#516. Tech Report: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2495 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Wiz

Tech Report: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2495 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wiz

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.
  • In a recent development, NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API.
  • Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.

In a recent development, NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server, it powers more than 225 million websites.

Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

Recent findings suggest that the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.

We reported our findings to F5, the manufacturer behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released.

We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes.

Sources indicate that october 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability.

November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review.

November 16, 2026: Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5.

November 17, 2026: F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release.

November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure.

Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered  CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the manufacturer behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules.Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas, the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution, to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure.The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell, disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.

Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out.In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2.

NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server, powering more than 225 million websites. It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user.

Recent findings suggest that NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer, distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it.

Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety concerns in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

Sources indicate that both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution.

On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.

In a recent development, the flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module.

An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs.

We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes.

In a recent development, F5's security release addresses several other vulnerabilities in NGINX. Below is a summary of these additional CVEs, as well as the two critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaws detailed in this post (captured in the first two rows of the table):.

Identify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available.

If you cannot upgrade immediately, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances:.

Set http2 off; in affected server blocks on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, and remove the http2 parameter from any listen directives.

Test application compatibility, reload NGINX, and confirm the old workers have exited.

Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading.

Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities.

NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts.

We start by sending only part of a HEADERS frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest:.

When we send the rest of the frame, ngx_http_v2_create_stream() creates a request stream and increments h2c->processing. However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close.

Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this.

Recent findings suggest that opening an upstream connection calls ngx_get_connection(). When free connection slots run low, ngx_drain_connections() selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request.

In a recent development, before closing it, NGINX tries to send a GOAWAY frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free.

The freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the fresh contents as the original request or connection.

This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

Industry observers note that HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called h2c->send_window.

Industry observers note that when NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance:.

Industry observers note that this refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur.

The next problem is in ngx_http_v2_state_window_update(), which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit:.

if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window).

The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases.

The invalid counter eventually reaches ngx_http_v2_send_chain(), where it is converted to the signed integer type off_t to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer.

Sources indicate that when the TLS send path in ngx_ssl_send_chain() processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module.

Recent findings suggest that to confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time.

Like other memory-safety problems, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets.

In a recent development, any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation.

Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration.

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

It has been revealed that with NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them.

It has been revealed that as we saw with PHP2Shell, AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve.

The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it.

It has been revealed that hi there! We are Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team (@wiz_io). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding newly introduced attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation problems in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the experiment, conducted by KPMG UK using more than 100 AI agents, marks an notable development in the application of artificial intelligence to one of the most labour-intensive areas of the financial services industry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LONDON, November 18, 2026 — Artificial intelligence has taken another significant step into the world of professional services after KPMG revealed that AI agents examining the accounts of a major UK-listed manufacturer sometimes investigated financial problems more deeply and asked better questions than its human audit team.

It has been revealed that the experiment, conducted by KPMG UK using more than 100 AI agents, marks an notable development in the application of artificial intelligence to one of the most labour-intensive areas of the financial services industry. It also raises an uncomfortable question for the accountancy profession: if machines can increasingly perform the analytical work traditionally undertaken by highly trained professionals, how swiftly will the economics of auditing change?

Sources indicate that according to the Financial Times, the project, codenamed Project Exponential, examined the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The AI agents worked alongside a conventional audit team, undertaking tasks across the audit process rather than simply assisting with isolated administrative functions.

KPMG UK head of audit Cath Burnet remarked the technology had, in several instances, gone considerably deeper into concerns than the regular audit team, identifying areas requiring further investigation and asking questions that human auditors had not necessarily raised.

The findings suggest that AI’s potential in professional services may extend well beyond improving productivity. It could fundamentally change how complex financial information is examined, interpreted and challenged.

Project Exponential represents a shift from using AI as a supporting tool towards deploying autonomous agents across an entire audit workflow.

It has been revealed that the agents collected information, analysed and documented data, developed draft conclusions and observations, and suggested subsequent steps. They were also able to work alongside one another, effectively dividing responsibilities and coordinating elements of the investigation.

The technology was developed over approximately four months. However, KPMG was careful to distinguish the experiment from a formally approved statutory audit. Although an audit partner signed off on the experimental exercise, its findings were not used as the basis for formally approving the tech giant’s accounts.

Human oversight remained essential. During the trial, an auditor had to intervene when one AI agent failed to correctly match regulatory requirements with the tech giant’s documentation. The episode illustrates both the capabilities and limitations of current AI systems when dealing with complex regulatory frameworks.

KPMG prepares to expand the initiative to as many as 20 larger audits, although the firm acknowledges that the technology is not yet sufficiently mature to be deployed across thousands of engagements. Data quality also remains a significant obstacle, with some businesses lacking the clean, structured information required for AI agents to operate effectively.

The implications for the accountancy industry could be substantial.

According to recent reports, traditional auditing relies on large teams of junior accountants undertaking detailed and repetitive work, supervised by experienced managers and partners. AI agents potentially offer a different operating model, automating significant portions of data collection, analysis and documentation while allowing senior professionals to concentrate on complex judgements and exceptions.

For firms such as KPMG, Deloitte, PwC and EY, the attraction is clear: faster audits, potentially lower operating costs and the ability to analyse much larger volumes of financial information.

However, whether those savings will ultimately be passed on to clients remains uncertain. KPMG has acknowledged the potential for significant time savings but has not confirmed whether AI-driven efficiencies will translate into lower audit fees.

The transition also presents regulatory and professional challenges. The UK’s Financial Reporting Council has warned that the use of AI must not undermine auditor independence, integrity or professional scepticism.

It has been revealed that there are also concerns about data security, over-reliance on automated conclusions and the possibility of AI generating inaccurate or fabricated information. The fundamental responsibility for an audit opinion remains with the human auditor, regardless of the technology used.

The KPMG experiment does not establish that AI can replace accountants or independently deliver a reliable statutory audit. It does, however, demonstrate that AI agents are beginning to challenge professionals in areas that were once considered dependent on human expertise.

Industry observers note that for the accountancy profession, the question is no longer simply whether AI will become part of the audit process. It is how much of that process will eventually be performed by machines — and what role human accountants will play when it does.

#506. The Magic of Partial Evaluation

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1884 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jimmyhmiller

The Magic of Partial Evaluation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jimmyhmiller

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there are certain ideas in software that are simply beautiful.
  • In a recent development, for me, the most beautiful pieces of software are those that reveal something about the nature of programming languages.
  • It has been revealed that so when I find something that makes me rethink the nature of programming languages, I start rethinking computation as a whole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there are certain ideas in software that are simply beautiful. It doesn't matter if they have any practical use. It doesn't matter that you will never convince your coworkers to consider them. There is just something captivating about the way some computational systems work.

In a recent development, for me, the most beautiful pieces of software are those that reveal something about the nature of programming languages. Programming languages are my obsession. I have never met a problem that couldn't be solved by introducing yet another programming language. Solving a problem at the programming language level is about solving the meta problem. Instead of trying to solve a particular problem, we take a step back and ask how we can solve a whole class of problems at once.

It has been revealed that so when I find something that makes me rethink the nature of programming languages, I start rethinking computation as a whole. One of these incredibly beautiful but tricky concepts goes by the name partial evaluation. If you are fascinated by interpreters and compilers, partial evaluation will teach you how they are related, and how you can get a compiler for free.

It has been revealed that partial evaluation has been a fascination of mine for a while. But this whole thing came up when James Long revealed he had revived Meta's partial evaluator for JavaScript called prepack. When I first heard about prepack, I had some high hopes and expectations for the project, but was sadly let down. This revival brought to light those same dreams. But sadly, just as with the original aim, prepack was not designed for beauty, but for practicality. So I figured it was time to renew my own efforts.

Yes, in some ways this is a post repping my own library I'm releasing. But I'm not doing this because I want it to be used. I'm doing this because it lets you play with the idea I find so beautiful. That is what this post is about.

According to recent reports, as a person who reads code, you can think about how this code computes and what answer it will give. But you can do more than just give the answer. You can see the expanded form of this particular code for these particular calls. This code is spiritually the same as the following expression, once we expand it out.

In this case, there is really nothing at all that this code needs to do at runtime. A sufficiently smart compiler will just run this code directly at compile time and give the answer. But this is a bit less clear if things come in at runtime.

It might seem like we can't do anything here, but again, if you are used to thinking about how programs run, you can trace this out and realize this is just the same as:.

Recent findings suggest that what we have done in both of these cases is called partial evaluation. In the first, it was a trivial case because everything was statically known. But in this latter case, we have reduced a program down into the essentials of its dynamic structure. There are no recursive function calls left. All of this has been expanded as far as it could till we get just the dynamic parts of the code remaining.

This intuitive notion of partial evaluation is all you need to know to appreciate the beauty here. Partial evaluation just evaluates the part of the program we can evaluate at build time and leaves all the rest. When we do this with certain programs in certain combinations, we get some quite surprising, incredible behavior.

In a recent development, here we have a very simple interpreter for a language that just supports arithmetic. For the above expression, you should be able to think about how we could start "partially" evaluating it. (In this case, it can be a full evaluation.) If this kind of partial evaluation isn't quite clicking for you, I've put the steps below to hopefully help it make sense.

Industry observers note that this is a simple evaluation of the code. But what happens if we throw a value we don't know into the expression?

Recent findings suggest that here we can see that clear partial evaluation difference. We don't know how to evaluate Number(process.argv[2]). We have no idea what the answer to that will be. But as part of this process, we do know some partial information about it. For example, when we get to.

In a recent development, we know that Number(process.argv[2]) is indeed a number. So we can partially evaluate it further. Hopefully this is all making sense. But if you are like me, this all might seem a bit trivial and uninteresting. So let's look at a more complicated example.

Recent findings suggest that here we have a brainfuck interpreter. And the example program we want to partially evaluate does not require any input at all (in brainfuck , is the way you get input). So when we go to partially evaluate this, we will just get an answer. In this case, this program is actually brainfuck's "hello world". But what about a program with input?

When we do our partial evaluation, we get the following:.

Industry observers note that what is this? A compiled brainfuck program! This is the first incredible fact: when you take an interpreter and partially evaluate it with a program, you get the compiled program out! Now this particular exact form is an artifact of how my partial evaluator works. You could imagine slightly different code. But the key is that what we've done is remove the interpreter completely.

What we've discovered here is the first of three so-called Futamura Projections. Our partial evaluator, when applied to an interpreter and given a program, can give us a compiled version of that program. Or to put it in pseudocode.

Sources indicate that depending on your exposure to interpreters and compilers, this might seem miraculous or mundane. Writing an interpreter and writing a compiler can seem like significantly different undertakings. In the age of AI, perhaps less so, but I think even then many things still hold. It is quite easy to instrument an interpreter, quite a bit harder to do so for a compiler. Changing an interpreter to support newly introduced features is quite easy, less so for a compiler. But more than that, there are all sorts of things that can be thought of as interpreters, that we'd almost never write a compiler for.

Consider this simple schema setup. This is code that can easily be partially evaled into something where we have created specialized functions for our particular schema. While not the most crucial code, this can give us a 5x performance boost when our objects start getting more complicated. You may think that we should just hand-write those functions. Or hand-write a compiler for these schemas. But what about those schemas that exist only at runtime? Now we either need to compile those on the fly, or we have to keep both a compiler and interpreter. Having a way to partial eval lowers this burden quite a bit.

But if the Futamura projections stopped here, they would be exciting, but not quite the craziness they are. To understand how this can go further, we are going to take this a step beyond your raw intuition of what it means to partially evaluate something and give a different frame. We can think of partial evaluation as a process of "specializing" a program.

What exactly is specializing a program? Well, it is taking a program that is generic and making a version that instead works for a single program. Let's think about a simple pattern matcher program like an overly simplified regex.

Sources indicate that this program is generic. It lets you match on many different patterns. That can be great if we need that flexibility. But if you don't have a bunch of patterns, it might be worth it to just make specialized code. Now, exactly what kind of specialized code? It might be that you only have this literal pattern; then you want to specialize very particularly.

Or you just have *** as a pattern.

For any bit of generic code, we can think of how to move our code to a more specialized form.

In a recent development, partial evaluation is a form of specialization that figures out what it should specialize on based on what input is static and what is dynamic. In many ways, a partial evaluator is a generic specializer. Given any program, we can make a specialized version of it for any input. What happens if we specialize an interpreter for a given input? We get back that interpreter for only exactly that one program. But what do we need then? Do we need all this generic dispatch? No, we know the full program. We don't need any operations we don't actually use. We can fully get rid of all the generic interpreter mechanism.

But if the specializer can specialize any program, can it specialize itself?

This leads us to the second Futamura projection. Put in our pseudo-code format, we get:.

It has been revealed that or, to put it in our specializer language, what if we make a special version of our generic specializer? What is it specialized for? A particular interpreter. Now we have a function that, given any program, will spit out newly specialized interpreters just for that program. Or, in Java speak, we have a specialized interpreter factory.

Let's see a real example of one of these compilers to make this concrete. Here is the interpreter we are going to specialize.

When we apply our second projection, we get out the following compiler:.

And if we compile one of these very simple programs, we can see the output:.

According to recent reports, now, of course, this is not a very interesting language. But hopefully you can see this general idea. Given an interpreter, we automatically derive a compiler! Pretty incredible.

But we can't stop at the second projection. We have to push on and get to the final mind-bending projection. If you apply our specializer to itself as input, you get a compiler generator.

So now we have a generic function that will spit out compilers for any interpreter we give it!

According to recent reports, I have implemented a reasonable, but still very limited partial evaluator for JavaScript in Rust. I have taken it further to try to make it work quite well for a number of different interpreters and interpreter-like programs in JavaScript. I've also tried to get limited versions of the second and third projections working. Go play with it, see what works, what doesn't, file issues, or better, use some of your tokens to help me make more cases work.

Industry observers note that but most of all, explore. This is such a rich space. Below are some papers, blogs, and projects about partial evaluation in some way, shape, or form. There has never been a better time to play with these kinds of crazy techniques for programming languages. Don't let what is practical stop you from exploring the cool, interesting aspects of programming.

#505. Genie 4 is now available

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (762 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Blog

Genie 4 is now available

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (762 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blog

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie, an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds.
  • Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser.
  • With Genie 4, our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Group Product Manager, Google DeepMind.

Group Product Manager, Google Labs.

Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie, an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them.

Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser.

With Genie 4, our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a newly introduced prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue.

Recent findings suggest that while Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include:.

Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas.

See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around.

Watch how Genie 3 combines longer runs, 360-degree panorama grounding, and real-time promptable events - transforming the world as you fly and even summoning a dragon to ride on command.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced Project Genie agent takes creation beyond a single text or image prompt. Now crafting an interactive universe is as effortless as having a conversation. Simply describe your vision in natural language, and the agent orchestrates Google’s suite of multimodal models to craft initial visuals establishing your world’s signature look, paired with custom background scores tailored to the mood.

You can also bring Gemini models into the session as you explore: it observes what is happening on screen, surfaces context-aware suggestion chips for where to go next, or triggers in-world events automatically as your journey unfolds.

Turns a natural language prompt into an interactive spacewalk, then an alien spaceship appears on command.

Remix a hillside cafe into a glass pavilion in the desert.

Publish custom worlds to the gallery for others to explore and remix.

Industry observers note that when you just want to jump straight into exploring, the new Project Genie gallery brings together a rich collection of curated worlds alongside creative work from the community. Transform personal photos into explorable spaces in “Living Memory,” wander through rich prehistoric habitats grounded in 360-degree panoramas in “Dino Field Guide,” or pit themed objects against one another on a desk with Gemini serving as your real-time referee in “Rock Paper Scissors.”.

Browse curated and community-built worlds and jump straight into exploring.

“Villa Giallo,” created with Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, uses Genie 4 to turn a gothic manor into an interactive, room-by-room mystery.

“The Life of Ants,” built with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, uses Genie 4’s photorealism to let you navigate a colony from an ant’s perspective.

The gallery also showcases inspiring collaborations with pioneering creators who had early access to these tools. Teaming up with creative technologist Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, we created “Villa Giallo,” an atmospheric, room-by-room mystery inside a gothic manor. And with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, we built “The Life of Ants,” inviting you to navigate a complex colony from an ant’s perspective, drawing on Genie 4’s stunning photorealism.

According to recent reports, beyond exploring curated worlds, you can also launch your vision with a simple prompt or remix existing gallery experiences alongside the Project Genie agent — tweaking the underlying world structure, soundtrack, or rules to make it uniquely your own. Once you’ve crafted something special, publish your creation to the community gallery for others to explore and remix.

According to recent reports, we are committed to developing and rolling out interactive world models responsibly. All video and audio generated in Project Genie includes SynthID watermarking, and all model inputs and outputs go through safety screenings.

Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain world models in the frontier research space. As the research continues to evolve, we are actively tackling key challenges such as camera latency, intricate physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence. For a deeper look into model limitations and our progress on these fronts, read our Genie 4 model research overview.

#504. DaisyRose-27B: 1,200-task RL took Qwen3.8 from 5.6% to 12% on Terminal-Bench 4.1

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (942 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Radixark

DaisyRose-27B: 1,200-task RL took Qwen3.8 from 5.6% to 12% on Terminal-Bench 4.1

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Radixark

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
  • We are releasing BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints for everyone to try and build on.
  • DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

We are releasing BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints for everyone to try and build on. In this post, we explain how carefully designed tasks and efficient infrastructure made these gains possible on a limited compute budget.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above1. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, a notoriously hard long-horizon benchmark. Our magic lies in the following three key ingredients: high-quality training data, efficient training backend, and robust sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from Eigent AI’s large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 of them made it into the final training set. The training tasks are selected based on three criteria.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

In a recent development, 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU's peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

Sources indicate that 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Industry observers note that stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

During training, every attempt the agent makes runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task's environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. All of the RadixArk team's work on this release ran in sandboxes on our own service, built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, the service ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running at the same time.

Reliable as it grew. The service grew from a single machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all of them while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded, and since late October more than 99.95% have. Getting there took a steady stream of fixes and improvements, such as keeping a machine from freezing when it runs out of memory.

Recent findings suggest that 80% lower cost. Our cloud infrastructure cost for the project's sandboxes was about 80% lower than the cost of running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to give each sandbox memory that grows and shrinks with what it actually uses. A sandbox usually uses only a small part of the memory it asks for, so each machine can run many more sandboxes.

You can download DaisyRose-27B from Hugging Face, and you can train your own agents with our open source reinforcement learning framework Miles.

DaisyRose-27B is one example of what high-quality data and efficient infrastructure can make possible. We are bringing this approach to teams building specialized models, with a focus on improving the capabilities they need while preserving the model’s broader strengths. If you are exploring post-training for your own model, reach out at contact@radixark.ai.

We are deeply grateful to Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and to the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B, the foundation of our work. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, as well as other open-source projects, including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

According to recent reports, how we evaluated: Terminal Bench 4.1 is averaged over 8 runs per task, using our internal mini-swe-agent harness with summarization turned on. Terminal Bench 2.1 is averaged over 5 runs per task, using the Terminus 2 harness. DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE Bench Pro v2 are averaged over 8 and 5 runs per task, both using the mini-swe-agent harness. HLE (text-only) is averaged over 5 runs per problem, graded by GPT-6 Luna, with no tools. IFBench is averaged over 4 runs on each of its 300 prompts, scored by the official allenai/IFBench scorer as prompt-level loose accuracy on the final response, with the thinking left out. GPQA Diamond is averaged over 8 runs on each of its 198 questions, using the simple-evals multiple-choice template and answer extraction, with the answer order reshuffled on every run. ↩.

Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.

SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google.

Your browser does not support the audio element.

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.

Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index, Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the upcoming Agent Arena Index. Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing.

The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window.

Sources indicate that enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index, it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench.

Neon also demonstrates strong wins across categories on Surge AI, ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's upcoming Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.

On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%).

Recent findings suggest that engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions.

It has been revealed that across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0. For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks.

Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon.

In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets.

Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk.

In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes.

We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs.

Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon indicates its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting.

Industry observers note that as agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench, achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%).

It has been revealed that securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2, Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models.

To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models.

Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program.

Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack— maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on:.

For more details, see the Gemini 4 Neon model card.

In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Neon excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses.

According to recent reports, neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Current education system focuses on wrong things, and is subject to traditional practices that were developed due to need of scaling, instead of due to improvement of the system itself.

In a recent development, the core glitch is that school is not actually focusing on brain development and "learning how to learn". By the way, this is what I was told as the reason of studying history and all those other subjects I didn't like. Instead it focuses on developing concrete skills in a bunch of different practices, and I will explain why it is completely wrong.

The brain develops when it is exposed to a fresh experience/task, because first brain is doing the task inefficiently using several existing neural centers, and then in around ~15 minutes it finds a neural center in between of those, and now performs the task much more efficiently.

It needs more studying, but at this point I am pretty sure that to become a genius at math, the best play is to learn everything except math for multiple years, to develop brainpower, and only then to go into math when your brain is ready, and reach the frontier much faster.

Instead the school system does completely opposite - the student can't choose what to study, needs to memorize concrete facts and crevices of systems (the grades measure that instead of measuring how well the student was exposed to various experiences). As provider of education the school should be graded on how well it provides the service of education, instead of users being graded on how well they consume the service.

Substantial thanks to my parents for letting me not to go to college, and for developing me with lots of different experiences in childhood.

We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Violetpixel

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit.
  • In a recent development, when I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are.
  • The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 @ 7:01 PM PST.

Industry observers note that something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions.

In a recent development, when I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable.

The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things:.

Industry observers note that those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is crucial or critical infrastructure.

Industry observers note that now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I stated remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse.

According to recent reports, and collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365, Air Traffic Control, United Airlines' systems, the NSA's network, many major banks, Apple's systems, and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI.

I guess that depends on how you look at it.

I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit.

Capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity.

According to recent reports, now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea.

Sources indicate that people who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from?

It has been revealed that it matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. What seems like care, concern, and attention is just generative AI doing what it's designed to do: telling you what you want to hear. The math and logic that power LLMs are as cold, unfeeling, and indifferent as the laws of physics.

Smart people who give a shit notice things. They connect dots. They notice when things don't feel right. They know when something is about to go off the rails, and they know how to get things back on track. They know how to handle edge cases. They know how to manually handle a unique situation. They know what the right thing to do is, and they know when they need to put in extra effort or time to make something happen. Generative AI falls far short in these areas, but this is the glue that holds complex systems together. More prompting and more output isn't a substitute for this.

It's hard for capitalist leadership to internalize any of that, though. It would be such a relief for them, such a burden lifted, to replace all those smart people who give a shit with generative AI. It would be so much easier to win at capitalism if generative AI lived up to the hype, and there's so much pressure for leadership and management to believe that the hype is real.

In a recent development, thus, a lot of the smart people who give a shit have been laid off, and the ones that remain are hollowed out. Telling people to stop doing the job they signed up for in favor of babysitting LLMs so they can do that job instead is a great way to make people less smart about the system they used to work on and give less of a shit about it. Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out. Every generated output that becomes part of the system means those people understand less about how the system actually works. Those people are robbed of the things that make them smart (the struggle of building and learning) and the things that made them gave a shit (a sense of ownership and close connection with the system).

We've moved from a world dependent on complex and fragile systems held together by smart people who give a shit to a world of complex and fragile systems run by generative AI. The people running the generative AI are not as smart, nor do they give as much of a shit. There are, of course, exceptions (which is why a lot of things are still humming along), but we are on a course where the number of smart people who give a shit are decreasing, and that's a massive problem. As long as the number continues to go down, more systems will fail.

Recent findings suggest that I think what we have here is a hot stove moment for capitalism. When you tell a young kid a stove is hot and they shouldn't touch it, you'll find there are two kinds of kids. For one kind of kid, the warning is the lesson, and they don't touch the stove. For the other kind of kid, the only lesson that works for them is being burned. They have to touch the stove at least once to learn the lesson. Capitalism was told the stove was hot, but their hand is on it right now.

Unfortunately, we're all getting burned.

#496. How to Fix Presigned Downloads: Filename, Content-Type, and Content-Disposition

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (766 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

How to Fix Presigned Downloads: Filename, Content-Type, and Content-Disposition

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that large receipt exports change the answer.
  • In a recent development, TL;DR: set Content-Type and Content-Disposition on the object before creating a signed URL.
  • Browsers make two decisions from response headers: how to render the bytes and what name to suggest when saving them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that large receipt exports change the answer. A 20 KB CSV that opens in a tab is annoying; a 2 GB PDF that opens in a tab can pin a browser process and make a support ticket look like a storage outage.

In a recent development, TL;DR: set Content-Type and Content-Disposition on the object before creating a signed URL. Verify the stored metadata with a HEAD request, then glitch a fresh private link. The URL is only a delivery token. It does not repair bad metadata.

Browsers make two decisions from response headers: how to render the bytes and what name to suggest when saving them. Object storage makes those headers from metadata saved with the object. A presigned URL normally signs a request for that object; it does not infer that receipt-2026-09.csv is a CSV just because the key ends in .csv.

That distinction explains the familiar symptoms:.

According to recent reports, the fix belongs in the write path. Set metadata at upload time, or immediately after upload if the producer cannot send headers. Then check it before signing. I keep this as a hard invariant in export jobs: an object is not downloadable until its metadata check passes.

The following adapter calls the storage capability over plain HTTP, but the application-facing contract is deliberately boring. If the storage provider changes, the receipt processor should still call setExportMetadata and presignExport.

Sources indicate that the metadata call is idempotent, so a worker retry does not create a second export. The response is checked before the link is returned, and a 429 honors Retry-After with exponential backoff. In production I also call the object HEAD route between these two calls; it is cheap compared with reprocessing a failed export and catches the trap where a local object model changes while the already-uploaded object keeps old headers.

For an existing object, use the provider's metadata-update operation, then repeat the HEAD check before issuing another link. I test filenames with spaces, cafe-au-lait.csv, quotes, and a 180-character stem. I also run the same matrix at 50 MB, 500 MB, and 2 GB. The numbers are test inputs, not promises about throughput; they expose buffering, proxy limits, and browser behavior early.

The useful comparison is about operational shape, not a sticker price.

The unified contract is useful when the receipt worker may switch vendors without changing its call sites. Its practical advantage is one REST API and one key across many backend capabilities, so there is less glue around the storage adapter. It does not remove storage engineering. Keep the object private and mint a short-lived signed link for each user request. Public URLs are not a fallback here.

For large files, benchmark the complete path: producer upload, metadata write, HEAD verification, signing, and browser download. Measure time to first byte and peak memory separately. A fast upload with a proxy that buffers the download is still a bad export experience.

According to recent reports, single-request uploads are a reasonable first implementation. At larger sizes, use multipart upload where the backend supports it. Keep the finalization step idempotent, and record the object key plus an export ID in your database before publishing the link. If a worker retries, it should resume or safely replace the same planned object, not create a second receipt with a new name.

Retention is another throughput concern. Lifecycle rules help remove old exports, but a one-day minimum expiration is not the same as hour-level cleanup. Multipart parts can also need explicit abort handling. Track unfinished uploads as a queue metric instead of waiting for a storage bill to reveal them.

In a recent development, do not use object metadata as a search index. If you need “all receipts for customer 481,” store that relation in your database; metadata is for delivery headers and small invariants, not server-side queries.

In a recent development, this pattern suits private, user-triggered downloads. It is the wrong foundation for a public image host, static-site origin, or an audit archive that requires WORM guarantees. Without versioning and object lock, an accidental overwrite is an application-level incident. Without conditional If-Match writes, strict concurrent ownership needs a queue or database lock. Without configurable CORS, browser-direct uploads need a controlled proxy or a platform that exposes the required bucket policy.

Those limits are design inputs. Write them into the decision record alongside your throughput test results. The practical rule is short: metadata first, HEAD second, presign third. Keep that sequence behind an adapter and the storage vendor becomes a replaceable implementation detail while the download behavior remains stable.

#495. Four ways to estimate a development project (and what each is good for)

Four ways to estimate a development project (and what each is good for)

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (335 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every estimate argument starts the same way: "it's just a simple app".
  • Recent findings suggest that estimation is not guessing.
  • Industry observers note that "We built something similar and it came to this much." Fast, useful for a rough range, and wrong the moment the scope differs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every estimate argument starts the same way: "it's just a simple app". Then three weeks later the same app has a payment provider, an admin panel, two integrations and a data migration.

Recent findings suggest that estimation is not guessing. It is a process with a few known methods. Here are the four that actually get used, and what each is good for.

Industry observers note that "We built something similar and it came to this much." Fast, useful for a rough range, and wrong the moment the scope differs. Good for a first conversation, dangerous as a contract.

Each stage is estimated separately: prototype, core, integrations, release, support. More work upfront, but the client can see where the money goes and can stop at any stage. This is the format I use most, because it turns an argument about the total into a discussion about one stage at a time.

It has been revealed that an experienced contractor looks at the list of work and gives a range. Fast and usually decent for scoping, but it is a range, not a commitment. Treat it as a filter, not a quote.

Industry observers note that pay for hours. Flexible, good for exploratory work where nobody knows the shape yet. Requires control: without a written scope, T&M quietly becomes an open-ended retainer.

In practice the best result is a combination: a range by analogy, a breakdown by stages, and a fixed price per stage.

Not the one with the lowest bid. It is the one where the scope was clear from day one: nobody paid for features that were cut, and nobody argued about what "done" means.

Industry observers note that if you only take one thing from this: ask for the estimate broken down by stage, and ask what is not included. The second question is where the real number hides.

#493. A local AI agent whose citations cannot be invented

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (846 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

A local AI agent whose citations cannot be invented

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most RAG demos look great until the model invents a page number.
  • In a recent development, I built a local-first agent that answers questions about contracts and invoices.
  • In a recent development, the interesting part is not the retrieval.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most RAG demos look great until the model invents a page number. This one refuses instead.

In a recent development, I built a local-first agent that answers questions about contracts and invoices. It runs entirely on your laptop — no API key, no cloud, no data leaving the machine.

In a recent development, the interesting part is not the retrieval. It's that the citations are checked by code, not trusted from the model.

According to recent reports, everyone builds a RAG in an afternoon. Upload PDFs, chunk, embed, search by similarity, pass the fragments to the model. It works, and the demo looks great.

"The contract expires on December 15, according to clause 4.2, page 3.".

Industry observers note that the problem: clause 4.2 says something else, and page 3 doesn't exist. The model didn't lie on purpose. It filled a gap with something that sounded probable. And since nobody checks, the wrong answer ships.

That's not a retrieval problem. It's a verification problem. And you don't fix it with a better model — you fix it with code.

According to recent reports, every answer comes back with structured citations: a chunk_id and a literal quote. The app doesn't trust the model; it verifies it.

A citation is valid only if its quote is a substring of the chunk, after whitespace normalization. If it fails, the model gets one more try. If it fails again, the answer becomes a refusal.

Sources indicate that this is not another LLM checking the first one. It's string containment, and anyone can reproduce it by opening the database.

This is the part people usually skip.

1. The embeddings were fake and the tests were green.

In a recent development, the first version called ollama embed, a CLI subcommand that does not exist. Every call failed and silently fell back to a three-dimension mock vector. The tests passed because they only checked structure, not values.

According to recent reports, the fix wasn't "improve the mock". It was removing the fallback entirely: if embeddings fail, ingestion fails loudly. A system that degrades silently is worse than one that breaks loudly.

Sources indicate that 2. The vector search wasn't vector search.

sqlite-vec was never loaded. chunks_vec was created as a regular table and the "KNN" was brute force. It worked by accident with 13 chunks and would have collapsed with 1,300.

I found it by inspecting sqlite_master:.

3. Three times, a subagent reported files it never wrote.

That's not a model problem, it's a trust problem: I accepted self-reports. The lesson was procedural. Before accepting any delivery, run the repo:.

If the file isn't on disk, it doesn't exist. Full stop.

It has been revealed that everyone asks "which model?". The honest answer: it matters less than you think, and more than you measure.

The 4B is 7× faster and 4.5× less accurate. Fine for a demo. Not fine for a contract.

And a detail nobody expects: a 9B can be slower than a 12B. Qwen3.5:9B kept a 262k context resident and didn't finish a single answer in 90 seconds. The 12B answered in 50.

The conclusion isn't "use the biggest model". It's measure on your machine, with your corpus, with your questions. Someone else's benchmark is a prior, not a truth.

Recent findings suggest that one of the 18 questions asked for the sum of two contract totals. The 12B failed it consistently: it can't add.

The fix wasn't a better model. It was admitting arithmetic is not the LLM's job and writing eight lines of deterministic code. The agent retrieves and composes; the calculator adds.

Same principle as the citations, applied one layer down: what can be verified by code, is verified by code.

Three proofs, not three promises:.

And a consequence almost nobody mentions: if the data doesn't leave, nothing comes in either. The model has to be local because privacy isn't a feature — it's the architecture.

In a recent development, saying this doesn't weaken the project. It makes it credible. A repo that admits its limits is a repo someone can use without surprises.

It was planned as a step-based program, implemented by separate role agents (developer, designer, auditor, critic), and every claim in the docs was verified against the running code rather than accepted from a report. That process produced its own lesson, documented above: three times a delegate reported a module it never wrote, and the fix was procedural, not technical.

It has been revealed that this started as a design exercise for the DEV.to Hacktoberfest 2026 Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend. The official window closed on October 5, 2026 — after that, so it is not a submission. The case study (“a freelance photographer with contracts she can't upload”) is a persona, not a real person. It exists to give the design a constraint, not to claim a testimonial.

If you build something similar, the one thing I'd steal is not the code: it's the habit of making the verifier independent from the thing being verified.

#491. Four AWS defaults that quietly inflate your bill (priced for Paris, Frankfurt, the UAE and Bahrain)
