Four AWS defaults that quietly inflate your bill (priced for Paris, Frankfurt, the UAE and Bahrain)

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (498 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that most expensive AWS bills I review are not caused by one big mistake.
  • Sources indicate that I priced four of them with AWS list prices (checked on 18 November 2026) for Europe (Paris, Frankfurt), the Middle East (UAE, Bahrain) and US East (N.
  • Private workloads that read from S3 through a NAT Gateway pay NAT data processing on every gigabyte:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that most expensive AWS bills I review are not caused by one big mistake. They come from defaults that nobody questioned: a NAT Gateway in the data path, microservices that talk across Availability Zones, batch jobs kept On-Demand, a DynamoDB table provisioned to hide a hot key.

Sources indicate that I priced four of them with AWS list prices (checked on 18 November 2026) for Europe (Paris, Frankfurt), the Middle East (UAE, Bahrain) and US East (N. Virginia) as a reference.

Private workloads that read from S3 through a NAT Gateway pay NAT data processing on every gigabyte:.

At 100 TB a month that is about $5,000 in Paris and $5,280 in the UAE.

Fix: an S3 gateway endpoint, which AWS provides at no additional charge, plus one route in the private route tables.

Data transfer between Availability Zones in the same Region is billed $0.01/GB in each direction. With 500 TB a month of internal traffic spread evenly over three zones, about two thirds crosses a zone boundary: roughly $6,700 a month.

Fix: keep calls inside the zone when possible. In Kubernetes, trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone on the Service (PreferClose is the older name). Keeping 80% of calls in-zone saves about $5,300 a month in this example.

Note: if your design relies on AWS App Mesh, it reached end of support on 30 September 2026.

100 instances running all month in Paris: $32,704 On-Demand. Moving 90% of the hours to Spot, with job state checkpointed to EBS or S3 and an EventBridge rule on the two-minute interruption notice, brings it to about $13,000. Spot prices change by zone and over time, and capacity is not guaranteed, so keep an On-Demand fallback.

Industry observers note that A single partition accepts at most 1,000 write units per second. Over-provisioning the table does not fix a hot key: the extra capacity is spread over partitions that are not under pressure. Write sharding (a random or calculated suffix on the key) spreads the load, and you only pay for the capacity you need.

Provisioned write capacity costs $0.000772 per WCU-hour in Paris, $0.0008085 in the UAE and Bahrain, and $0.00065 in N. Virginia.

In a recent development, the same architecture does not cost the same everywhere. Compared with N. Virginia, On-Demand m5.2xlarge is about 17% more expensive in Paris, 20% in Frankfurt and 23% in the UAE and Bahrain. That is not a reason to leave your Region (latency, data residency and customers decide that), but it is a reason to fix the defaults first.

I put the four scenarios in a free calculator: pick a Region, enter your own volumes, and see the default cost, the optimised cost and the trade-offs: AWS cost scenarios calculator.

Prices are public list prices, excluding tax and discounts (Savings Looks, Reserved Instances, private pricing). Always confirm against your own Cost and Usage Report.

Mohamed Ali Dridi, electromechanical and IT engineer, founder of Koyotec Engineering (Tunis), Registered AWS Partner.

The test is simple: if a feature can be postponed without changing whether you learn the answer, it is not in the MVP.

They usually follow each other: agree first, then test the hypothesis, then scale.

In a recent development, one metric, decided before launch. Not "people liked it" but:.

If you cannot name the metric before the build starts, the MVP will be judged on vibes — and vibes always say "we need more features".

In a recent development, building the MVP for the wrong user: the one who pays, instead of the one who uses. The person who approves the budget is rarely the person who will press the buttons every day. Watch the second one.

A focused MVP fits in 2–6 weeks, and a landing or bot in days. The rule of thumb: if the estimate is longer, the scope is not an MVP — it is a full product with an MVP label on it.

The pattern I'm seeing in AI agents lately is that they keep asking for more access to your data, but nobody's really thinking about who controls that model of you.

When an AI knows your relationships, habits, and priorities, that's essentially a digital twin. The data involved is incredibly sensitive, and most products just... store it wherever. That's the gap First Person Labs is targeting with their approach to keeping that model on your device with you in control.

What strikes me is that privacy isn't just compliance theater here—it's actually a product differentiator. Developers building agentic AI have a real decision to make early on: do you centralize user data for convenience, or build for control from day one? It's a tradeoff that affects architecture, UX, and trust.

The technical challenge of running these models locally while still being useful is substantial. But if you pull it off, you solve a real adoption blocker for personal AI assistants.

For indie hackers or solo builders in this space, is there a leaner angle on privacy-first personal AI worth exploring, or does the problem really require the kind of resources a funded team brings?

Critical Apache Roller RCE Flaw Under Active Exploitation, No Authentication Required

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (300 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A critical security flaw in Apache Roller, an open-source, Java-based blogging platform, has come under active exploitation in the wild, according to the Apache Software Foundation (ASF).
  • The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of unauthenticated deserialization in the XML-RPC endpoint that could lead to remote code execution.
  • "Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code," project maintainers said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A critical security flaw in Apache Roller, an open-source, Java-based blogging platform, has come under active exploitation in the wild, according to the Apache Software Foundation (ASF).

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of unauthenticated deserialization in the XML-RPC endpoint that could lead to remote code execution.

"Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code," project maintainers said. "The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester.".

ASF also noted that the vulnerability is the same as CVE-2026-82384 (CVSS score: 9.8), which was patched in September 2026 and listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected.

"This issue is being actively exploited," it added. ASF did not share any details on how the vulnerability is being exploited, or who is being targeted as part of these efforts.

A security researcher named n0mi1k has been credited with finding the flaw, and Matt Raible has been acknowledged for reporting it.

Owners are advised to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled.

If immediate patching is not an option, it's recommended to set "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and then restart Roller.

"Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting," ASF noted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every client who states "we need an app" usually means one of three things: a website, a PWA, or a native app. The cheapest wrong decision is to build a native app before validating demand. Here is how we decide, and what it costs.

Industry observers note that A PWA (progressive web app) is a website with a manifest and a service worker. It installs to the home screen, works offline, and feels like an app — without app store review.

Figures are ballpark for a typical scope; the real price depends on screens, integrations and design.

In these cases we say "native" before the project starts, not in the middle of it.

A car dealer needed vehicle inspections: the driver photographs 8 angles, the manager approves or marks a defect with a comment. Instead of a native app we built a PWA: form, camera, client-side compression, offline queue, simple PHP admin panel.

A PWA is still a website, so pages index normally — and often rank better thanks to speed and caching. Keep canonical URLs, sitemaps and meta tags in order; do not block the offline shell in robots.txt; measure installation as a separate analytics event.

Mostly "yes" → PWA. Heavy background work or a store requirement → native.

It has been revealed that cross-post: the long version with price ranges, iOS caveats and a decision table lives on my site — Website or PWA: what to choose. Real examples: an inspection PWA and a glare-free scanning app.

#486. How to upgrade one dynamic zone block in Strapi 5 (without deleting the others)

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1327 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

How to upgrade one dynamic zone block in Strapi 5 (without deleting the others)

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You have a Strapi 5 page built from a dynamic zone: a hero, a feature grid and a call to action.
  • It has been revealed that that is how Strapi 5 writes lists.
  • One GitHub issue reads, "found that I cannot revision component".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You have a Strapi 5 page built from a dynamic zone: a hero, a feature grid and a call to action. You want to change the hero's heading and nothing else. So you send an patch with the hero block, and the feature grid and the call to action are gone.

It has been revealed that that is how Strapi 5 writes lists. A dynamic zone, a repeatable component or a rich-text blocks field is replaced as a whole: the array you send becomes the latest list, and anything you left out is deleted. The REST API works this way, and so does the update_ tool in Strapi's built-in MCP server. With one writer, that is a matter of sending the right array. With two writers, it is a race: each one sends a list built from its own read, the second write wins, and the first writer's block disappears with a 200 and no error.

People keep running into this. One GitHub issue reads, "found that I cannot revision component". A docs issue is blunter: "Updating dynamic zones via REST API does not work." It does work. It just doesn't work the way most of us assume the first time.

Below are three routes, in order of how much control you have over the writer.

Recent findings suggest that disclosure up front: the third route uses writesafe, a plugin my manufacturer, IsoKron, built and maintains. It's free and MIT-licensed. Routes 1 and 2 need nothing but Strapi.

In Strapi v4 you could send a component's id and enhancement that one row. The v4-to-v5 breaking changes document two things about that in Strapi 5:.

It has been revealed that the reporter of the issue above, on 5.32.0, got a 400 Invalid key id for sending id in a REST body at all. On 5.62.0 the server has moved on from the first point. A REST GET returns an id on every block, and if you read the draft (?status=draft) and send those ids back, the PUT returns 200 and updates the rows in place. Published ids still get a 400: "Some of the provided components in sections are not related to the entity".

None of which saves you. An id only decides whether Strapi updates a row or recreates it. The list is still replaced as a whole: a block you leave out is deleted, id or no id, and nothing in the request says which version you read.

According to recent reports, strapi's documented pattern for REST is still to leave ids out, so that is Route 1. I wouldn't build on undocumented id handling that changed between 5.32 and 5.62. The Document Service, which reads and writes the draft by default, accepts draft component ids by design; that is Route 2.

According to recent reports, strapi's recommended pattern for Content API clients is to omit component ids and send the complete list you want. Their docs put it in one line: "Include every component you want to keep.".

In a recent development, read the draft with the zone populated. For dynamic zones, Strapi 5's docs use on fragments, one per component; list every component the zone allows:.

Then change the one block and send the whole zone back, every entry with its __component and without id:.

This route is correct for one writer. It has no version check, so if an editor adds a testimonial block between your GET and your PUT, your PUT removes it. Nothing in the response tells you.

Sources indicate that if the write happens in your own Strapi code (a controller, a cron job, a migration script), you can do what the REST docs say not to count on: load the draft with its component ids and update one entry in place. This is the second workaround in Strapi's breaking-change note. Wrapping it in a transaction keeps the read and the write together:.

Strapi 5 ships an MCP server, which is how a growing number of pages now get edited: an agent connected at /mcp, sometimes while a person is in the admin panel. The built-in update_ tool behaves like REST. It replaces each list it is sent, it can't send component ids, and it has no version check.

We measured that during development on Strapi 5.62.0 with SQLite. An agent writing from a stale read while a colleague added a block deleted the colleague's block in 12 of 12 trials, for each of dynamic zones, repeatable components and blocks fields. None of 233 responses carried a conflict signal.

According to recent reports, writesafe adds ws_* tools to that same /mcp endpoint through Strapi's plugin API (strapi.ai.mcp.registerTool), with the same admin tokens and permissions. Two of them do the work here.

Industry observers note that ws_get returns the draft with a version token and a _key on every row of each top-level list. Over plain HTTP it's a JSON-RPC tools/call; the server is stateless, so no initialize is needed first:.

Abridged, the part you care about looks like this (version and keys shortened; yours will differ):.

Then ws_patch edits one row by key:.

Row ops (add, patch, remove, move) apply to the current list inside the write transaction, under a row lock, not to the list as the agent last saw it. So a block a colleague added a minute ago survives, and the rows you didn't name keep their database ids. Row ops need no version, because a key is bound to the row's content: if someone changed the hero since your read, the call is refused with stale_row_key; if the hero is gone, row_not_found. Either way the agent reads again. It doesn't guess.

Industry observers note that sometimes you really do mean to replace the whole list. That's a set, and a set needs the version you read:.

If the draft changed since that read, nothing is written. The reply is version_conflict with the current version, the current document and a retry hint telling the agent to re-apply only its own change.

In the same trials as above: with row ops, 0 of 36 colleague rows were lost and no ids were recreated. With a stale whole-list set, 36 of 36 writes were refused with version_conflict, and 36 of 36 landed after one re-read and retry. The table and conditions are in the reference.

It has been revealed that to be plain about scope: this only applies to MCP tool calls. writesafe adds no REST routes and does not change what PUT /api/pages/:id does. Any HTTP client can make the calls above, not only an AI agent, but they go to /mcp, not /api. If your writers are REST clients, Routes 1 and 2 are your options.

By default (builtinUpdates: 'guard') the plugin also makes Strapi's built-in update_ refuse list and component writes and point the agent at ws_patch, so an agent can't take the old path by accident.

Then npm run build (the plugin adds a jobs page and a settings page to the admin) and restart. Create an admin token with Read and Revision on your content type; tools/list on /mcp should now show the ws_* tools. Client setup for Claude Code, Cursor and others is in docs/clients.md.

According to recent reports, none of this is a Strapi bug. Whole-list replacement is a reasonable contract for a REST API, and Strapi documents it. It just assumes one writer, and that assumption got quieter and less true once agents started editing content. If you only have one writer, send the full list and move on. If you have several, give each one a way to say which row it means and which version it read.

writesafe is on npm, in the Strapi Marketplace and on GitHub. If you hit a list edit the row ops don't cover, open an issue. The general idea behind it is written up in Send the change, not the object.

IsoKron built and maintains writesafe. I'm IsoKron's founder.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that claude Code or Cursor?
  • Both companies changed their looks this year, so ignore any comparison older than a few months.
  • It has been revealed that claude's pricing page lists Pro at $20 a month ($17 a month if you pay $200 for the year), Max at $100 for "5x Pro usage", and Ultra at $200, which drops the 5-hour limit for verified accounts and gives "10x Pro usage" a week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that claude Code or Cursor? If you are a founder who doesn't read code, pick Claude Code and run it on the $20 Pro initiative first. If you or someone on your team reads diffs line by line, Cursor's editor makes that easier. That is the short answer, using the pricing pages as they stood on November 17, 2026. The longer answer is that the choice matters a lot less than what you put around either tool, and I'll get to that, because it is where the apps we get sent actually break.

Both companies changed their looks this year, so ignore any comparison older than a few months.

It has been revealed that claude's pricing page lists Pro at $20 a month ($17 a month if you pay $200 for the year), Max at $100 for "5x Pro usage", and Ultra at $200, which drops the 5-hour limit for verified accounts and gives "10x Pro usage" a week. Claude Code is included on every paid plan. The free plan doesn't include it. Limits reset every 5 hours and every week, and how fast you hit them depends on the model you pick. Team seats are $25 a month billed monthly ($20 annually), or $125 for a premium seat.

Recent findings suggest that cursor's pricing page looks quite different now. Plus is $8 a month and only runs Grok models. Premium is $30 and adds third-party models "at API list price", which means the Claude and GPT models inside Cursor are billed on top, by usage. Super is $100 (15x Plus usage) and Ultra $200 (50x). Allowances refresh weekly, and when you run out you either buy top-offs or wait. You can set a spending cap, and you should, on day one.

So the honest monthly number for a founder building most days: Claude Code is $20 until you keep hitting the weekly wall, then $100. Cursor is $30 plus whatever the third-party model usage comes to, unless you are happy on Grok only. I'd budget $60 to $100 for Cursor if you want the same models you'd get in Claude Code. What drains a Claude Code proposal faster than you'd expect, and when paying per token through an API key is cheaper, is in our Claude Code pricing breakdown.

According to recent reports, cursor is an editor. It's a fork of VS Code with the AI built into every panel, and you see the files, the tabs and the diff the whole time. That's great if you understand what you're looking at. It's a wall of green and red if you don't.

Claude Code started as a terminal program (claude in your project folder) and now runs in VS Code and JetBrains, a desktop app, the browser and the phone app too, according to its own overview page. The same engine sits behind all of them, so a project's settings follow you around. Most non-technical founders I talk to end up in the desktop app because it shows diffs visually and runs a few sessions side by side.

It has been revealed that there's a funny overlap here: Claude Code ships an extension for Cursor. Plenty of people run Claude Code inside Cursor and pay for both. I don't recommend it unless you have a reason, because now you have two usage meters to watch.

Both tools read a plain text file of rules from your repository before they write anything. This file is the closest thing you have to a senior developer sitting next to the AI.

Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md in the project root at the start of every session. Cursor reads project rules from .cursor/rules/, and those have to end in .mdc. The Cursor rules docs are blunt about it: a plain .md file in that folder "is ignored by the rules system". I've seen a team keep a careful security.md in there for weeks, wondering why Cursor kept putting a Stripe secret key in a client component. It never read the file once.

Both also understand AGENTS.md, which is the one file to write if you might switch tools later.

What goes in it doesn't depend on the tool. The lines we add to almost every client file:.

Industry observers note that the last one sounds obvious. It's ignored constantly unless it's written down.

A founder sent us a booking app in October. He had built it with Cursor, then switched to Claude Code halfway "because it was smarter", and wanted to know which one had broken his checkout. The answer was neither. Both had done exactly what he asked. Somewhere in week three he had asked for "make the admin page faster", and one of them had replaced a database call with a cached list that never refreshed. Paid bookings stopped showing up for staff. Nobody noticed for nine days because nothing ran a test, nothing reviewed the change, and the deploy happened the moment he clicked accept.

It has been revealed that swapping the tool wouldn't have caught that. A pull request with a second pair of eyes would have, in about two minutes.

Neither one sets up a staging copy of your app, runs a security scan on each change, keeps backups of your database, or tells you a migration will lock a table with live users on it. Both will happily do any of those if you ask, and both will happily skip them if you don't. That's the gap, whichever logo is on the app.

In a recent development, if your app is about to take real money or real user data, we take Claude Code and Cursor apps to production at a fixed price from $500, usually in 5 to 7 days: details on the job page. If you want to keep building with the AI yourself and have someone review what it writes, that's our AI build partner retainer, from $500 a month after a one-time setup from $600. And if you are still deciding whether to build it yourself at all, the app development cost calculator puts the AI-built route next to an agency quote.

According to recent reports, pick the tool you'll actually open every day. Then write the rules file before the next feature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until the TMM restarts.

Each flaw needs a specific setup on a virtual server: an iRule that uses a particular command, or an APM policy that includes two particular kinds of agent.

Recent findings suggest that F5, which makes BIG-IP, disclosed the flaws today and notes they may also allow remote code execution. The organization has released engineering hotfixes and lists no workaround.

Industry observers note that the company rates all six 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.3 under CVSS v4.0. They are stack-based buffer overflows in BIG-IP's data plane, the part that processes almost all of its network traffic. The management side is not exposed, according to the company.

It has been revealed that none of the firm's advisories says the flaws have been exploited. WatchTowr researcher Sina Kheirkhah reported four, and the company found the other two itself.

According to recent reports, five of the flaws are in iRules, a SUBSTANTIAL-IP feature that administrators use to manage traffic, and one is in BIG-IP's APM module. Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and BIG-IP CNF, part of the organization's BIG-IP Cloud-Native Edition.

Each flaw needs the setup listed below on a virtual server:.

F5's security notification lists the 22 advisories it published today, including 10 for NGINX.

Industry observers note that for the six critical flaws, the only fixes are engineering hotfixes, builds that the company complications between its normal software releases. No scheduled release is listed as a fix, and the advisories provide no workaround until a hotfix is installed.

The company warns that "engineering hotfixes do not undergo the extensive QA assessment of scheduled software releases." Its hotfix policy adds that they come with no warranty or promise that they will work.

A system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from the company's support team.

It has been revealed that SUBSTANTIAL-IP Next for Kubernetes is fixed in BNK-2.4.2-EHF1, BNK-2.3.4-EHF1 and BNK-2.2.5-EHF1, for versions 2.4.0 to 2.4.2, 2.3.0 to 2.3.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.5. BIG-IP CNF, on the same version ranges, is fixed in CNF-2.4.2-EHF1, CNF-2.3.4-EHF1 and CNF-2.2.5-EHF1 for CVE-2026-121805 and CVE-2026-120285.

The firm checks only versions that are still within technical support, so an older release missing from its tables has not been shown to be safe.

Today's flaws differ from CVE-2026-94127, an APM flaw that F5 disclosed on September 22 and that was later exploited. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day.

It has been revealed that that flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow in APM setups that serve as OAuth authorization servers, allowing attackers to run code without logging in. Today's six are stack-based overflows that need different settings.

According to recent reports, today's advisories also cover six lower-rated flaws in BIG-IP and BIG-IQ, each with its own fix. The scores below are CVSS v3.1:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Found this when support kept forwarding the same complaint: "my card was declined, I tried again, now it says duplicate order.".
  • Our checkout created one order, then sent the order id to the gateway as the merchant reference.
  • The gateway treated the reference as unique per transaction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Found this when support kept forwarding the same complaint: "my card was declined, I tried again, now it says duplicate order.".

Our checkout created one order, then sent the order id to the gateway as the merchant reference. Customer pays, issuer returns a soft decline (05 or 51). Customer fixes the card and hits Pay again. Same order, same reference, second attempt.

The gateway treated the reference as unique per transaction. The retry came back as a duplicate-reference error before it ever reached the issuer. So a recoverable decline became a dead end. About a third of those customers never came back.

Sources indicate that we had also half-solved it the wrong way. In one path we generated a fresh reference on every click, which fixed the error but broke the other direction. Double-clicks and network retries of the same attempt produced two real charges.

The fix was to separate two ids we had collapsed into one:.

It has been revealed that the gateway reference is built from attempt_id. Idempotency lives at the attempt level. Reconciliation groups attempts by order.

How do you model order vs attempt in your own systems? Do you keep them in separate tables, or a single payments table with a parent id?

Payneteasy handles this kind of payment flow for merchants and PSPs — see how it works.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the decade-old flaw, CVE-2026-123007, dubbed "nginx2root," has been present in NGINX's open-source code since version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015.
  • F5, the company behind NGINX, states attackers can run code where ASLR is turned off or can be bypassed.
  • In a recent development, code run this way gets the permissions of an NGINX worker process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the decade-old flaw, CVE-2026-123007, dubbed "nginx2root," has been present in NGINX's open-source code since version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015. Fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 came out today.

F5, the company behind NGINX, states attackers can run code where ASLR is turned off or can be bypassed. Security researchers at Wiz remarked they bypassed ASLR and ran code through the flaw in tests. Xint's researchers said they ran code through it with nothing more than a reachable HTTP/2 port.

In a recent development, code run this way gets the permissions of an NGINX worker process. Getting root on the host takes a second way to raise privileges, according to CIRCL, the Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg.

In Xint's tests, code running as a worker could get root on the host through a separate bug in the Linux kernel's SCTP code, even when NGINX ran inside a Docker container.

Neither the vendor nor the Wiz and Rapid7 researchers have reported any attacks exploiting the flaw so far. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog did not list it as of today.

Proof-of-concept code for the flaw is publicly available on GitHub, but its notes state it is suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started Docker container on the same machine.

Industry observers note that every open-source release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is vulnerable, according to NGINX's security advisories. That includes 1.31.8 from October 21, as well as the October 14 security releases 1.31.7 and 1.30.6.

NGINX Plus is affected too, in 37.x releases before the fixed builds and in R34 to R36, according to the vendor advisory.

Today's releases also fix four more flaws that the vendor notes can lead to code execution under the same ASLR condition. It scores all five 9.2 out of 10 on CVSS 4.0.

Each flaw can be reached only in a particular setup:.

HTTP/2 is on where a listen directive includes http2, or where http2 on is set. Running openssl s_client with -alpn h2 against a server indicates whether it accepts HTTP/2: the output reads ALPN protocol: h2 if it does. Behind a CDN, test the NGINX origin itself, because an origin that accepts only HTTP/1.1 cannot be attacked through HTTP/2.

These releases fix CVE-2026-123007, according to F5:.

Versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 fix all five flaws, according to NGINX's release notes. On NGINX Plus, 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 fix four of the flaws, and the CVE-2026-123633 fix was introduced in the earlier builds 37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1.

After upgrading, restart NGINX fully or use its live binary upgrade. A reload alone leaves the old executable running, and existing connections can stay on old worker processes.

The official Docker images for NGINX had 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 tags as of today, including Alpine variants.

Recent findings suggest that ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages as of today. Ubuntu's CVE status page listed nginx as vulnerable on its releases from 16.04 to 26.10, and Debian's security tracker listed it as vulnerable in bookworm, trixie, forky and sid. A distribution package can carry a fix without changing the version number that nginx -v reports, so compare the full package version with the distribution's own advisory.

Industry observers note that the vendor lists workarounds for only two of the five flaws. For the resolver flaw, CVE-2026-123634, avoid SSI and mirror directives, and do not build a proxied server name from variables. For the mail proxy flaw, CVE-2026-113425, limit listeners to trusted networks.

In a recent development, CIRCL's response guidance lists turning off HTTP/2 as a temporary mitigation until you can upgrade. That blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, but not the other three flaws. Turning off HTTP/3 where it is used removes the setup that CVE-2026-121810 needs.

On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set http2 off; in each affected server block and remove http2 from its listen directives. On 1.9.5 through 1.25.0, remove http2 from the listen directive, so listen 443 ssl http2; becomes listen 443 ssl;. Then restart NGINX where needed and rerun the openssl check to confirm the server no longer accepts HTTP/2.

Sources indicate that until the Linux kernel's SCTP bug is fixed, the same guidance advises that hosts not using SCTP, a network transport protocol like TCP, block its kernel module from loading. One way is to add the line install sctp /bin/false to a .conf file in /etc/modprobe.d/. That does not unload a module already loaded or turn off SCTP built into the kernel.

For signs of an attack, CIRCL suggests looking for NGINX workers that start unexpected programs, workers that exit abnormally or leave core dumps, long-lived HTTP/2 connections with heavy incoming traffic but few logged requests, and unusual outbound connections or DNS lookups. A clean access log does not rule out an attack, because HTTP/2 control frames do not normally show up there as requests. None of these signs is proof on its own.

Industry observers note that rapid7's version of the attack needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, according to its technical analysis. The attack took two and a half minutes in its demonstration. On links slower than about 300 Mbit/s, the transfer would run past NGINX's default one-hour connection limit, and the attack would fail.

The method also depends on a glibc memory-copy routine that is chosen on x86-64 CPUs with the avx512f and avx512vl features.

Wiz ran its tests on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds, using HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems, according to its disclosure post.

Xint's attack worked against its test servers on AWS, GCP and Azure, including over a public IP address, according to its research report.

#473. Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review

Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Complexdiscovery

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D.
  • It has been revealed that for eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output.
  • A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton covering 718 firms. The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage.

It has been revealed that for eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also shows that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work.

A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review.".

News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat.

Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found.

In the study’s data, the extra coding produced no detectable rise in finished work, and code review became the bottleneck. Fiona Chen and James Stratton, both Ph.D. candidates at Harvard University, measured that pattern across 725,938 workers at 718 companies. Two legal AI announcements this month, Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and a court-filing redaction agent Cooley is developing with Google Cloud, place a lawyer at a comparable review step, and neither reports a measure of it.

In a recent development, how much weight that pattern can bear depends on where the numbers came from. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The sample runs from January 2021 to March 2026 and covers Jellyfish client firms that consented to research use of their data. The paper’s tables list 68.3 million Jira concerns, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data.

The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The paper says timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee’s firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months.

The authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters. They acknowledge one known imbalance, that larger firms adopted earlier, and they control for firm size. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI.

Sources indicate that the current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper, and nothing in the version reviewed for this article indicates journal acceptance or completed peer review. Her website lists coverage links to The Wall Street Journal and The Economist, and legal trade press picked it up this month, including an Oct. 12 eDiscovery Today post by Doug Austin that relayed an Ars Technica report.

With that provenance in view, the coding results are large. Lines of code added rose by 1,494 per worker-month against a baseline of 5,017, about 30 percent. Commits rose 20 percent, and pull requests, the bundles of code submitted for review, rose 23 percent. The authors note that these estimates capture the added effect of agents at firms that already had AI coding assistants, not the effect of AI from a standing start.

It has been revealed that output is where the gain stops. The paper counts finished work as Jira issues resolved, and an concern counts as complete when its code is deployed to production. Agents moved that measure by 0.12 issues per worker-month on a 3.67 baseline, with a standard error of 0.17. That result is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the 95 percent confidence interval rules out an increase above about 12 percent of the baseline, well short of the 30 percent rise in code written.

The authors tested the obvious escape route. If engineers had shifted to larger tasks, a flat concern count would understate real output. So the researchers labeled a 0.5 percent sample of concerns by size with GPT-4o and extended those labels to every issue with a text-embedding model. They found no shift in average issue size, and pull requests did not grow larger either, which the authors use to set aside the simplest explanation for what happened in review.

Industry observers note that the paper locates the shortfall in code review. The time from pull request submission to merge rose 3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline, a 49 percent increase. The share of pull requests receiving a formal change request increased by about 12 percentage points from a baseline of 13 percent, nearly doubling, and review comments per pull request rose 35 percent. The share of workers doing any code review rose 14 percent from a base of about 29 percent, while the share writing code highlighted no measurable change.

AI review tools did not remove the bottleneck. By March 2026, nearly 80 percent of the firms had used one, yet AI generated only 23.3 percent of review comments, and only 10.8 percent of pull requests received even one AI comment. The authors write that the bottleneck persists after firms adopt such tools. The paper’s interviews show what that looks like on a team: a junior software engineer described a project where only one senior engineer could approve changes and could review the interviewee’s code only once a week. “After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks,” the engineer said, in a quote the authors say they lightly edited for clarity.

According to recent reports, that account fits the model the authors use to explain their numbers, which has two channels. In the first, faster drafting sends more code to a fixed pool of reviewers, a problem that moving labor into review can largely relieve. In the second, the rise in change requests and comments, which faster drafting alone does not explain, reads through the model as a sign of lower-quality drafts. That problem, the authors say, would require better technology. Anyone buying an agent should care which channel dominates, because the two call for different spending.

It has been revealed that nor did the coding gains show up as job cuts. The estimates rule out a decline in overall employment larger than 2.9 percent. A noisier estimate rules out a decline in engineering employment larger than 13.8 percent. The authors caution that these are short-run effects measured in partial equilibrium, which could mask job losses at competing firms, and that the assistant estimate for engineering employment shows upward pre-trends that make it hard to read causally.

Recent findings suggest that those software results arrive as legal AI tools adopt a related design, and the Harvey and Cooley announcements both follow it: automate a first pass, then keep a lawyer at the checkpoint. Harvey’s workflow, co-developed with LexisNexis and unveiled Oct. 7, is the drafting case. Harvey says the multi-step process of reading the complaint, researching and drafting a motion to dismiss “commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work” and that its tool produces the research and a first draft “in a matter of hours.” The announcement describes “human checkpoints at the moments where a lawyer’s judgment matters most,” but it does not state how long lawyers spend at those checkpoints or how long it takes to reach a motion ready to file.

Industry observers note that cooley’s Oct. 8 announcement applies the same posture to a different task, since its agent recommends redactions rather than drafting arguments. Cooley says the agent is still being developed and that attorneys make all redaction determinations before a filing goes to the court, which puts the human checkpoint at the last step before submission. As ComplexDiscovery reported Oct. 10, the announcement carries no error rate.

It has been revealed that for a motion filed in federal court, the checkpoint is a legal duty rather than a design choice. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b), an attorney presenting a motion certifies several things about it to the best of the attorney’s knowledge, information and belief, “formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.” Its legal contentions must be “warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law or for establishing fresh law.” Its factual contentions must have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, be likely to have it after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery. A first draft can arrive in hours, but that inquiry stays with the attorney, and the software evidence raises the possibility that review could absorb some of the drafting savings.

The paper’s method carries a second lesson, this one for information governance teams. The researchers identified agent use partly from traces inside the firms’ own systems, including bot accounts tied to AI tools and signatures such as “Co-authored-by” lines in commit messages and pull request descriptions. AI authorship can leave its own metadata trail in collaboration systems. That trail is a record that a retention schedule and a legal hold may need to reach.

In a recent development, none of this means legal work will behave like software, and the limits of the comparison matter. Document review is not code review, a production is not a pull request, and Chen and Stratton studied no legal work. A separate National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, revised in September 2026, reports a similar falloff using data on over 500,000 GitHub developers. Its authors, Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, found a 240 percent cumulative rise in commits from autonomous agents shrinking to 30 percent for actual releases. That paper carries its own disclosure: Demirer and Musolff each previously held a postdoctoral research position at Microsoft, which owns GitHub, and each now works as a paid research consultant for the company. Two software studies point to a pattern in software, not a finding about law firms.

Discovery practitioners have argued a version of this question before, and Austin’s post draws that comparison. He wrote that discovery has seen a similar debate over generative AI review, with some practitioners saying manual validation offsets the gains and others, including him, saying statistical sampling of the kind used in predictive coding is enough. For coding agents, though, he wrote that the extra review time may be warranted, since code that is 90 percent correct can still fail to run.

Sources indicate that his comparison suggests a useful split between two kinds of legal output. Population-level work such as first-pass relevance review can be validated by sampling. A single filing is different, because its citations, factual assertions and sensitive data generally need direct examination when one fabricated citation or one missed Social Security number is the failure. Buyers can turn that split into a test. Ask a vendor which kind of output its agent produces, then ask for the downstream measure rather than the drafting one: hours from upload to an approved work product, the share of drafts a reviewing attorney sent back and reviewer time per matter. Budget review capacity before scaling drafting volume, and log what reviewers change, because that log reveals whether the bottleneck is volume or quality.

In a recent development, those questions apply to the paper’s own sourcing, too. The data partner has a commercial interest in the subject, and the relationship runs deeper than a data license. Jellyfish describes itself as an “AI Impact Platform,” and the authors have published on its blog: a Sept. 25, 2025, post by Chen and Stratton described itself as “part of our ongoing work with Jellyfish.” The paper thanks the Jellyfish team “for their partnership” and states that Jellyfish reviewed the manuscript only to check for proprietary disclosure, not for scientific content, and that the conclusions are the authors’. Its funders were the Stripe Economics of AI Fellowship, a Harvard Kennedy School program on wealth distribution and the Schmidt Sciences AI at Work Program.

Jellyfish has also promoted an earlier version of the work. A Jan. 28 post on its blog by Nicholas Arcolano called it “a preliminary version of a latest paper from our collaborators at Harvard Economics, Fiona Chen and James Stratton,” based on 100,000 software engineers across 500 companies. That post, and a March 17 Jellyfish press release after it, reported that AI was making coding faster and that “code quality doesn’t seem to be suffering.” The August version, built on a larger sample running through March 2026, reads the near-doubling in change requests through its model as a possible sign of lower draft quality. The two descriptions rest on different versions and samples, so they need not conflict, but a reader relying on Jellyfish’s summary would miss the quality question the current paper raises.

The paper also carries small internal inconsistencies that do not touch the headline agent estimates. Its introduction rounds the sample to about 700 firms and 700,000 workers, and its main text describes 17 interviews where an appendix describes 21. Other limits are structural rather than clerical: the underlying data are proprietary, and use of AI tools through individual licenses goes unrecorded.

Recent findings suggest that none of those caveats overturns the central result, though the March 2026 data cutoff means a revision could move the figures. What the paper offers is a standard the two legal announcements discussed here do not meet: named authors, a disclosed method, a confidence interval and a measured checkpoint. If an agent cuts 40 hours of research and drafting to a few, how many of those hours reappear on the desk of the lawyer who signs the motion?

#472. Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3354 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Revscope

Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Revscope

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google's AI answers are taking clicks from websites in the search results.
  • Recent findings suggest that search engine optimization (SEO) still decides whether you can be found, but where an AI answer appears, a ranking brings 40% fewer visits than it used to.
  • In a recent development, an AI Overview is a generated summary that Google places above the ordinary results, with links to the pages it drew on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google's AI answers are taking clicks from websites in the search results. In a randomized experiment, researchers hid AI Overviews from some US desktop consumers. Comparing them with users who still saw Overviews shows that an Overview cuts clicks to outside websites by about 40%. Those Overviews now appear on more than half the US keywords DataForSEO tracks, up from 6% two years ago. The industry's answer, GEO (generative engine optimization), has yet to show a way to compensate for the loss. While AI citations correlate with the same kind of link profile that goes with higher Google rankings, in March AI assistants sent websites just 0.3% of their traffic.

Recent findings suggest that search engine optimization (SEO) still decides whether you can be found, but where an AI answer appears, a ranking brings 40% fewer visits than it used to. Generative engine optimization (GEO), the practice of getting your content cited in AI-written answers, looks mostly like SEO plus two additions: being present on the third-party sites AI answers draw from, and writing pages that are easy to quote. We found little evidence for any other tactic.

In a recent development, an AI Overview is a generated summary that Google places above the ordinary results, with links to the pages it drew on. In DataForSEO's monthly panel of 20 million keywords, the share of results showing one climbed from 5.93% in September 2024 to 61.43% in August 2026. The chart at the top of this post shows that climb. Over the same period the featured snippet, the quoted passage Google used to show at the top of a page, fell from 8.96% to 0.44%, and the discussions and forums block fell from 21.13% to 7.42%. Video results rose from 9.67% to 19.98%, though that is down from a peak of 31.05% in October 2025, and local map listings rose from 19.98% to 25.99%. DataForSEO's dataset covers 190 million keywords, 165 million AI answers, and 1.1 billion backlinks, mostly for US English searches. Pew Research Center's data gives an independent check. Pew logged the searches of 900 US adults in March 2025, re-ran them in April, and found summaries on 18% of them. DataForSEO's figures for those months are 14.67% and 17.63%, close to Pew's.

You can't reliably avoid Overviews by choosing different keywords. Between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026, the rate rose for every type of search intent:.

Low-volume keywords aren't safer either. In the third quarter of 2026, keywords with 201 to 300 monthly searches demonstrated Overviews 58.59% of the time, against 48.62% for those above 600. A separate dataset, from June to September 2026, covers difficulty and price. The easiest keywords showed Overviews 60.64% of the time and the hardest 53.76%. Keywords costing advertisers more than $5 a click were at 49.55% and those under 25 cents at 50.54%, with a low of 42.63% between $0.51 and $1.00. More than half the result pages have no price data and show Overviews 60.06% of the time. The rate does vary by industry. Health is at 69.68% and finance at 68.80%, while apparel is at 37.48%, dining at 29.37%, and real estate at 22.27%.

According to recent reports, queries are also getting longer, especially on desktop. Over a year, queries of five or more words grew from 29.3% to 34.8% of unique desktop queries and from 29.6% to 31.9% on mobile. Three and four word searches are still the most common.

Industry observers note that the strongest evidence is an experiment. Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen gave US desktop Chrome people an extension that put each of them at random into a group. One group saw Google as usual, and another had AI Overviews hidden. The researchers then watched two weeks of real searches in January and February 2026. On searches that would show an Overview, the group that could see them averaged 0.37 clicks to outside websites per search, against 0.62 for the group that couldn't, which the authors report as a 39.8% reduction. Searches ending with no outbound click went from 54% to 73%. Clicks on ads didn't change, which suggests Google takes care not to cannibalize its own revenue. Across all searches, with and without an Overview, the authors put the loss at roughly 18.5% of the organic clicks a site gets from Google. The authors expect the loss to grow as Overviews appear on more searches. This is a randomized controlled trial, the most reliable kind of study for separating cause from correlation or coincidence. The effect was statistically significant for informational searches. The navigational and transactional samples were too small to settle anything. This is a working paper, not yet peer reviewed, and it covers desktop only. A separate preregistered experiment by Wang and colleagues, with 1,100 people, also found that removing AI Overviews and AI Mode raised clicks to publishers.

Observational data points the same way. Pew found people clicked an ordinary result on 8% of visits to a results page with a summary and on 15% without one, and ended their browsing session on 26% against 16%. Pew's comparison isn't a controlled experiment, because the searches that draw a summary tend to be longer and phrased as questions.

Click-through rate (CTR) is the share of people shown a result who click it. Across more than 2,000 websites in DataForSEO's panel, the desktop CTR of the first organic result fell from 17.83% in September 2025 to 7.43% in August 2026, a drop of 58%. Mobile fell from 25.17% to 20.80%, a drop of 17%.

Desktop plunged from 15.18% to 7.94% between February and March 2026. AI Overviews can't easily explain that step since the report has them almost flat that month, at 42.79% and then 43.38%. A change in the format or quality of the Overviews might explain part of it, though that is speculation on our part. Mobile, meanwhile, sank to 12.96% and then rebounded to 22.49% by May. The report itself says its data "does not establish" whether AI answers, layout changes, or changes in behavior are the cause. Its sample may also be shifting underneath it, since the unique desktop queries it counts fell by a third over the year, from 1.97 million to 1.32 million. Whatever the cause, a top ranking on desktop now earns less than half the clicks it did a year earlier.

Industry observers note that dataForSEO also estimates where clicks go on pages with and without an Overview. By its model, the first organic result holds 9 to 16 points less click share on pages with one, though these are different searches on a single day's snapshot:.

In a recent development, the click share for the Overview's cited links looks promising, but it comes from a model. Pew, which logged real browsing, saw people click a link inside a summary on just 1% of visits, against 8% for ordinary results. Eighteen months and a large change in the product separate the two measurements, so it is difficult to say which is closer to the truth.

According to recent reports, google disputes that search traffic to websites is declining. In August 2025 its head of Search, Liz Reid, wrote that total organic clicks were "relatively stable year-over-year" and that Google was sending "slightly more quality clicks", meaning clicks where people don't quickly come back. She gave no figures to back that up.

Recent findings suggest that your site can't see whether someone goes back to Google, so you can't check Google's quality-clicks claim yourself, but you can check what your Google clicks are worth. RevScope, our product, shows your revenue per visitor from Google, AI Overviews included, and which landing pages earn the most.

According to recent reports, if people read the summary and stop there, it matters which sites the summary cites. The report compares Google's AI Overviews with ChatGPT. Their most-cited lists overlap, but a different kind of site leads each one.

The report warns that the two platforms' counts aren't comparable, so compare where a site ranks within each list. Reddit and Wikipedia rank near the top of both, and by our count 16 of the 30 domains in each top 30 appear on both lists. The differences are still large. YouTube is first in AI Overviews and nineteenth in ChatGPT. Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok make Google's top ten and miss ChatGPT's top 30, while Reuters, The Guardian, AP News, and The Washington Post make ChatGPT's top 30 and miss Google's. ChatGPT also often cites nobody: 27.3% of its answers had no source, against 0.7% for AI Overviews. So, as the report puts it, strength on one platform "doesn't automatically guarantee" the same on another.

According to recent reports, reddit also appears in Google's ordinary top ten for 32.15% of the report's tracked results, nearly eight times Quora's 4.11%. Two limits apply to all of this. The first is that the answers come from prompts DataForSEO collected, and the report doesn't explain how they were chosen or whether they match what people really ask. The second is that major platforms do about as well in ordinary results: Pew found Wikipedia, YouTube, and Reddit made up 15% of the sources in AI summaries and 17% of those in standard results. Still, the common belief that AI favors Reddit holds up in this data.

Google's position is that there are "no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary", beyond a page being indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. Since that is a company describing its own product, we looked at outside data on two questions. The first is which sites get considered, and the second is which page on a site gets picked.

A referring domain is another website that links to yours. DataForSEO measured how closely referring domains track AI citations using Spearman's correlation, a score where 0 means no relationship between two rankings and 1 means they match exactly. The score was 0.406 for AI Overviews and 0.377 for ChatGPT. Links marked as coming from user-generated content, such as forum posts, scored lower, at 0.342 and 0.314.

Recent findings suggest that these are moderate relationships, and they don't show that links cause citations, since large, well-known sites tend to have more of everything. The samples also contain only domains cited at least once, so they can't tell you what it takes to get cited for the first time. A similar pattern indicates up in ordinary rankings: domains ranking first had a median of 111 referring domains against 85 for positions 4 to 10, with heavy overlap between the groups. For AI Overviews, the median cited domain had 282 referring domains on the easiest keywords and 1,571 on the hardest, after the report excluded giant platforms like YouTube and Amazon and any domain with fewer than 50 referring domains. Small sites weren't measured at all. The ranges are also wide, at 518 to 5,765 for the middle half of domains on the hardest keywords, so sites with very different link profiles get cited.

According to recent reports, ranking for a query and being cited for it are drifting apart. Ahrefs found 76% of pages cited in AI Overviews ranked in the top 10 for that query in July 2025, and about 38% in March 2026. The two studies differ in sample, parsing, and the Gemini model behind the Overviews, so the size of that fall isn't a clean measurement. One possible mechanism is what Google calls query fan-out: its documentation says these features may problem "multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources". A page could then be cited because it ranks for a related question the reader never typed. Ahrefs offers this only as a possibility, and its earlier study tested the idea and found that the data didn't support it.

According to recent reports, the most careful test of page-level tactics we found is a study by the SEO software firm SISTRIX, published in October 2026. It paired 48,527 pages cited by ChatGPT, AI Mode, or AI Overviews with uncited pages from the same site, which removes the site's overall strength from the comparison. In the table, a factor of 2.7 means pages with the feature were cited 2.7 times as often as pages without it.

An experiment in the paper that gave GEO its name points the same way as SISTRIX's correlations. Aggarwal and colleagues rewrote web pages and measured how much of a generated answer drew on them. On their 10,000-query benchmark, adding quotations raised a page's visibility by about 41%, adding statistics by about 31%, and citing sources by about 27%, while keyword stuffing lowered it by about 8%, all on their main measure, the position-weighted share of the answer's words. Lower-ranked pages gained the most: citing sources lifted a page ranked fifth by 115% and cut the top-ranked page by 30%. They also tried Perplexity, an AI search product, on 200 samples, uploading the source text as files rather than letting it search. The gains on that measure were smaller, at about 21% for quotations and 9% for statistics. The main test used GPT-3.5 reading the top five search results, which is well behind today's products, so the percentages are dated even if the direction still holds.

It has been revealed that the most debated shortcut has nothing behind it so far. llms.txt is a proposed file that tells AI systems what a site contains. SE Ranking analyzed nearly 300,000 domains and found no correlation with citations. SISTRIX also concluded there is "no measurable effect", though it cautions that domains with the file differ from others in many ways, so this part of its data doesn't have the same-site pairing. Google says "you don't need to create new machine readable files, AI text files, or markup" for its AI features. The data agrees about the files, though SISTRIX's FAQ structured data result suggests some markup may help.

Recent findings suggest that to count what AI visits are worth on your own site, RevScope reports when ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and other assistants send visitors and whether they buy. It also tracks when AI and search engine bots crawl your pages.

Google's own reporting has a gap too. It counts traffic from its AI features inside the overall "Web" numbers in Search Console. Since 2026 Search Console also has generative AI reports, which Google notes show how often your URLs appeared in those features, along with pages, countries, and devices. The announcement describes impressions and doesn't mention clicks, so you learn how often you appear, not how many visits or sales that brings. Rank tracking can't fill the gap, since a page can hold position 1 and earn fewer clicks than it used to.

The numbers above are mainly US English, and the products change promptly, so the 2025 figures may already be out of date. Nearly all the large datasets come from companies that sell SEO data or software, including DataForSEO, Ahrefs, SISTRIX, and SE Ranking, and we sell analytics. Almost everything about what earns a citation is correlation. Three findings hold up. Controlled experiments show fewer clicks to outside websites when Google's AI features are present, domains with more referring domains tend to be cited more often among those already cited, and we found no proven shortcut to being cited.

According to recent reports, revScope connects your web traffic to your payments, so you can see which channels, pages, and keywords bring in revenue. Start on the free plan and put your time and budget where it pays.

Rather run it yourself? RevScope's source is public. Self-host it for free.

Recent findings suggest that search Insider: 2026 Edition DataForSEO Â· Annual research report Â· October 2026 DataForSEO collects search and AI answer data for a living and publishes its tables and methods, which allowed us to check the monthly figures behind its headlines. It sells this data, its answer prompts aren't explained, and its click shares are modeled. We rely on it for what appears where, and treat its click estimates and correlations as indications. Our charts are redrawn from its published values.

Recent findings suggest that the Impact of Google AI Overviews on Publisher Traffic and User Experience: Evidence from a Field Experiment Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen Â· Working paper Â· SSRN Â· draft of June 2026 University researchers ran a preregistered randomized experiment on 1,065 US participants, 770 of them in the two groups compared here. Random assignment makes it the best evidence that Overviews themselves reduce clicks. It isn't yet peer reviewed, and it covers desktop Chrome for two weeks. We read a copy of the June draft hosted outside SSRN.

AI in Search Reduces Publisher Referrals Without Improving User Experience: Experimental Evidence Stephanie T. Wang, Jeffrey Gleason, and colleagues Â· Preprint Â· arXiv Â· August 2026 A second preregistered experiment, with 1,100 people, which independently supports the direction of the result. We read its abstract only, so we use it for that direction and not for any figure.

Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears in the results Athena Chapekis and Anna Lieb Â· Short read Â· Pew Research Center Â· July 2025 A nonprofit research organization with no search product to sell, logging the real browsing of 900 consenting US adults. It covers one month, March 2025, re-collected the summaries in April, and doesn't control for which searches draw a summary.

Sources indicate that AI Features and Your Website and the Search Console reports announcement Google Search Central Â· Documentation, last updated December 2025, and blog post, June 2026 The primary sources for what Google states its AI features require and how it reports them. They are reliable on those rules, and they aren't independent evidence of what works.

Recent findings suggest that AI in Search is driving more queries and higher quality clicks Liz Reid Â· Manufacturer blog Â· Google Â· August 2025 Google's public position on total clicks, from the person running Search. Google can see the true numbers, but this post publishes none of them, so we report it as a claim.

Citation Worthiness: Which GEO Tactics Hold Up Across 96,418 URLs Johannes Beus, Julia Weissbach, and the SISTRIX Content Team Â· Industry study Â· SISTRIX Â· October 2026 Its same-site pairing and correction for multiple testing make it more careful than most GEO studies. It sells SEO software, covers only German-speaking markets, and reports correlations.

It has been revealed that GEO: Generative Engine Optimization Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, and colleagues Â· Conference paper Â· KDD 2024 Â· version 3, June 2024 The academic paper that named the field and ran controlled rewrites of pages. It indicates content changes can move visibility, but its test engine is now dated, and its authors' "up to 40%" should not be read as a current forecast.

Sources indicate that update: 38% of AI Overview Citations Pull From The Top 10 and 76% of AI Overview Citations Pull From the Top 10 Louise Linehan with Xibeijia Guan Â· Industry studies Â· Ahrefs Â· March 2026 and July 2025 Ahrefs sells SEO tools and tracks AI answers through its Brand Radar product, here matching about 4 million cited URLs against rankings in the later study. The two studies aren't like-for-like. The 38% counts results in every part of the page; for ordinary links alone it is 37.1%.
