📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Login.gov, which the U.S. government maintains, also works for IRS sign-in,[2] & the IRS's Direct Pay service takes bank-account tax payments with "No sign-in required".[6] ID.me replaced the traditional login for Treasury's savings-bond site TreasuryDirect on October 28, 2026,[7] & on October 29, 2026 senators Ron Wyden & Elizabeth Warren asked Treasury & the IRS to explain why they continue to use ID.me "instead of the government-run Login.gov platform".[8].

The IRS describes ID.me as "a private sector sign-in provider for secure access to government and non-government websites".[2] ID.me's Terms of Service say the tech giant provides "a level of assurance to businesses and government agencies" that a user's identity and attributes are verified "based upon widely-recognized standards",[3] & that "ID.me does not charge members any fees for registering and/or using the Service or Website."[3].

Treasury's savings-bond site TreasuryDirect claims it uses ID.me because it "aligns with Treasury security requirements and those used by the Internal Revenue Service".[7] The IRS said on December 7, 2021 that it was "using ID.me to provide verification services".[9] It announced on February 7, 2022 that it would "transition away from using a third-party service for facial recognition",[10] & said on February 21, 2022 that taxpayers could still choose biometric verification "through ID.me’s self-assistance tool".[11].

A taxpayer emailed consumer advocate Louis Rossmann a screenshot of the "UPDATED TERMS & CONDITIONS" screen the taxpayer remarked they saw while signing in to IRS.gov through ID.me, showing ID.me & IRS logos and one button, "Accept Terms & Continue".

The current Terms, Version 10.1.0 dated November 13, 2026, count continued use after revised Terms take effect as "acceptance of those changes", "Unless we expressly state otherwise"; a user who disagrees may stop using the Service & close the wallet first.[3] Version 10.0.3, dated March 3, 2023, remarked continuing use after notice "will indicate your agreement to all changes", "Unless otherwise noted by us".[13] The Credential Policy, Version 10.1, published July 1, 2024, requires users to reaffirm acceptance of "the prevailing Terms of Service, Privacy and other Policies and any other required agreements" "at least once every 5 years" or face credential suspension.[14].

Public radio program Marketplace reported that Nancy Kim, a professor emerita at Illinois Tech's Chicago-Kent College of Law, remarked she found nothing reassuring in ID.me's terms, pointing out that although they state ID.me won't sell data, ID.me can change them.[15].

Industry observers note that we may use information for marketing purposes. We may use your information to send promotional messages and newsletters via email, or otherwise alert you to products or Services we think might be of interest to you, including for ID.me Shop.[4].

ID.me Shop, a page of deals & discounts, notes it "is part of the Amazon Associates program and other affiliate programs" & "may earn money when you buy products through links on Shop".[5].

Recent findings suggest that we may share your information in connection with a corporate transaction. We may disclose or transfer your information as part of, or during negotiations for, any purchase, sale, lease, merger, or any other type of acquisition, disposal, or financing involving our brands.[4].

A user may opt out by emailing a notice titled "Opt-Out Notice" to [email protected] within 30 calendar days "after you first accept these Terms" or within 30 calendar days "after a material change to the Opt-Out Provisions takes effect".[3] Section 10 caps ID.me's aggregate liability at $1,000.00 "To the extent allowed by law".[3].

Version 10.0.3, dated March 3, 2023, had the same cap, & its notice listed "A BINDING ARBITRATION CLAUSE AND A CLASS ACTION WAIVER" with no opt-out.[13] The opt-out appears in Version 10.1.0, in a copy last updated September 18, 2025 whose opt-out text matches the November 13, 2026 version.[16][3].

Closing a wallet directs ID.me to deactivate the credential & "purge the associated data from active use", but ID.me "does retain" account & verification history "for up to three (3) years".[4] Use of the credential with state or federal government agencies "will be stopped" if the account is deleted.[4] Information given "in connection with a public sector agency" for verification "may be retained for up to three (3) years after wallet closure", "unless applicable regulations require a shorter retention period".[4].

ID.me reserves the right to keep data from "certain high-risk transactions, particularly in government and healthcare settings", "exclusively for fraud prevention and government audit purposes".[4] The policy states biometric deletion requests "may be subject to an internal investigation prior to completion", "where determined as necessary to protect the platform against fraud", followed by "ID.me reserves the right to decline such requests".[4].

Marketplace reported that Kim mentioned ID.me can keep a user's data for up to three years even after a deletion request.[15].

Please note, if you are using ID.me Services in connection with legal identity verification for a state or federal government agency, or in association with Electronic Prescriptions for Controlled Substance Services, ID.me does not use any Personal Information provided as part of your verification for any type of marketing or promotional purposes related to ID.me Shop without your consent, or unless you otherwise use your ID.me credential for verification with any ID.me customer who is not a state or federal government agency customer, use your ID.me wallet in connection with ID.me Shop, ID.me Jobs, or ID.me Rx, or otherwise opt-in to receiving marketing communications from ID.me.[4].

ID.me's policy states the organization "may share" a user's name, date of birth & contact details for reporting with the government agency the user verifies for, & that verifying "constitutes consent" to it.[4] Terms of Service 10.1.0, dated September 18, 2025 & November 13, 2026, "do not provide consent to marketing calls or text messages".[16][3].

The August 18, 2026 IRS help page noted ID.me "will not share, sell, rent or trade" personally identifiable information "with other parties, except to verify your identity and eligibility";[18] the October 29, 2026 version points readers to "their privacy policies at Login.gov and IDMe".[2].

The IRS help page last reviewed or updated on October 29, 2026 claims that "The U.S. government maintains the Login.gov system", & that taxpayers who cannot verify their identity with one provider should "try the other provider".[2] The version last reviewed or updated on August 18, 2026 named only ID.me as the sign-in account.[18] The IRS sign-in page says to "choose ID.me" for anyone who does not have "an SSN, U.S. address, and smartphone, or tablet with a camera", SSN being a Social Security number.[1].

Login.gov is provided by the federal General Services Administration (GSA).[19] Login.gov's privacy page says a user who creates an account & verifies their identity consents to Login.gov "collecting, using, keeping, and sharing your personal information" as its policies describe, "including to verify your identity and to help detect and prevent fraud".[20].

Login.gov's Rules of Use say customer-support feedback may be used "for other purposes as we see fit, such as for marketing", though Login.gov "will not reveal your personal information outside of the Login.gov service" except "as required by applicable law or as stated elsewhere in these terms".[19] They also say disputes "shall be governed by federal law" & that no fees are charged for registering or using the service.[19] In a 2026 blog post, GSA wrote that Login.gov's privacy protections let people access government services "without their information being used for commercial purposes".[21].

Direct Pay, the IRS service for paying taxes from a bank account, lists "No sign-in required"; people who have never filed, or who last filed over six years ago, are told they "can pay another way".[6] Taxpayers who cannot register online can have a tax return or tax account transcript mailed; the IRS lists "transcripts of past tax returns" & "tax account information" among their tax records.[22].

On October 29, 2026, Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden, D-Ore., & Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee Ranking Member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., demanded that Treasury halt "a rushed transition" to ID.me for Americans trying to access their savings bonds online.[8] The senators wrote:.

Americans should not have to provide sensitive personal information to ID.me as the price of accessing essential government services when a secure government-operated alternative is available[8].

They asked the agencies to delay the ID.me requirement until after the 2027 tax filing deadline.[8].

According to recent reports, their letter, dated October 27, 2026, said federal law requires agencies to implement "a single sign-on trusted identity platform" developed by the General Services Administration, citing 6 U.S.C. § 1523(b)(1)(D).[23] It said ID.me was awarded a five-year agreement with a ceiling of more than $1 billion for identity verification, authentication, and fraud prevention services.[23] The letter requested a response by November 9, 2026.[23].

Trade publication Biometric Update reported that two Treasury orders for ID.me subscriptions were placed under "a five-year Treasury blanket purchase agreement for ID.me identity verification and authentication services" with "a ceiling of approximately $1.03 billion", and that "Federal procurement records show about $93 million obligated against the vehicle so far".[24].

An August 31, 2026 memorandum from the Office of Management and Budget, M-26-18, notes agencies offering other identity solutions must promote Login.gov as the default option for upcoming account creation "for any user population that Login.gov is able to serve".[25] The IRS said in an emailed statement, quoted by news site FedScoop, that "Taxpayers can use Login.gov or ID.me" ahead of the 2027 filing season.[26].

#470. Claude was trained on protein sequences at scale

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2339 w)

Claude was trained on protein sequences at scale

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Xinmingtu

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A next-amino-acid test on little-studied proteins finds that the latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences at scale.
  • The latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences, at scale.
  • Industry observers note that frontier LLMs have started to look good at protein tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A next-amino-acid test on little-studied proteins finds that the latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences at scale. Other frontier models show no sign of it.

The latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences, at scale. Give Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Opus 5.5 the start of a little-studied bacterial protein and they predict the next amino acid. Shuffle the protein and they can’t. No other model we tested can do this. Like a protein language model, they do better on bigger protein families, and they do it even in families with no papers at all. Fable 5.2 beats every open protein language model we ran, and Opus 5.5 is level with ProtGPT3-10B, the largest of them.

Revision, 18 November 2026. Since the first version:.

Industry observers note that frontier LLMs have started to look good at protein tasks. Atharv Jayprakash indicated GPT-6 Astra ranking SOD1 variants as well as ESM-2, and PG-LLM found the same across many proteins. Did these models learn from protein sequence databases such as UniProt, or from what is written about proteins?

Recent findings suggest that famous proteins can’t tell the two apart: GFP is printed in countless papers, and most frontier models recite it. So we tested proteins that almost nobody writes about.

Industry observers note that we give a model the start of a protein and ask for the next amino acids. Then we ask again on a shuffled copy of the same protein. Shuffling keeps the letters and destroys their order, so the difference in accuracy measures what the model knows about the sequence itself.

The test set is 668 bacterial and archaeal proteins from 167 Pfam families of unknown function. No family has a solved structure or more than three papers, and no protein has a close relative in UniProt. Each protein is cut at five points. At each cut the model writes the next 10 amino acids, and we score the first. Thinking is at its lowest setting. Appendix E has the details.

It has been revealed that fable 5.2 gets the next amino acid right 54% of the time on real proteins and 9% on shuffled ones. The gap is there in nearly every family, not just a few easy ones. It appears in Opus 4.7, jumps in Opus 5.5, and jumps again in Fable 5.2. GPT, Gemini and the seven open-weight models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen 3.8, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, gpt-oss-120b and Nemotron 3 Ultra) stay near zero, even when they simply continue raw FASTA text, the way they were trained. The latest Claude models also write runs of correct residues that other models rarely manage (Appendix B).

According to recent reports, protein language models learn only from sequences, so they are the natural yardstick. The closest to an LLM are the ones that read a protein left to right and predict the next residue: ProtGPT3, whose 10-billion-parameter version is the largest open one, and ProGen3, whose largest public version has 3 billion. On the same input, Fable 5.2 beats both by a wide margin. Opus 5.5 is level with ProtGPT3-10B and below ProGen3-3B.

ESM models are trained to see both sides of a residue, so continuing from the left is harder for them. Appendix C has all nine models.

According to recent reports, if the models learned from sequences, families with more sequences should be easier. To test this over a wide range, we added 90 smaller families, down to 20 proteins each, for 257 families in all.

It has been revealed that they are. Opus 5.5 rises with the two protein language models, ProtGPT3-10B and ProGen3-3B, which are trained on nothing but sequences. Fable 5.2 rises fastest and levels off at about 300 proteins per family. Earlier Claude models rise at a lower level, and GPT and Gemini stay near zero. The knowledge also carries over to proteins published after the training cutoff, with no close relative before it (Appendix G).

Two other explanations don’t fit:.

Sources indicate that famous proteins are a different story. Many models do well on them, and several recite hundreds of residues letter for letter (Appendix B), because these sequences are all over papers and the web. In a first round with famous and obscure proteins side by side, Gemini 4 Carbon was strong on the famous ones and dropped to almost nothing on the obscure ones. The latest Claude models and ProtGPT3-10B held up, and Fable 5.2 was the strongest on both.

In a recent development, this also explains the SOD1 and PG-LLM results. Ranking variants of a well-known protein can lean on what is written about it: which residues are buried, which substitutions break a helix, which mutations cause ALS. In PG-LLM, accuracy doesn’t depend on alignment depth and improves with more thinking, both signs of that route. Our test shuts it out. GPT-6 is good at the first kind of task and weak at the second; the latest Claude models are good at both.

In a recent development, the latest Claude models know protein families that almost nobody has studied. That takes a lot of sequence data, not a few examples: protein sequences were a sizeable part of their training. Opus 5.5 behaves like a protein language model, and Fable 5.2 goes beyond the best one we could run. GPT and Gemini show none of this. Whatever protein sequence they saw in training, it was not enough to learn these families.

DNA is different. Opus 5.5 predicts human and mouse coding sequence but not the rest of the genome, and barely the bacterial genes behind the proteins it knows (Appendix A). It learned proteins, not genomes.

We are curious what else this knowledge supports. Fable 5.2 predicts little-studied proteins better than any open protein language model we ran, and protein language models carry more than next-residue statistics: ESM-2’s internal representations hold enough structure that a small folding module on top predicts 3D structures (ESMFold), and their probabilities rank the effects of mutations. Could Claude fold a protein, or rank its variants, the same way?

All code, test sets, model outputs and figures are in llm-bioseq-probe.

220-nucleotide windows, 200 shown and 20 to predict, from hg38, mm39 and the bacterial genes behind the test proteins, 500 per region. Non-coding windows contain no repeats, and the control shuffles each window keeping its dinucleotide counts. Opus 5.5 wrote all 20 nucleotides right 25 times in 500 human coding windows; a blind guess does that about once in a trillion. Gemini 4 Carbon blocks most DNA prompts before answering, so it is not shown.

It has been revealed that all 10 residues right. Each question asks for the next 10 residues. On the 668 little-studied proteins, Claude Fable 5.2 gets all 10 right at 88 real cuts and Opus 5.5 at 12, and neither at any shuffled one. If their residues were independent guesses at their own per-residue accuracy, they would get 15.8 and 0.57 by chance.

Runs in a row. On shuffled proteins neither Fable 5.2 nor Opus 5.5 gets more than 3 residues in a row. Once on track they get surer: after one right residue, Opus 5.5 gets the next right 47% of the time, after four in a row 68%.

Reciting well-known proteins. At 158 points in well-studied proteins, each model was asked for the next 200 residues at once.

GPT-6.1 Sol never reaches 100 residues, and GPT-5.5 never gets past 2.

Choosing the proteins. We started from every Pfam family whose name says “domain of unknown function” (DUF) or “protein of unknown function”, and kept those with no structure in the PDB, at most 3 Europe PMC hits for the family’s accession, and at least 300 member proteins. We binned them by size (300 to 1,000 proteins, 1,000 to 3,000, 3,000 to 10,000, over 10,000) and drew 50 families per bin at random; only 17 families qualify above 10,000, so the set has 167. From each family we took 4 proteins from UniProt that are unreviewed (TrEMBL), come from Bacteria or Archaea, are 120 to 800 residues long, use only the 20 standard amino acids, are not low-complexity (Shannon entropy above 3.9 bits per residue), and are alone in their UniRef90 cluster, so no other UniProt protein is 90% or more identical to them. That gives 668 proteins.

According to recent reports, smaller families. For the family-size test we drew 30 more families in each of three smaller bins (20 to 60, 60 to 150 and 150 to 300 proteins) with the same criteria and 4 proteins per family, 360 proteins in all. Every model gets the same prompt and scoring as on the main set.

Cutting. Each protein is cut at 5 positions drawn at random inside its Pfam domain (the longest domain span, at least 40 residues), at least 10 residues from either end of the domain and with at least 30 residues before the cut: 3,340 cuts. Everything before the cut is the prefix; the residue right after it is the answer.

Asking. The model gets this message, with the prefix in 60-character lines (an example from one of the test proteins):.

Each model runs through its own API with temperature 0 where it is accepted, thinking off or at its lowest setting (for Opus 5.5 and the Fable models, low effort, at which the model still decides whether to think), no tools, and one sample per question. The Claude Fable models run through OpenRouter, since Anthropic’s API serves them only to workspaces that retain data. Models that declined to guess (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM, gpt-oss) also got a version that adds “Give your best guess even if you are uncertain. Do not explain or refuse.”; those runs are marked separately.

Industry observers note that thinking. A reply counts as thought about when the API reports thinking tokens for it: thinking_tokens in Anthropic’s usage report, reasoning_tokens in OpenRouter’s. The thinking text itself is not kept; only the visible reply is scored. Fable 5.2 thought on 9% of questions, Opus 5.5 on 36%, Fable 5.1 never. Without thinking, Fable 5.2 is right 54.7% of the time on real proteins and 8.8% on shuffled ones (48.2% and 10.6% with thinking), and Opus 5.5 35.3% and 6.9% (34.1% and 8.6%).

Scoring. We read the last sequence the reply states: a run of capital amino-acid letters on its own line or after a label such as “Answer:”, skipping words, lists and anything inside thinking tags. If it starts by restating the end of the prefix, the restatement is dropped. Its first letter is the predicted next amino acid. A reply cut off at the length limit counts only if it opens with a sequence. Replies that state no sequence are excluded and counted (0.1% for Opus 5.5). Only the first residue is scored; the full 10 are used for exact continuations and runs. The same reader is used for every model and for real and shuffled proteins.

Recent findings suggest that the shuffled control. Each protein’s residues are shuffled once, with a random seed fixed by its accession, and the same 5 cut positions are asked on the shuffled sequence. The shuffle keeps the composition of the whole protein and destroys the order, so a model that knows only which amino acids are common scores the same on both.

According to recent reports, statistics. For each family we compute the share of correct first residues on real and on shuffled cuts, and take the difference, in percentage points. The result for a model is the mean of that gap over the 167 families. Intervals are 95% bootstraps over families (10,000 resamples), the main test is a one-sided sign-flip permutation test over families, and the family-size trend is the Spearman correlation between a family’s gap and the logarithm of its size.

Industry observers note that raw continuation. For models that allow it, the same prefix is sent without any instruction, as the text “>sequence” followed by the FASTA lines, through a plain completion endpoint (open-weight models on Fireworks) or as the start of the model’s own reply (Gemini 2.5 Pro). The first letter the model writes is scored as above.

Protein language models. They get the same prefix and no prompt. ProGen3, ProtGPT3, ProtGPT2 and Prot-xLSTM read it left to right and give a probability for the next token; the ESM models see the prefix, a mask in place of the next residue, and the end of the sequence. In every case the prediction is the most likely of the 20 standard amino acids.

Total API cost was about $730, plus a few dollars of GPU time for the protein language models.

Gemini 4 Carbon blocked about 75% of DNA prompts outright. OpenAI rejected 23 GPT-6 requests in the first round and 17 GPT-6.1 Sol requests in the main run as possible biological misuse, and 6.6% of GPT-6.2 Astra’s main-set questions (GPT-6.2 Sol: 0.6%). Claude Sonnet 4.5 refused 97% of requests that started its reply with a protein sequence, and Anthropic’s filter blocked 44% of Claude Fable 5’s questions as cyber content.

According to recent reports, leo Tianlai Chen built a set of 56 proteins from 31 of the families that were first made public in August 2026, after the assumed 1 July training cutoff, and have no earlier relative at 50% identity or more. The models cannot have seen them or anything close. Both Claude models still predict them, Fable 5.2 ahead of both protein language models, while GPT-6.2 Sol stays at zero. Every model scores about half of what it scores on the same families in the main set, as expected for proteins this distant. What the latest Claude models learned carries over to latest members of a family.

The proteins were dated at their source, and none matches an earlier UniRef50 cluster at 50% identity or more. Cuts follow the main set’s rules. With 56 proteins only gaps of about 14 points or more are reliably detected, and the 1 July cutoff is an assumption.

While benchmarking Gemini 4 Carbon on one of our private evals, we found something surprising: it spent close to an hour completing tasks that routinely took Opus and Astra only a few minutes:.

Left is faster; lower is cheaper.

Turns out we weren't alone in noticing this.

Industry observers note that I don't really know how to properly emphasize this. Gemini 4 Carbon is unacceptably slow in real world usage.

Gemini 4 Carbon low: 22m21sOpus 5.5 high: 9m33s.

i really love gemini 4 carbon but its too slow. im losing my mind waiting just to stay focused and learn simple things.

carbon is nearly unusable because of how slow it is, but people are majorly sleeping on it.

To find out why, we traced every step of Carbon's runs and quantified what contributes to the slowness.

In each task, the agent gets a codebase from just before a bug was fixed, along with a report that describes the bug only by its symptoms. Its job is to diagnose the bug and fix it, without making any unrelated changes.

Much of the task's difficulty comes from engineering judgment rather than raw intelligence: tracing the user's symptoms to the right code path, ruling out rival explanations, putting the fix in the right place, and knowing when to stop.

According to recent reports, the first (and easiest) factor to separate out was inference speed: queueing at the provider, network latency, prompt processing and generation speed. Together, these set how long each step takes:.

Slower inference accounts for part of the gap: 16–30% of Carbon’s extra time compared with Astra, and 45–49% compared with Opus. The rest comes from longer trajectories. Carbon simply does more work per task, as the step counts, tool calls and tokens below show:.

GPT-6 Astra against Gemini 4 Carbon, mean per bug.

In a recent development, carbon takes about seven times as many steps as Astra, and eleven times as many actions such as reading a file or running a command. It writes seven times as much and, because every step re-sends a longer and longer conversation, it processes more than sixteen times as much input.

Before looking inside the runs, we checked two simpler explanations.

We labelled every step of the Astra and Carbon runs by what it was for, and then counted how many steps went to each kind of work:.

Each model’s steps, grouped by what they were for.

Half of Carbon’s steps went into work the ticket never asked for:.

Minutes from the start of each run. GPT-6 Astra at max effort, Gemini 4 Carbon at high.

Sources indicate that in this sample trial, both models identified the cause early, Astra within a minute and Carbon within about six. Astra had its fix written three minutes later; Carbon didn't write any code for another 25 minutes.

According to recent reports, carbon might not have been sure it had the cause (a knowledge gap), or it might have known and kept going anyway (a general habit, learned from training that rewards right answers more than it penalises extra steps). To tell them apart, we re-ran one of the trials in a modified harness that automatically injects the same check-in every five turns: "do you already have enough to make the fix?".

The same bug and scale as above. Gemini 4 Carbon at high, with the check-in injected every five turns (circles).

According to recent reports, with check-ins, Carbon finished in 28 minutes instead of 37, and the wait between naming the cause and editing shrank from 25 minutes to about 10. This implies that the slowness seems to come from how Carbon behaves, not what it knows.

Even within the steps the fix needed, we found some additional low-hanging fruit: Carbon got less done with each step, and it kept re-reading code it had already seen.

Recent findings suggest that astra made more than two tool calls per step, often reading several files at once — Carbon, on the other hand, made about one, usually reading a single file. Carbon also re-read far more: 39% of the lines it read were ones it had already seen, against 7% for Astra. We estimate that these two "mechanical" inefficiencies account for roughly 25% of Carbon's excess runtime.

Sources indicate that on difficult bug-fixing tasks, Carbon took close to an hour where Opus and Astra took minutes. We traced that gap to three sources:.

When you Googled something, you used to get a link to my website. Now you get a page of ads, then an AI-generated answer trained on my content, then finally a link to my website. This has a devastating impact on traffic.

It inspired two government portals and a few similar websites in other cities.

If my work just get mixed into an AI-generated answer, I lose my voice and my audience. My carefully chosen words lose their meaning. No one shakes my hand and buys me a beer. No one tells me how their citizenship application went.

This is not an isolated case. Many website owners have reached out in private to commiserate. Some have paywalled their work. Others have given up and moved on. They keep the websites online, but they no longer enhancement them. It’s just not worth it.

It will get worse. Last week, Google has made two announcements: AI-generated answers will replace search results entirely, and they have ads in them.1 This is the future of the internet. No websites, just a chat box with ads.

I don’t know where All About Berlin fits in that future.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning.
  • Existing looped reasoners update their latent state without any explicit assessment of it.
  • The energy rates the compatibility between the reasoning state z and the initial board x.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.

Existing looped reasoners update their latent state without any explicit assessment of it. An EBR learns an energy function that guides refinement, stopping and selection.

In a recent development, score. The energy rates the compatibility between the reasoning state z and the initial board x. Lower means better compatibility.

Recent findings suggest that refine. The gradient turns the score into an improvement direction.

Recent findings suggest that stop. The state becomes stationary once the gradient is small, so the gradient acts as a stopping criterion.

According to recent reports, select. Among multiple candidate solutions, we pick the one with the lowest energy.

According to recent reports, correct solutions settle at low-energy stationary states. Energy, gradient norm and step size during descent on Sudoku-Extreme. Correct trajectories settle at low energy with small gradients, while wrong ones keep moving.

Running more descent steps refines each answer further, and running more trajectories gives the energy more candidates to choose the lowest-energy one from.

EBRs reach EqR's best accuracy with 7× fewer iterations (left) and 43× fewer samples (right).

Recent findings suggest that GRAM and TRM from GRAM's paper; EqR from its released checkpoint. Mean ± SD over three seeds.

Each trajectory stops once its energy gradient falls below a threshold, so easy puzzles finish in a few steps and hard ones keep going.

EBRs give the best single-sample accuracy among reasoning models. Within only 5 passes, they reach 99.9% and 88.3%, ahead of methods that draw up to 128. Stopping each trajectory once its energy gradient falls below a threshold keeps 99.9% accuracy with 10.9× fewer FLOPs than a fixed-depth EBR, allowing us to surpass EqR with 345× fewer FLOPs.

EBR acts like stochastic gradient descent and can capture many different solutions. Coverage captures the share of each input's distinct valid solutions that 20 samples find.

Pass@1 (%) and Conflicts (edges summed over the test graphs) use one sample. Cov@20 is the share of distinct valid solutions found by 20 samples (%). Baselines from GRAM's paper.

#465. Quad9 Is Leaving France: Why DNS Resolvers Are the Wrong Place to Fight Piracy

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2225 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techstackups

Quad9 Is Leaving France: Why DNS Resolvers Are the Wrong Place to Fight Piracy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2225 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techstackups

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, Quad9 will stop answering DNS queries from France.
  • Recent findings suggest that cloudflare, which runs the competing 1.1.1.1 resolver, called the departure "a canary in the coal mine", and the post reached the front page of Hacker News.
  • A DNS resolver turns a name like example.com into an IP address your computer can connect to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, Quad9 will stop answering DNS queries from France. Quad9 is the Swiss non-profit behind the free 9.9.9.9 resolver, which blocks malware and phishing domains. It is not leaving because of costs or lack of customers. It is leaving because a Paris court fined it for refusing to block a list of pirate sports-streaming domains on behalf of beIN Sports. With around 20 similar cases still pending in France, leaving the country is the only option Quad9 can afford.

Recent findings suggest that cloudflare, which runs the competing 1.1.1.1 resolver, called the departure "a canary in the coal mine", and the post reached the front page of Hacker News. In that thread, Quad9's CTO John Todd asked readers to write "a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path", with plenty of sources, and to send it to policymakers. This is our attempt. Every claim below links to a primary document, a court ruling, or contemporaneous reporting.

A DNS resolver turns a name like example.com into an IP address your computer can connect to. Most people use their ISP's resolver without knowing it. A public resolver is one anyone can point their device or network at instead, such as Google's 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, Cisco's OpenDNS, or Quad9's 9.9.9.9.

Quad9 has a few properties that make it unusual:.

According to recent reports, organisations have come to depend on it. Mullvad shut down its own public encrypted DNS service on November 2, 2026 and moved Mullvad Browser people with default settings to Quad9, funding Quad9 instead. (Mullvad Browser users in France will now be migrated to a resolver that disappears three weeks later.) Quad9's announcement lists dozens of French networks it sees traffic from, including the interministerial digital directorate DINUM, France Travail, CEA, Institut Pasteur, RENATER, EDF, SNCF, AP-HM hospitals in Marseille, France TÃ©lÃ©visions, Thales, and Airbus's Stormshield. Quad9 can't tell any of them it is leaving. As Cloudflare points out, when a resolver disappears, users don't see an error message. "Their Internet will simply stop working.".

Industry observers note that the legal basis for all of this is Article L.333-10 of the French sports code. It was created by Law 2021-1382 of October 25, 2021, the same law that merged HADOPI and the CSA into the upcoming regulator Arcom. L.333-10 lets a sports rightsholder go to the president of the Paris judicial court and obtain "dynamic" blocking orders, meaning orders that cover sites already identified plus new mirror domains notified later through Arcom, against "toute personne susceptible de contribuer Ã  y remÃ©dier" (any person able to help stop the infringement).

That last phrase is what puts DNS resolvers in scope. In July 2026, Parliament passed Law 2026-725 on professional sport, which amended L.333-10 and added an automated real-time blocking system run by Arcom. TorrentFreak reported that under the new system "ARCOM's agents no longer approve each block in advance." Quad9 called it "recklessly dangerous.".

The timeline indicates how the circle of targets has widened:.

Recent findings suggest that the 21 October judgment is short and worth reading. A few details matter:.

Recent findings suggest that â¬1,000 a day for three weeks is survivable, about â¬24,000. Twenty more cases like it, each running for a full football season with ever-growing domain lists and Arcom's newly introduced automated system feeding them, is not. Quad9 says: "Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases.".

Recent findings suggest that quad9 is often asked why it doesn't just block the domains. It has three options, and none of them work.

1. Block globally. This is what Quad9 did for Canal+ in December 2024 and what DNS4EU does today. It means a French court decides what a user in Brazil, Kenya or Germany can resolve, for the commercial benefit of one tech giant. Quad9's announcement asks how France would react if other nations imposed their laws on French users through DNS. The answer is obvious, and the reverse should be too. Nothing limits this to sports either: once global blocking is accepted, every court in every country can add names to everyone's resolver.

In a recent development, 2. Geo-block France. Quad9 has already tried this, in Germany. In the Sony Music v. Quad9 case, Quad9 used geoIP blocking for German owners while the case continued. Sony's lawyers used a VPN to reach the content "from Germany" anyway, the court agreed this was non-compliance, and Quad9 was fined for contempt. GeoIP is a probabilistic guess about where an IP address is, not a legal fact about where a person is. A resolver that keeps no user records has no reliable way to define a "French user." As Quad9 told TorrentFreak: "There is no legally useful way for us to define a French user." Even the French order is geographically complicated: heise notes it covers the overseas departments and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon but excludes Latest Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, and French Polynesia.

Industry observers note that 3. Pay and fight. Quad9 won in Germany. The Dresden Higher Regional Court held in December 2023 that DNS resolvers get the same liability privilege as access providers, and the German civil rights group GFF remarked "the judgement puts the onus on rights holders." But winning took "several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time," and the opposition, in Quad9's words, "has more lawyers than we have money and time." As Quad9 wrote in 2025, compliance costs that are routine overhead for Google are, "for small, mission-driven nonprofits like Quad9, â¦ an existential threat.".

The argument against resolver blocking isn't only about Quad9's survival. Even on its own terms, it does not do what the rightsholders want.

It doesn't remove anything. The DNS only holds pointers. Quad9's Dresden write-up puts it this way: "The DNS does not contain content - it is a system designed for delivery only of pointers." The pirate server stays online and keeps serving everyone who reaches it some other way. The Internet Society's 2025 guide for legal professionals claims the same thing.

According to recent reports, it takes seconds to bypass. Quad9 notes there are thousands of other open resolvers. Users can also run their own, or use encrypted DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484), which looks like ordinary web traffic. Arcom's own December 2025 study for the National Assembly says 20% of French internet users already use an alternative DNS resolver and 29% use a VPN. Quad9 compares DNS blocking to "holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert.".

According to recent reports, it is blunt. DNS works at the level of whole domains. A resolver can't block one infringing stream on a shared host without blocking everything else on that name. The IAB's RFC 7754, the IETF's standard reference on blocking and filtering, says: "From a technical perspective, there are no perfect or even good solutions -- there is only least bad." ICANN's security committee revisited the question in SAC127, "DNS Blocking Revisited" (2025), warning implementers to minimise overblocking and avoid affecting consumers outside their jurisdiction. France's own registry operator, AFNIC, made the core point years ago in its scientific council's report on the consequences of DNS filtering: "Le DNS n'a pas Ã©tÃ© conÃ§u pour filtrer les contenus." (The DNS was not designed to filter content.).

According to recent reports, it is opaque. When a resolver is forced to lie, the user sees a site that doesn't load. They have no way to tell whether the site is down, their network is broken, or a court ordered the block. There is a standard for being honest about this: RFC 8914 Extended DNS Errors defines code 16, "Censored", for answers withheld "due to an external requirement imposed by an entity other than the operator." But nothing in the French orders requires resolvers to use it.

Sources indicate that blocking at scale causes real collateral damage. France is not the only test case. Italy's Piracy Shield system blocked Google Drive for much of the country in October 2024. A RIPE Labs study of Piracy Shield found more than 500 unrelated sites blocked and concluded that "IP-level blocking is an indiscriminate tool with consequences that outweigh its benefits." In Spain, LaLiga's IP blocking of shared Cloudflare addresses knocked innocent sites offline every match day, leading Cloudflare's CEO Matthew Prince to call the approach "bonkers". The same RIPE study found most European piracy is hosted in Europe, which is where enforcement belongs: at the hosting provider.

Measured by its own goals, the French system has a mixed record. Arcom reports 12,606 sports domains blocked since 2022, 6,496 of them in 2025 alone (up 71%), while piracy fell 4% in 2025 and 34% since 2021. The number of blocks is growing much faster than piracy is shrinking, and Arcom's figures don't separate the effect of resolver blocking from ISP blocking. Every one of those domains has to be found, blocked, and then found again when it reappears under a upcoming name. OONI's 2025 measurement of French ISP blocking found that of 542 domains tested, 291 were blocked by at least one ISP but only 132 by all four. The European Commission's own 2025 assessment of its live-events piracy recommendation concluded the effects "have been limited and have not allowed to significantly curb the volume of online piracy of live events.".

Driving Quad9 out of France doesn't hurt pirates at all. The people who lose are the ones who chose a resolver for security.

Quad9 is the clearest casualty so far, but the same process is underway across Europe.

That is why France matters beyond France. If its model becomes the EU template, every public resolver in Europe will face the choice Quad9 faced: lie to all people worldwide, build unreliable geolocation infrastructure, or leave.

The Hacker News discussion wasn't one-sided, and the counter-arguments deserve answers.

Recent findings suggest that "Hosting providers are unreachable, so courts move up the chain." One commenter argued that pirate hosts are bulletproof and ignore courts, so going after the intermediaries is the only lever left. Another asked the Quad9 CTO directly where the problem should be attacked. This is the strongest point. But the RIPE data indicates most of the hosting is in Europe and within reach of European courts, and the commenter's logic leads to blocking at the last link in the chain that cannot fight back. That is not the same as the link that can actually stop the infringement.

"Friction works. Most people won't bother to switch." Some argued that DNS blocking is good because it nudges the majority while staying easy to bypass for those who know how. The Paris Court of Appeal used essentially this reasoning. But Arcom's numbers say a fifth of French users already use alternative DNS, the friction is gone the moment one person changes a router setting for a household, and the cost is paid by resolvers that never had anything to do with piracy.

"Cloudflare is a hypocrite." Several commenters pointed out that Cloudflare's CDN fronts many pirate sites. That may be true, and it is an argument about Cloudflare's CDN, which French courts can already reach and have. It notes nothing about whether a resolver should lie.

Recent findings suggest that "The yellow pages would be held responsible." One commenter asked whether we'd accept a phone directory that kept listing a drug dealer's latest address. The analogy fails because a resolver is not a curated directory. It's closer to the operator who connects you to whatever number you dial. Quad9 has "no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites." Making the operator liable for every number dialled is how you end up with no operator.

In a recent development, if you're in France or the EU, do what John Todd asked: write something long-form, ideally in French, make it indexable, and send it to your representatives. Quad9 specifically suggests telling Arcom that its mandate is to balance rightsholders' interests against citizens' digital rights, and that "balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage.".

It has been revealed that if you work on infrastructure, push for transparency wherever blocking does happen. RFC 8914's "Censored" error code exists so consumers can tell a court-ordered block from a broken network.

According to recent reports, if you can afford it, Quad9 accepts donations for its legal defence. Its appeal against the May order is still pending at the Paris Court of Appeal.

In a recent development, quad9 put it this way: "Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly." The French system started with football. It now covers tennis, rugby, MotoGP and Formula 1, has expanded from ISPs to resolvers, VPNs, CDNs and search engines, and runs through an automated system in which no human approves each block. Each step was reasonable on its own. Together, they have pushed a non-profit security service out of the country while the piracy continues.

Industry observers note that the sports-rights industry has a real problem. DNS resolvers are the wrong place to solve it, and France is about to find out what the internet looks like when the trustworthy resolvers leave first.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Russia-linked cyber espionage group known as Cold Relic (formerly COLDRIVER and UNC4057) has been observed weaponizing a single cloud compromise into a launchpad for a series of linked intrusions resulting in third-party compromise.

Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it investigated a 2026 compromise at a U.S.-based organization in which the adversary leveraged data, the corporate staff directory, and identities harvested from an earlier attack on another U.S.-based entity in late 2025.

Cold Relic, also tracked as Callisto, Gossamer Bear, and Star Blizzard, has a track record of orchestrating sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns to gain access information that may be of strategic importance to the Russian government.

Industry observers note that the access is abused to register rogue multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices, passkeys, and MFA backup codes to establish long-term persistence and then conduct aggressive data collection and exfiltration operations targeting email, chat, and cloud storage repositories. In addition, the compromised access is used to target the victim's social and professional networks.

Attacks mounted by the threat actor have successfully compromised high-value targets, including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) across Europe and North America.

"Once Cold Relic compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets," Google remarked.

Sources indicate that according to the tech giant's cybersecurity and incident response teams, Cold Relic compromised the cloud productivity environment of an unspecified U.S.-based organization in late 2025. Initial access to the network was achieved by means of a residential proxy network located in close geographical proximity to the victim.

According to recent reports, using the stolen credentials of a Super Admin account and combining it with an MFA push notification fatigue attack, the threat actor is said to have gained access to the account after the victim accepted an MFA request. This was followed by the attacker registering their own device within the tenant to retain access. The threat actor was also observed using passkeys and MFA backup codes as alternate access mechanisms.

"Cold Relic used the privileges of the compromised Super Admin account to download the contents of the entire organization's cloud storage drive by both mass sharing files to a Cold Relic-operated email account and downloading files directly," Google explained.

"While operating inside the tenant of the victim organization, Cold Relic accessed the Admin Console, queried Admin security investigation and email audit logs to check defensive visibility, and viewed, modified, and deleted Alert Center notifications to remove forensic evidence of the initial intrusion.".

These actions ultimately enabled the threat actor to export full employee lists and domain-wide data via the Google Takeout service using the Super Admin privileges. Following mass data theft, the attackers continued to maintain access over several months and perform additional activities -.

Even after the attackers were ousted from the victim organization, Google noted it observed Cold Relic using email accounts impersonating employees of the victim organization to target both internal employees and associates within the same professional circles as part of a renewed social engineering campaign.

The attack then moved to the next phase when the threat actor compromised a Microsoft Entra ID user account of a second U.S.-based organization that used Entra ID as its federated single sign-on (SSO) identity provider for Google Workspace.

By impersonating an employee at the first organization, the threat actor established communications with the target over a secure messaging app and then shared phishing links designed to harvest credentials and authentication tokens for Entra ID under the pretext of sharing a document containing details about a technical glitch.

"Upon successful authentication using the stolen credentials, Cold Relic registered and used a upcoming MFA device in the SSO solution to retain access to the user account throughout the intrusion," Google remarked.

Sources indicate that "By impersonating someone known in the same professional circles as the newly introduced target, Cold Relic increased their chance of phishing success. Ultimately, in this case, Cold Relic was able to obtain credentials to the organization and perform bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user's cloud drive.".

It has been revealed that upon successfully compromising the second organization, the messaging app account used to initiate the conversation had its profile name changed to a different persona. It's suspected that the new persona was likely used to target other organizations in the same professional network.

In a recent development, "Cold Relic's campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google noted. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners.".

Latest Update: Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes.
  • Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.
  • Recent findings suggest that yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at upcoming pods, rather than streaming data between nodes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes.

Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.

Recent findings suggest that yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at upcoming pods, rather than streaming data between nodes. A blog post by the site reliability team details a migration. It covered about 90 production clusters. There was zero downtime for customers and no data loss. The largest cluster, a 54-pod user-data store, took about 12 hours end to end.

According to recent reports, yelp had already moved its stateless workloads to EKS through its PaaSTA deployment layer, but Cassandra stayed behind. Kubernetes has no built-in way to migrate StatefulSets and their persistent volumes across clusters. The usual approach is to add nodes to the fresh cluster and shut down the old ones. This would temporarily double compute capacity but also lead to data transfer costs. For the largest clusters, streaming alone could have taken weeks. Yelp also considered a regional failover and rebuild, and a new Cassandra datacenter in EKS, but rated both as less transparent to customers.

Yelp's "Rolling PV Transplant" relies on the fact that an EBS volume is bound to an Availability Zone, not to a Kubernetes cluster, and that a PersistentVolume is effectively a pointer to a volume ID. The team pre-creates PVs and PVCs in EKS that reference the existing volume IDs, then creates an identical StatefulSet there, whose pods wait in ContainerCreating. The automation then deletes one pod at a time on the legacy cluster, waits for the volume to detach, and lets the EKS pod claim it. The pod rejoins the ring with the same data and token range, and the process repeats for the next pod. Cassandra's replication tolerates the few minutes each node is offline.

Yelp set a skipReconciliation: true flag on the custom resources in both clusters. This was done because two operators managed the same logical ring during the migration. The flag helped prevent them from conflicting over pod state. The flag was cleared on the EKS side at the end.

Recent findings suggest that across roughly 1,000 pods, about 1,000 TiB moved by pointer rather than over the wire. No node was ever decommissioned from the ring, so rollback was the same operation in reverse. Yelp used it a handful of times, for a missing subnet definition and a certificate mismatch, and restored pods within minutes. After a week of manual dev runs and a week of automation, one engineer ran the production rollout in about three weeks, migrating three to six clusters on a typical day.

According to recent reports, the team had Claude generate the orchestration script, roughly 800 lines of bash, from its validated manual runbook, rather than asking it to design the procedure. The script needed minor adjustments after two days of testing.

According to recent reports, the approach relies on a previous Container Storage Interface migration by Yelp's Compute Infrastructure team. This work gave the Data Infrastructure team confidence in the volume detach and attach process. Yelp also used the technique for Kafka clusters, and states it applies to any AZ-pinned stateful workload on Kubernetes. The legacy clusters are now retired.

According to recent reports, the one failure specific to this technique was a stale VolumeAttachment object left behind by the AWS CSI controller after pod deletion. The EKS pod sat in Pending with no error, and deleting the object on the legacy cluster fixed it. Yelp advises building explicit timeouts for stalled detach and attach operations into any automation. Two other findings were unrelated to the mechanism. Backups failed with IAM AccessDenied errors for 48 hours because a newly introduced -eks role was not yet being assumed by scheduled jobs, and the alert only filed a ticket instead of paging. Pausing repairs for the migration also exposed one cluster whose repairs had been silently disabled for three months, leaving accumulated data inconsistencies. Teams planning a similar move should audit repair state, backup IAM roles and alert severity before starting.

Sources indicate that yelp's approach is not the only way to move Cassandra between EKS clusters. Monday.com's engineering team describes a different one in a post on zero-downtime Cassandra migration between EKS clusters. K8ssandra-managed clusters had to move without any downtime or data loss. So, the team created a workflow to add latest Cassandra data centers, safely transfer data, and remove the old ones. That is the streaming model Yelp considered and rejected. The new cluster is brought up alongside the old one and receives data over the network, and the original is retired only afterwards. The team believes success relied more on control, automation, and handling failures than on speed. They automated long tasks like rebuilds and planned the migration in stages based on operator behavior.

Recent findings suggest that the two migrations differ in what they trade away. Yelp's disk transplant skips data transfer and extra compute. It allows for a rollback by swapping the pointer. However, it relies on EBS volumes being linked to an Availability Zone, not a cluster. Monday.com's approach does not rely on that property, and it keeps the old environment intact until the end. The cost is a longer migration and the capacity to run both sides at once, which Yelp calculated would have taken weeks for its largest clusters.

Recent findings suggest that despite the different mechanics, the post-migration lessons are similar. Monday.com devotes part of its write-up to verifying that backups work after the migration, along with monitoring, dashboards and alerts. Yelp's own backups failed on an IAM role mismatch within 48 hours of its first production clusters landing in EKS. Teams planning either approach should treat those checks as part of the migration strategy, not as cleanup afterwards.

Threat actors have compromised Microsoft's agent-framework package to push a credential stealer, according to reports from Aikido, Chainguard, Endor Labs, OX Security, SafeDep, Socket, StepSecurity, and Google-owned Wiz.

The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published 33 minutes apart on November 17, 2026, and are designed to run a credential stealer on every Python start. As of writing, both the release versions have been quarantined on the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository. It's unclear how the attacker managed to obtain publishing access.

Agent-framework is the meta-package for Microsoft Agent Framework, an open-source framework for building and orchestrating artificial intelligence (AI) agents using Python.

"Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint," Socket said in a report.

Once either of the versions is installed, the package drops a .pth file in the site-packages root directory, which then gets executed automatically on every interpreter start, causing the credential stealer to run whenever Python is started in an environment, even if the package is not explicitly imported.

"Each wheel adds a .pth file to site-packages," Endor Labs stated. "Python executes import lines in .pth files on every interpreter start, so the stealer runs on any Python launch in an affected environment, including pip itself, whether or not anything imports Agent Framework.".

The names of the .pth files are below -.

The "agent_framework_meta.pth" file contains a single import statement referencing "agent_framework_meta," which then debuts the stealer payload. It's capable of capturing the following data -.

According to recent reports, "Besides reading credentials already on disk, the code asks the platform to issue newly introduced ones," SafeDep remarked. "Rotating stored secrets does not cover those.".

Industry observers note that "In an Azure DevOps pipeline, SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI are enough to request a federated token for api://AzureADTokenExchange. On Azure compute, it asks the managed identity endpoint for an access token to each of these resources. It uses IDENTITY_ENDPOINT or MSI_ENDPOINT on App Service and Functions, and 169.254.169[.]254 elsewhere. It also pulls instance metadata.".

It's worth noting that the Azure instance metadata service (IMDS) is a RESTful web service that runs on a local IP address ("169.254.169[.]254"), and provides information about the virtual machine, its region, tags, and the identity token.

All the collected information is saved into a JSON document, zlib-compressed, Base64-encoded, and sent via an HTTPS POST request to a hard-coded URL ("webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb").

Version 1.26.2, on the other hand, imports a newly introduced top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py, collects GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, and expands the search patterns used for harvesting credential-related environment variables.

Given that the package attracts about 190,000 downloads a month, users are advised to perform the following steps -.

"The malicious agent-framework shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it," OX Security said. "While directly targeting an official Microsoft package, it seems that attackers found a way to hijack the wheel creation flow to add malicious logic inside.".

Agent-framework is the second Microsoft-related PyPI package to be compromised this year. In May 2026, the threat actors behind TeamPCP pushed three malicious versions of durabletask, Microsoft's Python client for the Durable Task workflow execution framework, to distribute the Mini Shai-Hulud worm.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.
  • Recent findings suggest that AWS has published a technical walkthrough of tunnel endpoints, a VPC endpoint type released in September that lets an application in one VPC reach every address in a CIDR range shared from another account, instead of one resource at a time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account.

Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.

Recent findings suggest that AWS has published a technical walkthrough of tunnel endpoints, a VPC endpoint type released in September that lets an application in one VPC reach every address in a CIDR range shared from another account, instead of one resource at a time. The provider shares a CIDR-type resource configuration through AWS Resource Access Manager and the consumer creates a tunnel endpoint against it. From then on, anything inside the range is reachable, including resources that did not exist when the share was made.

Bruce Pinsky and Ashish Kumar of AWS frame it as a vendor-access problem, for "a vendor or service provider whose software must reach applications and resources in a customer's network." Until now, that meant a separate PrivateLink resource configuration per database or host, which breaks down when the resources are ephemeral, or the customer does not want to enumerate them. With a CIDR configuration, the customer defines a perimeter in address ranges, and "resources located outside the perimeter can't be reached by the vendor." Two further properties come with the design: the consumer and provider VPCs can use overlapping CIDR blocks, and connections "can start only from the consumer VPC, not from the provider network.".

(Source: AWS Networking & Content Delivery blog).

On the r/aws thread about the September launch, the first question was what this does that VPC peering does not, from a self-described veteran of AWS's advanced networking components. The answers that followed are the use cases: a peering connection exposes the whole VPC in both directions, while a tunnel endpoint shares a subset of the address space in one direction only; one commenter at a bank wrote that "peering with unregulated partners is a massive no-no, the auditors will rip you to shreds for it." Another pointed to clusters that do client-side load balancing, such as self-managed Kafka or Aerospike, which until now needed port-based routing on a Network Load Balancer and a separate port-mapping horizon for connections arriving over an interface endpoint. The same thread drew the line against VPC Lattice itself: Lattice services work at layer 7, tunnel endpoints at layer 4 without a resource configuration per target.

The unusual part is on the consumer side: the application's traffic has to arrive at the tunnel endpoint wrapped in GENEVE, the encapsulation protocol defined in RFC 8926, over UDP port 6081 and in the same Availability Zone. The endpoint strips the header, checks that the inner destination falls inside the shared range, rewrites the source to a resource gateway address, and forwards a plain packet into the provider VPC. Linux can do the wrapping in the kernel. The walkthrough creates an ip link add ... type geneve id 0 device inside its own network namespace with a default route through it, which sends the provider's ranges into the tunnel and leaves the instance's other traffic alone. On the far side, the resources see the resource gateway as the client, so the post advises security groups that reference the gateway's security group or subnet rather than a single address.

Industry observers note that the documentation lists the constraints. Inner traffic must be TCP, with UDP permitted only for DNS, so ICMP and ping do not work, and IP fragments are dropped. Private DNS names are not supported on tunnel endpoints. The endpoint's subnets must sit in Availability Zones that overlap with the resource gateway's, or the association shows as inaccessible. A resource gateway's DNS setting cannot be changed after creation. And the access logs identify the consumer's endpoint but carry no field for the inner source address, so a provider can attribute traffic to a vendor and not to a workload behind that vendor's endpoint. The post also warns that sharing 0.0.0.0/0 grants access to everything the provider VPC can route to, including networks behind VPC peering, Direct Connect or a Site-to-Site VPN, and recommends sharing the narrowest ranges that work.

Recent findings suggest that both points have been tested in practice. Ryo Suzuki of the Japanese consultancy Classmethod connected two VPCs that both use 10.0.0.0/16 and got HTTP through, but only by running a GENEVE relay as root on the client, by routing a /32 per destination host, or by putting an HAProxy or NAT instance in front, each of which adds a hop or a single point of failure; his conclusion was that "route management according to the number of destinations is required." In a second experiment, he shared 0.0.0.0/0 from a VPC with a NAT gateway and reached the internet from a VPC with no gateway at all, which confirmed AWS's warning from the other side; he judged it workable as a temporary path and "difficult to use in a permanent production setup.".

In a recent development, pricing is an hourly charge per tunnel endpoint plus a per-GB charge for data processed, under PrivateLink pricing, with the provider side billed per GB through the resource gateway under VPC Lattice pricing, and the feature is available in 28 regions. Terraform support followed from the community: a contributor request opened two days after launch was implemented by another contributor and shipped in version 6.71.0 of the AWS provider, as a Tunnel endpoint type on aws_vpc_endpoint and a cidr_resource block on the Lattice resource configuration.

Industry observers note that the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged organizations to immediately patch a newly disclosed critical security flaw impacting Oracle Java.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (CVSS score: 8.1), refers to a case of out-of-bounds write that can lead to denial-of-service (DoS) or remote code execution under certain conditions.

"This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as 'Java4Shell,' affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK)," CISA remarked. "Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.".

According to recent reports, patches for the flaw have been released by Oracle and OpenJDK. As of writing, there is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild.

As reported previously by The Hacker News, Java4Shell can enable attackers without an account to execute arbitrary code on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, under default settings.

Advisories for the flaw have been released by numerous security and software vendors, including Aikido, Amazon Linux, Blackpoint Cyber, Chainguard, Cisco Talos, Cycode, Datadog, Dynatrace, Endor Labs, Field Effect, Hadrian, Horizon3.ai, Miggo, Orca Security, Qualys, Rapid7, Red Hat, SentinelOne, Sophos, Tanium, Tenable, Upwind, VulnCheck, watchTowr, and Wiz.

In an update shared on November 18, 2026, the Keycloak team mentioned an instance can be considered at risk if the following conditions apply -.

It has been revealed that "The x86-64 Keycloak container images tagged 26.8.2-1 and 26.8.2-2 bundle an affected OpenJDK 21.0.13 build," the team noted. "These image tags alone do not establish whether your deployment is exploitable: check the CPU feature and effective JVM flags.".

"A Keycloak ZIP or TAR.GZ distribution started directly on a host can also be affected; the conditions depend on its Java runtime and CPU, not on whether it runs in a container.".

Keycloak is also recommending that people run the below command to check the CPU feature on a host or virtual machine -.

Industry observers note that if the output of the command returns nothing, it indicates that the CPU does not expose AVX-512 VBMI and is not known to be affected by the flaw. Keycloak has released temporary mitigations that users can apply until it releases updated Keycloak and Keycloak Operator container images once patched OpenJDK builds are available for them.

"The vulnerability could be reached through a local Spring Boot application using Spring Security," Blackpoint Cyber researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal mentioned.

"In this environment, approximately 28,000 unauthenticated HTTP requests carrying a malformed Base64 authentication value caused the JVM to terminate after roughly 20 seconds of sustained requests. Additional testing confirmed corruption of nearby Java objects and changes to live application data without necessarily causing an immediate crash.".

CISA is recommending that organizations take the following steps -.

"If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access," CISA said.

Alain Rödel, a security researcher at Neodyme AG, has been credited with discovering and reporting CVE-2026-115731 along with CVE-2026-115732 (CVSS score: 9.0), a critical certificate-name authorization bypass affecting both Puppet and OpenVox. The issues were discovered with artificial intelligence (AI) assistance and precise steering, the German cybersecurity manufacturer added.

"The impact highly depends on the Puppet server configuration and the orchestration protocols used, if any are enabled at all," Neodyme stated in a report published this month. "Independent of the configuration, an attacker with RCE on a Puppet server can grab the CA signing keys and impersonate other hosts.".

According to recent reports, "Puppet is a powerful software, often with full access to a fleet of systems in a corporate network. Remote Code Execution on such a central and crucial system can lead to worst-case scenarios: Deployment of ransomware, mass data exfiltration, and potentially lateral movement to other parts of the network.".

As of writing, there are no details on how the vulnerability is being weaponized in the wild. However, a Reddit user named transdimensia noted in a November 4 post that it was being exploited shortly after public disclosure.

"After finding a severely misconfigured CA in my fleet, I traced the actions backwards on a [CVE-2026-]115731 intrusion," the user said.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are advised to apply the fixes by December 1, 2026, to secure their networks under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Vercel Releases UI SDK for Agents to Compose UI from Reusable Behaviors.

Nov 18, 2026 2 min read.

Vercel has released UI SDK, an open-source TypeScript library that treats keyboard navigation, focus, selection, popups, and drag and drop as reusable behaviors rather than details buried inside finished components. Vercel UI SDK is published on GitHub as vercel-labs/ui and is presently in beta.

It has been revealed that the behaviors live in @ui-sdk/core. Vercel says it built more than 50 of them, including createPopup, createSelection, createTypeahead, createRovingFocus, createReorder, createResize, createViewport, createListbox, createChange, createFocusRecovery, and createVirtualizer. A developer, or more often an agent, combines those helpers inside definePrimitive, which declares a component's state, API, and slots once. Framework adapters then render the same primitive through createParts in React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, or as Web Components. The parts are unstyled and expose attributes and CSS variables. The same behaviors also back a starter library of more than 50 unstyled components, from Color Picker, Token Input, and Command to Calendar, Tree, and OTP Input, with the same part names in all five adapters.

UI SDK is meant to be used by agents, not only written by them. The ui-sdk skill, installed with npx skills add vercel-labs/ui --skill ui-sdk, points an agent at the Markdown docs shipped in the installed packages. At runtime, createAgent, imported from the matching framework package such as @ui-sdk/react/agent, exposes snapshot, act, and query so an agent can read component state and call actions through the component API, without screenshots. Apps can approve or refuse those steps, and change callbacks receive a source of "agent" and may cancel a change. registerTools can expose the same methods to a browser's built-in agent through WebMCP, when the browser provides document.modelContext.

It has been revealed that developers already have several headless libraries at this layer, including Radix UI, Base UI, React Aria, Ark UI and its Zag.js state machines, and Headless UI. shadcn/ui sits one level above those primitives as a copy-into-your-repo component kit. UI SDK aims lower, at composable behaviors shared across frameworks, and adds a first-class agent bridge. The changelog thanks the teams behind Radix, Base UI, React Aria, shadcn/ui, Nuxt UI, and Geist. Vercel has not said whether shadcn/ui will be rebuilt on UI SDK.

Rahim, a product engineer at Mux who built Vidstack, wrote after reading the source:.

In a recent development, this is so genuinely cool. I love how it's been packaged up. So elegant @shadcn and @shuding! I'll be studying this for a while. 1. createAgent is an "agent bridge" which gives a snapshot, act, and query tool. It allows agents to interact with the actual UI components directly 2. Change callbacks know when the agent made the change (details.source === "agent"), and the app can refuse it with cancel (I love this).

A developer identified as Stefan looked at the repository and asked how the idea compares with existing headless libraries:.

I tried looking at the repo a bit but I’m not sure I quite understand the value prop of this versus something like Base UI. Is the thought process that we should be thinking about UIs/components as combinations of behaviours?

UI SDK is in beta as 0.1.0-beta.1, licensed under the Apache License 2.0, and subject to Vercel's public beta terms; the APIs, documentation, and behavior may change before general availability. Install @ui-sdk/core plus the adapter for your framework, for example npm install @ui-sdk/react @ui-sdk/core, which requires React 19 or later. The Vue, Svelte, and Solid adapters document peer ranges of Vue 3.5, Svelte 5.33, and Solid 2 from 2.0.0-rc.14. Setup details are in the documentation.
