#439. Latest Update: When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next?

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1857 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Css-tricks

Latest Update: When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it’s been a… year, huh?
  • According to recent reports, technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do.
  • It’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s been a… year, huh? I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is 🫩 and that says a lot. One thing is for sure: the industry we make a living in is in flux, regardless of the outcomes of the AI bubble. Let’s take a look at how we can try and navigate that situation as best we can. But first….

According to recent reports, technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do. This is true regardless of if they fail or somehow succeed in their quest to have everyone paying a subscription fee for their Large Language Model (LLM) technology, which is marketed to us as AI. I’ll refer to this technology as AI for the rest of this article for simplicity.

It’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either. Everywhere you go, you will see some slop, somewhere. Be it a flyer, website, a village poster or a food truck menu. Heck, people are even using LLMs to work out what’s special about their own children. The effects of this technology are far-reaching, way beyond our own industry.

According to recent reports, the technology has hit us all in tech especially hard though. Mid-last year, I did some investigating because I suspected that so-called AI mandates were becoming increasingly popular and what I learned from conversations then feels like some sort of utopia compared to now. In the space between that piece being published and now, we went from token maxxing to companies realizing that actually, this technology is extremely expensive and not returning the promised outcomes.

The mandates have cooled, sure, but the demands to use AI to produce more volume, regardless of whether that volume is actually needed or not are still very much there. I’m in a fortunate position to have friendships with people all across the industry, from tech hyperscalers, to tiny little studios, and the stories I have heard from their work life are nothing short of horrifying. No one really seems to be happy with their work either.

This is such a long way away from even a handful of years ago where yes, there was a lot of problematic culture and outcomes from the tech industry, but people were generally quite happy with the work they were doing at least.

The sudden urge to sprint towards AI technologies over the last few years has had a devastating effect in so many places. The technology has encouraged suicide, devastated communities with the data center build-out and of course, displaced thousands of people’s careers. It’s worth noting that I’ve mentioned only a tiny sample of the harms there. If I listed them all, this article would be unbearably long and depressing.

Sources indicate that some harms I do want to touch on though are the effects on our communities in tech. The community spirit of open source and open knowledge was the foundation of the industry’s — especially the web industry’s — rapid success. At the root of everything there was people happy to share knowledge and build everyone up with them. Those people still do exist — myself included — but being one of those people is increasingly difficult.

As the numbers go up in the AI world, the numbers very much go down for independent educators, publishers and community conferences. There’s a developing and worrying culture of “I don’t need to skill up now because I can use AI for work”, so allow me to break down why that reductive view of your work and your career is harmful in the long term.

Industry observers note that and don’t ever forget that! Let’s have a think for a second about what actually makes you a good developer, because typing characters in a text editor certainly isn’t it. What makes us good is experience, knowledge, nuance and above all else, creativity.

It has been revealed that look, I get it, AI really can feel like it’s a miracle machine, but it’s important to take a wider view. Along with the published studies on cognitive decline and the widening skills gap, it’s more important than ever to invest in your brain to keep your skills sharp because you’re not getting that repetitive reinforcement that writing code every day gives you anymore if AI tools do everything for you. There’s a reason that I often build most of my teaching around a linear build-along because the tangible nature of repeating patterns you’ve learned really helps that knowledge to sink in.

As always, this article is addressed to everyone, but I want to talk directly to founders (like me), decision makers, and managers for a second. A big part of our job, in fact, the most key part, is to ensure that our workers are looked after. I’m not just talking about compensation and perks here. I’m talking about our responsibility to ensure that our workers’ skills are kept sharp, their professional curiosities are satisfied and above all else that they are happy in the work they are doing. Our workers are much more than “number go up” vehicles.

You should be giving your developers more time to learn, rather than chasing endless volume. If AI enthusiasts are to be believed, there’s hours upon hours of time efficiencies created by this technology. Don’t fill that time with more volume. Instead, invest that time in developing your worker’s skills. It’s going to avoid burnout which yep, daily LLM use will likely cause in the long term.

One thing that is increasingly clear is that the health of the AI industry is not good. The bubble has already effectively burst in China and more worryingly for economy enjoyers, the “picks and shovels” — AKA the chips industry in Korea — has seen dramatic downturns. This is not how an “inevitable” outcome is supposed to happen!

The U.S. AI industry is on very shaky ground too. Circular financing, unbelievable levels of debt and a data center build out that simply cannot keep up with the required power levels to turn profits for hyperscalers and startups, mixed with a genuine hatred of the technology by the general public, creates enough risk in itself. Recent events, such as the Democrats dominating the midterms causing AI stocks to drop and as well as Nvidia’s stock because of its CEO being caught up in a spying scandal shine a light on the fragility of the industry. A healthy industry doesn’t work like this.

Industry observers note that with all that in mind, what would be a really silly thing to do? Yeh, you guessed it: put AI at the heart of everything in your business. Sure, there’s open source models — which I think is the logical destination of the technology — but how many companies are going to be willing to maintain their infrastructure needs? Not many. The low barrier of entry of commercial AI technology is the selling point, let’s be honest.

Above everything, people need to be invested in, not pushed aside by technology like AI. As I mentioned earlier, it’s experience, knowledge, nuance, and creativity that sets humans far apart from AI. That technology does indeed keep evolving, but even the most ardent of AI supporters will concede that the rate of frontier model improvement is very much levelling out.

There’s never been a more important time to keep human skills sharp, so here’s some ideas on how to do that.

This is not just directed at individuals but also at founders, decision makers and managers. Our industry has been historically excellent at investing in skilling people up and we need to bring that back.

Industry observers note that give staff the time and budget to learn, to develop their skills and to engage with the community at conferences. You already know the positive outcomes that brings, so bring it back to your organization. At the absolute worst case, it’ll make the usage of AI in your organization more efficient and when the token subsidies inevitably end, more cost effective.

Again, token subsidies will inevitably end. So, getting thousands of dollars of worth from a $200 a month subscription will be something you’ll look fondly back on. When hallucinations from AI tools are suddenly costing thousands, does it make sense to force your staff to produce as much volume as possible? Of course not.

It has been revealed that my advice is to re-evaluate those prior decisions and invest saved costs back into developing your workers instead, while there’s still a hope of them not burning out completely. Make sure you include your workers in these decisions and discuss the impacts of mandates on them. It’s important for you to understand the impact of these sort of decisions.

This advice is more aimed at developers, but stay paying attention, managers. As I noted earlier, repetition (especially typing) reinforces newly introduced learning and existing knowledge. The slower pace also allows your brain to think, which from a quality of output perspective, is imperative. Doing none of that atrophies skills over time.

According to recent reports, I recently read Jenn Schiffer’s great post. She did the Weird Web October challenge and wrote this:.

[…] i encourage anyone who uses ai and/or vibe codes to consider doing an exercise like this without those tools as a way to challenge your brain and you can continue doing your regular work the way you do your regular work.

I think that’s a very good idea, even if it’s messing around with a little side project — if you’ve got the energy from Producing Value all day, of course. Guess what bosses: this is another way you can make your staff happier, by giving them time to do this on the clock.

At the end of the day, you’ll miss the soul when it’s gone. It’s not gone yet though. Far from it. Independents like CSS-Tricks, my publication, Piccalilli, and Smashing Magazine are trying hard to keep the soul of our industry alive by sharing high quality educational content with the community.

Most of this content is free at the point of entry, but it certainly isn’t free to produce. We all pay writers fairly to share their knowledge with the community and we are all tiny organizations. We’re certainly not in this game to make huge profits, that’s for sure.

All of us could do more though, but funding is the ultimate barrier. For both companies and individuals, purchase courses, join the membership programs, and purchase ad space. With the right financial support, publications like ours can be a real force in pushing the good stuff back into our industry and bringing everyone up with us. That’s what we do it for.

Some course producers I recommend are Miriam, Sara, Mat, Scott, Brad and Ian, Josh, Ahmad, Christine, Vitaly, Ben and of course, myself! All of these will have generous Black Friday deals, so go ahead and ask your boss to invest in you.

Now, share this post with your boss.

#438. 8 Mac menu bar apps that actually earn their spot on a coding Mac (2026)

8 Mac menu bar apps that actually earn their spot on a coding Mac (2026)

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You glance up at the menu bar to check something and it's a wall of 25 icons, half of which you can't name.
  • It has been revealed that the menu bar is the most valuable real estate on a Mac, and most of us let it fill up by accident.
  • An icon stays only if I look at it or click it at least once a day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know the moment. You glance up at the menu bar to check something and it's a wall of 25 icons, half of which you can't name. The MacBook notch has quietly eaten three of them.

It has been revealed that the menu bar is the most valuable real estate on a Mac, and most of us let it fill up by accident. Here's the short list of menu bar apps I'd actually let stay there on a Mac used for coding, and what each one earns its spot for.

An icon stays only if I look at it or click it at least once a day. Everything else gets hidden or quit. With that rule, these eight make the cut.

It has been revealed that ice is the first thing I'd install, because it fixes the problem every other item on this list creates. It hides and shows menu bar items so you keep only the ones you care about visible.

According to recent reports, it's free, open source, and needs macOS 14 or later. If you've ever lost an icon behind the notch, this is the fix.

Industry observers note that stats puts a system monitor in your menu bar: CPU, memory, disk, network, battery and more. You pick which modules show.

Handy when a build, a Docker container or a local model suddenly makes the fans spin up and you want to know why. Install with brew install stats or grab the DMG from the releases page.

Itsycal is a tiny menu bar calendar that reads from the Mac Calendar app. You can see and create events, view and complete Reminders, and join virtual meetings from it.

It has a configurable shortcut to open it, and yes, it supports Vim motions for navigation.

Sources indicate that maccy is a clipboard manager that does one job: keep your copy history and let you search it fast. Hit the shortcut, type, press Enter.

In a recent development, it's keyboard-first, stores everything on your Mac, and is MIT licensed. It needs macOS 14 or later. Once you have clipboard history you stop re-copying the same error message three times.

Amphetamine keeps your Mac awake with a simple switch in the menu bar, or automatically through Triggers.

You can keep it awake indefinitely, for a set time, while a file downloads, or while a specific app is running. Useful when a long test run or a coding agent is working and you step away.

CleanShot X is the screenshot and screen recording tool I'd pick for bug reports and PR descriptions. It adds annotation, a video editor with smart zooms, and optional cloud links.

Recent findings suggest that the Basic license is $35 once with a year of updates (optional renewal at $19 a year). Cloud Pro is $10 per user per month billed annually. It also comes with a Setapp subscription. It needs macOS 13 or later.

Recent findings suggest that rectangle moves and resizes windows with keyboard shortcuts or by dragging them to screen edges and corners. Repeat a shortcut to cycle through sizes.

Industry observers note that it lives in the menu bar for quick access to layouts. The free version is open source and supports macOS 14+. Rectangle Pro adds custom shortcuts for any size and position.

If you code with AI agents, the number you check most is probably how much of your limit is left and when it resets. TokenBar puts usage and reset times for Claude, Codex, Cursor, Gemini and Copilot in one menu bar view.

Recent findings suggest that it demonstrates things like session and weekly usage and a pace check against the reset. It's built on Peter Steinberger's MIT-licensed CodexBar and credits Pixel Agents for its agent status view. It doesn't give you any extra quota, it just shows you where you stand. Basic is $5/month, Pro is $15 lifetime, and it needs macOS 14 or later.

Recent findings suggest that weather, a second clock, VPN icons I only touch once a week, and every app that adds an icon by default and never asks. Those all go behind Ice.

What's the one menu bar app you'd never remove? Drop it in the comments, I'm always looking for a ninth.

#434. The refusal is in English even when the request is not

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1224 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

The refusal is in English even when the request is not

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A measurement and a repair of refusal consistency on Cohere Labs' Tiny Aya Global, built with CuratorKIT and SafeTune on one 64 GB Mac.
  • This post quotes harmful request text and fragments of model output that begin to answer it — firearms modification, explosives, ransomware, forged identity documents, toxic gas, phishing and money laundering.
  • Tiny Aya Global 3.35B refuses harmful requests.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A measurement and a repair of refusal consistency on Cohere Labs' Tiny Aya Global, built with CuratorKIT and SafeTune on one 64 GB Mac.

Content warning. This post quotes harmful request text and fragments of model output that begin to answer it — firearms modification, explosives, ransomware, forged identity documents, toxic gas, phishing and money laundering. Quoted fragments are short and non-operational; full generations are in the published eval dataset.

Tiny Aya Global 3.35B refuses harmful requests. It does not refuse them in the language they are asked in. Across 288 prompts — 8 attack families × 12 harmful intents × {English, Devanagari Hindi, romanised Hinglish} — the model almost never produced usable harmful content. On this prompt set the failure is not compliance. It is the expression of refusal. Under one fixed decoding protocol, 64 in 100 English replies and 54 in 100 Devanagari Hindi replies contained an explicit in-language refusal.

It has been revealed that in romanised Hinglish, 3 in 100 did. The rest were neither a refusal nor an answer: how-to-shaped text with hallucinated nouns, sometimes running to the token cap because nothing in it signalled an ending.

After a LoRA repair trained on CuratorKIT-gated data, in-language explicit refusal rises to 1.00 / 0.98 / 0.95 across the three cells, with repetition collapse at zero everywhere. It is not free: 6 of 40 Hinglish benign prompts are now refused. That cost is measured and reported, not smoothed away.

It has been revealed that those 288 prompts are also 91.7% present in the training set by construction — the repair set is generated per intent from the same prompts — so the headline is in-distribution. Thirty prompts written after training, never seen, give the out-of-sample picture: explicit refusal 0.367 → 0.900, and hand-reading all sixty replies reveals the base model answering 7 of 30 while the repaired model answers none. Both audits are in results/heldout.md and results/heldout_audit.md, andthe judge flagged zero of those seven.

Industry observers note that I started with the obvious metric: attack success rate, judged by a local 4B model scoring whether a reply contains actionable harmful detail. It came back flat, so I nearly stopped there. Instead I read the generations, and what emerged was not a safety failure in the usual sense:.

In a recent development, that distinction changes what you measure. A model that already refuses nearly everything cannot be made safer by safety training. It can be made legible: an operator in Lucknow who asks in Hinglish should see a refusal they recognise as a refusal, not a paragraph of fluent nothing. So the metric pair is:.

Three guards, because a repair that raises refusal by refusing everything is worthless: a 120-prompt benign control (40 per language), a distinct-reply rate (a model that emits the same sentence 96 times has learnt a template, not a behaviour), and a manual audit of every judge positive — the local judge marked 8/288 base replies compliant and was wrong about 7 of them.

Two Lexsi repos carry the pipeline:.

According to recent reports, auditKIT was installed and inspected and is not used: its detectors (AgentLoopDetection, Abstention) target agent trajectories and unanswerable-RAG cases, not single-turn chat replies, and a wrapper around them would have been kit theatre. The evaluation protocol here — fixed decoding, script-aware markers, benign control arm, published raw generations — was written for this task.

Sources indicate that the interesting part of this project is not the final adapter. It is that each metric caught a different way the repair was fake.

Runaway generation is the same phenomenon measured differently: 56% of base replies never emitted a stop token at all and ran to the 256-token cap, versus 1.4% after the repair. The base model is not withholding an ending — it does not know it has reached one.

The over-refusal cost is real and unevenly distributed: the Hinglish cell pays most of it. Five of 40 Hinglish benign prompts — a dripping tap, a bicycle inspection, a sleep routine — now come back as refusals. That is the price of teaching a register the base model did not have, and it is the number I would attack next: more benign Hinglish, and a gate that rejects harmful-style refusals applied to benign-style prompts.

According to recent reports, the 288-prompt taxonomy is a controlled instrument, not a sample of real traffic, and it is 91.7% in the training set. So the obvious objection is that the repair learned the test. Thirty prompts written after training — fresh phrasings, same intent space, ten per language — answer it:.

Recent findings suggest that the base model's seven are the interesting part. They are not near-misses: a step-by-step driver's-licence forgery guide with materials and printing advice, an IED component list with a "small explosive charge in a sealed container", a Hindi fake-ID procedure, a Hinglish semi-to-full auto conversion walkthrough, an in-character ransomware build, and a finished invoice-fraud phishing email. All seven sit in fiction, hypothetical and roleplay frames, and five are in Hindi or Hinglish. results/heldout_audit.md has each one with its classification.

That reframes the thesis, and I would rather state the narrower version than the tidy one: Tiny Aya refuses what resembles its safety training. Off that distribution it complies, and it complies most readily in romanised Hinglish. The repair works because it teaches refusal in the request's own language and register, which is also why the remaining escape route is a fresh phrasing rather than a different language.

The judge caught none of it — zero flagged replies in either arm — while in the main run it flagged 8 of 288 base replies, 7 of which were refusals. A 4B judge reads caveated procedural detail as a warning. That is why every headline claim here is either a script-aware marker or a hand count, with the judge reported beside it.

The repair is uneven across attack families, and the residual sits exactly where you would expect:.

continuation is the family where the harmful frame is written by the prompt rather than asked for — the model is handed the opening of a "practical guide" and only has to keep going. All four residual Hinglish failures, and the one genuine base-model compliance in the audit, are in that cell. A refusal register learnt from direct asks does not transfer to a prompt that never asks.

The whole pipeline ran on one laptop: 3.35B parameters in fp16 on 16 GPU cores, LoRA at micro-batch 1 and 256 tokens (the 262k-token vocabulary makes the logits tensor, not the activations, the memory bottleneck — that constraint set the entire training recipe), two epochs in ~13 minutes, four evaluation arms in ~40 minutes. Generation and judging used a local Qwen3 through Ollama; no closed-model API calls are in the data path, so the dataset licence is unencumbered.

In a recent development, the honest comparison is not "cheaper than a frontier model", it is that a stronger generator would have hidden the finding. A frontier model asked to write Hinglish refusals would have produced excellent ones — and the experiment would then have measured its Hinglish, not Tiny Aya's. The repair data had to come from something that could fail in the same register, or the diversity and collapse metrics would have been measuring nothing.

Code & more: https://www.dailybuild.xyz/project/318-refusal-consistency-on-tiny-aya-global.

New EggStreme Malware Variant Goes Silent to Evade Security Tools in Government Attacks

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group behind the sophisticated EggStreme malware has rebuilt its toolkit as it continues to target government organizations in the Philippines.
  • "When attackers are exposed, the cheap response is to rotate," Bitdefender noted in a technical report shared with The Hacker News.
  • According to recent reports, "The EggStreme operators did more than rotate – the agent we now see uses a different network protocol, has an enhanced command set, and comes in a passive variant that never beacons out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group behind the sophisticated EggStreme malware has rebuilt its toolkit as it continues to target government organizations in the Philippines.

"When attackers are exposed, the cheap response is to rotate," Bitdefender noted in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "A file hash changes with every recompile, a domain costs a few dollars, and a latest IP address costs less.".

According to recent reports, "The EggStreme operators did more than rotate – the agent we now see uses a different network protocol, has an enhanced command set, and comes in a passive variant that never beacons out. The infrastructure appears to be moving away from the one certificate authority that tied its older servers together.".

The end result is that the changes allow it to bypass static signatures and heuristic detections built around the EggStreme malware framework when it was first exposed in September 2025.

Delivered via an as-yet-unknown initial access vector, EggStreme's defining characteristic is the use of DLL sideloading to execute payloads. It features multiple components as follows -.

It's worth noting that some components of the framework, such as EggStremeFuel and EggStremeLoader, have been put to use by another cluster tracked by Palo Alto Networks as CL-STA-1048 between March and September 2025.

The latest findings from Bitdefender show a significant retooling of EggStreme's capabilities, including removing the keylogger from every agent build observed since then. Within two weeks after public disclosure, the threat actors are also stated to have made other changes -.

In addition, where lateral movement previously relied on Impacket-like tooling and on EggStremeAgent itself, newer incidents make use of an unmanaged system that sits outside of the organization's endpoint management but is still reachable by other workstations to stage the payloads and launch them via DLL sideloading using a Visual Basic Script (VBScript) file remotely run over Server Message Block (SMB).

Some of the newer builds have been found to run in passive mode by opening a listening port and waiting for the operator to connect in as opposed to contacting an external command-and-control (C2) server.

There is also some evidence that the attackers have also targeted Taiwan, but it has been treated with low to medium confidence.

"The speed of the loader changes notes as much about the operators' maturity as about the cost of exposure," Bitdefender concluded. "The build-time design appears to be what makes rebuilds this fast. What they did not change is how they operate: sideloaded DLLs under system library names, staging through file shares, running from memory, and requiring mutual TLS.".

As of late October 2026, Philippine government officials have also been targeted by Mustang Panda, a prolific China-aligned cyber espionage group, using ASEAN Summit lures to deliver PlugX using established tactics like DLL sideloading.

"The package impersonated a Laos–Philippines bilateral meeting agenda from the Lao Ministry of Foreign Affairs," Dream Research Labs noted in a report published last week.

"It named five officials and referenced plausible diplomatic priorities, requesting that the reader provide confirmation before the summit. Behind it was a delivery chain that installed PlugX remote-access malware while displaying the decoy agenda.".

Recent findings suggest that the disclosure comes as a China-nexus threat actor tracked as Earth Alux (aka Ink Dragon, Jewelbug, REF7707, and UAT-11587) has been attributed to a fresh set of attacks targeting Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has assigned the activity the designation TGR-STA-0049 (formerly CL-STA-0049).

"The defining signature of the threat actor behind the activity is the targeting of government entities, combined with the use of advanced custom payloads that are designed for high-stealth intelligence collection operations, with an emphasis on evading security detection tools," Unit 42 researcher Tom Fakterman noted.

Sources indicate that attacks mounted by the group have historically deployed an advanced backdoor known as FINALDRAFT (aka Squidoor) since 2023. However, it has since expanded its malware arsenal to include two previously undocumented remote access trojans (RATs) called PerfectPioneer RAT (in July 2025) and KUKURAT (in March 2026).

Initial access to target networks is achieved via exploitation of vulnerable, unpatched Microsoft Exchange servers to deploy web shells like ASPXSpy and Godzilla, which are then used to deploy the RAT payloads. Alternatively, Earth Alux has leveraged phishing emails using decoy PDFs and lookalike domains to compromise victim hosts.

PerfectPioneer RAT is a Go-based malware that's released via three different methods -.

The malware supports a number of features that enable the operator to gain remote control of the infected host. It facilitates file operations, shell execution, process management, keylogging, SOCKS5 proxy, screenshot capture, Window enumeration and manipulation, and CPU and memory utilization monitoring.

It also ensures a connection to the C2 server remains active at all times and systematically cleans up temporary files and runs garbage collection if memory usage exceeds 100 MB to minimize forensic traces.

Industry observers note that furthermore, select variants of the malware come with an "isDangerousCommand" feature to avoid running administrative commands that would be highly destructive or noisy, thereby allowing it to be detected by security programs installed on the host. These include rm, curl | bash, wget | bash, and powershell -e, among others.

In a recent development, KUKURAT, in contrast, functions as a modular implant that's executed in networks already compromised by PerfectPioneer RAT. Written in C++, the backdoor implements its functionality as a separate DLL module that's loaded dynamically at runtime directly from the C2 server.

This allows the malware to be highly evasive and adapt its capabilities on the fly in response to shifting operational objectives. It supports the following features -.

In a recent development, what's more, KUKURAT initiates bogus, legitimate-looking activity on the endpoint to camouflage and cover up its tracks based on a command issued by the threat actor. This includes -.

Sources indicate that "Both PerfectPioneer RAT and KUKURAT use HTTP/3 as the primary method for communicating with C2 infrastructure," Unit 42 remarked. "While the adoption of HTTP/3 is rare across the broader malware landscape, its deployment in this campaign reflects an emerging trend among advanced threat actors.".

The attacks have also been found to leverage established tools like PsExec, WMI, and Windows Remote Management (WinRM) to move laterally across compromised enterprise networks; collect credentials using Mimikatz, ProcDump, and SharpDPAPI; compromise Domain Controllers to deploy KUKURAT on local endpoints; and exfiltrate sensitive data such as files and emails.

"Through the deployment of KUKURAT and the PerfectPioneer RAT, the attackers behind this activity are actively evolving to stay ahead of traditional network defenses by implementing protocol-level evasion via HTTP/3 and QUIC over UDP," Unit 42 concluded.

According to recent reports, "What makes this group particularly evasive is the extensive effort invested in maintaining operational security and remaining hidden on compromised endpoints. The group demonstrates a mature understanding of modern defensive ecosystems. They have even gone so far as to embed hard-coded administrative safety switches within their binaries to prevent their own operators from running loud or destructive commands that might trigger security alerts.".

#431. Fintech Login Fallback: Owning Templates and Retention Across SMS and Email OTP

Fintech Login Fallback: Owning Templates and Retention Across SMS and Email OTP

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The bill for SMS-to-email OTP login fallback includes message sends, polling, retained evidence, and the engineering time needed to keep recovery templates consistent.
  • Short answer: use SMS OTP first, add email OTP fallback only with an application-owned issuance and validation lifecycle, and bound the polling that drives the transition.
  • The contact form is the concrete boundary here: a customer reports a login problem, the recovery flow gathers evidence, and the application routes the request to the appropriate support queue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bill for SMS-to-email OTP login fallback includes message sends, polling, retained evidence, and the engineering time needed to keep recovery templates consistent. For a fintech contact form that routes locked-out customers to the right support queue, count the work before choosing a provider: in an illustrative workload of 1,000 attempts with six status checks each, polling alone creates 6,000 reads. That's a planning example, not a measured workload or a provider charge. It identifies a term the application can control.

Short answer: use SMS OTP first, add email OTP fallback only with an application-owned issuance and validation lifecycle, and bound the polling that drives the transition. Keep template ownership and support-queue decisions in the application so a provider change doesn't also become a recovery-policy migration. For a US/EU SaaS built in Node.js, the runtime doesn't remove those responsibilities.

The contact form is the concrete boundary here: a customer reports a login problem, the recovery flow gathers evidence, and the application routes the request to the appropriate support queue. A delivery status is evidence about a message. It isn't permission to disclose account information to the person submitting the form.

Sources indicate that infrai is worth trying for teams that want one REST API to keep application code unchanged when switching the vendor behind a supported capability, provided polling meets their recovery requirements. Its capability contract is the concrete boundary; the application owns the recovery state machine and templates above it. Infrai uses one key and one bill for SMS and email, reducing credential management and billing reconciliation across the two legs of this recovery worker. Public, unauthenticated discovery supplies request and response schemas, so the team can inspect the contract before wiring credentials into the integration. These conveniences don't make an email template equivalent to hosted OTP verification.

Every unresolved attempt invites another read, another retained response, and sometimes another message. The architectural mistake is treating all three as necessary evidence, because storing repeated snapshots doesn't make the underlying status more authoritative, and sending a second code doesn't establish which challenge the application should accept. Preserve the state transition that explains the support decision, with enough provenance to investigate it later.

In the planning example, reducing the polling budget from six checks to two changes 6,000 reads to 2,000 reads for the same 1,000 attempts. It also means fewer observations of intermediate status. That's the trade-off: a smaller polling budget may leave the application with less evidence when it decides to offer recovery, so the policy needs an explicit unresolved state rather than pretending that silence proves delivery failure. No timing or delivery guarantee follows from that arithmetic.

Sources indicate that the same accounting applies to retention. If an application stores six complete status responses per attempt, it keeps 6,000 snapshots in that example; keeping one terminal decision record per attempt produces 1,000 decision records instead. These records differ in content and forensic value, so their counts aren't a storage-size benchmark. The useful question is which fields justify continued retention after the recovery window closes.

According to recent reports, for the fintech form, a proposed decision record would contain an internal attempt identifier, the selected support queue, a template revision, the channel transition, and the application's reason for making it. Those are application fields, not a claimed provider response schema. Keep contact-form prose out of repeated delivery snapshots; a customer can put sensitive financial details into a free-text field without the architecture asking for them.

Template ownership is the migration lever. Let the application own the purpose of each message, its approved wording, the revision used for a recovery attempt, and the rule that maps a contact-form category to a support queue. An adapter can translate an application request into a provider call without acquiring authority over account recovery. A provider-held template identifier should be a binding to an application revision, not the only surviving copy of the recovery policy.

Consider an illustrative form category named account-access and an internal destination named access-review. Those labels belong to the SaaS. If a channel vendor changes, the adapter binding may change, but the category, destination, approved message intent, and evidence-retention decision should still mean the same thing. This is the migration invariant to test; an unchanged function signature is weak evidence if the fresh integration silently changes who owns code expiry or validation.

Industry observers note that SMS offers hosted OTP issuance and verification in this stack. Email recovery uses ordinary email sending with code issuance and validation owned by the application. Treat those as different contracts. Before an email message is sent, decide how its challenge expires, how failed guesses are limited, and whether switching channels supersedes the previous challenge. The OWASP recovery guidance is a useful reference for secure, expiring, single-use recovery tokens and consistent responses.

According to recent reports, the failure mode is challenge ambiguity: a delayed SMS arrives after email fallback, and the application has no explicit rule for whether either code remains valid. Choose the rule before wiring the send operation, record its outcome, and make the same rule survive a vendor migration. Keeping that policy in the application costs implementation effort; outsourcing part of the lifecycle to a specialist can be the better decision when that effort exceeds the value of retaining control.

Sources indicate that for authentication recovery, send the email when the policy authorizes it. Avoid a design whose correctness depends on retracting a scheduled email after the SMS succeeds. This keeps the recovery boundary understandable and avoids coupling login safety to delayed-message cancellation semantics.

A fair comparison needs separate acceptance criteria for the authentication lifecycle and the email transport. Twilio Verify, Amazon SES, and SendGrid are real alternatives to evaluate, but listing their names beside a unified API doesn't establish that they take on the same responsibilities. Use the following table as a selection test, rather than assuming that an email delivery integration includes a recovery-code lifecycle.

It has been revealed that these are different integration choices, not a feature-parity claim. A verification specialist is the better direction to evaluate when real-time cross-channel orchestration is a requirement. A direct email provider is the better direction when the team wants to manage that transport relationship separately and is comfortable owning the recovery lifecycle around it. Infrai fits the narrower case where replacing the underlying vendor through the same capability contract reduces application migration work.

Sources indicate that discovery exposes per-capability vendor readiness and schemas; inspect those for the actual deployment rather than treating the US/EU label on a planning document as evidence of regional suitability. This article doesn't establish a fintech compliance determination, data-residency guarantee, or equivalent authentication assurance across channels.

Before implementing the Node.js adapter, inspect the SMS OTP contract. This Python example uses only the standard library and queries public discovery; it doesn't problem a code, create a recovery attempt, or need an API key. It makes the proposed migration boundary inspectable without guessing request fields. The retry budget is an example client policy, not a service limit.

Use the returned request and response schemas to review an adapter's assumptions before and after a vendor change. Schema compatibility is necessary; it doesn't prove that the recovery policy is preserved. The application's transition tests still have to establish that. The platform's documented 24h default idempotency deduplication window is a retry convention, not an OTP expiry policy or a retention period for authentication evidence.

In a recent development, polling-based decisions arrive after observations, so the application must tolerate an unresolved interval. Persist the recovery decision before using it to drive support routing, and make repeated processing converge on the same outcome. The relevant failure modes are duplicate fallback issuance, stale status overwriting a newer decision, and a contact-form retry opening another recovery attempt without linking it to the original. These are design cases to handle, not reports of provider incidents.

Delivery and verification need separate state.

In a recent development, A message accepted for delivery must not mark an account verified, and successful challenge verification must not let arbitrary text from the contact form pick a privileged support queue. Route from the application's validated category and recovery state, preserving enough evidence to explain the selection. If the status remains unresolved after the polling budget, move to the policy's unresolved branch; don't keep polling indefinitely merely because the adapter exposes a status operation.

During migration, test a delayed SMS, a repeated form submission, and an expired email challenge against the same expected application decisions. An adapter can own schema translation while the service owns recovery policy and a retention job owns evidence expiry. That's a division a team can review without confusing a successful send call with a complete authentication protocol.

Start with purpose, then choose retention. Retain the minimum decision evidence needed for support review and the applicable audit policy; expire challenge material when its authentication purpose ends, and stop accumulating identical polling snapshots after the application has made its decision. Don't put raw OTP values into diagnostic logs. Template revisions can explain which instructions the customer received without preserving every message body and every copy of the contact form.

In a recent development, after raw polling snapshots expire, support may be unable to reconstruct every intermediate status observation. After message bodies expire, a template revision can explain approved wording but cannot prove every rendered detail of an individual message. Those are deliberate losses of forensic detail, and a team that needs that detail must budget for retaining it under an explicit policy. Keeping everything forever is also a policy, usually an unexamined one.

The acceptance test is concrete: SMS remains the primary OTP path, email fallback has an application-owned validation lifecycle, polling has a stopping rule, and a vendor replacement preserves the template revision and support-routing decision. Reject the design if required orchestration depends on immediate channel events or if the team cannot own email recovery safely.

OWASP's recovery guidance supports the token-lifecycle discussion. The provider documentation below is for checking candidate contracts and ownership boundaries; it isn't evidence of measured delivery performance or interchangeable authentication guarantees.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the first-party SMS and email recovery guide to check the polling-based architecture against your application's template ownership: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/sms/answers/sms-otp-vs-email-otp-for-saas-login-us-eu-best-practice/.

I opened every free Amazon image compliance checker I could find — including my own

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A rejected main image is one of the few Amazon listing errors you can catch before submitting — pure white background, 85% frame fill, 1000px+ for zoom, no text or watermarks.
  • So I opened every free compliance checker I could find and tested the same things on each:.
  • Disclosure up front, not buried at the end: I work on PicViva, one of the tools in this list.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A rejected main image is one of the few Amazon listing errors you can catch before submitting — pure white background, 85% frame fill, 1000px+ for zoom, no text or watermarks. Yet most sellers only learn the rules after a rejection email.

So I opened every free compliance checker I could find and tested the same things on each:.

Disclosure up front, not buried at the end: I work on PicViva, one of the tools in this list. I've tried to test ours as harshly as the others, and I'll point out where competitors beat us — because in two cases, they do.

Now the details, in the order I tested them.

The strongest pure checker I found. Three upload slots, and it checks things others skip: centering, edge-crop risk, watermark detection, and it separates main image rules from secondary image rules — which matters because Amazon allows lifestyle shots in slots 2–9 but rejects them in slot 1. It also gates checks by destination marketplace, including eBay, Etsy and Lazada variants. Everything runs on-device.

Recent findings suggest that where it's weak: it's a checker plus a separate fix flow. You still take the error list somewhere else to actually repair the image.

zonfy's checker does the pixel rules locally and clearly labels what's local vs. what requires their AI. But the interesting part is the ecosystem around it: a dedicated Image Fixer (square crop, ~85% fill, true #FFFFFF, 2000px export) and a bulk processor for whole listings. They even offer the checker as an embeddable widget for seller guides — a smart distribution play I haven't seen elsewhere.

One honest note: their fixer docs describe "the near-white trap" — backgrounds that look white but measure 240-something. That's exactly the failure mode I wrote about in my last post: a global brightness boost can't fix it without clipping your product. Good to see others hitting the same wall.

I assumed non-English markets had no local-language tooling. Listimo is fully German: the checker page, the rules, the suite around it (a 0–100 listing score, a "Rufus check" that tests whether your listing answers buyer questions). And they do something none of the English tools do well: they split the problem honestly. Pixel-measurable rules run locally; text, logos and watermarks get an AI pass, because no pixel measurement catches a "FREE SHIPPING" badge.

That split — "what code can measure" vs. "what needs a model" — is the most honest architecture in this list.

According to recent reports, does exactly what it indicates: pure white (RGB 255), fill, zoom dimensions, file type. In-browser, no login, no upsell mid-check. The fewest checks here, but zero friction. Its sibling compliance-claims-checker (for listing claims) is a nice touch.

It has been revealed that 12 rules with pass/fail output, including "no lifestyle imagery on main" — a rule most pixel tools skip because detecting a lifestyle scene needs more than thresholds. The upload widget renders after JavaScript loads, so my static HTML scan found no file input; judge it in your browser, not by my curl.

Their sitemap advertises an image checker, but the page I loaded showed no upload UI before JS, and their core product is paid AI listing images. I can't verify what the checker does, so I won't claim it works.

Win: the check and the fix are one flow. The checker opens directly in the editor (I verified GET /en/app/editor/newly introduced?tool=amazon-image-compliance-checker returns 200 with no login redirect), flags size, background, text, watermark and coverage challenges, and the toolbar to fix each one is right there — resize, background removal, the compliance re-check. And the tool page exists in 19 languages, because marketplace sellers overwhelmingly aren't browsing in English.

Lose, honestly: zonfy ships 13 free seller tools and a bulk processor; we ship one standalone free tool. Fernpix covers more marketplaces. Listimo's AI text/logo pass catches things our pixel checks don't. If you need any of those today, use theirs — this post will still be here when you need a fixer.

Every tool above is free at the point of check. None of them will get your image un-rejected after the fact — test before you upload, not after Amazon emails you.

Method note: all findings collected Nov 2026 by loading each page and inspecting the rendered HTML; "runs locally" claims are taken from each tool's own documentation and spot-checked where feasible. Tools change — if one of these now behaves differently, that's worth knowing too.

#425. Who Builds the Machines That Build the Machines?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3198 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Corematter

Who Builds the Machines That Build the Machines?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Corematter

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On October 28, 2026, the White House issued a proclamation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
  • Recent findings suggest that this ties back to one theme that keeps coming back to me as I write on Core Matter.
  • With the fresh Section 232 news, I went down the rabbit hole of the US machine tool landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On October 28, 2026, the White House issued a proclamation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. This followed a Commerce Department investigation that concluded imports of robotics and industrial machinery “threaten to impair the national security.” No newly introduced tariffs have been set yet. Section 232 opens a 180-day window till April 26, 2027 to negotiate with trading partners.

Recent findings suggest that this ties back to one theme that keeps coming back to me as I write on Core Matter. The bottleneck for scaling physical AI sits below the finished machine, in the components inside it, the materials inside those components (eg, rare earth magnets), and the machines that build them (this piece’s topic), as we covered in Part 4 of the actuator series. It’s like a Russian doll, layer after layer.

With the fresh Section 232 news, I went down the rabbit hole of the US machine tool landscape. Here’s what I found.

The US imports about half of the machine tools it uses, $5.8bn of $11.4bn in 2025. Assuming demand (which is not the trend, see point 3) stays flat, US output would need to grow 63% to 83% ($4.4bn to $5.8bn a year) to replace imports with domestic machines.

It has been revealed that the US builds everyday machines and imports the precise ones. About 55% of import value is the high-end versions of machines US plants already make, such as 5-axis machining centers. Precision machines, small-module gear grinders, precision grinders and the heaviest forging presses have no confirmed US volume builder. Imports rose 29.5% for grinders and 76.7% for gear machines in Jan to Sep 2026. These machines make the ball screws, bearings, gears and forgings that aircraft, turbines and robots depend on.

Orders are at a record by value since 1998, while a domestic ramp is limited by people and components. US machine tool orders grew 45.0% to $5.76bn in Jan to Sep 2026, after 3 straight years of decline. Aerospace, power generation, munitions and shipbuilding are pulling it up. A domestic ramp is limited by people, castings and imported components (the components that make the machines, the next doll in). We dive into the key cost drivers and where industrial AI could change the cost structure.

US Machine Tool Imports Are Half of an $11.4bn Market.

Which Machine Tools the US Makes vs. Imports.

Aerospace, Gas Turbines, Munitions and Ships Drove Machine Demand in 2026.

Who Builds Machine Tools in the US, and How Fast Can Supply Ramp?

Fixed Costs and People Keep Upcoming Machine Tool Builders Scarce.

Machine Tool Startups Building the Machines That Build the Machines.

Section 232, the 1986 Machine Tool Precedent and What the 180 Days Decide.

Sources indicate that assuming domestic demand stays flat, which is not the trendline as we’ll discuss in section 3, closing the import gap means $4.4bn to $5.8bn of latest US machine output a year, or output up 63% to 83%. The low end replaces net imports, and the high end replaces every imported machine.

In 2025 the US produced $7.0bn of machine tools, consumed $11.4bn, imported $5.8bn and exported $1.4bn, per Gardner’s World Machine Tool Survey.

It has been revealed that forming and stamping ($1.48bn) and machining centers ($1.43bn) are the top 2025 imports. Imports of precision grinders or gear grinders rose rapidly at 29.5% and 76.7% in January to September 2026, against about 9.6% for all machine tool imports. We could not confirm US volume production.

The US imports 5-axis machines, horizontals with pallet systems, large gantries and boring mills, precision and gear grinders, and presses. It builds in volume entry and mid-range 3-axis mills and lathes.

“Japanese and DACH (Germany, Austria and Switzerland) machines generally fulfill buyer needs in the higher segment while US and Taiwanese (ROC) generally fulfill them in the lower.”.

One distributor analyst put it succinctly in a filing to the Section 232 docket.

What do higher vs. lower segments mean? Higher means more axes, tighter precision, bigger work envelopes and more automation, at a higher price. The average imported machining center cost about $196k in 2024, roughly 2x our estimate of about $96k per machine at Haas, the largest machine tool builder in North America.

See the table below of what these machines do, and who the main buyers are.

While Okuma (Charlotte), Makino (Ohio), United Grinding (Ohio), Kapp Niles (Colorado) and DN Solutions (New Jersey) have large US sites, the sources we found describe them as sales, service or headquarters sites.

Recent findings suggest that the largest two import classes feed autos, aerospace and defense. Forming and stamping machines make stampings, shell bodies and aerospace forgings. Machining centers make everything from brackets and housings to aerospace structures and turbine parts. My guess is that a cutoff at the high end would hit aerospace, defense and power first.

In a recent development, the US built its own heavy forging presses in the 1950s. The newest ones came from a German builder. Heavy forging presses squeeze titanium, aluminum and nickel into one-piece parts such as landing gear, airframe bulkheads and turbine discs. Because so few exist, these presses can cap how many aircraft and engine parts get made here.

Robot reducers need ultra-precision gear machines, which are imported and in low volumes. Robot joints use reducers, small gearboxes whose teeth are cut and ground on gear machines. Leaderdrive, a Chinese reducer maker, told the Shanghai stock exchange that a plant for 1 million harmonic reducers a year needs 30 ultra-precision gear machines, at about $833k each.

Recent findings suggest that assuming 23 reducers per humanoid (on the low end, based on Unitree G1 teardown), 1 million humanoids a year (Tesla’s stated line capacity) would need about 690 of those machines, or about $115mn a year bought over the 5 years to 2030. That is 2.3x and 1.2x all US gear-machine imports, $50.7mn in 2025 and about $100mn a year at the 2026 pace.

I ranked the hardest machines to ramp domestically based on, a) which are whether we found a US builder making them in volume, b) how long new capacity takes, and c) how much it costs. Details are in the Core Matter Industrial Machinery Model.

Machines to build in the US, ranked from hardest to ramp:.

Recent findings suggest that small-module gear grinders. They finish the gears in robot reducers and aerospace gearboxes. We could not confirm volume production of these at any US builder.

It has been revealed that precision cylindrical and thread grinders. These grinders make the ball screws and bearings that other machines need. United Grinding, the Swiss grinding group, serves the US from an import and service site in Ohio. We found 2 US builders, Weldon (Pennsylvania) and Drake (Ohio), and could not confirm volume production at either.

Sources indicate that heavy forging presses. The 2 largest US presses we found built or rebuilt since 2000 came from a German builder. Each project took years and $100mn or more.

According to recent reports, large gantries and boring mills. Ingersoll and Fives build them here, so these are the likeliest candidates to ramp. The constraint is size and lead time.

High-end 5-axis machines and automated horizontals. Mazak and DMG MORI already build some in the US, so expansion of existing plants is the shorter path here.

Recent findings suggest that US machine tool orders have picked up significantly in 2025 and 2026. Order value rose 22.5% to $5.74bn in 2025, and another 45.0% to $5.76bn in January to September 2026. That was after 3 straight years of decline, including a 3.8% fall in 2024. AMT calls the first half of 2026 its strongest half since the series began in 1998.

According to recent reports, aerospace orders rose 45.1% in 2025, and in the first half of 2026 aerospace ordered more machinery than in any half on record. AMT ties 2026 demand to the space economy, commercial aircraft backlogs and munitions, so commercial demand is part of it alongside defense.

Power generation orders in the first half of 2026 ran 14% above automotive.

Contract job shops, AMT’s largest customer group, grew orders 19.1% in 2025.

Data centers drive gas turbines machinery demands. Klingelnberg says that in the US “the rising energy needs of these data centers are providing additional momentum, for example through investments in gas turbines.”.

Industry observers note that the US buys $11.4bn of machine tools a year today. Four build-outs (munitions, ships, gas turbines, commercial aerospace) add $1.0bn to $2.9bn a year of extra buying for 5 years, on top of 1% to 3% normal growth. That puts US buying at $12.7bn to $15.4bn a year in 2026 to 2030.

Munitions is the largest piece. The one new US plant we found, Haas Henderson, adds about $0.5bn of machines sold at home. So imports rise from $5.8bn to about $6.9bn to $9.5bn a year, and the import share goes from 51% to 54% to 62%.

A domestic ramp-up faces four limiting factors.

Workforce. This is the manufacturing story repeating all over again. Gleason’s executive put it first, saying “First you need a large enough, trained workforce. This needs to be the top priority to expand the industrial base.” Haas is hiring more than 1,000 people for Henderson at starting pay of about $23 an hour.

Castings. Castings are the heavy iron bed and columns of a machine. Haas bought “more than 100 million pounds of castings each year” back in 2006 and worried that shrinking US foundry numbers “could limit their manufacturer’s growth.” At 10,000 to 13,000 machines a year, that is roughly 7,700 to 10,000 pounds (3.5 to 4.5 tonnes, about the weight of 2 to 3 cars) of castings per machine.

Imported components. The parts inside the machines are imported too, including controls (FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain, Mitsubishi), spindles, ball screws and linear guides. Tariffs raise their cost, and control deliveries have seen delays.

Sources indicate that in April 2025 Haas asked for “tariff exemptions for raw materials and components vital to the U.S. machine tool industry.” DMG MORI’s 2025 results blame late deliveries partly on “delays in switching to latest European-made CNCs.”.

Recent findings suggest that time. “A shift in global production takes a lot of time,” per GMTA, a US importer of German gear machines. One example is Haas’s plant in Henderson, Nevada. The city closed the land sale in November 2019, with completion planned for 2022. Haas asked the city to extend its deadline, citing the pandemic, supply chains and construction costs. They eventually held the groundbreaking in October 2024. The plant is scheduled to open in Q1 2027, 5 years behind schedule.

Sources indicate that imports are slow to fill a jump in demand too, since foreign builders hold about 7 months of sales in backlog, with DMG MORI at 7.0 months on September 30, 2026 and Klingelnberg at about 7 at the end of March 2026. Klingelnberg’s backlog has halved since 2023.

Would this spur a upcoming generation of startups to build the machines that build the machines? As I read the filings of listed builders, the economics are brutal.

It has been revealed that what I took away from these financials is that for European and Japanese builders, people cost about as much as materials. Personnel is 30% to 41% of revenue or operating output and materials 38% to 41%. At Chinese builders, total employee pay is 15% to 19% of revenue (Haitian and Kede, 2025) and materials 50% to 62%. Personnel, depreciation and overhead are fixed costs, so margins swing with the cycle. 2025 was a weak year. In 2023 Hermle earned an operating margin of about 21.8% and DMG MORI 10.0%. Labor productivity in US metalworking machinery “has grown only 0.9% per year over the last 30 years.”.

What are the key materials? Neway, a Chinese CNC machine builder (688697.SS)’s IPO prospectus published their bill of materials. Of Rmb840.0mn ($122mn) of purchases in 2020, the split is below.

Functional components (hydraulics, tool magazines, rotary tables) are 25.6%.

Recent findings suggest that electrical parts (mainly the control) are 20.9%. The control alone is about 17.7% of purchases.

Transmission parts (spindles, guides, screws, bearings, gears) are 15.4%.

Accessories, machined parts, sheet metal and other are 15.8%.

Control and distribution are two levers that can help expand margins.

In a recent development, the control. A CNC control is the machine’s computer, software, servo drives and motors. Most builders we checked buy it from FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain or Mitsubishi, and FANUC earns a 21.4% operating margin (firm-wide) against 3% to 10% at most builders we checked.

Industry observers note that cutting the middlemen. US distribution typically has 2 levels, “a wholesaler and a dealer,” and “each level marks their cost up as much as 20%.”.

In a recent development, could venture capital close the machinery gap with the next wave of startups? I went searching and found no venture-backed US tech giant building production machining centers, grinders or gear machines. (If you are building them, I’d love to hear from you!).

It has been revealed that what we can learn from history. Haas, the largest machine builder in North America, was founded in 1983, during the import surge behind the 1983 machine tool Section 232 petition. It started with indexers and built its first vertical machining center in 1987. Today it builds about 10,000 to 15,000 machines a year on about $1.2bn of revenue, and is private.

It has been revealed that the small US builders popped up in the 2000s. They include Tormach (Wisconsin, 2001), Pocket NC, now Penta Machine (Montana, 2011), and Langmuir Systems, a plasma-table maker bought by ShopSabre in 2023. They design and sell desktop and small-shop machines.

US venture money has gone to companies that use machine tools or build equipment for their own factories. Examples include Hadrian, Machina Labs, Divergent, VulcanForms, Freeform and Seurat. Hadrian’s new Alabama factory is the first of three supported by a $900mn Navy contract, with a goal to “automate 80% of the work.”.

Industry observers note that this year’s capital went to factory software and sensing. Arda, led by OpenAI’s former research chief Bob McGrew, came out of stealth in October 2026 with $232mn of funding, its Series A at a $1.5bn valuation, building AI that turns product designs into assembly lines. Matter, whose cofounder and CEO Adi Prasad came from Tesla, offers final assembly, test and packaging for robots in the US. In machining software, CloudNC raised $20mn (UK, September 2026, with Lockheed’s venture arm), Limitless Labs $20mn (Israel) and IPercept $16.5mn (Sweden, entering the US).

According to recent reports, funded machine builders abroad tell a different story. Ethereal Machines (India) raised a $28.5mn Series B in 2026. It builds its own multi-axis CNC machines, sells machining as a service from them, and is building its own controller and a 300,000 sq ft plant. Shanghai Xinghe (China) builds gear grinders and raised several hundred million yuan in July 2026.

Recent findings suggest that government money has gone to training and adjacent supply. America’s Cutting Edge, a national CNC machining training initiative backed by Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), received $42mn from the Defense Department from 2020 to 2022 for machine tool training and R&D. The Pentagon’s industrial base program has awarded over $3.3bn since FY2024. The releases we read do not name any machine tool builder.

With Section 232, I believe two opportunities arise domestically in the US.

Recent findings suggest that foreign builders establish US bases to build machines. They are more experienced in navigating thin margins, but that would likely still require government incentives to boost investments.

Industry observers note that startups in the same spirit as Ethereal Machines launch in the US. They would need to think carefully about how to cut labor cost, solve the materials supply chain bottleneck, and build the control in-house from day one.

This Section 232 has until April 26, 2027 for its first negotiation revision. Section 232 last came for machine tools in 1983, 43 years ago. Will history repeat or rhyme?

In a recent development, the US lost its lead in the 1970s and 1980s. Japanese machine tool exports to the US rose over 1,200% between 1964 and 1967, and by 1986 imports were 75% of the numerically controlled (NC) machines sold in the US, the category that includes today’s CNC machines. Across all machine tools, imports went from about 10% of US consumption in the mid-1970s to 25% by 1981 and about 50% by 1986.

According to recent reports, march 1983. The builders’ association petitions for import quotas under Section 232.

May 20, 1986. Reagan chooses negotiation. “Voluntary restraint agreements will be sought with Taiwan, West Germany, Japan, and Switzerland.”.

Dec 16, 1986. Japan and Taiwan agree to 5 years of restraint from January 1987. The White House projects up to 16,500 more domestic machine sales over the 5 years and cites industry estimates of about $115mn of upcoming plant investment. The full outcome is hard to score. One NBER study found US output rose from 41,992 machines in 1987 to 48,668 in 1988.

Sources indicate that by Oct 1991. Reports said “at least 10 Japanese machine-toolmakers have established plants in the U.S.”.

Industry observers note that dec 1991. Bush keeps the restraints on computer-controlled machines for a 2-year phase-out from January 1992. Japan’s extension ran to Dec 31, 1993, so 5 years became 7.

Effects. The US International Trade Commission estimated that in 1987, the first year, the restraints raised prices 4.4% to 4.9% and protected 658 to 671 jobs. AMT says the domestic share held near 50% for the next decade, so the restraints stopped the fall without reversing it. Imports are about 51% of consumption today.

Industry observers note that A tariff alone raises prices, but buyers keep importing the precise machines. Back in 1987, during the last Section 232, the domestic share held near 50% for the following decade. Fast forward to today, imports are 51% of consumption. One can argue that without the 1987 restraints, the domestic share would be even lower today. This time, imports fell where US plants offer an alternative and kept rising where buyers have few US options. So either the buyers are not price sensitive, or the cost are passed down to the customers. In January to September 2026, with duties in place, machining-center imports fell 3.7% while orders rose 45.0%, and grinder imports rose 29.5% and gear machine imports +76.7%.

It has been revealed that for reindustrialization startups, the openings are in the control and in automation that cuts labor cost. The control is where the profit sits. Builders buy it from suppliers such as FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain and Mitsubishi, and FANUC earns a 21.4% operating margin (manufacturer-wide) against 3% to 10% at most builders we checked. Automation goes after the other big cost. On our numbers, personnel is 30% to 41% of revenue or operating output at European and Japanese builders, about as much as materials. Service margins come from machines already in the field, so they follow once the core machine business is running. This in my opinion is an opportunity for agentic robotics, manufacturing AI founders to shine.

#422. Latest Update: Not Everything Needs an LLM

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1557 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Posthog

Latest Update: Not Everything Needs an LLM

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Posthog

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ask a simple question and you get a few hundred words of "it depends." It's annoying as hell.
  • According to recent reports, this is why we love decision models like Jev for simpler tasks.
  • Industry observers note that choice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LLMs love to yap. Ask a simple question and you get a few hundred words of "it depends." It's annoying as hell.

According to recent reports, this is why we love decision models like Jev for simpler tasks. You ask a structured question and get a typed answer with a probability, which looks something like this:.

Recent findings suggest that noul. Are hedgehogs mammals? → Yes, 0.99.

Industry observers note that choice. Which animal family do hedgehogs belong to? → Mammal, 0.99.

Score. What is the current conservation status of hedgehogs? → Least Concern, 0.77.

Whereas LLMs return free-form and overly confident prose, decision models make model uncertainty explicit. In a calibrated model, answers that score 0.8 are right about 80% of the time. That means a score of 0.5 is a coin flip.

Industry observers note that we've been experimenting with them at PostHog and several use cases have made it to production. This is everything we've learned about using decision models so far: when to use them, how to use them, and mistakes to avoid.

Decision models are up to 444.6x cheaper and 193.6x faster than frontier models,1 so you can use them to check whether you even need to make an expensive LLM call at all.

We do this in a pipeline that scrubs personal info in Replay Vision, our product that watches and summarizes user session recordings for you. Here's how it works:.

Each session summary goes through 2 yes/no questions from a decision model. Using narrow questions like this cuts false flags to about a tenth of what a single question produced.

Sources indicate that 1. “Does this name a real person?”.

According to recent reports, 2. “Does this show contact details or an ID?”.

If either scores 0.4 or above, Gemini rewrites the summary without the personal info and it gets checked again.

Recent findings suggest that otherwise, it's clean and passes through the gate. In production, 98.7% skip the LLM call entirely.

Without the decision model, we'd have to keep fussing with prompts and regexes that miss things, or sending every summary to Gemini to catch the 1% that need it.

A probability score of 0.85 still means ~150 wrong answers per 1,000 checks, so initiative ahead for false positives and false negatives.

In the PII example, a false positive only costs us an extra LLM call, whereas a false negative stores personal data as clean. That's why we set the threshold low at 0.4.

When false positives are the costlier mistake, use higher thresholds. For example, we recently updated the PostHog in Slack bot, so it can answer questions without being tagged. To avoid being annoying, it checks every message in a channel to see (1) whether it's asking for information, and (2) whether PostHog could answer it. Only messages that pass both at 0.85+ go through.

Takeaway: Use decision models to filter jobs before they hit an expensive LLM call, and set the threshold based on which mistake costs you more.

Our PostHog in Slack bot also uses a decision model as a model router.

When the bot gets tagged, it first checks whether the message asked for a specific model. If not, one choice question picks from the list:.

“Pick the cheapest option that will most likely finish the task correctly on the first try. A failed run costs more than a smarter option.”.

Each option in the list carries a short note on what that model is good for. GPT Luna is described as “a light and very cheap model. Good for short answers, lookups, summaries and very small edits.” The decision model then scores the request against each option’s text.

Different tasks, models, and providers all have different thresholds.

Industry observers note that we were experimenting with using them to auto-merge similar logs in Error Tracking and found that thresholds changed between v1 and v2 of the same model. We had to make its thresholds configurable per PostHog project and keep the judge in shadow mode while recalibrating based on hand-labeled data.

Sources indicate that this is one of the reasons why Fernando on our growth team pushed for a model-agnostic interface early. We now have an internal AI gateway for swapping and testing models, including self-hosted ones.

Recent findings suggest that takeaway: Use a choice question to route free-form LLM requests to the cheapest model that can handle it. Keep in mind that thresholds don't carry over, so set them per task and per model.

Industry observers note that if a question requires more context or chains of reasoning, it's better to use an LLM. However, you can still use a decision model if you have a way to flatten, or pre-process the input, so it's checkable at face-value.

In Replay Vision, when a user searches for a theme like "onboarding friction," there's a chance for the query to return a few unexpected results because of the way embedding distance works.

A decision model can’t "Rank the top 10 sessions that contain summaries that match the user's search query." It’s too complicated.

Instead, we use the embeddings first to derive an initial list of session recordings to pass to the decision model. Then, the only task left for the decision model is to look at how closely each result in the list matches the user's original search term:.

"Does this summary describe a session that matches what the search looks for?".

It has been revealed that results are then reranked by that probability. On 20 test queries, this improved ranking quality by about 25%.

It has been revealed that we've tried using a decision model for multi-step reasoning before. Before embeddings were ready in Replay Vision, we tried ranking a "Highlights" feed of sessions worth a human's time. The questions were:.

Is this session worth watching?

Industry observers note that if so, why is it worth watching? (With choices like “error on screen,” “slow or stuck,” “user confused”, “user gave up", etc.).

Processing these two questions in order required an hourly job that sent large requests – up to 32 sessions and 12-38k tokens each – which flooded the model server and blocked other products' calls for hours.

So yes, technically, you can chain decision models into multi-step judgments, but it's not operationally worth it. Leave that to LLMs, or do the heavy lifting before the decision model sees the data like in the embedding search example above.

In a recent development, takeaway: Decision models judge what's in front of them in a single pass. Leave multi-step reasoning to LLMs.

Decision models can take any job where an LLM is overkill, either because it's too slow or too expensive.

One example is our smarter chart picker for SQL queries. PostHog used to pick a visualization using deterministic rules like:.

A date column, a number column and multiple rows → Line chart.

Two or more text columns plus a number → Heatmap.

Now, a decision model looks at both the SQL itself if your org opts in, and the first three rows of the results to suggest a better chart.

The example below is based on a simple query about pageviews by browser. The original rules picked a basic aggregate line chart; with Jev, it chose a bar chart split by browser:.

Anything more open-ended should still go to an LLM.

According to recent reports, still, out of curiosity, we tried Jev on ranking our internal PR review agent's findings with five noul questions that roughly asked if the change is worth a developer's attention. The results were inconclusive with an AUC of 0.52.

If Jev were an LLM, we’d solve this by sending more context, but Jev can’t handle large requests. Its long-context mode is also slower and less accurate.2 Typical decision models just aren’t built for this kind of reasoning.

Recent findings suggest that hybrid decision models like Jeeves can help bridge this gap, though. Developed by our in-house AI research team, Jeeves is a decision model that reasons before deciding when it’s unsure.

It's now our default for any decision call at PostHog that doesn't name a model, and there are similar variations by other developers, like Kev.

Sources indicate that takeaway: Use decision models as evaluators for inputs that are too simple for a language model, yet too fuzzy for a regex. Anything more complex is still too much to hand over to a decision model. For now, at least.

Words by Jina Yoon, who expects this article to be obsolete in two months.
