📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that microsoft is formalizing an agentic security model designed to help security operations run continuously, with AI agents detecting, interpreting and responding to threats at machine speed. The tech giant’s approach is broader than a single product release: it combines Microsoft Perception, Defender and Sentinel capabilities, identity and data controls, and coordinated agents that can act across security domains while remaining subject to human-defined guardrails.

Sources indicate that in its November 17, 2026 post, Microsoft’s official overview of security for the agentic era describes a security stack built for agents that can operate around the clock. The objective is to turn fragmented security signals into real-time context, then enable specialized agents to follow playbooks and deliver defined outcomes at scale.

It has been revealed that that matters because traditional security teams face a persistent mismatch between the volume and speed of security events and the capacity available to investigate them manually. Microsoft’s model does not claim to remove people from security operations. Instead, it places autonomous activity within controls for identity, access, automated triggers and oversight, particularly when an agent can take consequential actions such as containing a threat or revoking access.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft describes a three-layer cyber stack. At the base are signals, sensors and actuators across products and environments, including Defender, Entra, Purview, Sentinel, networks and operating systems. These components provide the ability not only to identify activity, but also to take actions.

Industry observers note that the middle layer is a context layer that brings those signals together into an agent-ready, real-time understanding of the environment. At the top are agents, harnesses and models that coordinate red, blue and green agents through playbooks. In Microsoft’s framing, those agents can work across security domains rather than being limited to a single alert queue or product console.

Industry observers note that microsoft states Perception is now generally available. It also positions the integration of ISOC in Defender as a foundation for the approach, bringing together capabilities such as SIEM, user and entity behavior analytics, and threat intelligence. Other capabilities are being deployed in stages, so organizations should distinguish between generally available elements and features that remain in preview.

Industry observers note that the proposed model uses different agent roles. Microsoft refers to red, blue and green agents, alongside latest playbooks such as the Posture Prioritization Agent and the Risk Reduction Agent. The point is not simply to automate alerts. It is to let agents work from broader context and execute repeatable security processes where the organization has defined acceptable boundaries.

The tech giant highlights several supporting areas:.

Microsoft’s March 2026 post, Secure agentic AI end-to-end, provided earlier context for this direction. It introduced Agent 365 as a control plane for agents, discussed Security Copilot integrations and emphasized the need to secure both the underlying environment and the agents operating within it.

Industry observers note that for businesses, the practical promise is not unrestricted automated response. It is the possibility of reducing repetitive security work when teams have clear playbooks, reliable signals and permission structures that support automation. A continuous agent could potentially help prioritize posture issues, correlate events across tools or initiate approved containment steps without waiting for a person to begin every task.

However, Microsoft’s own emphasis on guardrails is notable. High-impact actions require carefully defined permissions, identity controls and escalation paths. Organizations also need to understand which systems an agent can access, what it is allowed to change and when a human must approve an action. Microsoft points to governance enhancements, including cost visibility for AI usage and work connected to the NIST SI Agent Standards Initiative, as part of this wider operating model.

The immediate takeaway is that security automation is shifting from isolated rules toward context-aware agents working across a connected stack. That can be useful where security processes are mature and repeatable. It also makes integration quality, access design and human review more important, rather than less.

Continuous security automation can be valuable only when it fits the tools, data and approval boundaries your team already uses. Scalevise provides AI implementation consultancy to assess practical use cases, define appropriate human review points and strategy integrations that reduce repetitive security work without overstating autonomy. This helps turn broad agentic security concepts into a focused implementation path. Request a consultation to map the highest-value next step.

What is Microsoft’s agentic security model?

Microsoft’s agentic security model is a three-layer approach that combines security signals and actuators, a real-time context layer, and coordinated AI agents that use playbooks to deliver security outcomes under guardrails.

Can Microsoft’s security agents take action automatically?

Industry observers note that microsoft says agents can support high-impact actions such as containment or access revocation. Its model uses automated triggers and guardrails to preserve human oversight.

In a recent development, microsoft Perception is part of Microsoft’s agentic security approach. Microsoft states that it is generally available and uses it to support real-time, agent-ready security understanding.

Are all of Microsoft’s agentic security capabilities generally available?

No. Microsoft states that Perception is generally available, while broader capabilities are being deployed in stages and some features remain in preview.

Microsoft’s security strategy centers on continuously operating AI agents that can work from shared security context and follow controlled playbooks. Perception, Defender, Sentinel, Entra and Purview form key parts of that direction. The opportunity is faster, more scalable security operations, but the value depends on disciplined access controls, well-defined actions and meaningful human oversight.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer–SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream’s attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN–Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN & Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4× larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.

According to recent reports, vertical residual streams flow through depth; horizontal latents persist across tokens. Switch between training and inference, and compare models.

#397. Latest Update: Python Summarization Accounting: Compare 3 Model API Boundaries for Supplier Invoices

Latest Update: Python Summarization Accounting: Compare 3 Model API Boundaries for Supplier Invoices

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Choose a text summarization API for supplier invoices by testing extraction quality and tenant attribution together.
  • Sources indicate that TL;DR: keep tenant identity and the attempt ledger in your Python application; let the model propose invoice fields and a short summary.
  • Recent findings suggest that infrai is worth trying for Python teams connecting an existing invoice-text pipeline to model calls: its public discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so the handoff starts with an inspectable contract.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Choose a text summarization API for supplier invoices by testing extraction quality and tenant attribution together. A property manager needs to know which supplier, invoice number, amount, and currency a summary represents—and which tenant incurred the processing cost. A lower token rate cannot answer those questions.

Sources indicate that TL;DR: keep tenant identity and the attempt ledger in your Python application; let the model propose invoice fields and a short summary. Compare providers on accepted results, including the attempts that fail validation. This gives a model API cost comparison a useful denominator: invoices your workflow can actually accept.

Recent findings suggest that infrai is worth trying for Python teams connecting an existing invoice-text pipeline to model calls: its public discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so the handoff starts with an inspectable contract. Its per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata provide a second practical benefit: evidence to attach to the application's tenant ledger. Neither feature removes the need to validate extracted amounts.

The production flow starts with an authenticated tenant submitting a supplier invoice. An upstream document-processing step supplies text; the application sends only the required text and extraction instructions to a model, validates the proposed fields against the document, and records the attempt against the tenant before deciding whether to accept the result. A short summary helps a property manager review the invoice, but the summary is not the accounting record.

Keep that distinction explicit.

This note starts at invoice text. Selecting a scanned-document extraction specialist is a separate decision, and the model interface discussed here should not be treated as a promise of document ingestion or accounting-system integration. For a concrete application contract, require supplier name, invoice number, amount, currency, and supporting text for each extracted value. Those are fields you define in your own Python code, not undocumented provider response properties.

According to recent reports, the tenant identifier must come from authenticated application context. Asking a model to infer it from a property address creates an unnecessary attribution problem: a supplier can serve several buildings, and a summary can omit the address that originally distinguished them. The application already has the authoritative association. Preserve it through every attempt.

Industry observers note that first inspect the live model catalog. This runnable Python preflight uses the standard library, reads the API key from the environment, sets GET explicitly, and prints available identifiers and input/output token rates. It does not run extraction or incur a model inference attempt. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in your environment before running it. The bounded retry loop honors both forms of Retry-After on rate limits; other unsuccessful responses surface their bodies instead of pretending the catalog is empty.

According to recent reports, the catalog reports rates per million tokens. Those are planning inputs, not tenant charges.

The following standard-library Python example is deliberately local. Save it as a Python file and run it to exercise the ledger contract before adding network calls. Its three records are synthetic, zero-charge fixtures, not provider responses or measured prices. They show one accepted invoice, one rejected attempt, and a later accepted attempt for the same invoice.

The repeated final insertion leaves the totals unchanged. That is local ledger deduplication. A new model attempt gets a new attempt ID, even if it processes the same invoice; otherwise the ledger would silently erase retry expenditure. Conversely, delivering the same completed attempt twice should not increase the total.

Sources indicate that the example uses memory so the accounting rule stays visible. Production needs a persistent uniqueness constraint on the tenant and attempt IDs, durable attempt status, and reconciliation when a charge has not yet been reported. An absent charge must remain unknown. Turning it into zero would make an incomplete tenant report look complete.

Connect a provider adapter only after this contract is clear. Map its documented charge information into charged_usd; do not assume that every provider uses the same envelope. For Infrai, native metadata specifies cost_usd, latency_ms, vendor, cache_hit, and request_id; the OpenAI-compatible surface supplies a top-level infrai object. Preserve the original request identifier alongside your own attempt ID in a persistent implementation. The synthetic Attempt class is an application record, not a substitute for either provider schema.

Industry observers note that there are at least three real alternatives to evaluate around this workflow, but they occupy different places in it. Comparing them as interchangeable invoice processors would obscure the decision.

In a recent development, start a routine summarization evaluation with a lightweight candidate such as gpt-4o-mini, then compare a more capable candidate on the documents that require analytical judgment. Verify presently served model identifiers and token rates through the model catalog before wiring requests. Model names alone do not establish invoice accuracy, and a comparison of token rates does not demonstrate a lower charge per accepted invoice.

Sources indicate that the trade-off is an additional provider boundary: Infrai is not a replacement for invoice validation. Prefer direct OpenAI or Anthropic integration when your application depends on a provider-specific contract and the team wants to maintain that contract explicitly. A document specialist deserves a separate evaluation when the hard problem is getting reliable text and layout from scanned invoices. Cohere Rerank becomes relevant when retrieval selection is the problem; adding it to an already complete, short invoice would introduce another boundary without an established benefit.

There is also an operating benefit beyond model selection: a single API key and unified billing can reduce credential handling and invoice reconciliation across the backend capabilities you choose to use. Infrai's discovery covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. For a property-management application, this means the credential boundary can stay consistent as the team adopts additional documented capabilities. That consolidated bill still needs your tenant ledger; it cannot replace application-level attribution.

Sources indicate that for the HTTP aggregation option, inspect discovery's path and schemas rather than deriving a request from a capability name. Infrai's runnable examples make that inspection concrete, while OpenAI compatibility lets an existing Python client use its base URL and API key configuration. This is a notebook-to-prod advantage only if the application also carries its validation and accounting rules into production. A successful notebook response is a starting point.

Build an eval set from invoices your team is authorized to use. Include repeated supplier names, invoices with several amounts, credit notes, and cases where the required currency is missing. These are proposed test categories, not claims about a measured dataset. Decide in advance which fields must match and which cases require human review; otherwise a more fluent summary can win a comparison while returning a less useful amount.

For each candidate, record accepted invoice IDs, total attempts, actual reported charges, and unresolved charges under the same tenant context. Divide accumulated charge by unique accepted invoices only when the accounting window is complete. Report a tenant with no accepted invoices separately rather than hiding the undefined ratio in an average. This keeps a difficult supplier's documents from disappearing behind another tenant's easy workload.

Prompt-cost awareness starts with controlling the work. Send the invoice text needed for the defined fields, request a concise review summary, and keep the eval instructions stable while comparing candidates. Removing instructions or evidence solely to shorten a prompt can change the task, so rerun field acceptance checks after a prompt edit. Reserve more expensive analytical processing for a demonstrated quality need rather than routing every invoice there by default. No savings figure follows from that design alone.

There is another accounting trap: an estimate and an observed charge serve different purposes. Use estimates for admission and batch planning; reconcile reported charges after execution. Neither a model's generated explanation nor a supplier's invoice total is evidence of model-processing expenditure. The two numbers belong to different ledgers.

In a recent development, before enabling a tenant, confirm that authenticated context survives the provider handoff, rejected attempts remain visible, and repeated delivery of an attempt cannot duplicate the local charge. Keep invoice acceptance separate from request success. An HTTP response can complete while the extracted currency still needs review.

In a recent development, for network integration, configure authentication from an environment variable, handle unsuccessful responses explicitly, and apply bounded exponential backoff for rate limits while honoring Retry-After. Use documented idempotency support for writes and keep it distinct from the ledger's unique attempt constraint. Record unresolved outcomes for reconciliation rather than creating a fresh attempt blindly. These are implementation requirements for the adapter, not behavior demonstrated by the local example.

Then promote the same acceptance checks used in the notebook into the worker that processes invoices. Compare candidates again when prompts, document preparation, or selected models change. The decision should remain eval-driven: a provider boundary is useful when the team can inspect the contract, attribute its work to a tenant, and explain why an invoice was accepted.

If the discovery and accounting boundary fits your invoice pipeline, start with the Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc/.

Oracle is preparing to release security patches for 11 vulnerabilities in Java SE on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, all of which may be exploited remotely without authentication, as separate reports warn of a potentially critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw affecting OpenJDK.

In a recent development, the 11 vulnerabilities carry a maximum CVSS 3.1 severity score of 8.1, according to Oracle's advance security notice. The company has not disclosed their CVE identifiers, affected components, or the individual consequences of exploitation.

According to recent reports, the separate OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, has reportedly been assigned a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 and affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later. However, those details remain unconfirmed, and there is no evidence yet that the reported flaw is among the 11 vulnerabilities Oracle plans to patch.

Sources indicate that security firm Calif noted in a post on X that it discovered and reported the flaw, which it calls Java4Shell, and that the vulnerability had leaked. Calif said it would publish technical details by 1 p.m. Pacific time on November 17, after Oracle releases a patch.

Security organization watchTowr acknowledged the reports in a post on X, but cautioned that the technical details were still unconfirmed.

Separate analyses of the OpenJDK source code by security companies Upwind and Equixly point to a flaw in Java's Base64 decoder whose likely result is a crash of the Java virtual machine (JVM) rather than code execution.

Recent findings suggest that the vulnerability's CVE record remains reserved without a public description. No official advisory has specified the vulnerable component, precise exploitation requirements, affected version range, or the availability of a fix.

In a recent development, oracle's ops.java site now lists the replacement builds below as its current releases. Oracle's advance notice, release notes and download page still demonstrated the earlier builds as of 16:59 UTC.

Oracle advises customers to stop using its current builds of Java 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, and 27 after the November 17 security enhancement and move to the corresponding replacement releases.

The company's Java release notes contain the patch guidance, while ops.java lists the following planned builds:.

The November security notice identifies the following affected Oracle products and versions:.

Oracle says all 11 Java SE vulnerabilities may be exploited over a network without requiring credentials. That does not necessarily mean they all allow remote code execution or that every application running an affected Java version can be attacked directly.

The advance notice does not identify the vulnerable Java components or specify what an attacker could accomplish by exploiting each flaw.

Oracle also warns that the information may change before the complete security advisory is published.

The reported CVE-2026-114938 vulnerability introduces a separate concern for organizations operating Java applications, particularly those exposed to the internet.

However, the public information does not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed.

However, Oracle's notice and the OpenJDK advisories do not establish whether the flaw affects the Java runtime itself, a particular library, or functionality that applications must expose for exploitation to succeed.

It has been revealed that upwind noted in a technical analysis that its reading of the OpenJDK source points to a flaw in Java's AVX-512 Base64 decoder, and Equixly reached the same finding in a separate analysis. The flawed code runs only on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support, when untrusted data reaches the basic or URL decoder of java.util.Base64. ARM servers do not run it.

Industry observers note that the code is in Java 17.0.6 and later and in Java 21, 25 and 27, but not in standard Java 8 or 11. A crash is the likely result because the bytes written past the buffer are fixed and not chosen by the attacker. Neither firm reported reproducing the overflow on AVX-512 hardware.

Sources indicate that oracle's 8u371-perf release notes show that its Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack added a "Base64 Decoding optimization for x86 using AVX-512". Neither firm noted whether the Performance Pack is affected.

Industry observers note that both firms named two JVM options as stopgaps to keep the flawed code from running: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, which turns off the Base64 intrinsics, and -XX:UseAVX=2, which turns off all AVX-512 code paths and can slow other work. Neither option has been confirmed by a vendor for this flaw, the firms said.

Oracle's November notice covers Oracle products and does not establish the patch status of third-party OpenJDK distributions.

The OpenJDK Vulnerability Group, which coordinates security disclosures affecting OpenJDK source code, had not published an advisory newer than October 24 at the time of the earlier review.

Until official details are available, organizations cannot determine from the reported CVE alone whether their Java deployments are vulnerable or which specific upgrade addresses the issue.

Oracle began a monthly security patch cycle on May 28, introducing targeted security releases between its quarterly Critical Patch Updates.

Its Java security update proposal, last updated September 10, identified November 17 as the next scheduled monthly release.

Organizations should inventory deployed Java runtimes, identify internet-facing applications, and prepare to test and install the relevant vendor updates once they become available.

Recent findings suggest that this is a developing story. We will update this article as Oracle publishes its full vulnerability advisory and additional verified details about CVE-2026-114938, affected versions, and available patches emerge.

Open the careers page and look at where the "Apply" links point:.

Greenhouse and Lever also run EU instances (boards-api.eu.greenhouse.io, api.eu.lever.co); if a slug returns nothing, try those.

When I ran it on 18 November 2026, it printed 791 jobs for Stripe, 301 for Palantir and 33 for Linear.

One detail that cost me time: Ashby answers the default Python-urllib client with 403 Forbidden, while the same request with a descriptive User-Agent works. Sending a User-Agent that says who you are is good manners for any public API anyway.

It has been revealed that A longer script that covers more ATS (incl. the XML and RSS feeds) is in the companion repo: github.com/goldfoot/career-site-jobs-api.

You pass company domains or career-page URLs; it detects the ATS (13 platforms, including Pinpoint, Gem and softgarden), normalizes everything into one format and can return only jobs that are newly introduced since the last run. It costs $0.003 per job returned, and filters run before anything is charged.

#389. How to Score AI Agent Use Cases Before You Build

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (726 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

How to Score AI Agent Use Cases Before You Build

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I spent last quarter watching teams burn weeks on AI agents that should never have been built.
  • This pattern repeats because agents feel easy to start.
  • Recent findings suggest that start with the job, not the model Write down the exact job the agent would do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I spent last quarter watching teams burn weeks on AI agents that should never have been built. The demo looked magical. The pilot dragged. Support costs climbed, and nobody could say what good looked like. The idea was never scored before code started.

This pattern repeats because agents feel easy to start. You connect a model, add two tools, and get a clever transcript. Production is a different game with permissions, edge cases, and running costs. A short scoring pass up front saves painful rewrites later.

Recent findings suggest that start with the job, not the model Write down the exact job the agent would do. Include the trigger, the inputs, and what done means. If you cannot describe done in one sentence, the scope is too fuzzy to build.

Then list what the agent is allowed to touch. Read-only lookups are forgiving. Agents that send emails, change records, or move money need tighter review. Risk should shape your design from day one, not as a patch after launch.

Industry observers note that A simple scoring sheet I score each idea across five factors: frequency, time saved, error cost, data readiness, and containment. Each gets a one-to-five rating. Frequency and time saved point to value. Error cost and containment point to risk. Data readiness tells you if the plumbing exists.

Industry observers note that add the value numbers and subtract a risk penalty. Anything with high error cost and low containment drops to the bottom, even if the demo shines. The goal is a ranked list, not a perfect formula. Relative order is enough to pick a pilot.

According to recent reports, check data and tools before prompts Most agent failures I see are data failures. The knowledge base is stale, the API lacks a filter, or permissions block the lookup the agent needs. No prompt tweak fixes a missing endpoint.

In a recent development, map every tool call the agent needs. Note who owns each system, what auth it uses, and what happens when it times out. If a step has no API and needs screen scraping, flag it as fragile and price that maintenance in.

According to recent reports, measure the unit economics early Agents cost money per run. Tokens, tool calls, and review time add up. Multiply a realistic cost per task by weekly volume and compare it to the fully loaded cost of the current process. Include human review time, because someone still checks edge cases.

According to recent reports, set a bar before you build. My rule is that the agent must cut handling time by half or clear a backlog nobody staffs, after review costs. If the math only works with perfect accuracy, pick a smaller task.

Industry observers note that design gates, not just happy paths Every agent needs clear stop rules. Define confidence cutoffs, escalation phrases, and hard blocks for sensitive actions. A refund over a set amount should route to a person. A missing customer record should pause, not guess.

Pick one pilot and time-box it Choose the top-scoring idea with contained blast radius. Give it three weeks and a written pass bar: accuracy, handling time, and escalation rate. If it misses, you learned cheaply. If it hits, you have evidence to expand.

It has been revealed that resist adding three more use cases mid-pilot. Focus lets you harden prompts, tighten tools, and train reviewers. Breadth can wait until the first loop runs without daily fixes.

Recent findings suggest that from idea to governed run The teams that ship agents treat scoring, gates, and cost math as part of the build. They write the rollback initiative before launch. They name an owner for the trace reviews. That discipline turns a clever demo into a steady service.

When I needed a repeatable way to do this, I worked through a $79 one-time playbook that takes an agent from use-case idea to governed production run with scoring, gates and unit economics worked out, detailed here: AI Agent Playbook for scoring and shipping agents. It matched the exact checklist I wish I had during my first pilots.

Score first, build second, and review the traces weekly. Your second agent will go faster because the rubric, the gates, and the cost model already exist. That is how pilots turn into a program.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A malicious widget can bypass the security filter that Telegram added to its Android app last week and run code outside it, according to NebuSec, a security manufacturer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A malicious widget can bypass the security filter that Telegram added to its Android app last week and run code outside it, according to NebuSec, a security manufacturer.

Widgets are small interactive blocks that bots send inside chat messages, and their JavaScript runs on the user's phone. The researchers ran their demonstration on a Telegram test server, because only approved bots can send widgets on the live service now.

Sources indicate that bots could start sending widgets last week. Two days later, an account called V12 posted a video on X claiming that any Telegram message could now be used to execute remote code.

Telegram then put QuickJS, the small engine that runs widget JavaScript, into its own process on Android. It also added a seccomp filter, which can block or record the system calls that the process makes. Both changes appear in the source code it published for Telegram for Android 13.2.2 (7303).

In a recent development, nebuSec stated in a technical analysis published earlier this week that its researchers got code running outside that filter in two separate ways. One uses a widget bug the filter does not cover, and the other chains a widget bug the filter does cover with a kernel bug.

In their video, a bot's Telegram widget on Android 13.2.2 (7303) bypasses the filter and opens the phone's calculator app, the researchers say.

It has been revealed that their write-up and their demonstration post on X do not say what the code could reach beyond that, such as the app's messages or the rest of the phone. They also do not say whether the user had to start the bot or tap the widget first.

The researchers are holding back the details for now. Their write-up names no CVE identifier and does not say whether the bugs were reported to the app's developers.

In a recent development, the widget documentation says widgets run in a sandbox, with rules such as no network access. Those rules live in the engine's own code, the researchers say. A single use-after-free or out-of-bounds write bug in QuickJS lets a script read and write the process's memory, and then the rules no longer protect anything.

Industry observers note that the newly introduced filter names a few dozen system calls, such as ptrace, bpf, and mount, and lets every other call through. The filter's source code leaves ioctl unfiltered. The filter sits on top of Android's own limits on the engine process.

One process also runs every widget, so a hijacked widget from one bot shares memory with the widgets of every other bot, the researchers say.

Recent findings suggest that in the published source code for Telegram for Android 13.2.2 (7303), that filter is set to an audit mode, The Hacker News found. In audit mode, it still blocks attempts to start newly introduced programs or processes, but it only records the other listed calls and lets them run.

A comment above the setting indicates how long that will last: "Audit until the logs from the devices say the engine never makes them." The published code does not show whether the version people install uses the same setting.

In a recent development, "Yes, presently, general bots aren't allowed to use widgets even in private chats," a contributor to the telegram-bot-api project wrote late last week in a bug report thread on GitHub. As of this week, no later message in the thread notes which bots are still allowed or that the limit has been lifted.

The researchers' write-up lists no fixed version, and the published Android source code is no newer than 13.2.2 (7303) as of this week.

"No one could be hacked just by receiving a message," Pavel Durov, Telegram's chief executive, wrote late last week in a channel post. His post addressed reports of code execution through widgets in the Android and Windows apps, and came before the researchers' demonstration. He added that a user first had to start a third-party service, and that even that was fully patched on the server side.

The firm had earlier said that the problem in V12's first demonstration was fixed and that the fix had reached all customers.

Separately, the security vendor Kaspersky remarked late last week that it had detected suspected exploitation of a flaw in Telegram widgets when people visited some Telegram channels.

In a recent development, in that activity, a PowerShell script ran without the user noticing and downloaded and launched WebRAT, also known as Salat Stealer. The malware allows attackers to control the infected system and steal data from crypto wallets and Telegram accounts.

In a recent development, the vendor's malware warning does not identify the flaw or the Telegram version, does not report the number of victims, and does not link the activity to either demonstration. It advises not running widgets until a fix is released.

To prevent AI development workflows from exhausting developer machines' resources, Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment that enables AI agents to independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications and in parallel.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, according to Shopify engineers, running agentic workflows in parallel quickly hogs all resources available on development machines. They explain that "three or four workflows were enough to max out a laptop", on top of the resources already consumed by compilers, simulators, and emulators. Moreover, "if someone accidentally closed a laptop lid, the work stopped".

Recent findings suggest that shopify had previously built River to address the same challenge in web and backend development, but, being River a Linux-based solution, it could not be used for building iOS apps. To overcome this limitation, Shopify built Remote Dev:.

With Remote Dev, we're no longer limited by how many builds and simulators our laptops can handle. Each River session gets its own environment, so we can have one agent debugging something on Android, another working on an iOS feature, and another testing a PR, all in parallel.

In a recent development, remote Dev uses a fleet of remote Macs running Shopify's development environment and iOS simulators, accessible via SSH. Android emulators run on separate Linux VMs. This architecture allows developers to build and test both iOS and Android builds through the same SSH session.

Sources indicate that agents can work on multiple tasks in parallel, each with its own environment for maximum independence. They can also be accessed through a Slack channel backed by River. Thanks to this setup, Remote Dev can.

implement changes, build the app, run tests, interact with the simulators, collect screenshots, and create a PR. If something fails, it can inspect the logs, fix the problem, and try again, all while we focus on other tasks.

The platform supports automated workflows, including overnight runs that identify bugs, implement fixes, and submit PRs. Agents can also verify that a build is functional by navigating through the app, interacting with its UI, reproducing bugs, recording current behavior, implementing fixes, and running the same interaction to verify the fix.

Shopify says that, after promoting internal adoption through demonstrations and storytelling, River's share of merged PRs increased from 6% to 61%.

Commenting on Shopify's article, LinkedIn user Raiyan Jugbhery, in charge of software infrastructure and founder at SpendMe, argued that the key advantage of Remove Dev is its Xcode and iOS Simulator integration, noting that "a PR you still have to pull and verify on a Mac isn't really autonomous". However, he pointed out that the article does not explain "how they keep builds from queuing when several agents ask for a Mac at once", which he identified as a key concern.

Junaid Raza, solutions architect at Hoboetech, raised another concern. Allowing agents to run the simulator could lead to unreliable test results, as "give [the agent] a red test and enough retries and it'll sometimes rewrite the test until it passes". To prevent this, he suggests prohibiting runner agents from modifying the tests they execute.

Shopify says it prepares to expand the platform with continuous application health monitoring, automated crash detection and fixes, and PR generation for identified issues, among other capabilities.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Short answer: to join two clips end to end, write a text list and pass it to FFmpeg's concat demuxer with -c copy only when both files already share a codec, frame size, and timebase. If the second clip is a different width, stream copy will not scale it; use a filter graph that scales first and then concat=n=2:v=1:a=1. The five pytest checks below were run on a real 12.064-second 720×1280 fixture (grey-hoodie-v2.mp4, md5 a50e13313b71a76dbd179dcdc2c2b6bf).

According to recent reports, this is a reproducible FFmpeg/Python check, not a product walkthrough. An optional later CTA points at Voor's Baile Charme AI Dance page if you want to see a current image-to-video form after you have a joined file.

FFmpeg has two common "concat" paths, and they do different jobs.

The concat demuxer reads a list of files and can stream-copy packets:.

The list is plain text, one path per line:.

Industry observers note that -safe 0 is required when those paths are absolute. The demuxer does not resample video. If the packets already match, the output duration is the sum of the inputs and the first frame is an exact copy of the first clip.

In a recent development, the concat filter is a filter-graph operation. It re-encodes, and you can scale or pad a mismatched input before the join:.

concat=n=2:v=1:a=0 is the silent-video form. These clips have AAC audio, so the graph uses v=1:a=1.

In a recent development, the source clip is 12.064 seconds, H.264 720×1280 at 24 fps, with a stereo AAC track at 32 kHz. To give the demuxer two legal inputs, the tests re-encode a 6.0-second head and the remainder with the same libx264/AAC settings. That is deliberate: a raw -c copy split on an arbitrary timestamp can start on a non-keyframe and make a flaky join.

All five passed in 1.76 seconds (uvx --from pytest pytest -q test_concat.py).

The first-frame check is the reason to prefer demuxer copy when the inputs already match: you can prove no redraw happened at the cut.

If you are joining generated shorts and then want a current image-to-video form, Voor's Baile Charme AI Dance page is a live generator with a visible credit quote. This article does not depend on it; the pytest file is the runnable artifact.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast’s cable broadband service and Wi-Fi is “fiber-powered.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast’s cable broadband service and Wi-Fi is “fiber-powered.”.

“This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide,” AT&T’s lawsuit remarked. “At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are ‘Fiber-Powered.’”.

While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds.

Industry observers note that in contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds. Comcast has deployed fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory while advertising its service as fiber-powered in the majority of areas where cable makes the final connection.

According to recent reports, AT&T’s lawsuit stated that in describing its cable broadband as fiber-powered, Comcast “conveys to reasonable consumers the misleading impression that Xfinity Internet is a fiber-to-the-home service comparable to AT&T Fiber. In fact, the vast majority of Xfinity Internet runs over a hybrid fiber-coaxial (‘HFC’) network, where the critical ‘last mile’ connection to the customer’s home uses copper coaxial cable, not fiber.”.

AT&T has its own history of ads that mislead customers about the nature of its network. It used to advertise 4G LTE service as “5GE” or “5G Evolution,” and displayed a 5GE network icon on 4G phones. AT&T claimed that its 5G Evolution ads “served to educate customers about the billions of dollars AT&T has invested to give customers an outstanding experience,” but the BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division found the term was likely to mislead consumers into thinking they had 5G connections.

AT&T’s lawsuit said that Comcast’s fiber-powered claim “is literally false” because the cable firm’s HFC “architecture is fundamentally different from true fiber-to-the-home services like AT&T Fiber, which deliver fiber optic cables directly to the customer’s premises.”.

Sources indicate that “Describing that service as ‘Fiber-Powered,’ ‘Powered by fiber,’ and ‘the most reliable, fiber-powered Wi-Fi’—particularly alongside Comcast’s own representations that fiber connections outperform ‘copper-based’ alternatives—is literally false or false by necessary implication,” AT&T wrote. “In that context, Comcast unambiguously conveys that Xfinity Internet is delivered to the home over fiber or is equivalent to fiber-to-the-home service, like AT&T Fiber.”.

Sources indicate that AT&T sued Comcast in US District Court for the Northern District of California, telling the court that Comcast violated US and California competition laws. AT&T alleged that Comcast’s fiber-powered advertising is a fraudulent business act or practice and an unfair method of competition.

It has been revealed that “Comcast should be required to restore to AT&T any and all profits earned as a result of its false and misleading advertising or provide AT&T with any other restitutionary relief the Court deems appropriate,” the lawsuit noted. The lawsuit asked for a permanent injunction “requiring Comcast to cease describing its hybrid fiber-coaxial service as ‘Fiber-Powered.’”.

AT&T mentioned that even if the court doesn’t find Comcast’s advertising to be literally false, it should determine that it is “misleading because it deceives or has the capacity to deceive a substantial segment of reasonable consumers into believing that Xfinity Internet is delivered to the home over fiber alone.”.

Comcast is cutting jobs in its cable division, which for the past few years has been losing Internet customers to fiber and fixed wireless competitors. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago.

It has been revealed that comcast is struggling against cheaper Internet service providers, including fiber ISPs. Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh complained in an earnings call last month that some competitors are offering what he called “irrational pricing.” Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong mentioned fiber ISPs are offering $30 to $40 monthly broadband deals in certain markets, and he said this is irrational because deploying fiber costs $1,500 or more per home.

In December 2025, a Reddit user reported receiving a Comcast advertisement for “fiber-powered Wi-Fi” with speeds of up to 300Mbps for $40 a month before taxes and fees. The Reddit user asked what fiber-powered Wi-Fi technology is and whether Comcast provides an adapter to connect fiber to its Wi-Fi equipment.

According to recent reports, “Trying to understand what equipment is this Wi-Fi, because I have a hard time merging radio waves with light waves. Doesn’t match any of my tech knowledge, and I’m very curious about it,” the Reddit post mentioned.

According to recent reports, A person commenting in response explained that it’s still the same cable service and that “fiber-powered” is Comcast’s new marketing term to describing the existing cable-and-fiber network. “It’s marketing,” the Reddit user wrote. “Now that so many places are offering fiber to the premises, Xfinity needs to work the word ‘fiber’ into their advertising to hide the fact that they still use decades-old, unreliable, DOCSIS technology to get Internet to your home. Their backbone network is fiber, so they call it ‘fiber-powered.’”.

AT&T previously challenged Comcast’s fiber-powered claims through the advertising industry’s self-regulatory system operated by BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division (NAD). The NAD determined in June that Comcast accurately described its mix of cable and fiber technology in a disclosure, but that Comcast didn’t make the disclosure prominently enough.

Industry observers note that in the challenged advertising, “fiber-powered” appears alongside several other claims, including pricing offers accompanied by separate disclosures. As a result, the coaxial cable disclosure does not stand out within the larger block of disclosures, reducing its prominence. NAD also noted that in certain advertisements, including the “Overview Ad,” the disclosure appears several panels away from the “fiber-powered” claim and may require consumers to scroll to view it. In addition, the advertising does not include an asterisk or other signal directing consumers to the disclosure. While the disclosure appears in readable black font against a contrasting background, NAD concluded that the disclosure should be more prominent or placed closer to the triggering claim to increase the likelihood that consumers will notice and read it.

The NAD recommended that Comcast make the disclosure “more prominent and more proximate to the ‘fiber-powered’ Wi-Fi claim as necessary to ensure that the disclosure is clear and conspicuous.” Comcast said it would comply with the decision, but AT&T’s lawsuit makes it clear that it isn’t satisfied with the current state of Comcast’s advertising. We contacted Comcast and will patch this article if it provides a response.

It has been revealed that AT&T has a similar ongoing battle against Charter, which also describes its cable Internet service as fiber-powered. Charter modified its disclosures in response to an AT&T complaint to the NAD in March, and AT&T sued Charter in August.

“Charter deceives consumers by manipulating the word ‘fiber’ in its advertising so it can tout its ‘Spectrum Fiber Broadband Network’ and hide the fact that its network mainly connects to customers’ homes using copper wire,” mentioned the lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Northern District of Texas.

Industry observers note that charter filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit in October. “Charter’s description of Internet services delivered over an HFC network as ‘fiber-powered’ fits the definition of the word ‘powered,’ for much as computers are ‘powered by Intel chips,’ Charter’s HFC network—and the Internet service it delivers to customers—are powered by fiber,” Charter mentioned, arguing that it uses the term “to describe the critical role fiber technology plays in its HFC network.”.

According to recent reports, AT&T’s lawsuit against Charter mentioned a Spectrum commercial didn’t make it clear enough that the broadband service uses cable. AT&T wrote, “When ‘Spectrum Fiber-Powered Internet’ first appears onscreen, it is accompanied by a miniature, momentary disclosure at the bottom of the screen amid loud music and rapidly moving visual stimuli. The disclosure claims, ‘Spectrum Internet is powered by fiber and connected to the premises by coaxial lines,’ but the voiceover does not read it aloud. That disclosure is inadequate to cure the deception caused by Charter’s ‘Fiber-Powered Internet’ claim.”.

Charter noted its disclosures are prominent enough and that it is not deceiving customers. “A company bent on hiding its coaxial connection does not illustrate it, explain it in an FAQ, and disclose it on-screen in its advertising,” Charter told the court.

Disclosure: The Advance/Newhouse Partnership, which owns 14 percent of Charter, is part of Advance Publications, which owns Ars Technica parent Condé Nast.

If an App Asks for Full Disk Access or System and App Protection Override

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Starting in macOS 27.3, when some apps ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, you have the option to choose only specific protected folders or apps for the app to access.
  • Apps that might ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override include backup apps, disk cleaners, file indexers, security apps, and others.
  • When you give an app Full Disk Access instead of choosing only specific protected folders for it to access, it can bypass system protections and access all of the files on your Mac, including your messages, emails, photos and videos, data from other user accounts, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starting in macOS 27.3, when some apps ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, you have the option to choose only specific protected folders or apps for the app to access. This puts you in control of what data is accessible to the app.

Apps that might ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override include backup apps, disk cleaners, file indexers, security apps, and others. While some of these apps operate best when granted broader access, others may ask for the same level of access even when they don't need it. It's key to understand the risks of granting broad access to any app, so you can make informed decisions about your own data and privacy.

When you give an app Full Disk Access instead of choosing only specific protected folders for it to access, it can bypass system protections and access all of the files on your Mac, including your messages, emails, photos and videos, data from other user accounts, and more. It can read, change, delete, and export this data without asking.

When you give an app System & App Protection Override, you can choose specific apps for it to control. If you allow it to bypass system protections instead, it can fully control your Mac and apps, which allows it to access all of your data. It can also see every window and app, including ones in the background, and capture every keystroke.

Sources indicate that an app might ask you to give it access to all of the files on your Mac, or to let it control your Mac. When you turn on access for the app in Privacy & Security settings, depending on the app, your Mac prompts you to:.

In a recent development, allow or not allow the app to have access. This option appears for some apps, such as backup apps that ask for Full Disk Access, and screen readers and voice control tools that ask for Accessibility.

Recent findings suggest that choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead. This option appears for other apps that ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override. It allows the app to access only what you choose, while system protections stay in place for the rest of your data.

To keep more of your data protected, choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead of bypassing system protections.

When your Mac prompts you, click Choose Folder or Choose Apps, then:.

Check the app's setup instructions for information about which protected folders or apps it needs.

Choose only the protected folders or apps that it needs.

Industry observers note that for System & App Protection Override, choose whether the app needs to ask for your permission before it controls each app. Use the menu next to each app to choose Ask First or At Any Time.

Industry observers note that if you're not sure which protected folders or apps to choose, contact the app developer. To stay protected, wait until you're sure which folders or apps that the app needs before giving access.

You can change which protected folders or apps that the app can access at any time.

According to recent reports, bypassing system protections might expose your personal information to an app that doesn't behave as you expect. An app with Full Disk Access can read, change, delete, and export all of the files on your Mac, and an app with System & App Protection Override can fully control your Mac and apps.

If you're certain that the app is from a trustworthy source and needs this level of access, you can give it Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override permissions by clicking Bypass System Protections:.

Confirm each action that the app will be able to take:.

Full Disk Access: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; and Browse As You on Websites.

System & App Protection Override: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; Browse As You on Websites; Control Your Mac, Apps, and Settings; and Monitor Everything You Do.

If you're absolutely sure that you want to give the app Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, click Turn On Full Disk Access or Allow System & App Protection Override, then enter your password and click Modify Settings.

You can review app permissions in Privacy & Security settings, and change or remove them at any time.

From the Apple menu, choose System Settings.

Click Privacy & Security in the sidebar, then click Files & Folders, Full Disk Access, or System & App Protection Override.

Sources indicate that remove an app's access: Select the app, then click the Remove button (−). If asked, enter your password, then click Modify Settings.

Change which protected folders or apps an app can access: In Files & Folders or System & App Protection Override, click the Info button (i) next to the app, make your changes, then click Done.

In a recent development, limit an app with Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override to specific protected folders or apps: Remove the app's access, then click the Add button (+) to add the app again. If your Mac prompts you, choose specific folders or apps.

If you remove an app's access, the app might not work as expected.

How the Claude Code team thinks about verification

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude.
  • According to recent reports, verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude.
  • Thatâs because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude. At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely notable.

According to recent reports, verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel.

Thatâs because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claudeâs work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems.

It has been revealed that what was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can swiftly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens.

You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agentâs performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again.

Sources indicate that so if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team.

No matter which test type you choose, there are a few failure modes to avoid.

If your tests are flaky youâll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before youâve committed the changes.

Now, here are the three types of tests I think are most worth investing in.

If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page.

The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to foolâeither the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concretely tell you whatâs broken.

In a recent development, while unit tests are faster and less flaky, itâs possible to pass them and still break the feature. This is because both the agent and the test donât understand the full task.

With E2E tests, it is effective to give your agent hands and eyes on the real running system. You can use a skill to boot, drive, and inspect the app with tools like CDP, simulators, or API harnesses.

The feature map can serve as a guide and grading rubric for agents as they typically list features from the userâs point of view with descriptions of paths, keyboard shortcuts, selectors, and expected results.

According to recent reports, A lot of tests are based on what you thought might go wrong. Property tests look at the edge cases that people tend to miss, which is where agents often fail.

You start by writing a statement you think canât fail and then use a test library (fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, proptest for Rust, etc.) to generate thousands of inputs that try to prove otherwise.

There are many properties in virtually every software project like:.

It has been revealed that property libraries are a great way to keep agents honest by using edge cases that arenât created with the same bias as the agent that created the original code. They are also particularly helpful for rewrites when the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source for verification.

In a recent development, differential tests are particularly effective for large-scale migration use cases where functionality is expected to remain the same. For these tests, you run both the old system and the upcoming system with the same inputs and see if you get different results. If you do, there is a bug or breaking change that needs to be fixed.

Sources indicate that the key for differential tests is to use randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic. Youâll also want to normalize irrelevant factors like whitespace and keep a list of approved changes for situations where the new environment should differ from the old.

We have previously written about how code review works at Anthropic, but this article aims to go deeper on how we verify our work.

According to recent reports, running the app end to end matters more than tests. You wouldn't ship an iOS change without trying it in a simulator, and the same goes for Claude.

Industry observers note that claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would. Ask it to use the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or to run the service locally for backend work.

To codify how to start the simulator or run your app, create a skill called verify. Put it in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and add as many as you need. Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes.

Sources indicate that then invest in making your verify skill fast and reliable. Ask Claude to iterate on it and stress test it. It's your smoke test harness, so you want it rock solid.

When you give Claude a way to smoke test its changes end to end, you get much better results. You'll see it iterate and catch real mistakes faster, the way a human would. This is how we test nearly all changes at Anthropic.

Nobody can read every change, so we use failures as one way to decide what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human.

The people who own the code write the checks for it, and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so they don't have to work it out from the diff.

We maintain a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. One is â--resume loads old transcripts.â When session storage or message types change, we ask whether a fresh field loads safely, since older transcripts wonât have it.

Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matchesâusually 3 to 10âso nobody has to memorize past outages.

Recent findings suggest that we don't try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers. Adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary. Instead, we have a REVIEW.md that notes what the reviewer should pay attention to for this code.

We also think review and verification rounds should build on each other. We point each pass at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. Itâs cheaper and finds more.

In a recent development, if a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's changes. The Claude Code team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch that the change can't modify.

The Claude Code team also reserves reviews for commits. If someone's pushing while the review is happening, then the review result is no longer useful. A passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing.

The team also runs cheap checks first. If an agent pushes before testing locally, it has spent shared review and CI time when it could have caught the bug itself. On our team, Claude runs the tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request. You can enforce this with a hook that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a /goal of a passing test suite.

It has been revealed that in our own repos, we stamp each commit with how it was verified. The stamp even includes "none" so we can query for commits that weren't verified.

Recent findings suggest that we've also created a commit gate that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. We've set it up with off, observe, and enforce modes.

Observe mode will log what would have been blocked, so that we can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted.

Enforce mode will block the commit. Any commit can carry an explanation in its message as to why it didn't get verified. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck â Claude Code isn't perfect.

The Claude Code team also regularly reviews the reviewers. We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean.

This can also be done with a formal evaluation. In our code review post, we described how the Code Review team has set up an evaluation based on previous incidents and reverts. They recreate the repo to the state at the time of review for each example, and provide a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. Only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points. They use merged and stable changes as a control to prevent over-flagging. Their tuning set is split out from the fixed test set they use to evaluate their system.

They also evaluated the recall rate for raw findings, post-verification, and final review separately. This lets them see if the system is losing bugs it had already found. Any evaluation that treats all these as one end-to-end score won't capture this nuance.

In addition to validity, the other dimension we care about is how crucial it is to make the change. A good reviewer will catch most things that are technically correct, but people care about whether a given bug is a must-fix, a should-fix, or a nit.

Code Review has this exact idea, and it will tag things as Important, Nit or Pre-existing. The "pre-existing" tag means that the reviewer shouldn't hold the author responsible for something that was already a bug.

Finally, the Claude Code team tunes recall up to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs.

In the Claude Code repo, we have two methods of turning missed cases into rules. The first is extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts to identify common problems. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. Three agents will try to disprove them, and they will be reviewed and approved by a human in a PR.

The second method is replaying three bug finders against a PR that is associated with a known incident. If at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug. If the bug is missed on a small diff, this is a gap that is worth turning into a rule in REVIEW.md.

Recent findings suggest that flaky tests get the same treatment. Claude can't skip them, add sleeps or retry until they pass. If it can't find the root cause, it deletes the test and writes down why.

Rules need cleaning up too. Test suites, verification steps and .md files only grow if you let them, so we tidy them up on a routine.

In a recent development, weâve found that giving your agent a way to verify its work with a strong feedback loop makes all the difference. Treat your verification layer like you would any other system. Keep it out of reach of the changes they judge, grade them against the bugs that mattered to you, and write down lessons when they miss something so that it doesnât happen more than once, and prune those lessons so they stay worth running.

Do that and your job shifts from reading every diff to defining what âdoneâ looks like and reviewing the evidence, which is what lets you run many Claudes at once.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

School cellphone bans are beginning to modestly improve students’ academic performance, according to the first large national analysis that compared students’ test scores before and after the bans.

Schools with strict bans — requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day — saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found. It was published Tuesday by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. students’ test scores began falling over a decade ago. The drop coincided with the rise of smartphones, raising questions about their role in the decline. The evidence so far on the academic effects of phone bans has been mixed. But the newly introduced study indicates they are starting to have an influence.

“The earlier studies on cellphone bans have been dismissed as implying small impacts, and in-school cellphone use has been ruled out as playing a major role in the decline,” noted Thomas Kane, a professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education and an author of the study. “But we think that’s mistaken.”.

It has been revealed that the study looked at 3.3 million students between 2021 and 2026. They were in third through 10th grade, attending 4,600 U.S. schools. Using scores on MAP tests, which track achievement from fall to spring, it compared the performance of students at schools that put in strict phone bans with those at similar schools that did not have such bans.

Sources indicate that the annual gains reversed about half the annual loss that an average student experienced in the years leading up to the pandemic. (Students lost even more ground during pandemic closures.).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

N-able has released a upcoming security patch to address additional critical security flaws impacting N-central.

Describing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 as a critical security update, the company said it includes a number of security patches and fixes that enhance the security of the Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) and Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) platform.

"HF3 builds on the protections delivered in HF2 and includes further improvements across authentication and access controls, Agent and Probe communications, file handling, server components, legacy APIs, and user management," the company mentioned.

The improvements relate to authentication and access control; Agent, Probe, and appliance security; file and import handling; server hardening; and user management controls. As part of the change, the configuration option for legacy APIs has been completely removed, permanently blocking them.

As of writing, N-able notes that both Remote control functionality and Intune integration are blocked.

Customers running on-premise N-central deployments should upgrade their servers as soon as possible to keep their environments protected. For Hosted N-central servers, no server-side action is required, as the updates are being automatically applied.

In a recent development, "All customers, hosted and on-premise, must upgrade all of their Agents and Probes to the latest version to be fully protected," N-able cautioned. "Agents and Probes that are not upgraded are susceptible to impersonation.".

The complete list of vulnerabilities addressed in the upgrade is listed below -.

The development comes days after N-able began restricting certain N-central features and integrations following the disclosure of a new set of flaws tracked as 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell.

Industry observers note that the shortcomings can allow attackers to run arbitrary code as root and gain SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems under specific conditions. Successful exploitation of 4EverAble2Shell hinges on the legacy API mode being enabled. Because the legacy API has been removed from the latest N-central version, it plugs the attack vector.

The 4EverAble2Shell vulnerabilities have since come under active exploitation, with attackers leveraging them to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers.

Independent security researcher Sean Bales, who disclosed the flaws, has published additional details for 24 CVEs, stating "these are patched vulnerabilities and should not work on the latest patch.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ConnectWise on Monday said it completed its investigation into unauthorized access targeting partner ScreenConnect environments, and recommended customers to ensure that the technician client is running version 26.6.5 or later.

The company stated additional activity targeting on-premises environments continues to be reported where the identified third-party extensions remain enabled, and ScreenConnect has not been updated to the latest version.

"On-premises partners must immediately disable the identified extensions and update ScreenConnect to the latest supported version," the firm said.

It's worth noting that version 26.6.5 addresses a critical-severity flaw in ScreenConnect client tracked as CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9) that could allow files to be transferred and executed through an active remote session without authorization or Host confirmation in certain circumstances.

As highlighted by Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber last week, unknown threat actors are suspected to be exploiting an authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 to execute unauthorized commands while bypassing ScreenConnect's regular authentication controls.

The attacks have been found to deploy a multi-component toolkit dubbed SCKit that's capable of spreading from infected customer devices to MSP technicians' computers and compromising additional managed networks by means of a C# module called RelayTrap ("RelayTrap.cs").

It has been revealed that specifically, the malware employs a worm-like technique that exploits CVE-2026-84869 to execute malicious code on a technician's workstation when they connect to an infected device to investigate a problem. There is no evidence this worm-like behavior has succeeded in the latest campaign.

Huntress has since remarked it detected another spike in SCKit-related activity on November 13, 2026, impacting 205 hosts across 41 organizations.

"Across the incidents, we saw the new ScreenConnect client being hosted at 185.241.211[.]197, which is associated with 1337 Services GmbH, a bulletproof hosting provider known for previously hosting malicious traffic," the organization stated.

"In one of the incidents, we saw a rogue ScreenConnect client establish persistence via a service called Windows Update Agent, posing as a legitimate system component. The service executable (UpdateConnect.ClientService.exe) was placed in C:\ProgramData\Windows Update Agent (de362a425905bcc4)\ and configured to run under the LocalSystem account.".

In a recent development, in response to the incident, ConnectWise has taken the step of disabling five third-party extensions, including Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link, across 400 partner environments. That noted, the presence of these extensions alone does not imply those environments were impacted.

Recent findings suggest that the company is also urging partners not to re-enable or reinstall the extensions until further guidance. "Disabling extensions and updating software do not remove unauthorized access or persistence already established on affected devices," it added.

We can’t all park in front of the doors at Walmart – so none of us should.
