#368. Hijacked Optimizely Scripts Served Card Skimmer and iOS Exploit Kits to CNN, BBC and Zoom Visitors

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1252 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thehackernews

Hijacked Optimizely Scripts Served Card Skimmer and iOS Exploit Kits to CNN, BBC and Zoom Visitors

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1252 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely Web Experimentation to plant malicious code in some of the scripts that customers' websites load from the service, Optimizely stated early today.
  • Visitors to sites run by at least 178 organizations, including CNN, the BBC and Zoom, received the code yesterday, according to Report URI, a firm that monitors the scripts websites run.
  • Industry observers note that the code was built to replace crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's own addresses and to capture card details, but the firm cannot see how many card numbers were exposed to the attacker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely Web Experimentation to plant malicious code in some of the scripts that customers' websites load from the service, Optimizely stated early today.

Visitors to sites run by at least 178 organizations, including CNN, the BBC and Zoom, received the code yesterday, according to Report URI, a firm that monitors the scripts websites run.

Industry observers note that the code was built to replace crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's own addresses and to capture card details, but the firm cannot see how many card numbers were exposed to the attacker. The vendor says it has fixed the flaw and removed the code.

On iPhones and iPads, the code was also set up to load a second stage that the firm identifies as an iOS exploit kit, but it reports no iPhones actually being taken over.

In an incident notice posted at 01:02 UTC, Optimizely noted the attacker had "exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.

It has been revealed that the vendor has also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and added protections to stop unauthorized code from being delivered. The notice does not say how the flaw worked, how many projects were changed, when the fix went in, whether the attacker still has any access, or what customers should do.

Smartsheet's script was cleaned once and then re-infected with a hidden version of the code, which indicates the attacker still had access at that point, according to the firm.

Writing before the notice appeared, the firm stated it did not know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: "That's for Optimizely to explain.".

It has been revealed that sites that use the service to run experiments on their pages load a script from the vendor, called a snippet. The snippet updates itself whenever the customer changes a setting, according to the vendor's snippet documentation. Each time it loads, it runs a field of custom code called Project JavaScript.

Recent findings suggest that the attacker wrote a loader into the Project JavaScript of customer projects and left the rest of each snippet untouched, Report URI noted in its technical analysis. The snippets were still served from cdn.optimizely.com with the vendor's own certificate, so every page that loaded one also ran the loader.

Some sites serve the snippet from their own domain, and those were affected too, because the content comes from the same project.

The loader came in three versions. Most snippets loaded 1688360[.]cc/track.js directly, one version hid that address in base64 so a text search for the domain would miss it, and another carried a full copy of the payload that runs if the domain is blocked.

Cynet, whose endpoint detection flagged browser connections to the attacker's server, traced the loader to a file served from cdn.optimizely.com in an endpoint investigation. Its researchers also captured the code on CNN and Zoom pages. A site that delivered the code has not necessarily had its own systems compromised, the researchers say.

The firm checked 1,611 Optimizely snippets, mostly identified through its own crawl data, and found code in 188 of them, belonging to 178 organizations. It says the real number is likely higher because it could only check the snippets it found in time. Its post lists all 178, with their domains.

Besides CNN, the BBC and Zoom, the infected snippets belonged to Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock, among others. The vendor's own main site and login page also carried the code. Some researchers call the campaign OPTIMJACK.

In a recent development, the first injection was seen at 04:21 UTC yesterday, in the BBC's snippet. A mass cleanup began at about 20:40 UTC, and by 21:52 UTC only TalkTalk's snippet still carried the code.

That first injection loaded webshell[.]lol, which the firm calls the same actor's injector. The injector had also been planted through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts since late last week, and it first appeared on Turkish sites on September 17.

The payload, a file called track.js, replaces valid crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's in page text, forms, links, the clipboard and outgoing requests.

It swaps only an address that passes its chain's checksum and sits near a payment word such as wallet, deposit or send, according to a payload analysis by StepSecurity. Copying is not safe either: an address a visitor copies from one of these pages may already be the attacker's by the time it is pasted into a wallet.

Sources indicate that A card skimmer, added at 13:43 UTC, captures the card number, expiry date, and CVV when they are submitted via the site's form fields and sends them to the attacker's server. It cannot read cards entered in a cross-origin payment iframe, such as Stripe's hosted fields or Adyen's.

According to recent reports, the firm identifies the iOS exploit kits as Coruna and DarkSword, as documented by Google researchers. The Coruna exploit kit targets iOS 13.0 to 17.2.1, and the DarkSword exploit kit targets iOS 18.4 to 18.7.

On iPhones and iPads, the code loads a script called boot.js from two .icu domains. That script reads the iOS version and opens an exploit chain in a hidden iframe: Coruna for iOS 13 to 17, DarkSword for iOS 18, and, for iOS 26, a separate chain that so far only collects details about the device.

Industry observers note that between 17:13 and 17:57 UTC, the attacker also added a Coruna iframe to every visit from iOS 18.6 or earlier. Those pages reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, a sign a visitor could notice. The kit's own comments mark iOS 18.7.3 and later, and iOS 26.3 and later, as patched, according to the firm.

Cynet's researchers retrieved the second stage using an emulated iPhone browser and describe what they saw as conditional delivery, "not a successful compromise of a physical iPhone or iPad.".

Industry observers note that the firm states crypto has already been stolen. As of 19:25 UTC yesterday, the attacker's wallets had received about $7,040, all within roughly nine hours.

Recent findings suggest that stepSecurity put the total across the same addresses at about $6,600. Two of the addresses were already in use before the injections began, and its analysts wrote that "the chain does not show which transfers came from victims.".

Report URI recommends these checks for sites that use Optimizely Web Experimentation:.

The firm kept a copy of every infected snippet, with hashes and timestamps, and could share them with affected organizations and CERTs (computer emergency response teams) on request.

For anyone who visited an affected site on Monday, the firm advises:.

According to recent reports, A snippet that is clean now may still have served the code on Monday. StepSecurity also advises:.

Cynet treats cdn.optimizely.com as a legitimate delivery host rather than an indicator, and it advises against broad blocks of that host or of the affected news sites.

The payload changed multiple times during the day, so a single file hash will not capture every version. These indicators come from the researchers' published lists:.

#367. Industry News: Ten Years On, Google Updates the SRE Book for the AI Era

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1096 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq

Industry News: Ten Years On, Google Updates the SRE Book for the AI Era

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1096 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Ten Years On, Google Updates the SRE Book for the AI Era.
  • Nov 17, 2026 5 min read.
  • Google has unveiled a completely rewritten second edition of their seminal book Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems, ten years after the original book was first published.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Ten Years On, Google Updates the SRE Book for the AI Era.

Nov 17, 2026 5 min read.

Google has unveiled a completely rewritten second edition of their seminal book Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems, ten years after the original book was first published. The book updates thinking on site reliability engineering (SRE) to encompass modern cloud architectures, platform engineering and AI workloads, whilst keeping the original emphasis on applying good software engineering techniques to operations work.

Revealed by Google's SRE programme manager Betsy Beyer and software engineer David Huska, the latest edition is positioned as a response to a production environment that has changed substantially since 2016, when the first edition appeared. The authors argue that the central problem is no longer adopting cloud infrastructure, but maintaining reliability as systems become more distributed, interdependent and continuously changing.

Sources indicate that the original SRE book became influential because it gave a public account of how Google operated large-scale services. It described practices such as service level objectives (SLOs), error budgets, toil reduction, incident management and postmortems. InfoQ's 2016 review noted that the book presented SRE as the application of software engineering to an operations function, with engineers expected to automate repetitive operational work rather than simply respond to it.

Sources indicate that the second edition does not present SRE as a fixed set of practices. Instead, it describes how those practices have changed as organisations have moved from early cloud migration and monolithic applications towards microservices, multi-cloud deployments, serverless systems and internal developer platforms.

One of the clearest changes over the years concerns SLOs and error budgets. Google says that teams once relied on basic availability metrics and manually applied error-budget policies. The revised guidance describes user-centred, multi-tiered SLOs, dynamic burn-rate alerting and automated policy enforcement. Reliability practice itself has evolved away from infrastructure uptime alone and towards measures that describe the effect of failures on owners.

Observability has also evolved, and the book's latest edition talks this through. The first edition's world of static dashboards, basic logs and manual alert triage has given way, in Google's account, to OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing and automated anomaly correlation. The aim is not merely to collect more telemetry, but to reduce the time between an alert and a credible explanation of what has failed.

Automation is the third major area of revision. Google describes a movement from custom scripts addressing isolated tasks towards declarative infrastructure as code, internal developer platforms and self-healing systems. This aligns with the platform-engineering model now common in larger organisations: reliability capabilities are built once into a platform and consumed by product teams, rather than being reimplemented by every team.

Sources indicate that reliability testing has also changed. Google contrasts scheduled game days and synthetic load tests with continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing and live production canary verification. The practical implication is that resilience becomes part of the delivery pipeline rather than an occasional exercise performed before a major release.

According to recent reports, capacity management is another area where the book has been updated. Google says that manual provisioning and static forecasting have been replaced by dynamic auto-scaling, cloud FinOps alignment and optimisation for GPU and TPU clusters. This matters because AI training and inference workloads can concentrate demand on scarce accelerated computing resources, making capacity planning, networking and cost control more operationally significant.

Industry observers note that generative AI inevitably appears in the second edition, in two facets. First, SRE is presented as a discipline needed to operate AI infrastructure. The book covers the reliability of large GPU and TPU clusters, network topologies, non-deterministic model outputs, latency behaviour and the pipelines used for training, fine-tuning and data processing. These are different operational problems from those posed by a conventional stateless web service.

In a recent development, second, AI is presented as a tool for reliability engineers. The post welcomes generative AI support for incident triage and postmortem writing, natural-language queries over telemetry, and predictive models that identify resource bottlenecks before they cause an outage. The examples in the announcement mostly place AI in a supporting role, gathering and organising evidence for engineers, rather than claiming that AI can replace operational judgement. Recent industry activity appears to support this, with InfoQ reporting in October 2026 that Datadog had released Scout, a specialist model intended to investigate production problems inside its Bits AI SRE product. Other vendors are exploring similar territory, including Honeycomb's Canvas Agent, Splunk AI SRE and New Relic's SRE Agent. InfoQ also reported in February 2026 on Google Cloud SREs using the Gemini CLI during real outages; using AI to help engineers work through incidents, rather than as an autonomous replacement for on-call staff.

The announcement also revises the organisational side of SRE. Google describes a move beyond dedicated SRE teams attached to particular applications, towards hybrid models, platform-engineering integration and reliability champions embedded in product teams. This has come about because many organisations cannot staff a central SRE team for every service, so reliability expertise has to be distributed more widely.

Despite the technological updates, Google argues that the underlying culture has not changed. The authors restate the importance of reliability-focused culture and expand the book's coverage of the human aspects of systems engineering. David Blank-Edelman made a related point in a presentation, You Are Asking the Wrong Questions (about Reliability and SRE), delivered at InfoQ Dev Summit Boston in 2025. He argued that reliability work should start from the customer's perspective rather than the component's perspective, and described SRE as fundamentally collaborative. He also challenged the conventional focus on a single root cause, favouring an examination of the contributing factors behind a failure.

Recent findings suggest that the second edition is available in physical format through Google Books and in digital format from O'Reilly. For teams already practising SRE, its value is likely to lie less in introducing familiar concepts than in showing how those concepts have been adapted for platforms, distributed systems and AI-heavy infrastructure. For organisations earlier in their reliability journey, it remains a substantial reference on how to make operations a software-engineering problem rather than a collection of manual tasks.

#366. A reader found a hole in our AI inbox. Postgres closes it now

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1050 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

A reader found a hole in our AI inbox. Postgres closes it now

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in my last post I wrote about how our AI assistant can write to exactly one table.
  • Industry observers note that I ended that post with "the inbox is where the real control happens".
  • A proposal can go stale in the inbox too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in my last post I wrote about how our AI assistant can write to exactly one table. Claude, connected to Reperline over MCP, can only insert rows into pending_changes. A person approves or rejects each one in an inbox, and apply_pending_change writes the real tables with the approver's own rights.

Industry observers note that I ended that post with "the inbox is where the real control happens". In the comments, Mike Johnstone pointed out that the inbox had a hole of its own:.

A proposal can go stale in the inbox too. If someone changes a milestone before approval, the reviewer may be looking at a diff against an old value.

He was right, and the bug was worse than a confusing screen. This post is the fix, migration 064.

A milestone proposal carries an absolute value, not a delta:.

Here is the sequence that broke it:.

Recent findings suggest that progress just went down by five points. Our normal entry path refuses to lower progress without a note explaining why, but that rule lived in the application function that records a fact from the UI and Telegram. The approval path wrote the journal directly, so the drop went in silently. Nobody did anything wrong, and the database accepted a value that was already false when it was approved.

The grants from the first post did their job. Claude still wrote nothing by itself. A person approved a stale diff, and the approval was the hole.

It has been revealed that the quick fix is to show the current value next to the proposal and hope the reviewer notices. We do show it now, but a check that lives only on the screen is the same kind of promise the first post was about avoiding. Another client, a script or a second tab can still approve. The check had to be inside apply_pending_change, in the same transaction as the write.

According to recent reports, mike suggested storing the base row version with the proposal. The idea is right; choosing which version took most of the work.

Industry observers note that A row version such as xmin. It changes on any upgrade of the milestone row, including a renamed milestone or a corrected planned date. Every unrelated edit would strand every open proposal.

The current progress value alone. It misses the case 70 → 55 → 70: someone records a drop, then measures again and records 70. The value is back where it was, but two facts were entered that the proposal never saw. The reviewer should look again.

In a recent development, the id or timestamp of the latest journal row. Facts can be back dated (reported_at is when the work was measured, not when it was typed), so "latest by reported_at" misses a late entry of an older measurement. created_at is the transaction start time, so rows inserted in one transaction tie, and a transaction that started earlier can commit later.

It has been revealed that what we used: the number of journal rows plus the progress value. Every fact for a milestone is a new row in milestone_updates, and a trigger moves milestones.progress on every insert. So the count changes exactly when progress may have changed, regardless of dates. Comparing progress as well covers the remaining blind spot (a delete plus an insert keeps the count). Our app never deletes a fact, but the role technically still holds DELETE, so we did not want to rely on that.

If Claude sent the base, a prompt could make it send whatever value makes the check pass. So the base is stamped by a BEFORE INSERT trigger, and anything the client put in those keys is overwritten:.

In apply_pending_change the milestone branch now does this before writing:.

Recent findings suggest that the split into two statements matters. Under READ COMMITTED, each statement inside a PL/pgSQL function gets a fresh snapshot. If the count ran in the same statement as the lock, it could use a snapshot taken before the lock was granted. A fact that committed while we were waiting would be missing from the count, and we would approve over it.

It has been revealed that the lock also closes the window from the other side. Inserting a fact takes a KEY SHARE lock on the milestone (the foreign key) and the trigger then updates the row, so no fact can land between our check and our own journal insert.

is distinct from instead of <> matters too: it treats null as a value, so a null base never compares equal to anything.

Rejecting is never checked. A stale proposal can always be thrown away; it just cannot be approved.

Recent findings suggest that the UI shows the same thing the database enforces. A stale proposal gets a red notice ("It was 55% when proposed. A fact was entered since, so the proposal can only be rejected.") and a disabled Approve button. That is a display hint only. The function refuses on its own, and the error key proposal_stale is translated for anyone who reaches it some other way.

Proposals that were already waiting when the migration ran were backfilled with the current state, so the existing inbox was not stranded by the upgrade.

Each case runs against a real Postgres, with Claude's role filing the proposal:.

That last one is the case that is easiest to get wrong and hardest to see in review, so it is the one I would not ship without.

Sources indicate that the first post was about making sure the AI cannot write. This one is about the next layer: a person approving is only meaningful if they approve against the data as it is now. Optimistic concurrency is an old idea; the work was in choosing a version marker that changes when it should and only then, and in making the stamp something the proposer cannot fake.

And thanks to Mike. A comment section that finds a real bug in a week is worth more than any launch post.

If you are building an approval inbox for an AI agent: store what the proposal was based on, stamp it on the server, and check it under a lock in the same transaction that writes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've moved to Poland, you've heard the horror stories about the karta pobytu (residence card). Forums are full of guesses. So we stopped guessing.

Industry observers note that on 7 October 2026 we sent identical freedom-of-information requests to all 16 voivodeship offices (urzędy wojewódzkie) and asked for the average time from application to decision. 11 have replied so far. Every number below is copied from their official letters.

* Decisions issued 1 Jan to 30 Sep 2026 (Poznań and Kielce didn't state the end date; Poznań's figures are approximate).

It has been revealed that these are means, not medians, so a few very long cases pull them up. They describe past decisions, not a forecast for a upcoming application, and offices count differently. Details are in the README.

The 5 missing offices (Lublin, Gdańsk, Katowice, Białystok, Wrocław) will be added when they reply. If you build something with it, I'd love to see it.

Collected by Expat Essentials Poland, free plain-English guides for foreigners in Poland.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Scaling LLM-Based Ranking Systems for Latency-Critical Search & Recommendation Workloads.

It has been revealed that sundara Raman Ramachandran shares how LinkedIn productionizes LLM ranking under strict P99 latency SLAs. He discusses distilling a 7B model down to 400M parameters, compressing job contexts into single-token embeddings for a 10x throughput leap, and eliminating hidden system bottlenecks - from custom flash attention masks to Python GIL workarounds, gc.freeze, and non-blocking CUDA memory copies.

Sources indicate that sundara Raman Ramachandran is a Lead Engineer on LinkedIn’s LLM Inference team, where he plays a key role in designing and scaling the infrastructure powering LLM-based ranking systems for search and recommendation. His work centers on building latency-critical, high-throughput LLM serving platforms that operate reliably at global scale.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Sources indicate that these are like user culprits. You go rule them out, and then you have to spend more time debugging what's happening, and the root cause turned out to be the garbage collector. In model server, when you load the model and there are a lot of long-lived Python objects that get created that lives through the lifecycle of the overall process. What was happening is this Python garbage collector was kicking in every few seconds and was scanning each of these objects to figure out which one it should free. In a recent development, after this, whatever temporary object that gets created during the request path is the one the garbage collector will be interested in. With this fix we were able to get the P99 in a stable way. The next bottleneck was Python's infamous Global Interpreter Lock, which effectively makes Python bytecode executable by single thread only once at a time. It's different from how Java and C++ and all those things can give you true parallelism when you are working with threads. Python is a different thing all together. In LinkedIn's system, we take the open-source engines we have, and we take the SGLang engine, and then put it behind a gRPC servicer process. In a recent development, because of the Global Interpreter Lock, and when we send large QPS the single servicer process became the bottleneck. In order to fix this, we replaced a single process with multiple processes, so that all of them can do this work in parallel in separate CPU cores. Once we solve the bottleneck on a servicer with multiprocessing, the SGLang worker process which is effectively preparing the work and dispatching the work to the GPU became the bottleneck. The fix here is again the same, instead of one process you will have multiple processes. The callout here is, each process has its own model copy and it's going to have its own CUDA stream and do the kernel releases and MemSync and whatnot, and it's effectively going to time slice the GPU. In our case we were able to do it because the model was smaller. Nowadays I think we get enough HBM in the GPU, so you should be able to deploy this as well. The callout again here, in production systems based on Python, is, worry about this Global Interpreter Lock and this can be your single fix which can help improve the throughput.

It turned out, we were doing our benchmarks incorrectly. When we are simulating synthetic traffic, we were effectively using even distribution to send the request. What it means is within a second interval, you are estimating based on QPS. You're going to say that my throughput is 1000 jobs per second, 1000 items per second, or something of that sort. When you're simulating the synthetic traffic, the requests are getting sent in an equally spaced manner.

All of them arrive in a uniform distribution with equal spaces. In production, when you're serving real time user traffic, you cannot expect the owners to follow the same patterns. Within a second interval, you might have a surge in requests so the queue depth increases. After that, there could be some quieter periods. The major takeaway from this here is if you are serving systems in production, the closest possible result you can get is if you can record and replay your production traffic. If you don't have that option, the second closest thing you could get is if you can simulate the synthetic traffic using a Poisson distribution instead of an even distribution. Just make sure you're doing the right thing there. The second learning is what I call offline must match online. What do we mean by this? When you're working with a model-based system in production, there is an engineer who's going to work on fine-tuning the model.

There'll be prompt engineers who are designing the prompts, and they have their own set of code. The system that gets deployed in production is entirely different. You might be leveraging an open-source system, or you might be leveraging your own model server. There are a set of defaults which is different from both these. Like for example, a simple tokenization config like add end of sequence or beginning of sequence config, can change the entire prompt in itself. You have to make sure there is absolute parity between the offline and the online system. Don't discover all these disparities or discrepancies in production. Disparity has to be a gate without which you cannot launch in production at all.

The third learning is the crux of the talk. There is no single fix here when you are serving systems in production, models, LLMs, anything of that sort. You have to squeeze in throughput from all the possible places. You have to make the model as small as possible, and you have to make the context as short as possible and make the inference as efficient as possible. The final learning, if there are any tech leads, managers, and leaders, this is for you guys. When you are dealing with production systems, there are multiple actors here. You have the inference engineers. You have the model engineers. You have the prompt engineers. You have the product managers who are defining the product policies. It's very crucial that we bring all of these actors into one setup, one meeting which is recurring. You can have a standup or a meeting every week so that each of them can share their idea, cross check, cross validate everything.

You will be surprised how many issues you can catch in these meetings before even you get to production. We often think about optimizations as, if we have to optimize the code, we have to optimize the CPU, GPU, Python, Java, C++, Rust, and all those things. The first and foremost optimization we had to do is with respect to bringing the right people together, you remove the communication barrier and make sure you allow them to share their ideas, and then effectively improve the overall system in play.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple on Monday introduced fresh controls that allow Mac people to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.
  • The changes, presently previewed in macOS 27.3 beta 2, relate to increased transparency and more options for two of its APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access.
  • It has been revealed that "Before granting an app such extraordinary access, customers should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk," Apple said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple on Monday introduced fresh controls that allow Mac people to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

The changes, presently previewed in macOS 27.3 beta 2, relate to increased transparency and more options for two of its APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access.

It has been revealed that "Before granting an app such extraordinary access, customers should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk," Apple said in a statement. "These changes are designed to help them do that and to empower them to make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.".

To that end, Device Control and Data Access is being split into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility.

Apple stressed that app permissions previously granted by users will remain intact, adding that developers should be prepared to make changes to their onboarding workflows to ensure their apps can handle scenarios where access is granted to only a limited set of folders or apps via these APIs.

In addition, apps that use Full Disk Access for disk backup or the fresh Accessibility settings for assistive technologies can request entitlements to offer the same experience for new installations that they offered before macOS 27.3.

"Presently, known apps aren't affected and will keep the same experience without an entitlement," the tech giant added. "Additional entitlement details will be available soon.".

The development comes a little over a month after Apple began taking steps to tighten controls around a macOS setting called Full Disk Access (FDA) due to security risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An AI-simulated client is an AI-powered character that allows trainees to practise realistic counselling conversations without requiring a human role-play partner for every session. The system can respond to what the trainee claims, maintain a scenario, adapt the conversation and provide structured feedback after the session.

That is the idea behind PraxisAI, an AI human-skills simulation and assessment platform built by ThinkShift. Trainee counsellors can practise conversations with AI clients through voice, avatar and chat, with sessions evaluated against defined competencies.

The interesting engineering challenge isn't simply making an AI that can talk.

It is making an AI that can stay inside a scenario, behave consistently, create a useful training experience and turn a conversation into measurable feedback.

That became the core problem we explored while building PraxisAI.

An AI-simulated client is a virtual client powered by AI for training or role-play.

Instead of following a fixed dialogue tree, the simulated client can respond dynamically to the trainee's questions and statements. This makes the interaction less predictable than traditional scripted practice.

For counselling training, that distinction matters.

A trainee shouldn't only practise asking a predefined list of questions. They need to experience what happens when a conversation changes direction, when a client gives an unexpected answer, or when important information emerges gradually.

Recent research has started evaluating generative AI in exactly this role. Studies have found that AI can provide a flexible environment for practising counselling skills, while also identifying limitations around emotional nuance, authenticity, cultural dynamics and overly agreeable responses.

So the product challenge becomes:.

How do you make an AI conversation useful for learning, rather than simply interesting to interact with?

Traditional role-play is valuable, but it has practical limitations.

Sources indicate that two students need to be available at the same time. One person has to play the client. The scenario may change depending on the person playing the role. And repeating the same exercise many times isn't always easy.

An AI client introduces another option.

A trainee can practise a scenario, review the interaction, try again and compare the results.

Practice → Conversation → Feedback → Reflection → Practice again.

The value is not that AI replaces a supervisor or a human client.

The value is that it can create additional opportunities to practise between structured teaching and real-world experience.

Research published in 2025 similarly found that AI-simulated counselling sessions could offer a psychologically safer and flexible environment for practice, while concluding that AI should supplement rather than replace live training.

A generic chatbot can answer questions.

A useful training simulator needs to do more.

Imagine a scenario where a client is initially reluctant to discuss a particular problem.

If the trainee asks an open-ended question, the client might gradually reveal more.

If the trainee interrupts or asks a leading question, the client might respond differently.

If the trainee demonstrates empathy and creates space, the conversation may develop in another direction.

The system therefore needs to maintain more than conversational fluency.

It needs to maintain scenario state.

Without this context, an AI client can swiftly start behaving like a generic assistant.

And that breaks the simulation.

Realism doesn't mean making the AI sound human in every sentence.

In a training environment, realism means creating behaviour that makes sense within the scenario.

These behaviours create opportunities for the trainee to practise actual communication skills.

Research into AI-simulated counselling has identified a similar challenge: AI can produce convincing interactions, but overly idealised responses, limited emotional nuance and missing non-verbal cues can reduce authenticity.

That means realism has to be treated as a product design problem, not just an LLM prompt.

This was one of the biggest distinctions in building PraxisAI.

A chatbot answers a user's message.

A training simulator has a learning objective.

Those are very different systems.

For example, the objective might be to help a trainee practise reflective listening.

The system then needs to evaluate the conversation against that competency rather than simply deciding whether the final answer sounded good.

This creates a second layer around the AI conversation:.

AI client → conversation → competency evaluation → feedback.

That second layer is where the product becomes a training system.

A realistic conversation is useful.

A realistic conversation followed by useful feedback is much more useful.

After a practice session, trainees need to understand what happened.

Instead of receiving a generic score such as:.

the feedback should connect the assessment to the actual interaction.

This creates a connection between what happened and what to practise next.

PraxisAI is designed around this assessment layer, with sessions evaluated against competencies rather than treating the conversation as an isolated chatbot interaction.

One of the interesting product challenges is that counselling isn't one single skill.

Different approaches can emphasise different techniques and competencies.

So an assessment system needs to understand the context in which a conversation is taking place.

That means the evaluation layer needs to consider:.

Scenario + approach + conversation + competency framework.

Conversation + generic AI score.

This is vital because the same response could be appropriate in one context and less useful in another.

The assessment therefore becomes part of the product architecture, not something added after the AI conversation has been built.

Another useful distinction is between practice and assessment.

During practice, the trainee is learning.

They may want guidance, feedback and opportunities to repeat a scenario.

During assessment, the objective is different: the trainee should demonstrate their skills with less intervention.

Separating these experiences makes the product more useful because the system is supporting two different user goals.

This is a broader lesson for AI product development:.

Don't build one AI experience and expect it to serve every stage of the user's journey.

The AI behaviour, interface and evaluation system should change according to what the user is trying to accomplish.

PraxisAI is designed around multiple interaction formats, including voice, avatar and chat.

This creates another product consideration.

Text-based interaction gives the system a clean representation of the conversation.

Voice introduces additional dimensions such as:.

An avatar adds another visual layer to the experience.

The underlying training objective, however, should remain consistent.

The interface can change without losing the core learning loop:.

Interact → Evaluate → Understand → Improve.

That separation between the interaction layer and the learning layer is useful when designing AI training products.

It is easy to demonstrate an AI role-play by writing a detailed prompt.

Building a reliable product around that interaction is much harder.

You need scenario management, user flows, evaluation logic, feedback, persistence and a clear learning objective.

Giving an AI complete freedom doesn't necessarily produce the best simulation.

Training scenarios need constraints.

The AI should have enough freedom to create natural conversations while remaining consistent with the scenario and learning objective.

If every assessment is generated from scratch, results can become inconsistent.

A useful training system needs defined competencies and a consistent evaluation framework.

The AI can then interpret the conversation within those boundaries.

The most visible part of an AI simulator is the conversation.

But the less visible parts, scenario setup, evaluation, feedback and progress tracking, may create much of the product's actual value.

This is perhaps the most key lesson.

AI simulation can create more practice opportunities, but it doesn't reproduce everything that happens in a real human interaction.

Current research continues to identify limitations around emotional depth, authenticity, cultural sensitivity and non-verbal communication.

ThinkShift is based in Dubai and focuses on building working products that can be tested with real consumers rather than spending months building around assumptions.

That approach influenced how we thought about PraxisAI.

"How can we build a chatbot for counsellors?".

That change in framing affected the product.

The AI conversation became one component.

The competency framework became another.

And the feedback loop connected everything together.

That is an important distinction when building AI products in Dubai—or anywhere else.

The technology is only one part of the product. The real work is connecting the technology to a measurable user problem.

AI-simulated clients should be considered a supplement to human-led training, not a replacement for supervisors, educators or real human interaction.

AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms. Andrew leads the … More about Andrew ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

Lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up.

We asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most stated they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage.

These results point to a two-speed workflow. AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible?

Accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now.

According to recent reports, this matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor.

In a recent development, so how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace?

We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently.

Industry observers note that here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge indicates up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training, communication, and a culture of accessibility.

In a recent development, A quick caveat: This is survey data, so it only indicates correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore.

Recent findings suggest that and it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize issues. They were also nearly three times as likely to say it helps them tackle accessibility more proactively in development.

In other words, AI works best as an amplifier of a strong program. With context, testing, environments, and guardrails in place, agents can take on a large share of the work from drafting through to operations, and much of the time lost to waiting and handoffs goes away. People stay responsible for deciding what to build and for approving what ships.

So let me ask you: When it comes to accessibility, where does human judgment sit in your workflow today?

According to recent reports, not sure? Here’s a quick way to find out.

Pick a feature you shipped recently and trace it from the first Figma frame to production. Mark every moment a person decided whether it would work for someone using a keyboard, a screen reader, or their browser at 400% zoom.

How many marks did you get? If most of them cluster at the end of creation, you’re likely heading to one of two places: You’ll either ship accessibility barriers or spend the time you saved upstream fixing them later, when they’re harder and costlier to fix.

Here’s how to avoid both outcomes by building the right accessibility checks and judgment calls into the work your team is already doing.

As AI takes on more work, people need to stay involved at three points: finding complications, fixing them, and documenting the evidence. Each one plugs into a step your team already takes, like a handoff, a pull request, or a review, so nothing upcoming gets added to the timeline, and accessibility keeps pace with the work that’s in motion.

Context fades fast. Put the first judgment checkpoints as close to the creation work as you can:.

Industry observers note that found the issue? Great. Fix it while it’s fresh. When complications end up as tickets, make sure the context travels with them. They should carry the element, the repro, the related WCAG criterion, a suggested fix, and the PR link, so context doesn’t leak.

The worst time to start gathering evidence is when somebody’s asking for it.

Every check, fix, and judgment call throughout the process described above should ideally leave a trail. A fix isn’t done until something fails if the glitch comes back. Ask your AI assistant to write the regression test with the fix and put the finding link and any judgment call in the PR description. That’s the receipt.

According to recent reports, A passing test shows a known issue hasn’t returned. It doesn’t show the experience works. For what automation can’t cover, add a short note to the PR: what you tested, with which assistive technology, and any judgment calls you made.

AI has given digital creation a speed boost, but broadly speaking, validating the work hasn’t kept pace. Closing that gap isn’t about adopting more AI in more places or abandoning the toolset that helped make your team faster.

According to our data, the opportunity in front of teams is to build the practice around that toolset, so that human judgment is flagged, embedded, and acted on earlier, and more often.

Industry observers note that we’ve only scratched the surface of what our data tells us about AI and accessibility. If you’re curious about what else we found, check out the 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. There’s plenty more to unpack.

  • The model has been trained on a lot of “always memoize callbacks passed to children” advice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the PR “cleans up” a form by wrapping every event handler in useCallback and every derived boolean in useMemo. The commit message says “performance.” There is no profile, no skipped render that mattered, and two stale-closure bugs in the validation path.

According to recent reports, I’ve started treating agent-added useMemo / useCallback without a stated reason as noise, not as an optimization. React is not cheaper just because the call site looks official. The wrappers are extra dependencies to get wrong.

The model has been trained on a lot of “always memoize callbacks passed to children” advice. Some of that advice was aimed at class components, or at a child wrapped in memo that actually sits in a hot list. A one-off in a settings page is not that situation.

In a recent development, useMemo also lies about cost. Memoizing a boolean const isEmpty = items.length === 0 is slower to think about than the comparison. Memoizing a massive filtered list can be real — if the input is large and the parent renders often. That sentence should be in the PR, not implied by the hook.

Stale closures show up when the dependency array omits a function or a piece of form state. The memo was added to help, and now a submit handler sees yesterday’s values.

If the team already has a lint rule (react-hooks, react/no-unstable-nested-components), the agent should follow it, not pre-empt it with wrappers everywhere.

Sources indicate that in review, if the hook was not there before the bugfix, ask whether the bugfix still works with the hook removed. Many times it does.

Industry observers note that A useful exception is a context provider that passes a large value object into a wide tree. Stabilizing that value can be real work. Stabilizing a click handler on a leaf button, in the same PR, is still decoration. If the agent “also memoized the context value,” make it show the provider file and the consumers, not a blanket hook pass.

useMemo is not a substitute for moving expensive work out of render — a filter over 20,000 rows belongs in a worker, a query library, or a precomputed index, not in a hook that still runs on the main thread the first time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A CVE record can create an assumption that a vendor patch exists somewhere and that the main task is deployment. CVE-2026-111461 breaks that assumption. The affected OnCell G3150A-LTE Series is end of life, and Moxa's mitigation is to keep SMS management disabled rather than to install a upcoming firmware release for this line.

According to recent reports, moxa's MPSA-269510 advisory assigns CVE-2026-111461 to an OS command injection flaw in the OnCell G3150A-LTE Series. The concern is CWE-78, the CVSS 4.0 score is 7.5, and the SMS upgrade argument reaches system() without escaping. The vendor says all firmware versions are affected and unauthenticated remote exploitation does not apply.

Industry observers note that the advisory also covers CVE-2026-111459 and CVE-2026-111460. An inventory should preserve the exact CVE and product relationship instead of treating the whole advisory as a generic Moxa event.

An operator cannot disable SMS on an unknown gateway. An operator also cannot verify a management path when a device is represented only by a spreadsheet row with no network owner. The first evidence gap is usually completeness.

Industry observers note that build a list from procurement records, network discovery, firewall addresses, and site maintenance logs. Match each candidate against the OnCell G3150A-LTE Series. Record firmware, site, operational purpose, management address, account owner, SMS state, and replacement status. Mark duplicate addresses and devices behind NAT so that a count is not mistaken for a unique asset count.

Industry observers note that configuration records age quickly. A device that was installed with SMS disabled may have been changed during a field test or restored from a backup that enabled it. Verify the setting on the device or through an approved management channel.

The same applies to privileges. The CVE requires high privileges, so the account list is part of the inventory. Determine which consumers can perform SMS or upgrade operations and whether shared or stale accounts remain.

ZoomEye returned 330 matches for app="Moxa OnCell". The exact CVE query returned 0. The product count is not proof of vulnerability, and the zero CVE result does not mean no affected assets exist. The comparison is useful because a product fingerprint can reveal a gateway that the internal inventory missed.

According to recent reports, do not place an external match directly into a victim list. Verify ownership, reachability, configuration, and evidence of compromise separately.

In a recent development, for each affected gateway, choose one of three documented states: retired, approved for controlled use with SMS disabled, or approved for controlled use with SMS enabled for a specific operational requirement. The last state needs a stronger exception with limited access, monitoring, and an end date.

In a recent development, moxa's general recommendations support this approach. Limit communication to trusted networks, avoid direct internet exposure, disable unused services, enforce least privilege, and review logs. None of those controls should remain only in a policy document.

The inventory is ready for risk decisions when every known OnCell device has an owner and verified SMS state, management-network paths are documented, and every remains-in-service exception has an accountable approver. That is a higher bar than a scanner count, and a more useful one for an end-of-life command injection flaw.

#358. Industry News: We don't need more apps. We need better open source

Industry News: We don't need more apps. We need better open source

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, every day, a dozen people post a fresh app they built with AI over a weekend: a habit tracker, a to-do list, another note-taking app.
  • But far less of that energy goes into the open source software we already rely on.
  • In a recent development, people call this latest way of building “vibecoding.” I hate the name; it makes a real shift in who gets to write software sound like a joke.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every day, a dozen people post a fresh app they built with AI over a weekend: a habit tracker, a to-do list, another note-taking app. I’m glad! More people building things is one of the best parts of this moment.

But far less of that energy goes into the open source software we already rely on.

In a recent development, people call this latest way of building “vibecoding.” I hate the name; it makes a real shift in who gets to write software sound like a joke. I’ll call it AI-assisted coding, and I think it could aim somewhere more useful.

Free and open source software already does most of what my clients and I need. What it often can’t do is run well on a cheap server, install in one step, or stay up without forum threads at 11pm.

According to recent reports, I self-host a lot of my own stuff, and I help progressive nonprofits with their tech for a living. I run a Matrix server (Synapse, Element and a moderation bot) for a community with thousands of users. I also run apps on Coolify and Hetzner, keep my paperwork in Paperless-ngx, and own a Mac Mini that’s always one download from a full disk.

The software is usually great. Running it is the hard part. Install guides assume you know five other tools. Upgrades break things. Apps eat 4GB of RAM to serve a handful of people. Error messages tell you nothing.

My nonprofit clients would love to leave Big Tech for privacy, cost and owning their data. But the open source option usually needs a part-time sysadmin they don’t have, so they pay for the corporate tool.

Sources indicate that A new to-do app usually helps the few people who find it. Making a tool millions already use 20% lighter helps all of them, every day.

This is also the work that slides when maintainers are tired, and many are unpaid volunteers. We saw the risk in 2024. Someone spent years earning the trust of the worn-out solo maintainer of xz, a compression tool inside most Linux systems, then slipped a backdoor into it.

In a recent development, I think this unglamorous work suits AI well: profiling slow code, writing tests that make massive changes safe, testing installers, rewriting cryptic errors, writing the missing docs. It takes patience more than brilliance, plus a person who checks every line.

According to recent reports, it matters politically too. If organizations are going to own their data instead of renting it from a few giant companies, open source has to be something a 20-person nonprofit can run. I want AI’s gains shared widely. Better public tools that anyone can use, change and share are one way to get there.

Sources indicate that maintainers have already seen the wrong way. The curl project ended its bug bounty in January 2026 after a flood of fake, AI-generated security reports. By April, its lead developer wrote that the fakes were mostly gone and almost every report used AI, most of them very good. The latest problem is volume. Even good work can bury a maintainer. So:.

Sources indicate that pick one open source tool you use. Find the most annoying thing about installing or running it. Spend a weekend fixing it, with the people who maintain it. Then tell me about it.

#357. Hybrid Search, Measured

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1245 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

Hybrid Search, Measured

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1245 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ask a retrieval system about one error code and it may answer from the record for a different one.
  • According to recent reports, this is the standing argument for hybrid search: keep the vector index for meaning, add a keyword index for the strings that must match exactly, merge the two lists.
  • Most of it is our own writing: 325 chunks cut from fifty of the posts on this blog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Originally published at Trida AI.

It has been revealed that ask a retrieval system about one error code and it may answer from the record for a different one. The two records read almost identically: same service, same shape of incident, codes differing by two transposed digits. An embedding model, which scores meaning rather than characters, can rank the wrong one first. The assistant downstream then writes a confident, fluent answer about the wrong fix. Nobody sees a retrieval error. They see a wrong answer.

According to recent reports, this is the standing argument for hybrid search: keep the vector index for meaning, add a keyword index for the strings that must match exactly, merge the two lists. The advice is usually asserted rather than measured, so we measured it, on a corpus we control, with the awkward queries left in.

The corpus was 373 chunks. Most of it is our own writing: 325 chunks cut from fifty of the posts on this blog. The rest is 48 operational records we wrote for the test: incident notes, part records, runbook owners, product notes, policies, host records, seeded with near-neighbours on purpose (error codes differing by transposed digits; a gasket for the P-9 pump and a near-identical one for the P-6; a Dana Whitfield and a Dana Whitmore who own different queues). Real corpora grow these confusions on their own. We planted ours where we could see them.

Thirty-two queries, written and frozen before anything ran. Twelve were exact-term lookups: a bare code, a part number, a name. Ten were paraphrases of passages in our posts, worded to share as little vocabulary with the passage as we could manage. Ten were mixed: an exact term inside a real question, or a choice between two confusables. Each query has exactly one correct chunk, and we scored every method on whether that chunk came back in the top five, and at what rank.

It has been revealed that three retrievers over the same chunks. Vector search with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, cosine similarity. BM25, the keyword ranking function, in a small implementation we wrote for the test (k1 = 1.5, b = 0.75). And a hybrid: reciprocal rank fusion with k = 60, merging the two top-50 lists. No reranker and no query rewriting: we wanted the retrieval layer's own behaviour, not a pipeline's.

The rig: 373 chunks in one corpus, two retrievers over it, and one fused list from reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60).

In a recent development, on the exact-term queries, BM25 was perfect: the correct record at rank one, twelve times out of twelve. A code is not a topic: it either matches or it doesn't, and a keyword index knows the difference between 1810 and 1180 in a way a vector does not.

Vector search never lost the record. The correct chunk sat in its top five every time, but a wrong near-neighbour took rank one in three of the twelve. ERR_AUTH_1180, a password-policy lockout, outranked ERR_AUTH_1810, the failover problem the query named. The P-6 pump's gasket outranked the P-9's. A connector error outranked the sync error. Each time, the right record sat at rank two. That sounds like a near miss and behaves like a failure, because the model downstream reads the top chunk first and builds on it — and the top chunk was a different incident with a different fix.

What each method returned for "AX-4410-B gasket", from the run output. The correct record is the P-9 gasket; vector search and the hybrid both put the P-6 gasket first.

In a recent development, on paraphrases the expected order flipped, then flattened. Vector search found the correct chunk in the top five for six of ten. BM25 managed four. The hybrid matched the vector score, six, and beat neither. If your traffic is mostly people asking questions in their own words, this test gives you no accuracy reason to run a second index.

The worst miss was shared. One question (how a system cautiously tests whether a failed tool has recovered before letting traffic back through) put the correct chunk at rank 126 under vector search and rank 76 under BM25. The hybrid never saw it at all: fusion only merges what the two retrievers surface, and neither surfaced it in fifty places. Asked about the same chunk with the words "circuit breaker" in the question, BM25 and the hybrid both returned it at rank one. The distance between those two outcomes is vocabulary, not meaning, and no blend closes it. Fusion did pull three buried answers closer — vector ranks 13, 25 and 22 became 7, 13 and 15 — still outside the five results a model actually reads. We count that as no rescue.

In a recent development, the mixed queries are where the hybrid earned its keep: ten of ten correct chunks in the top five, matching BM25 and ahead of vector search's eight. Across all 32 queries it found 28, against 26 for either method alone. That is the honest headline: a modest, real gain, concentrated where the two signals overlap.

According to recent reports, but fusion is an average of two opinions, and it can talk a certain answer down. Twice on exact-term queries (the P-9 gasket; ERR_AUTH_1810) BM25 held the right record at rank one and the fused list demoted it to rank two, because the vector list preferred the neighbour. Our read: run the hybrid as the default, but let an exact match on a code-shaped token outrank the fusion when one fires. A part number is not a vote. That rule is a judgment from this data, not a property of the method.

According to recent reports, the cost is not query time. On this rig a vector query took about 9 milliseconds and our from-scratch BM25 scan about 24, numbers that say more about a teaching implementation than about a production inverted index. The real cost is a second index to build, keep in step with the first, and interrogate at 2 a.m. when an answer is wrong and two rankings might be to blame.

It has been revealed that pay it when the corpus carries identifiers: tickets, parts catalogues, policy documents, logs, anything where customers paste strings that must match character for character. That describes most production corpora we meet. Postpone it for a pure prose corpus of questions and explanations, where our paraphrase results say the second index buys complexity and returns nothing at the top of the list.

Recent findings suggest that thirty-two queries is a direction, not a significance test. One embedding model, and a small one; a larger model may blur codes less, or blur them differently. Our 48 records were written to be confusable on purpose. Real corpora are too, but rarely so neatly. And at 373 chunks every retriever is effectively scanning the whole haystack; at a million chunks the dynamics change. What survives those caveats is the shape of the result: keyword search owns exact strings, vector search owns paraphrase, and a blend buys the overlap while importing a demotion problem you have to design around.

According to recent reports, retrieval is usually the first layer we audit in a RAG deployment, because its failures arrive disguised as the model's. If your assistant answers confidently from almost-the-right record, send us the corpus and the questions it keeps missing through Trida AI's intake, and we will show you which layer is actually failing.

Government sectors in Asia and Africa have been targeted by an active cyber intrusion campaign that delivers to previously undocumented backdoors that leverage legitimate services like Microsoft SharePoint and GitHub for command‑and‑control (C2).

According to recent reports, the activity has been codenamed Operation ShadowCloud by Kaspersky. The Russian cybersecurity tech giant said it identified the campaign in early 2026.

In a recent development, "The threat actor behind it is abusing the legitimate MeshAgent utility to drop two brand-upcoming backdoors," Kaspersky researchers Saurabh Sharma and Noushin Shabab noted in a two-part analysis. "These implants hide their command‑and‑control (C2) traffic behind cloud services Microsoft SharePoint, GitHub, and Ably, allowing the implants to blend in with normal traffic, effectively evading network-based detections.".

The modular backdoors, dubbed GraphDoor and GitDoor for their choice of the cloud platform used for C2, enable the download of additional plugins on demand and the execution of shellcode directly in memory to extend their functionality. Traffic between infected systems and the C2 servers is proxied by deploying a modified Erfrp client and Ably messaging service-based plugins.

In a recent development, the starting point of the attack has been traced back to a MeshCentral Agent, a legitimate remote access tool that's used for remote desktop control, command‑line access, and file management. The attack is said to have targeted an unspecified Taiwanese organization.

Sources indicate that the exact method by which the utility is installed on the host remains unknown. However, signs point to the "reuse of a prior infection already present on the network," Kaspersky added.

The MeshCentral Agent is configured to contact a hard-coded C2 server ("wss://27.102.66[.]162:443/agent.ashx") and then fetch three payloads staged on the endpoint -.

At least two different DLL loaders have been identified to date, each employing its own method to decode and launch the encrypted backdoor payload by injecting it into the current process's memory.

"Loader (Type 1) employs a hybrid scheme: first running the data through an RC4 stream cipher and then applying an XOR mask, while Loader (Type 2) simplifies the process by using a straight XOR operation alone," Kaspersky noted.

The end goal is to deploy backdoors like GitDoor and GraphDoor, which employ a number of encryption and obfuscation techniques like control flow flattening and nested helper functions to complicate analysis efforts and make it harder to trace genuine execution flow.

According to recent reports, gitDoor, as the name implies, uses GitHub for C2. It relies on two distinct repositories for receiving command payloads ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo") and uploading the results of the execution ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix"). While the Havo repository is public, the Trix repository is private.

The creation date of these repositories suggests that preparations for the campaign have been underway since at least the end of 2024. GitDoor supports 26 commands that allow the backdoor to -.

The custom shellcode feature is used to download and run different modules that facilitate the following functions -.

GraphDoor, on the other hand, opens a named pipe, creates a directory named "Intel_Log" inside the system's Application Data folder, and gathers system information to send back to the attacker.

To establish communications with the C2 server, it authenticates with a malicious application using "login.microsoftonline.com" on port 443 and uses the access token to communicate with the Microsoft Graph API and ultimately stage the data on the SharePoint drive.

The malware then fetches three plugin modules from the server and launches them in parallel to carry out screenshot capture, process listing, and keylogging. It also proceeds to reestablish contact with the SharePoint website to retrieve the commands to be executed on the machine.

The complete list of plugins supported by GraphDoor is as follows -.

In addition, GraphDoor's custom shellcode capability expands on GitDoor to support two additional commands that allow it to run commands using "cmd.exe," as well as MZ executables.

It has been revealed that the identity of the threat actor behind the campaign is unknown, but Kaspersky said it shares some degree of overlap with a China-nexus activity that Sophos tracks under the moniker Bronze Sandcastle. Tactical similarities have been observed with prior campaigns undertaken by FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle (aka BlackTech).

"On several victim systems, these groups shared the same staging directories as the GitDoor backdoor, with their implants deployed within a one-day window of GitDoor deployment," the firm concluded. "While this does not prove a direct link, it suggests that a Chinese-speaking group may be developing and/or utilizing the GitDoor and GraphDoor backdoors.".

"By using cloud-based storage and messaging services, the actors blend in with normal traffic (as cloud API calls to Microsoft Graph, GitHub, and Ably are indistinguishable from legitimate enterprise usage, evading many network-based detections), and enable dynamic payload delivery, where on-demand plug-ins and shellcode are retrieved from cloud repositories, allowing for rapid updates and functional extensions without modifying host files.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

⚠️ Mastering SPA Resilience: Playwright E2E for Error Boundaries How do you truly validate an SPA's graceful degradation and error recovery using Playwright, beyond just unit tests?

According to recent reports, 📌 Problem Statement Modern Single Page Applications (SPAs) critically depend on robust client-side error handling and error boundaries to prevent full application crashes. While unit tests verify individual error boundary components, a comprehensive End-to-End (E2E) strategy with Playwright is essential. It validates these mechanisms within the complete application context, including routing, data flows, and user interactions.

• The Core Challenge: Reliably inducing specific client-side errors and verifying the application's visual and functional response under controlled conditions.

❌ Antipattern: Relying solely on isolated unit tests which miss real-world interactions and cascading failures.

✅ Robust E2E Strategy: • Controlled Error Injection: Deliberately trigger JavaScript runtime errors or simulate API failures. • State Observation & Assertion: Verify error fallback UI presence, content, and proper functionality blocking. • Recovery Validation: Test if the application can recover (e.g., via a retry button) if applicable.

💡 Solution & Code Walkthrough Let's design a Playwright test to induce a client-side JavaScript runtime error and verify the SPA's error boundary. We'll use page.evaluate() to inject a fault.

Scenario: An vital DataFetcher component should trigger an error boundary if its critical logic fails during rendering or an event.

🔑 Key Takeaways • ✅ Controlled Injection: Use page.evaluate() for client-side JS errors. For network errors, page.route() is ideal. • ✅ Comprehensive Validation: Assert the error boundary's visual presence, specific messages, and the state of critical UI elements. • ✅ Real-World Scenarios: Ensure your E2E tests cover complex user flows that might trigger hidden error paths. • ❌ Avoid Flakiness: Design your error injection precisely to target specific components or logic without side effects.

Sources indicate that ❓ Quick Summary Q&A • Q: Why E2E for error boundaries? A: To validate the full user experience, graceful degradation, and recovery within the complete application context. • Q: How to induce client-side JS errors? A: page.evaluate() is powerful for injecting code that forces runtime errors. • Q: What should E2E tests verify? A: Presence of error fallback UI, correct error messages, blocked functionality, and successful recovery (if a retry mechanism exists).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Capacitor lets you take a web app — the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript you already know — and run it as a native app on iOS and Android. You do not rewrite your app. You wrap it in a native shell and add access to native features like the camera, storage, and push notifications through plugins.

Capacitor is made by the Ionic team, and it works with any web framework — React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, or plain JavaScript. Your web code runs in a native WebView, and Capacitor's bridge lets JavaScript call native code and get results back.

After that, your built web files live inside a real iOS and Android project that you open in Xcode or Android Studio. Native features are one import away:.

That single call opens the native camera on the phone — no platform-specific code from you.

According to recent reports, to start, build any small web app first — a notes app, a calculator, a weather page — then add Capacitor to it. Run it on a real device or an emulator to see your web code behave like a real app.

Capacitor is a great fit if you already have a web app and want a mobile version without learning native development or maintaining two codebases. It is also a good choice for teams that ship on web and mobile from one codebase.

Industry observers note that the limits are real. Heavy graphics and animations can feel slower in a WebView than in a fully native app. Some native features need custom plugins if no official one exists. And you still need a Mac to build for iOS, which is Apple's rule, not Capacitor's.

According to recent reports, take a web app you already built and wrap it with Capacitor this weekend. Seeing your own project open on your phone as a real app is the fastest way to understand what it offers.

#350. Researchers Detail iPhone Flaw That Let Apps Record Audio Despite Denied Microphone Permission

Researchers Detail iPhone Flaw That Let Apps Record Audio Despite Denied Microphone Permission
