⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A now-patched flaw in Apple's audio service let apps on iPhones and iPads record audio even after the user tapped "Don't Allow" on the microphone prompt.
  • Sources indicate that the first security updates with the fix came out on August 17.
  • Industry observers note that nik Tsytsarkin of Meta Red Team X published the technical details last week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A now-patched flaw in Apple's audio service let apps on iPhones and iPads record audio even after the user tapped "Don't Allow" on the microphone prompt.

Sources indicate that the first security updates with the fix came out on August 17. Neither Apple nor the two researchers who found the flaw report that it was used in attacks.

Industry observers note that nik Tsytsarkin of Meta Red Team X published the technical details last week. Mustafa Calap, a security engineer who reported the same flaw separately, published his own analysis the same day.

On iPhones, an orange indicator shows when an app is using the microphone. On one of the researchers' earlier test builds, that indicator stayed off while the app recorded.

In Tsytsarkin's tests, the prompt appeared the first time the app opened. Declining it did not stop the recording, and the prompt did not reappear on subsequent introduces.

In the earlier build of his technical analysis, the system logs revealed no record of the app using the microphone. They named the audio service itself as the recorder.

His demo video shows the indicator while the test app records with no microphone permission. He wrote that the video "was filmed on a later build that appears to have restored the orange microphone indicator.".

Calap's test app recorded while its permission still read denied, according to his detailed write-up. No orange indicator appeared in the Dynamic Island or in Control Center. He does not say which of his two test builds that was.

Recent findings suggest that neither researcher describes a way for users to check whether an app recorded them before the fix. Calap reproduced the bypass on iOS 26.6, released July 27, and on an iPadOS 27 beta.

Sources indicate that the bypass needed an app already installed on the device. His two test apps were sandboxed apps with no added entitlements. Their only privacy key was NSMicrophoneUsageDescription, which makes the microphone prompt appear.

In his tests, recording had to start while the app was in the foreground. Once started, it continued after the app went to the background and after the device was locked. The background version also set UIBackgroundModes = audio.

In a recent development, both apps were installed from Xcode and never went through App Review. So the tests do not show whether App Review would have stopped such an app.

It has been revealed that the Meta analysis compared two iOS 27 test builds. Neither researcher reports testing macOS, tvOS, watchOS, or visionOS, though fixes are listed for those systems too.

It has been revealed that the bypass covered microphone capture through the audio service only. It did not give the app other privacy permissions.

These releases fix the flaw, which is tracked as CVE-2026-65339:.

The researchers describe no setting that blocks the bypass, so installing these updates is the fix.

Sources indicate that the iOS 27 notes do not list the flaw, nor do those for later iOS 27 updates as of today. Meta's timeline says the fix shipped in iOS 27.0 beta 5 on August 10.

CISA gives the flaw a CVSS score of 5.0 out of 10. The agency's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities does not list it, as of the catalog's update late last week.

Apple's notes for the August 17 updates describe the flaw only as one that may let an app leak sensitive user information.

Tsytsarkin wrote: "That description leaves out the most striking part: the app could record after permission was denied, without the orange indicator appearing.".

According to recent reports, in his own tests, the indicator was missing only on the earlier build. An app does not decide for itself whether it may record. That decision goes through the Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC) system, which checks which process is asking.

The audio service, called audiomxd, accepted the app's own word about which process was asking. An audit token identifies a process. An app could send the service a token that named audiomxd itself.

It has been revealed that the service then treated the app as itself. It took a shortcut meant for its own internal audio and allowed recording without asking TCC. The kernel itself provided the app with the details it needed to impersonate the service.

Sources indicate that the fix makes the service check the real caller's identity, which the kernel supplies. Outside callers now need the private entitlement com.apple.private.audio.client-audit-token-override to replace the client identity the service relies on. An app cannot grant itself that entitlement.

#349. A US Federal Women's Prison Became a "Rape Club"

A US Federal Women's Prison Became a "Rape Club"

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 34 min read (6772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Propublica

⏱️ ~34 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
  • Officer Felix Wilder sauntered around the women’s prison like he owned the place.
  • Prone to showing up to work in gold chains and stylish jeans instead of his concrete gray government uniform, the slender 35-year-old moved, one woman noted, “like he had just gotten off of a horse from a long ride.” He spoke slowly and eyed the prisoners as they walked through the drab buildings and shadeless yards of the secluded federal lockup in Aliceville, Alabama.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

Officer Felix Wilder sauntered around the women’s prison like he owned the place.

Prone to showing up to work in gold chains and stylish jeans instead of his concrete gray government uniform, the slender 35-year-old moved, one woman noted, “like he had just gotten off of a horse from a long ride.” He spoke slowly and eyed the prisoners as they walked through the drab buildings and shadeless yards of the secluded federal lockup in Aliceville, Alabama.

By the fall of 2024, some of the women there had begun to notice him hovering over a soft-spoken immigrant from Mexico who’d been in prison for only a few years. Ela, as she asked to be called, had dark hair, dark eyes and children to get home to back in Utah. Wilder was just a little too close, a little too familiar.

Ela’s cellmate, who asked to be identified as Ana, watched it all with unease. At 40, she knew exactly what that kind of attention from an officer could mean in a women’s prison.

Recent findings suggest that for 15 years, Ana had served her time at Federal Correctional Institution Dublin, a low-security prison in California, where officers had preyed on the women in their care. Sexual misconduct became so rampant that staff and prisoners alike called it a “rape club.” Eventually, the FBI intervened, and prosecutors charged the warden, the chaplain and nine other officers with sexually abusing female prisoners. Hundreds of women — including Ana — came forward to tell what happened to them, not just to investigators, but also to outside lawyers who sued the system to demand change at the Bay Area prison.

In a recent development, ana had hoped to leave that all behind when she was transferred out of Dublin. But tucked between the pine trees and low-slung churches of rural Alabama, the Aliceville prison had its own brand of menace. The facility had newer buildings but fewer freedoms. The roofs leaked, and sometimes the air smelled faintly of mold. The shorthanded staff often locked the women in their cells for days at a time.

And then there were officers like Wilder, who seemed to be choosing their targets.

In a recent development, thousands of miles from families they couldn’t call during yet another lockdown, Ana and Ela became allies. They paced. They picked at the lukewarm meals delivered on Styrofoam trays. They stared out the narrow slit of a window.

And then Ela broke down, sobbing as her words tumbled out into the stale prison air.

Sources indicate that two years earlier, an officer had pulled her into a closet and raped her, she told Ana, her voice quavering. Now, she said, it was happening all over again — but this time it was the stylish officer in jeans: Felix Wilder.

Ela mentioned she’d reported the first assault and nothing happened. Now, she didn’t know what to do. If the prison didn’t care about one rape, why would it care about two?

Sources indicate that as she listened, Ana felt a dull rage churning in her stomach. She thought of all the things she’d seen and survived at Dublin: the rapes, the harassment, the uncertainty of a life subject to the whims of lascivious men with badges. As she tried to comfort her sobbing cellmate, she wondered whether Aliceville was any better. Maybe, she thought, no place was.

Sitting on her metal bunk, she opened the little address book she’d bought from the prison commissary and flipped to the phone numbers for the lead attorneys in the class action lawsuit against Dublin. “Here,” she told Ela, “you can talk to them.”.

It has been revealed that the arrests and subsequent convictions of Dublin staff — 10 in all — marked the largest sex abuse scandal in the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ history and a rare moment of accountability in a troubled system where many women had learned to stop expecting it. Suddenly, every branch of government stepped in. A federal judge appointed an outside monitor. A slew of agencies issued reports, and the Justice Department dispatched attorneys to visit and evaluate women’s facilities. Congress passed a law to create a new, independent office to oversee the prison system.

But after the judge made that unprecedented move to appoint outside oversight, in early 2024 the bureau abruptly unveiled it would shut down Dublin and transfer its more than 600 women — including Ana — to lockups across the country.

It has been revealed that then, quietly, the window of accountability shut. Little appeared to have come of the promised reforms, the site visits and the reports, and Congress never appropriated funding for the upcoming oversight office. More than a dozen current and former federal prison employees told ProPublica and The Marshall Project they’d seen few or no meaningful improvements. One Justice Department official said the only obvious sign of progress was new sexual assault prevention posters.

Industry observers note that “Nothing has really changed,” mentioned Alix McLearen, a top Bureau of Prisons official who retired in 2024 after serving as the agency’s first administrator overseeing the women and special populations branch. “We had a horrible crisis, and crisis leads to opportunity, and this is an opportunity that has been completely squandered.”.

An official with the federal prison workers union who — like nearly every current employee interviewed for this story — asked not to be named for fear of retaliation, put it even more bluntly: “Nothing has been done to effectively change sexual abuse of inmates within the BOP. Not on a large scale or small scale.”.

For the last five years, the culture that spawned a rape club at Dublin has persisted across the system. Reporters at ProPublica and The Marshall Project set out to determine how pervasive the problem of staff sexual abuse inside federal women’s prisons is — and what, if anything, officials have done to solve it. What we found was sexual assault, misconduct or harassment at most of the 27 facilities that currently hold women. We identified more than 185 cases in which prison employees have been accused of sexually abusing people in women’s prisons since 2021, the year the Dublin scandal broke. The cases implicate more than 96 officers at 16 prisons. Of those, just 19 officers have been arrested or convicted.In some cases, officers withheld food or medical care, or threatened to put women in solitary confinement if they refused to comply with sexual demands, court records allege. In others, officers locked them in windowless closets or bathrooms, choked them, or forced them to use sex toys or have sex with each other. In more than a dozen instances, the assaults were so brutal that the women were left bruised and bleeding.

It has been revealed that though some abusers have been prosecuted or removed, insiders say the culture of impunity that allows officers to prey on women remains. Officials have repeatedly refused to acknowledge or failed to act on signs of sexual abuse, we found. More than 25 women remarked that they were abused by officers who had been reported or investigated before, according to lawsuits we reviewed. In some cases, officers have covered for their abusive colleagues, court records allege. Other times, staff say that they, like the prisoners, have hesitated to report misconduct for fear of retaliation.

In a recent development, at a prison camp in West Virginia, an officer who’d been investigated repeatedly for suspected abuse — but allowed to remain on the job — raped a woman so forcefully that he tore her vaginal lining, according to a lawsuit she filed last year. The officer has been charged with sexually assaulting her and two other women at the camp and has pleaded not guilty. His case is set for trial early next year.

At Federal Medical Center Carswell, a facility in North Texas, an officer allegedly forced two women to have a threesome with him in his office, where he’d rigged up a doorbell to alert him if anyone came by, court filings show. A civil lawsuit has been stayed pending a criminal investigation.

“We had a horrible crisis, and crisis leads to opportunity, and this is an opportunity that has been completely squandered.”.

Sources indicate that and at Aliceville, Wilder, the officer who allegedly assaulted Ela, also abused at least 17 other women, many of whom were facing deportation after they finished serving their sentences, according to court records and interviews. He allegedly didn’t stop until the FBI revealed up at the facility in the fall of 2024, and federal prosecutors eventually charged him with sexually abusing seven women. He has pleaded not guilty and is awaiting trial.

“I’m pretty sure everybody knew what was going on and they just didn’t care,” one of the women told ProPublica and The Marshall Project in a phone interview from the federal prison in Fort Worth, Texas.

We found that abuse continued even as the facilities kept passing federally mandated sexual assault prevention audits. The Texas medical facility had a flawless audit the same year the FBI arrived to investigate a paramedic whom at least 18 women have accused of sexual assault, records show. Likewise, Aliceville got perfect marks during the same time period that Wilder was allegedly preying on Ela and other women.

The officers union called sexual abuse “completely unacceptable” and blamed persistent staffing shortages for helping to create an environment that allows it to go undetected. “If we are serious about protecting inmates and maintaining safe, secure federal prisons, we have to address the staffing crisis head-on,” the union mentioned in a statement, noting that more watchful eyes would mean “fewer opportunities for inappropriate conduct to occur behind closed doors.”.

Bureau of Prisons spokesperson Randilee Giamusso said the federal prison system has “zero tolerance” for sexual abuse and harassment. “We take all allegations of sexual abuse seriously,” she said.

Giamusso highlighted the bureau’s recently revamped policy on sexually abusive behavior, which is intended to ensure that allegations are more thoroughly investigated. It also eliminates any mention of transgender or intersex people, whom federal law identifies as particularly vulnerable to sexual abuse in prison. She did not provide further details or address any specific cases, saying the bureau does not comment on pending litigation. Officers mentioned in this story, as well as representatives for the prisons, either did not respond or declined to comment on specific allegations.

Sources indicate that as Ana and the other Dublin women, now scattered to other facilities, realized that no one was going to stop the abuse, they began to take matters into their own hands. Across the country, they encouraged other women to speak out about what had happened to them — and told them what they could do about it.

According to recent reports, the volume of abuse allegations ballooned so rapidly that the legal team handling the Dublin case had to refer scores of potential clients to other lawyers, some of whom have taken on so many federal prison sex abuse cases that it’s become the primary focus of their law practice. We continued receiving fresh lawsuits, tort claims and allegations of abuse up until publication of this story.

“There has been so much reporting on Dublin as an aberration,” said Susan Beaty, one of the lawyers spearheading the class action suit. “But I think it’s actually incredibly representative. I think it’s happening at basically every BOP women’s prison.”.

As she comforted her cellmate at Aliceville, Ana thought back to her first months at Dublin — before she’d learned how to recognize abuse in prison and before she’d seen just how much of it there was.

Back then, around 2010, it seemed that almost every day she saw a handful of women eating Mexican takeout for lunch — hot meals too mouth-watering to have come from the spartan prison kitchen.

At the time, Ana was just 25 and at the beginning of a lengthy sentence stemming from her involvement in her husband’s drug-trafficking operation. So while she suspected the smuggled-in meals were the sign of some nefarious quid pro quo arrangement with the officers, she didn’t ask questions, partly because she was afraid and partly because the women shared their coveted contraband meals. “So I would just eat it and shut up,” she noted.

Under federal law, all sexual contact between prison staff and people in custody is a felony — and for good reason. Prisoners cannot meaningfully give consent when they’re propositioned by people who control every aspect of their lives, from when they get fed to whether they face disciplinary sanctions that could land them in solitary confinement. So although prison sex abuse sometimes involves violent rape, it often relies on subtle coercion and grooming.

Poor conditions and scarcity behind bars turn basic necessities into valuable commodities that officers can leverage to create the illusion of a “relationship” — one built on exchanging sexual favors for extra privileges and little gifts, like contraband makeup, extra tampons or a few more minutes at visitation.

As one high-ranking prison official explained: “The women are getting small trinkets. It’s not substantial things that we can trace. He’s bringing in a hamburger, a Subway sandwich. It’s heartbreaking to look at the value of the things that are being passed.”.

Industry observers note that many times, those seeming relationships turn volatile — and violent. In Ana’s case, it began when one Dublin officer started being unusually nice to her, according to her lawsuit. He’d rush across the unit to unlock doors for her or call her into his office to talk alone. Ana thought they’d developed a rapport. But over time, he groomed her with personal questions and meager privileges. Once, he told her he’d had a sexual dream about her. Then, according to her lawsuit, he kissed her and eventually raped her.

According to recent reports, telling prison investigators didn’t seem like an option; Ana had already learned the hard way about the risks of reporting errant staff. A few years earlier, she had helped another prisoner file a complaint about staff misconduct. Afterward, she stated, both women were sent to solitary confinement. For two weeks, Ana spent 23 hours a day locked in a cell barely bigger than an elevator. She got cold food, had no access to the phone and was barred from seeing visitors.

Prison officials often isolate those who report abuse, ostensibly for their own protection, even though the Justice Department has found this practice has a “chilling effect” that discourages people from reporting abuse. A federal prison spokesperson remarked the agency’s policy does not require that people who report abuse be put in solitary — but that sometimes it is the only adequate option.

It’s not just prisoners who are afraid to report wrongdoing. Although staff are required to report misconduct under bureau policy, in lawsuits and interviews, officers say they, too, worry about retaliation.

“You see all the sexual abuse, how they treat inmates. If you bring that to their attention, it’s like you’re doing the wrong thing,” stated a former correctional officer at the prison camp for women in Bryan, Texas. In 2024, she reported several co-workers for having sexual contact with incarcerated women. She resigned last year after the warden moved to fire her for unprofessional conduct, documents show.

In a recent development, even when witnesses or victims do report abuse, investigators rarely conclude that it occurred. As of 2022, less than 10% of allegations against Bureau of Prisons employees were substantiated, meaning investigators found it more likely than not that the abuse happened in those cases. In some instances, investigators decided there was evidence the abuse didn’t occur. But more than 75% of the time, they said there wasn’t enough evidence to make a determination either way.

It has been revealed that officers accused of abuse face an internal disciplinary process that can take years. In many cases, they can simply retire or resign, knowing that the agency will no longer have jurisdiction to punish them once they leave. They could still face criminal charges — but bureau insiders say that many cases don’t reach that point because investigators abandon the criminal probes when an officer resigns. “Staff would know that if they were having sex with inmates, the worst that would happen is that you would have to find a new job,” one former prison official stated.

According to recent reports, the landmark law intended to combat sex abuse, the 2003 Prison Rape Elimination Act — widely known as PREA — mandates employee training and regular audits but lacks a serious enforcement mechanism. Auditors are primarily looking for policy compliance, not signs of abuse. “A facility may have widespread sexual abuse, but they’re still meeting compliance on the things they’re required to do,” mentioned Kendra Prisk, a PREA auditor who has evaluated several federal prisons, including Aliceville.

Beth Schwartzapfel and I are continuing to report on this problem and want to hear from any prisoners or prison staff who have been sexually harassed or abused in the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

I welcome any tips leading to tough accountability stories about the legal system. Right now, I’m particularly interested in hearing from federal prison employees and federal prisoners with information about untold and revelatory stories.

At Dublin, Ana mentioned she watched the officer who’d been bringing in burritos get walked off the job by investigators. He was, according to an Associated Press investigation and several agency sources, one of about a dozen Dublin workers in the early 2010s who were quietly removed from their posts — but not prosecuted — over sex abuse allegations.

In September 2021, a fresh round of problems at Dublin burst into public view when the FBI arrested the facility’s warden, Ray Garcia. He was eventually charged with sexually abusing multiple women all over the compound — then lying to cover it up. In one instance, prosecutors say he abused a woman while PREA auditors were visiting. Though Garcia was later convicted and sentenced to nearly six years in prison, his attorney, Kevin Little, told ProPublica and The Marshall Project that Garcia maintained that he is not guilty.

The arrest of such a high-ranking official sent shockwaves through the system. Members of Congress began asking questions. The head of the agency, Michael Carvajal, unveiled that he would step down, a move he said in a recent interview was driven by concerns that Congress would not support the bureau until he left. Ultimately, 10 Dublin officers pleaded guilty or were convicted at trial, and one walked free after two hung juries.

According to recent reports, while several of the Dublin officers could not be reached or did not respond to requests for comment, one did. John Bellhouse, who was a safety supervisor, emailed ProPublica and The Marshall Project from a federal prison in Louisiana, where he is serving a 63-month sentence after he was convicted of sexually abusing two women. Bellhouse insisted he is innocent and said the problem at Dublin was that the lower-ranking staff were “too comfortable” at the facility and too familiar with the prisoners. “It was very junior high school,” he wrote.

In a recent development, to Ana and the other women at Dublin, the rash of charges had made it seem for a moment like there might be change. But it soon became clear the problems were far more entrenched.

In the wake of the indictments at Dublin, prison officials were dispatched across the country beginning in 2022 to inspect other women’s prisons and generate internal reports.

That spring, at the low-security prison in Tallahassee, Florida, most of the women surveyed for the “Women’s Institution Cultural Assessment” noted they were afraid of reprisals if they spoke freely, according to a copy reviewed by ProPublica and The Marshall Project. The last time officials visited, they said, officers had punished the women with “shakedowns” — in which officers ransack cells and destroy belongings — and told them it was in retaliation for talking to the visitors. Despite noting this and “several concerning observations,” the bureau found that sexual safety was “not determined to be a problem” at the facility.

In a recent development, since then, at least 10 prisoners have filed legal claims saying they were abused by Tallahassee officers in the same year as the assessment. Six noted they were sexually assaulted by a single officer, Lenton Hatten, who had previously been reprimanded by prison officials at another facility for putting money in women’s commissary accounts, “which was a warning sign of inappropriate relations,” according to multiple lawsuits. He was ultimately sentenced to three months in prison for repeatedly abusing one woman after DNA tied him to the crime. In legal filings, attorneys for the prison system admitted that Hatten sexually abused that woman but denied that he assaulted any of the others. They also denied that officials had failed to train or supervise Hatten properly. Neither Hatten nor his attorney responded to requests for comment.

Industry observers note that at Carswell, in the summer of 2022, multiple prisoners told officials that prison staff had held town hall meetings before the site visit, threatening repercussions if anyone reported their concerns, the assessment found. Nonetheless, the team concluded that women at Carswell overwhelmingly felt it was a “physically and sexually safe environment.”.

Recent findings suggest that but that year, at least seven women were sexually abused by four different Carswell employees, according to allegations in civil lawsuits they’ve since filed. In one case, a woman who was partially paralyzed and required a wheelchair stated she was violently sodomized in the shower by an officer who attended her Bible study group. When he heard people coming, she said he dropped her on the floor, leaving her alone to crawl back to her wheelchair, crying and bloodied. Months later, when she finally reported the assault, the nurse on duty told her she’d reported that same officer for sexually harassing other prisoners and nothing had been done about it, according to her lawsuit.

All the suits are still pending. Among the staffers named in them, only Hatten has been prosecuted. In many cases, it’s not clear whether any of the employees were disciplined by the Bureau of Prisons. The prisons agency would not answer questions about the assessments’ findings, though a spokesperson mentioned it has continued to visit prisons and conduct assessments, which it does not release to the public.

Later in 2022, a highly publicized Senate subcommittee investigation found the problem of prison sexual assault was more widespread than previously understood and, around the same time, the Justice Department’s inspector general issued a report criticizing the bureau’s handling of staff misconduct investigations.

Meanwhile, the Bureau of Prisons’ parent agency, the Justice Department, put together a working group that recommended prison officials “enhance prevention of sexual misconduct” by promoting “stronger leadership” at women’s facilities, improving staff training and installing more cameras.

In mid-2023, the department began dispatching its own teams to survey women’s prisons and make sure they were carrying out the working group’s recommendations. Nikhil Ramnaney, a former Justice Department attorney who participated in a visit to the SeaTac lockup in Washington state that summer, noted the department notified prison officials in advance, giving them time to prepare. “BOP was putting on a show,” he said. And when Ramnaney and the other visitors interviewed women, the facility’s top officials stood nearby. When asked if they felt safe reporting abuse, the women offered “positive and lukewarm answers,” Ramnaney said. “In hindsight, what else were they going to say?”.

Industry observers note that another Department of Justice attorney who visited Carswell offered a similar assessment, and both said the department never released findings from those site visits. Neither could identify any meaningful changes the agency made.

Since then, officials from the Bureau of Prisons and the Justice Department have repeatedly said the agency is working to implement the working group’s recommendations. But when asked a series of detailed questions about the status of specific recommendations, the Justice Department deferred to the prison agency. Giamusso, the prisons spokesperson, said in an email that information was “not readily available.” She added, “We have more work to do, and we are committed to doing that work.”.

According to recent reports, by the end of 2023, there were growing signs that women were being abused at other facilities. At the camp in Bryan, Texas, it was an open secret that officers were groping women and pressuring them into unwanted sex acts, according to women and staff previously interviewed by The Marshall Project and NBC News. At the federal jail in Chicago, an officer groped and sexually assaulted at least four women in December alone, according to an indictment. That officer pleaded not guilty, and the case is ongoing.

According to recent reports, and perhaps most disturbingly, the abuse continued at Dublin, even while the prison was under the scrutiny of the courts and Congress in the wake of Warden Garcia’s arrest. In addition to the hundreds who remarked they were abused before 2021, at least 47 prisoners alleged abuse by staffers after that. Many of those allegations have not been previously reported, and many of the alleged abusers have not been prosecuted.

The abuse continued even after the agency replaced Garcia. And it continued after a sprawling legal team — including attorneys from the advocacy organization Rights Behind Bars, the law firm Rosen Bien Galvan & Grunfeld and the nonprofit legal group California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice — filed the class action lawsuit against the bureau in the summer of 2023 on behalf of Ana and hundreds of other Dublin women. They alleged the Bureau of Prisons’ systems for preventing and responding to sexual abuse were so inadequate that everyone at Dublin was at risk. The following year, the government claimed in court filings that sexual abuse was by then “virtually non-existent” at Dublin and that the facility was “not at the moment a sexualized environment.”.

A few weeks before that claim, a Dublin officer had allegedly slammed Antonina Troyer against the wall of her cell and raped her, according to a lawsuit she filed later, which has since been stayed. Troyer noted three years after she reported him, she received a letter stating that her allegation was not sustained but offering no further information. The officer, who did not respond to requests for comment, was not prosecuted and still worked for the agency as of November.

“You have a huge system that just steamrolls everybody, and you’re already considered to be not trustworthy,” Troyer noted in an interview. “Our word means practically nothing.”.

By March 2024, the federal judge overseeing the Dublin lawsuit had grown noticeably frustrated with what she called the prison agency’s sluggish response. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers issued a scathing order and appointed a so-called “special master” to oversee promised reforms.

Sources indicate that days later, the bureau abruptly announced that it would shut down Dublin — then asked the judge to dismiss the case. The judge demurred, saying the idea that closure solved the agency’s problems “strains credulity.”.

Recent findings suggest that ana and the other women at Dublin were shackled and taken to other facilities around the country in what seemed like an unusually torturous process. In letters and interviews, women recounted how some officers screamed at them, threatened to shoot them or left them without water for hours. “With their behavior and the noise of the cocked guns,” one woman wrote, “I was sure they were going to kill us.” An internal affairs investigation later determined that all the transport officers had acted “within policy” even though, in some cases, other prison staff corroborated the women’s accounts.

According to recent reports, for Beaty and the other San Francisco-based attorneys heading up the legal team for the class action lawsuit, building a case against the federal government now became much more complicated. To interview dozens more survivors, they had to travel across the country to remote prisons.

Recent findings suggest that that October, Beaty and fellow attorney Kara Janssen paid their first visit to Aliceville. They’d just come from a legal conference in Atlanta, where they’d given a presentation on their work at Dublin, then rented cars to drive four hours to a hotel in Tuscaloosa. After another hour on the road — once they’d nearly reached the Mississippi border — the bleak, boxy buildings of a federal prison rose up out of the endless forest.

According to recent reports, when the lawyers walked through the front door, the prison staff seemed so unaccustomed to legal visitors that they weren’t sure how to sign them in. “It felt like nobody had come there in a long time,” said Janssen.

Recent findings suggest that over the next three days, she and Beaty took down statements from more than 70 women, most transfers from Dublin. Some described the rough move or their trouble getting basic medical care. But others told fresh stories of abuse, this time at Aliceville. The medical staff who forced them to dance. The officers who assaulted them in closets, and the other staff who pretended not to see.

One of the women who talked to them was Ela. She’d landed behind bars five years earlier, after FBI agents arrested her in a meth bust. It was the first time she’d been in real trouble. She was sentenced to seven years in federal prison and eventually ended up in Aliceville, where, in early 2022, an officer pulled her into a closet and pushed her to her knees, forcing her to perform oral sex on him before vaginally raping her, according to a tort claim filed on her behalf. When she reported the incident to prison officials, she stated they yelled at her and fired her from her job in the prison’s safety department. Traumatized and distraught, she began cutting herself. Eventually, she asked to see a psychiatrist but left feeling worse after the psychiatrist made fun of her, according to the narrative laid out in her legal claim.

About a year later, Wilder — the officer in stylish jeans — started circling, according to the claim. He was flirtatious at first, talking about his own romantic encounters and asking about her family back home. Then, one day in the spring of 2023, she remarked he forced her into a utility closet and made her perform oral sex on him. A few months later, he locked her in that same closet for two hours, returning three times to rape her, according to the legal claim.

Industry observers note that ela wasn’t the only woman Wilder allegedly targeted. Other women had reported him for similar behavior, but his abuse continued until the fall of 2024, according to court filings and interviews. That September, investigators questioned Ela about her earlier abuser, who had by then pleaded guilty to assaulting two other women. But even though Ela had already confided in Ana about Wilder, she was reluctant to tell prison officials. “I was very scared to speak out,” she mentioned in emails in Spanish to ProPublica and The Marshall Project.

Industry observers note that investigators paid another visit days later — and that time she told them everything. “I would not want the chain of victims to continue,” she said. “We had to put a stop to it.” Wilder was walked off the prison property that day. But officers threw Ela into solitary confinement for nearly two weeks. They told her it was for her safety — “which really wasn’t safe at all because it was a nightmare,” she said.

According to recent reports, “You have a huge system that just steamrolls everybody, and you’re already considered to be not trustworthy. Our word means practically nothing.”.

And while Wilder was eventually indicted for sexually abusing seven women, 11 others — including Ela — have also accused him of sexual assault in civil claims, including two lawsuits. In both of those cases, a court has paused the proceedings until the criminal charges against him are resolved. Apart from his not guilty plea, Wilder has not responded in court or to repeated requests for comment.

By the time Beaty and Janssen arrived at Aliceville, the women were skittish, rattled by the abuse, the retaliation, the prodding FBI agents.

It has been revealed that “A lot of people were really scared,” Janssen said. “It felt just like another Dublin.” As she got in the car to leave, Janssen broke down crying.

In the months following the Aliceville trip, the lawyers traveled to prisons in California, Connecticut, Texas, Florida and Wisconsin to speak to Dublin victims. At almost every stop, women told them of abuse happening in that institution, too.

In early 2025, over the fresh Trump administration’s objections, Gonzalez Rogers, the judge in the Dublin class action suit, approved a sweeping consent decree — a first for the federal prison system. It included pathways to early release, increased protections against retaliation and two more years of court-mandated oversight for the Dublin survivors.

It has been revealed that it would not be enough to protect those who were still incarcerated. Even as their lawyers prepared civil suits, Ana and the other Dublin women became targets for harassment at their latest prisons. At some facilities, staff derisively referred to them as “Dublin girls” or “Dublin bitches” and refused to give them prison jobs, according to interviews and court papers. Elsewhere, other prisoners viewed them as snitches and held their decision to come forward against them.

It has been revealed that the women also continued to face sexual abuse. After getting shipped out of Dublin, the survivors reported almost 40 instances of abuse at their newly introduced prisons during the first six months of the court-appointed monitoring, according to monthly reports filed in federal court.

Abuse allegations continue to extend far beyond Dublin survivors. In interviews and legal filings, ProPublica and The Marshall Project uncovered accusations of sexual abuse at a prison camp in California, a low-security prison in Wisconsin and a notoriously troubled facility in West Virginia.

And earlier this year, the FBI demonstrated up at Carswell, a facility so troubled that one woman described it in court filings as “a federal prison that became a hunting ground.”.

Sources indicate that investigators uncovered a cluster of allegations against paramedic Preston Emert, who was removed from his job after 18 women accused him of sexually abusive behavior, according to court filings and internal bureau correspondence. Emert targeted women with addiction complications and medical problems, demanding sex in exchange for drugs and medical treatments, according to several women, their attorneys and a top bureau official.

“I have seizures and would need help and in order to get it I would have to have sex with him,” Olivia Floyd stated in a letter to reporters. Emert is one of 12 Carswell employees accused of sexual assault in the last five years. He has not been charged, and bureau officials said in November he is still employed as a paramedic at Carswell.

Sources indicate that last month, his boss — the health services supervisor who records show fielded at least one of the early complaints about the paramedic’s behavior — was arrested after he admitted to investigators that he was having sex with a woman incarcerated there. He has not yet entered a plea.

Despite evidence of persistent abuse throughout the system, the Bureau of Prisons now appears poised to have less oversight than ever. The landmark consent decree is set to expire early next year. The Office of Inspector General, the Justice Department’s watchdog that has the power to investigate and recommend reforms, has suffered staffing shortages in recent years as the Trump administration has pushed to slash its budget. Meanwhile, hoping to shore up its staffing levels, the bureau recently announced it would allow new officers to start with fewer qualifications and lower pay.

“It’s almost as if they’ve learned nothing,” said Shanna Rifkin, general counsel for FAMM, a nonpartisan organization that advocates for criminal justice reform. “They need staff who are well-trained and well-compensated, and to lower the qualifications when you already have rampant sex abuse and drugs being brought in — what do they think is going to happen?”.

Sources indicate that two years after Congress passed the Federal Prison Oversight Act, the ombuds office it mandated still does not exist. The Trump Department of Justice has failed to release a projected budget and progress report, even after both chambers of Congress directed it to do so by April of this year. And lawmakers have yet to appropriate any money for it.

Sources indicate that within the Bureau of Prisons, the effects of the intended reforms have been minimal. The agency has installed more cameras and restructured its Office of Internal Affairs, though under the new structure, staff at individual prisons typically still investigate their coworkers. “I think small things were changed — like the signage about how to report [abuse] needed fixing,” stated former Justice Department attorney Marnie Shiels. “There were no substantive long-term changes from this that I know of.”.

Recent findings suggest that lawyers say it’s also becoming harder for civil cases to succeed. So far, the federal government has agreed to pay $116 million to settle lawsuits with the first 103 victims of Dublin. Roughly 300 more cases are working their way through the legal system, including the one brought by Ana, who has since been released from prison. The man who abused her was never criminally charged, and he died while under investigation.

Sources indicate that trump’s Justice Department has offered paltry payouts in some cases and reneged on signed agreements that could have avoided protracted litigation in others, according to sources familiar with the situation. Lauren Bis, a spokesperson for the White House, referred questions to federal prison officials.

Recent findings suggest that legal experts also point to a recent, troubling precedent. In 2024, a federal judge in Alabama threw out a lawsuit brought by a woman at Aliceville who had been raped by an officer. The judge, Scott Coogler, sided with the Justice Department in ruling that the prison system wasn’t liable because the officer “was acting outside the scope of his employment” when he sexually assaulted her while on duty. The decision is pending appeal.

Recent findings suggest that “This case could make it incredibly hard for anyone abused in government custody to seek accountability from the BOP,” said Deborah Golden, who is representing dozens of women in cases about their sexual abuse at federal prisons. “I hope that doesn’t happen.”.

To the lawyers at the forefront of this fight, the fallout from Dublin has come to a disappointing conclusion. “It should not be hard to go to work and not force someone to give you a blow job,” Janssen said. “That is an extremely easy rule to follow. And I can only think that it’s just a complete lack of accountability.”.

In a recent development, as for the Bureau of Prisons, it’s already returning to a familiar playbook. Earlier this year, the bureau announced aims to stop housing women at Aliceville and turn the facility into a men’s prison. Ela has since been released. But the rest of the women will, once again, be scattered across the country.

Reporters searched federal court records and civil lawsuits and interviewed presently and formerly incarcerated survivors of sexual abuse, prison officials, and civil rights attorneys to compile a list of allegations that met the criteria for “sexual abuse” under the Prison Rape Elimination Act. They included only abuse allegedly committed by a BOP staffer against prisoners at women’s facilities operated by the Bureau of Prisons. There were 172 cases involving women and 15 in which the victims were transgender men. Allegations were sourced from an official record — including tort claims, lawsuits, criminal filings and internal agency documents — or the individual themselves, in which cases reporters corroborated their accounts with contemporaneous witness statements, journal entries, or letters; court filings; sworn statements; and other documentation.

I cover criminal justice, with a focus on prisons and the death penalty.

It has been revealed that I welcome any tips leading to tough accountability stories about the legal system. Right now, I’m particularly interested in hearing from federal prison employees and federal prisoners with information about untold and revelatory stories.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tuần này HN đang bàn nhiều về tin Optimizely bị compromise và phát tán malware lên các trang lớn như Zoom, GitLab. Chi tiết vụ việc vẫn đang được điều tra, nên mình sẽ không bình luận về nó. Mình chỉ muốn đặt ra một câu hỏi thực tế hơn: nếu ngày mai vendor analytics, A/B testing hay chat widget của bạn bị hack, website của bạn có tự động chạy malware cho toàn bộ user không?

InfoQ Homepage News Microsoft Releases .NET 11: C# 15 Union Types, Native AOT CLI Host, and CoreCLR by Default in MAUI.

Nov 17, 2026 2 min read.

Last week, Microsoft has released .NET 11, the latest version of its development platform, together with C# 15, F# 11, ASP.NET Core 11, .NET MAUI, and Entity Framework Core 11. The release is a Standard Term Support (STS) version and will be supported for two years.

It has been revealed that as stated in the announcement, .NET 10 remains the Long-Term Support option, while .NET 8 and .NET 9 reached end of support on the same day, November 10, 2026. The release coincided with this year's .NET Conf, held from November 10 to 13.

Industry observers note that C# 15 is the default language version for projects that target .NET 11. It adds union types, declared with the union keyword, and the compiler checks switch expressions over them for exhaustiveness. Closed hierarchies limit derivation to the declaring assembly.

The language also gains collection expression arguments, extension indexers, and labeled break and continue statements, while the memory safety work stays in preview. F# 11, according to the release, lowers compiler memory use and reduces collection allocations in FSharp.Core.

It has been revealed that in the SDK, the CLI now starts through a Native AOT host by default and keeps the MSBuild server warm between invocations. The dotnet test command gains run-level timeouts and failure limits, and container publishing can produce reproducible digests. In the runtime, Runtime Async remains a preview and is turned on with a feature flag.

Industry observers note that the JIT removes more bounds checks and improves devirtualization. As described in the documentation, the release also raises the minimum hardware requirements, and the x86/x64 baseline moves to x86-64-v2.

Recent findings suggest that the libraries add Zstandard compression to System.IO.Compression, upcoming Process APIs for running a process and capturing its output, and four in-memory stream adapters. System.Text.Json supports C# unions and JSON Lines output, and LINQ gains a FullJoin operator.

Recent findings suggest that ASP.NET Core 11 adds asynchronous validation and generates OpenAPI 3.2 documents by default, which the release notes list as a breaking change. SignalR can refresh authentication without reconnecting.

Industry observers note that blazor receives a CacheView component for static server-side rendering, client-side validation for static SSR forms, and an opt-in automatic circuit pause for inactive tabs. An experimental package with AI components for Blazor is also available.

.NET MAUI now uses CoreCLR as the default runtime, with Mono still available and Native AOT as an opt-in option. As reported, XAML Incremental Hot Reload is on by default for Debug builds, XAML namespace declarations are implicit, and the Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships.

Entity Framework Core 11 requires .NET 11. It generates fewer unnecessary joins, translates FullJoin, supports complex types and JSON columns with TPT and TPC inheritance, and adds experimental vector search for SQL Server.

Other changes in this release are the dotnet fresh mcpserver template, the dotnetup toolchain manager in public preview, .NET Skills for coding agents, opt-in modern visual styles in Windows Forms, and reliability fixes in WPF.

Industry observers note that on Reddit, the reaction was mixed. Several developers welcomed union types as a replacement for hand-written result classes, and others said that .NET 11 and .NET 10 share the same end-of-support date.

The most upvoted comments argued that AI coding tools have made fresh releases feel less exciting. Other users criticized the code fix for non-exhaustive switch expressions and asked for the decimal conversion change to be more visible.

For interested readers, the full release notes and the list of breaking changes are available in the official .NET 11 documentation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks.
  • In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool.
  • The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it.

In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check.

The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/concerns-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it.

The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it.

According to recent reports, that gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning. If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't.

Industry observers note that pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected.

GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it.

📅 Save Your Spot: Learn Why “Best Practice” Won’t Stop the Next GitHub Actions Attack.

But a pinned SHA leaves three questions unanswered:.

With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely.

GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later.

That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't presently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server.

Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you.

Led by Erika Heidi, Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard, the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers:.

Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you.

According to recent reports, attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability.

Nov 17, 2026 3 min read.

Datadog is extending its Agent Observability platform with Online Experiments, allowing engineering teams to compare AI agent versions against real production traffic rather than relying exclusively on predefined evaluation datasets. The capability combines agent evaluation scores with operational measurements such as latency, token consumption, execution cost, and errors, helping teams establish whether changes to models, prompts, retrieval strategies, or tools actually improve an agent.

It has been revealed that the announcement addresses a growing challenge in agent development: a change that performs better in a controlled test may behave very differently when exposed to unpredictable user requests. Datadog's approach brings controlled experimentation, production telemetry, and execution traces together, giving teams evidence of both the outcome and the behaviour behind it.

Offline evaluations remain an important part of agent development. Teams can run different versions against predefined datasets, assess responses and identify known regressions before deployment.

However, these evaluations are only as representative as the datasets and scoring criteria behind them. Latest user workflows, unexpected requests, and changing tool responses can expose weaknesses that existing test cases never anticipated.

Recent findings suggest that online experiments address this limitation by evaluating agent behaviour against real user interactions. Teams can compare a control version with a modified variant by randomly distributing production traffic between them, reducing the influence of differences in user requests.

This provides a more realistic view of how an agent performs under actual workloads, while also helping teams identify upcoming scenarios that should eventually become part of their offline regression datasets.

Datadog integrates its Agent Observability evaluators with its Experiments capability, allowing evaluation scores to be compared alongside conventional operational metrics.

Teams can measure response quality, accuracy, and completeness while tracking execution duration, token consumption, estimated cost, and workflow errors.Feature Flags manage traffic allocation, letting engineers expose a change to a small percentage of users before rolling it out more widely.

This is vital because improvements rarely come without trade-offs. A cheaper model might require more retries, while a revised retrieval strategy could improve evidence quality but increase execution time.

It has been revealed that datadog also connects experiment results to individual agent traces. Engineers can inspect tool calls, supplied arguments, and returned results to understand why a particular variant behaved differently.

Sources indicate that according to the article, the experiment compared GPT-5.6 Luna against GPT-6 Luna, splitting traffic evenly between the two. An LLM-based evaluator scored investigation quality from one to five, considering accuracy, completeness, and whether conclusions were supported by available evidence.

They claim the results showed a 44.3% reduction in estimated cost for the newer model, with quality scores remaining close at 3.84 and 3.86, respectively.

Sources indicate that however, the operational results revealed potential concerns. The newer model revealed estimated increases in execution duration and workflow errors, although the confidence intervals were too broad to establish definitive regressions.

Inspecting the traces revealed that the newer model also supplied invalid tool parameters more frequently, usually recovering after retries. This behaviour was not sufficiently visible in the overall quality score.

According to recent reports, datadog used that finding to improve tool handling before proceeding with the model change. The failed calls also provided candidates for additional offline regression tests.

Datadog is not alone in trying to solve this challenge. Tools such as LangSmith and Langfuse provide agent tracing and evaluation capabilities, while experimentation platforms such as LaunchDarkly support controlled feature rollouts. Datadog's approach connects these concerns within its existing observability ecosystem, linking evaluation results directly to production experiments and execution evidence.

Industry observers note that datadog's broader proposition is that online experiments can create a feedback loop between production behaviour and development testing. Unexpected failures become upcoming regression cases, while subsequent experiments establish whether changes actually resolve them.

The important shift is from asking whether an agent passes a predefined evaluation to establishing whether it performs better under real conditions. For agent engineering, production experimentation may become as important as traditional software testing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Is there an RDP server for macOS? Not built in. Here are your options from Windows, and what to expect.

This is for you if you sit at a Windows PC with Remote Desktop Connection (mstsc) and want to reach a Mac next to it.

mstsc speaks the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). A computer only accepts those connections if it runs an RDP server. Windows Pro has one. macOS does not.

What macOS ships instead is Screen Sharing and Remote Management, both based on VNC. VNC is a different protocol. Turning on Screen Sharing and pointing mstsc at the Mac fails, because nothing on the Mac answers in RDP.

Recent findings suggest that none of these is "best" in general. If you only need the Mac once a month, VNC and the built-in Screen Sharing cost nothing. If you sit at a Windows PC all day and want the Mac next to it, the third option avoids a second remote tool on Windows.

This part is where expectations usually go wrong, so it is worth reading before you pick anything.

Once a server is running on the Mac, read its local IP and port. RDP's default port is 3389. Then on Windows:.

Choose More choices → Use a different account, then enter the Mac's short account name (not the full name) and its login password.

Sources indicate that the first connection usually demonstrates a certificate warning, because the server uses a self-signed certificate. Before you click through, compare the certificate fingerprint Windows shows with the one the Mac server reports.

It has been revealed that do not forward port 3389 on your router straight to the Mac. Any RDP port open to the internet gets scanned constantly, whichever product is behind it. To connect from outside the office or home, use a VPN (Tailscale, WireGuard or your router's VPN) and connect to the Mac's VPN address.

We make RDPyon, a paid macOS app that runs an RDP server so the built-in Windows mstsc can connect to a Mac. The screenshot above is its menu. As of November 2026 it is a one-time $19 purchase (launch price until Dec 1, then $29) with a 14-day free trial that needs no card. The limits listed above apply to it too, and NLA is an optional switch that is off by default. Full setup guide with the error list: https://devjar.dev/go/G-1741.

If you already reach a Mac from Windows, which of the three options do you use, and what made you pick it?

Qwik, the resumable JavaScript framework originally created at Builder.io, has released its 2.0 Release Candidate, targeting a rewrite of how the framework encodes resumable state in server-rendered HTML and introducing experimental out-of-order streaming. The RC was published on 1st October 2026 as @qwik.dev/core@2.0.0-rc.0, around two years and eight months after the initial Towards Qwik 2.0 design article.

Sources indicate that in v1, Qwik propagated state updates by sprinkling HTML comment markers such as and throughout the rendered body to flag component boundaries and the text nodes a signal should upgrade. That approach forced a single ordered write pass, added CPU and memory overhead, and made out-of-order streaming impossible because a slow fetch blocked everything after it. In v2 the comments are gone, with state and virtual node information instead compressed into two.

#334. Tech Report: Reproducing a model is not validating it

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1516 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

Tech Report: Reproducing a model is not validating it

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What a deeper cross-validation audit revealed about reproducibility, evaluation composition, and the limits of machine-learning performance metrics.
  • There is a particular kind of confidence that comes from running an experiment twice and getting exactly the same answer.
  • Nothing crashes, and the outputs are reproducible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What a deeper cross-validation audit revealed about reproducibility, evaluation composition, and the limits of machine-learning performance metrics.

There is a particular kind of confidence that comes from running an experiment twice and getting exactly the same answer.

Your code executes. The metrics match. The predictions agree. Nothing crashes, and the outputs are reproducible.

It is tempting to consider that a successful experiment.

But reproducibility and validity answer different questions.

I recently spent time investigating this distinction in QueleaGuard, a machine-learning research project studying the environmental and spatial factors associated with Red-billed Quelea occurrence around the Ahero Rice Irrigation Scheme in Kisumu County, Kenya.

In a recent development, the project had already established a spatial cross-validation design and produced a baseline logistic regression evaluation. Rather than immediately moving to more sophisticated models, I decided to investigate whether the existing evaluation could be independently reconstructed from the committed data and code, and what its results actually represented.

The exercise became a much larger evaluation audit.

01 — The Experiment We Needed to Reproduce.

The baseline used logistic regression to distinguish recorded quelea presences from an approximate target-group background sample.

The modelling dataset contained 266 records:.

Dataset component| Records Confirmed occurrence records| 133 Background records| 133 Total| 266 Evaluation folds| 5.

The model used ten numerical predictors and three seasonal indicator variables.

The numerical predictors included rainfall, temperature, dewpoint, wind, vegetation index, elevation, slope, distance to water, and rice-related landscape variables.

Sources indicate that each fold was held out once. The remaining four folds were used to fit the model, with numerical predictors standardised using the training data.

The original evaluation produced:.

Metric| Mean across five folds F1-score| 0.593 ROC-AUC| 0.854.

Those numbers were interesting, but they were not sufficient evidence that the model generalised reliably.

I wanted to establish something more fundamental first:.

«Could I reconstruct the reported experiment using the committed inputs and implementation, without changing anything to make the numbers agree?».

02 — Building a Reproduction Gate.

I created a separate audit stage, M0, implemented in "src/cv_audit_m0.py".

According to recent reports, the objective was not to improve the model. It was to reconstruct the original baseline and compare its outputs against the previously committed results.

Before fitting anything, the script checked the integrity of the experiment.

The checks were deliberately strict.

If a critical input differed, the audit was supposed to stop rather than silently continue with a different experiment.

The model was then reconstructed using the same logistic regression specification, including the original feature construction, scaling procedure, five folds and classification threshold.

I also ran the reconstruction twice within the same execution.

The purpose was to distinguish agreement with the historical results from agreement between repeated executions.

03 — The Baseline Reproduced Successfully.

The reproduction gate passed all 51 assertions.

The largest absolute differences between the reconstructed and original metrics were:.

Metric| Maximum absolute difference Precision| 0 Recall| Approximately 1.11 × 10⁻¹⁶ F1-score| 0 ROC-AUC| Approximately 1.11 × 10⁻¹⁶.

The maximum difference between the two independently executed sets of predicted probabilities was also zero.

No convergence warnings were recorded.

The audit additionally checked the confusion matrices, calibration diagnostics and the composition of a particularly difficult evaluation fold.

But it did not establish that the baseline was a good model.

It did not establish that its probabilities were calibrated, that the spatial validation design was adequate, or that its performance would transfer to genuinely latest locations.

It has been revealed that reproducing an experiment confirms that you can regenerate its outputs. It does not independently confirm that the experiment measures what you intended it to measure.

04 — Looking Beyond the Fold Averages.

This distinction motivated the next audit stage, R.

Instead of fitting another model, I kept the reproduced out-of-fold predictions fixed and investigated the composition of their evaluation results.

How well did the model perform in each fold?

Which observations and locations contributed to those scores?

The analysis examined individual presence-bearing grid cells, decomposed focal locations from the remaining observations, tested the sensitivity of evaluation metrics to removing individual cells, and investigated residual spatial patterns.

Two folds deserved particular attention.

4.1 — Fold 3: A Strong Score Concentrated Around One Location.

Fold 3 contained 58 records, including 36 presences.

Metric| Result Precision| 0.882 Recall| 0.833 F1-score| 0.857 ROC-AUC| 0.886.

On its own, that looks encouraging.

However, one location, "cell_0156", contributed 27 of the 36 presence records.

It also accounted for 27 of the fold's 30 true positives.

When the audit separated that focal cell from the remaining evaluation records, the remaining subset contained only nine presences and 22 background records.

Its results were substantially different:.

Metric| Remaining subset Recall| 0.333 Precision| 0.429 F1-score| 0.375 ROC-AUC| 0.667.

The remaining sample is small, and the analysis changes the evaluation set rather than refitting the model.

It does, however, demonstrate why a single fold-level score can conceal crucial differences in evaluation composition.

4.2 — Fold 4: A Different Pattern, With a Similar Problem.

Fold 4 contained 113 records, including 69 presences.

Metric| Result Precision| 0.833 Recall| 0.362 F1-score| 0.505 ROC-AUC| 0.839.

Here, "cell_0080" contributed 60 of the 69 presence records.

The focal location accounted for 39 of the fold's 44 false negatives.

Removing that location from the evaluation subset left 51 records, including nine presences and 42 background records.

Metric| Remaining subset Recall| 0.444 Precision| 0.500 F1-score| 0.471 ROC-AUC| 0.918.

Interestingly, the remaining subset's ROC-AUC was higher than the full-fold ROC-AUC, even though its F1-score was slightly lower.

This is a useful reminder that different evaluation metrics describe different aspects of model behaviour.

A strong ranking metric does not necessarily imply strong classification performance at a particular decision threshold.

The subset also contained only two other presence-bearing cells, so its metrics must be interpreted cautiously.

05 — Why I Did Not Simply Remove the Difficult Locations.

There is an important methodological distinction here.

The R-stage analysis removed locations from the evaluation set while keeping the original model predictions fixed.

It did not retrain the model without those locations.

Consequently, it tells us how much the composition of an evaluation subset affects the reported metrics.

It does not tell us what would happen if the model were trained without the dominant locations.

This distinction is particularly vital in spatial machine learning, where the same geographic locations can contribute many observations.

Counting records alone can make an evaluation look more informative than it really is.

Sixty observations from two coordinates do not provide the same geographic coverage as sixty observations distributed across sixty independent locations.

The number of records, the number of distinct coordinates, the number of dates and the number of independent spatial sites all deserve attention.

06 — Reproducibility Needs an Audit Trail.

Another part of this work was making the audit itself reproducible.

The shared implementation in "src/cv_audit_common.py" records:.

Outputs are written into unique, timestamped directories rather than silently overwriting earlier results.

This matters because an evaluation is not just a number in a report.

It is the result of a particular dataset, implementation, configuration and execution environment.

If any of those change, the relationship between the upcoming result and the old one needs to be explicit.

The project's decision log also records what an analysis establishes, what it does not establish, and which questions remain open.

I find this especially valuable in research engineering:.

«Methodological decisions should be traceable, not reconstructed from memory after something goes wrong.».

The next stage of the audit moves beyond keeping predictions fixed.

The newly committed M1 analysis investigates the influence of training composition through controlled refits, including exact-repeat and cell-balanced weighting variants and reference ablations.

This is deliberately separate from the R-stage evaluation-composition analysis.

Only after those investigations can we make stronger statements about the baseline's sensitivity to the dominant spatial clusters.

Even then, QueleaGuard remains an active research project.

It has not established a validated early-warning system, and its current occurrence modelling should not be interpreted as confirmed infestation or crop-damage prediction.

That distinction matters because the eventual goal is practical: better information about where and when quelea activity may occur, so that agricultural interventions can be planned more intelligently.

Getting there requires more than a model with an attractive ROC-AUC.

I started this exercise wanting to establish whether I could reproduce an existing machine-learning experiment.

I ended up with a much clearer understanding of what its reported metrics did and did not tell me.

There are at least three separate questions worth asking about an ML experiment:.

Can the committed data, code and configuration regenerate the reported outputs?

Are the test observations sufficiently representative, and do the reported metrics conceal important differences in evaluation composition?

Does the model perform reliably beyond the particular observations, locations and conditions represented in the experiment?

Passing the first question does not automatically answer the other two.

For me, this is part of what separates building an ML model from conducting credible machine-learning research.

The objective is not to produce the most impressive metric.

It is to understand exactly what that metric supports, what it leaves unresolved, and what evidence is needed next.

Repository: "QueleaGuard — GitHub" (https://github.com/benardabuto081/QueleaGuard).
