Industry observers note that on 16 November 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organisations through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The list includes some of the most visited sites in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock.

According to recent reports, this is exactly the kind of attack Report URI is designed to detect. Our platform can identify unexpected changes to trusted JavaScript, detect newly introduced scripts being loaded and reveal suspicious connections to external destinations. In this case, those signals would have exposed the malicious activity, even though the original script was being served from a trusted Optimizely domain. With an appropriate CSP in enforcement mode, organisations could have gone a step further and blocked key parts of the attack before they succeeded.

It has been revealed that the notable lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.

In a recent development, most of the malicious code has now been removed. At 21:52 UTC we found it in only 1 of the 188 infected snippets, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC. If your site uses Optimizely Web, or you visited any of the sites below today, read on.

Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript "snippet" from Optimizely's CDN, for example https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/6395285578973184.js. The snippet contains Optimizely's code, the customer's experiments and an optional field called Project JavaScript (projectJS): custom code the customer writes in their Optimizely dashboard, which runs on every page.

According to recent reports, the attacker wrote their own code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, and the rest of each snippet was untouched. The file was still served from cdn.optimizely.com, with Optimizely's certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted. Here is what was added to Zoom's snippet:.

It has been revealed that the Ignite keynote is tonight, and if you listen to nothing else this week, listen for one word: agents. Not chatbots that answer a question and stop, but agents that can plan, call tools, pull in your data, and finish a task.

According to recent reports, everyone will hear about agents tonight. The more useful question is how you actually build one — and there is a free Microsoft Learn path that walks you through it, end to end, with Microsoft Foundry: Develop AI Agents on Azure.

Sources indicate that it is 9 modules, no cost, and you come out with a working agent instead of just notes. Here is what is inside, and how I would approach it.

According to recent reports, the first module, Develop AI agents with Microsoft Foundry and Visual Studio Code, is where the path earns its name. You build, test, and deploy an agent using the Microsoft Foundry Agent Service, both through the Azure portal and with the Foundry Toolkit for Visual Studio Code. That matters more than it sounds: the difference between reading about agents and building one is having a loop where you can change something, run it, and see what the agent actually does. Get that loop working first, before you worry about anything advanced.

An agent without tools is just a chat window. Modules two and three fix that. First you integrate custom tools, so the agent can call functions you wrote for your own problem. Then you connect MCP-hosted tools, which is the part I find most interesting — MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets an agent reach tools other people built, dynamically, instead of you hard-wiring every capability yourself. If you have ever wished your project could just talk to another service, this is the module that indicates you how.

The fourth module is the one I would not skip: Build knowledge-enhanced AI agents with Foundry IQ. An agent that only knows what the model was trained on will guess confidently about your data. Foundry IQ connects the agent to enterprise knowledge with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), so answers are grounded in your own documents and come back with citations. The module also covers tuning retrieval quality and writing instructions that keep responses consistent.

Module five adds Web IQ, which pulls current information from the web into the agent — useful when the answer depends on something that changed yesterday rather than something in your files.

Recent findings suggest that module six, Integrate your agent with Microsoft 365, is the payoff: you publish your Foundry agent to Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot, and connect it to workplace data with Work IQ. An agent that lives in a notebook is a demo. An agent your study group or team can actually message in Teams is a tool.

Sources indicate that the last three modules are the stretch goals. Module seven covers agent-driven workflows in Foundry — orchestrating agents and other components into an application. Module eight introduces the Microsoft Agent Framework for building agents in code. Module nine brings it together: orchestrating a multi-agent solution, where several agents collaborate on one problem.

It has been revealed that you do not need all nine on day one. My suggestion: do modules one through four this week, ship something small to Teams, and come back for workflows and multi-agent orchestration once you have felt the basic loop.

Recent findings suggest that the path suggests you come in with fundamental AI concepts and some familiarity with Azure services, so if those are newly introduced, the Get started with artificial intelligence path on Learn is the right warm-up. After that, the honest test is a first project: a study assistant grounded in your own notes with Foundry IQ, a small support agent for a club or society, or a tool-calling agent for a workflow you repeat every week.

If you build your first agent this week, what would you make it do? I am genuinely curious — drop it in the comments.

The full path is free on Microsoft Learn: Develop AI Agents on Azure.

#310. Your HMI Display Didn't Break. Your Integration Did.

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (814 w)

Your HMI Display Didn't Break. Your Integration Did.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A touchscreen that passes bench testing and then fails on the factory floor is one of the most expensive patterns in embedded work.
  • According to recent reports, the familiar version of this story: three weeks after commissioning, operators report ghost touches, the screen goes dark below 5°C, and the MCU logs UART timeouts nobody has seen before.
  • Software bug → firmware bug → communication bug → finally, environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A touchscreen that passes bench testing and then fails on the factory floor is one of the most expensive patterns in embedded work. The display did not change. The environment did — and the integration layer was never asked to survive it.

According to recent reports, the familiar version of this story: three weeks after commissioning, operators report ghost touches, the screen goes dark below 5°C, and the MCU logs UART timeouts nobody has seen before. The team assumes a firmware regression. They reflash the GUI project. They rewrite the comms layer. A month disappears. I have watched this loop run on TFT integration projects from EV charger rollouts in northern China winters to vending machines in humid Southeast Asian markets. The failure is almost never the panel. It is one of four things engineers routinely skip when they wire a display to an MCU.

Software bug → firmware bug → communication bug → finally, environment.

Most teams burn three of those four steps before somebody opens the temperature log and notices the failures cluster between 6 and 8 AM in January — exactly when the factory floor drops below freezing.

Industry observers note that the classic. Host transmits at 115200. The module is still configured for 9600. The result is garbage characters or a frozen screen, and every default diagnostic tool points at the display.

Both sides are working perfectly. They are simply not speaking the same rate, and nothing in a default configuration tells you so. Do not trust "transmit complete" as proof of delivery — add an application-level acknowledgement. A frame the display never parsed is a frame that was never acknowledged.

Recent findings suggest that A logistics operator deployed 200 intelligent parcel lockers. Simple requirement: show a keypad, accept a six-digit code, release the lock. One in eighty unlocks failed. Diagnosis took six weeks.

In a recent development, the unlock command shared the same UART line as temperature telemetry streaming from the lock body. Under specific timing conditions, the two packets overlapped. Nobody caught it during integration because the lab rig never had the temperature sensor connected while touch input was being tested.

In a recent development, the fix was a 50 ms guard between touch event and command send, plus a hardware flow-control line. Two lines of MCU code. The lesson is not about the bug. It is that the team validated against a consumer checklist instead of an industrial one.

Wire that guard into a retry with backoff and log every rejected attempt with a timestamp. The log is what turns a six-week investigation into a ten-minute one.

It has been revealed that A useful log line carries five fields: millisecond timestamp, direction, raw frame bytes in hex, acknowledgement latency, and the ambient temperature at the moment of the event. That last field costs one sensor read. It is also the field that ends arguments about whether a fault is thermal, because a plot of failures against temperature is not an opinion.

In a recent development, datasheets quote steady-state current. Modules draw a startup spike that runs two to three times that number. If the supply has poor transient response, the rail sags and the display resets mid-boot.

Recent findings suggest that the engineer sees a module that "fails to initialize" and concludes it is defective. Something did fail. It was the power design, not the panel. Scope the rail at power-on with the display connected — never with a resistive load standing in for it.

Capacitive panels derive touch from a capacitance reference. A floating ground plane corrupts that reference, and the controller reads the corruption as a finger. Check grounding topology before opening a supplier ticket. It resolves more "defective panel" claims than any firmware change ever will.

Baud rate → startup transient → ground continuity → shared-bus collisions → temperature and humidity logs → and only then, the panel itself.

Sources indicate that none of this is exotic. It is the difference between validating a module and validating an integration. The datasheet describes the module; only your test rig describes the system. When a display "stops working" in the first thirty days, the probability that the root cause lives in your configuration rather than in the glass is very high — and every hour spent reflashing firmware before you have pulled the timing log is an hour you are guessing.

Industry observers note that the industrial checklist and the consumer checklist differ in one dimension: the consumer version assumes a comfortable room. Add humidity, vibration, and thermal cycling to your own list, and run it against the assembled unit inside its enclosure — not against a bare panel on an antistatic mat.

So build the log first. Then build the display. The order is not a preference; it is the difference between a two-week bring-up and a quarter of field escalation.

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An open-source, self-hosted ontology platform.
  • Quick start · How it works · Proposals · Python SDK · Contributing.
  • Only small parts are still alpha: the model language and APIs may still change between versions, and parts of the user interface and docs are unfinished.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scarce Units, Typed, Related, Actionable.

An open-source, self-hosted ontology platform. Your data becomes one model you own: typed, linked, changed only through rules the server enforces, and every number traces back to its source.

Quick start · How it works · Proposals · Python SDK · Contributing.

Beta. Only small parts are still alpha: the model language and APIs may still change between versions, and parts of the user interface and docs are unfinished.

In a recent development, maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS is a one-person project so far. See Contributing.

Sutra-OS began in late 2025 as a thought experiment: a free version of the system described in Ontology-Oriented Software Development, whose creators I deeply admire.

Much talent today goes into software that sells attention, while the software everything else runs on is mostly free: by a rough estimate, 70–90% of US economic output depends on free software at some critical point. That openness is not guaranteed. In November 2026, Nvidia's board parted with the founder who had its AI models released openly. Sutra-OS adds to the commons under the AGPL, so that it stays readable by anyone.

Recent findings suggest that the past ten years have shown what it costs when nobody can see what depends on what. In 2017, NotPetya spread through a single Ukrainian accounting program and stopped Maersk's ports and Merck's factories. In 2023, a corrupted file in one FAA system halted every domestic departure in the US. In 2024, one faulty CrowdStrike update crashed millions of Windows machines, and airlines, hospitals and banks stood still. In November 2026, a single vendor took Outlook down for a day and some cities went back to fax. That same week, data flooded the FAA's telecommunications network, aging routers buckled, and the US saw only the third nationwide ground stop in its history. No one, it seems, had those routers on the map of what keeps planes in the air, so no one could ask beforehand what would stop if they failed.

That question is what Sutra-OS is built for. Every system, device, dataset and decision becomes an object with links to what it feeds and what feeds it, and every number can be traced back to its source. Whoever holds such a model can ask, before the outage, what stops when one piece fails, and get an answer, at every scale from a single person to a government (hopefully never a world government). Many small ontologies, each held by those it describes, keep power spread out; one model of everything would not.

According to recent reports, almost everyone. Whoever you are, someone else keeps a better-connected record of your affairs than you do. Sutra is for anyone who wants their own.

Requirements: Linux x86_64, JDK 21, the Clojure CLI, Node.js, Python 3, git.

This starts an embedded PostgreSQL and the server on 127.0.0.1 and prints the address. Data lives in $SUTRA_HOME (default ~/.local/share/sutra). The admin password is in zugang.edn ("access") there. Run the bin/sutra bind … line it prints once.

Recent findings suggest that three ideas carry the whole platform: object types, link types and action types. The examples below use the farm model in resources/presets.

You start by saying what exists: a lot of hay, from one field and one cut; a sale, to one buyer. Each is a typed thing with a kind and a key.

It has been revealed that nobody types or counts :in-barn: it is the bales made minus every bale sold, computed by the server. :bales is an integer, so "about forty" or -3 is refused before anything is written.

According to recent reports, an object type is a typed table with a name, a face in the UI and a class in the generated SDK. Properties are typed, constrained and can be derived, so a value nobody typed in still shows up like any other column.

A sale on its own is just a number. A sale linked to the lot it came out of is a fact everyone can see.

The sale names its lot and the link follows it: from the lot you see its sales, from a sale its lot, and :connected-sum above sums across that link. One line, and the barn knows what is in it.

Links are first-class: named in both directions, navigable in the UI, traversable in the SDK (lot.sales), and usable in derived values, filters and object sets.

Sources indicate that in most systems anybody may change anything, and nobody can say who did. Here there is no "update row". There are only actions: named decisions with typed inputs and rules the server enforces. Selling hay is one of them, and it has a condition.

In a recent development, ask to sell more bales than are in the barn and the server refuses and claims why, with the same sentence for the phone, the CLI, the Python script and the AI agent. A refused action writes nothing. Every sale records who made it, and nobody can put someone else's name there.

Actions are the only write path: typed parameters, validation, submission criteria and state transitions, defined once and enforced everywhere.

Sources indicate that every rule you would otherwise keep in your head has this shape: a fact the server computes, and an action that checks it. Declare it once, and stop remembering it.

Recent findings suggest that the same three ideas run the arable side of the farm. A field's margin is derived from its paid harvests and the hay sold off it, two links away. A harvest moves from planted to harvested, delivered and paid only through its actions, and Sell harvest refuses to run without a signed delivery note and a quality test of your own.

It has been revealed that in most software, deciding and doing are one step. In Sutra they are two. When you sell hay, the server first writes down what would change: one new sale, forty bales, your name on it. Nothing has happened yet. Only when that note is approved does the barn change.

Everything else follows from that:.

It has been revealed that and it is not a promise. A test fails if the part that decides ever does anything but decide.

Your data comes in as it is. Mail over IMAP, CSV exports, REST APIs, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and SSH, shaped by transforms in Python, SQL or Clojure.

Every number has a past. Lineage runs from each object back through the transforms and datasets to the mail, statement or row it came from (sutra lineage ). When someone else's figures disagree with yours, you open the source.

In a recent development, agents get only the tools you name. An action, a function, a query on one type. By default (:writes :propose) their changes are staged as proposals; a rejected one doesn't come back, and the model's prompt and answer are kept with the run.

In a recent development, the model is versioned like code. Model and data live on branches. You stage a change, commit it, open a proposal, see who consumes what you touched, and merge into main only when it's reviewed. Webhooks and notifications stay silent on a branch unless you say otherwise.

According to recent reports, share exactly what you choose. Markings on types and properties are mandatory access control; grants on projects decide who may read, act and invoke. A group (a co-op, a tenants' association, a family) can pool what its members agree to share, and nothing else, and the server enforces it on every read: lists, filters, counts and totals. One person's data can't show what everyone else was offered. A group's can.

Builders and users are different people. One person writes the model; everyone else gets apps with the build tools locked away, and a server that says no when no is the right answer.

Secrets stay out of reach. A separate egress agent holds every external credential, so the code that reads your mail never sees the password.

You described the farm once. Generate a Python SDK from it, and your code speaks the farm's language: lots, harvests and buyers, and the things you are allowed to do with them, not tables and joins.

In a recent development, farm_sdk.py is plain, typed Python: a class per object type, an attribute per property and link, a method per action with the action's parameters as its signature. Sutra's language server (clients/ent-lsp) runs pyright for Python and labels each completion as what it is in the model (property, link-type, action, state); any editor that lets you pick the language server can run it (Neovim config).

An action is a method. Its signature comes from the model; a missing argument is flagged before anything runs.

Recent findings suggest that states are types. A harvest's status is Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'], so the editor offers exactly those four.

In a recent development, filters are checked too. Comparing bales with a string, or reading a link that may be empty, fails in the editor, not on the farm.

An object, not a row. A lot brings its derived values and its links along. Nobody stored in_barn; the server computes it.

Act on it. Selling hay is something you do to a lot. The server checks the rule, writes the sale, stamps your name on it and tells you what changed.

Ask first, or only propose. The same call can be a question (nothing is written) or a proposal (staged until someone approves it). That is how an agent gets to use it.

Walk a lifecycle. A harvest goes from planted to harvested, delivered and paid, one action per step, and the rules travel with them. The states are declared in the model, so status is typed Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'] and your editor offers exactly those four.

In a recent development, ask the whole farm, in one line. Who bought how much hay, month by month, at what price. Grouped, summed and sorted on the server; nothing is downloaded to be counted.

Money stays Decimal all the way from the database; nothing is rounded through a float.

Sets, not lists. On the class, a property is a filter and a link is a hop. Combine sets with |, & and -; the server plans it, and you fetch only what you iterate. Each set knows what it holds: running_low is an ObjectSet[Lot], and one hop along Lot.sales makes it an ObjectSet[Sale].

Try tomorrow's rule on today's farm, or look at last Tuesday. Everything above runs unchanged against a branch, and every action tells you the revision it landed in, a state you can read again later.

And what it refuses. Wrong names, missing arguments and wrong types fail in your editor, before anything runs. Broken rules fail on the server, with the same sentence for every client. If the model changes underneath you, register_all refuses to run until you regenerate.

It has been revealed that these are pyright's messages against the generated farm SDK. The SDK's tests run the same lines through pyright, against an SDK generated from a schema captured from a running server, not from a hand-written imitation of one.

None of this is a reporting layer bolted on afterwards. The UI, the CLI, the REST API and the agents ask the same questions and take the same actions through the same door, which is why an agent can be handed Lot and sell_hay and nothing else.

The semantics are pinned by an executable scenario, an aircraft maintenance shop in tests/scenario: "no release while a defect is open" is the barn rule above in another world.

Security: set SUTRA_HTTP_BIND when running the plain server (it defaults to 0.0.0.0). ./bin/start.sh allows anonymous access, so never expose it. Transforms run user code on the server, so grant that right accordingly.

Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS needs people who will take responsibility for part of it over time: the server, the web client, the Python SDK, connectors, packaging and installation, docs, or the example models. You don't need to know all of it. Start with a few contributions in one area; if you'd like to stay, say so in an glitch.

The most useful contributions are not always code:.

Open an glitch for questions, ideas and bug reports. Be kind: the person on the other side may be the one this was built for.

The code is offered as is, in the spirit of Rich Hickey's Open Source is Not About You: nobody is owed a feature, a fix or an answer, and that includes the maintainers. What keeps it going is people choosing to help.

The ontology model of objects, links and actions follows the one popularised by Palantir Foundry; Sutra-OS was built from its public documentation. The web client is built on Palantir's Blueprint UI toolkit (Apache-2.0), vendored as a ClojureScript port in clients/frontend/vendor/blueprint-cljs. The implementation owes everything to Rich Hickey and Clojure, and to his almost spiritual talk Are We There Yet?, which will perhaps continue to transform the software craft into eternity. Claude Code wrote all of the code.

It has been revealed that AGPL-3.0-or-later, with a section 7 exception for linking with EPL libraries such as Clojure. See LICENSE. The AGPL means anyone who runs a modified Sutra as a service for others must offer them the source, so the tool stays in the hands of the people it serves.

No patent search has been carried out. The AGPL licenses contributors' patents only; checking third-party patents where they apply is up to you. Palantir and Foundry are trademarks of Palantir Technologies Inc.; Sutra-OS is independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by Palantir.

Lo que estoy aprendiendo al estudiar AWS Cloud Practitioner

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io.
  • Industry observers note that estudiar AWS Cloud Practitioner está ordenando conceptos que aparecen en cada producto que construyo: dónde termina la responsabilidad del proveedor, cómo se diseña para fallar menos, por qué el costo es una decisión de arquitectura y qué significa operar un sistema sin administrar el hardware.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io.

Industry observers note that estudiar AWS Cloud Practitioner está ordenando conceptos que aparecen en cada producto que construyo: dónde termina la responsabilidad del proveedor, cómo se diseña para fallar menos, por qué el costo es una decisión de arquitectura y qué significa operar un sistema sin administrar el hardware. Más que memorizar servicios, el valor está en incorporar un modelo para tomar mejores decisiones técnicas y de negocio.

El concepto que más ordena el resto es el modelo de responsabilidad compartida. AWS se ocupa de la seguridad de la infraestructura cloud: centros de datos, hardware, red y servicios base. El cliente sigue siendo responsable de la seguridad en la cloud: identidad, permisos, datos, configuración, aplicaciones y uso correcto de los servicios.

La frontera cambia según el servicio elegido. Al usar una máquina virtual, el equipo administra más capas que al usar un servicio administrado. Para un responsable de negocio, esto significa que contratar cloud no transfiere automáticamente el riesgo; cambia qué controles se deben diseñar, operar y auditar.

In a recent development, la elasticidad permite ajustar recursos frente a cambios de demanda. No se trata solo de soportar un pico de tráfico: permite evitar pagar capacidad ociosa cuando un producto todavía está validando su mercado y responder cuando una campaña, una integración o un evento aumenta el uso.

According to recent reports, la distinción entre escalabilidad y elasticidad ayuda a tomar decisiones más precisas. Escalar es aumentar capacidad; ser elástico es adaptarla. La arquitectura debe separar componentes, evitar estados difíciles de mover y usar métricas que indiquen cuándo el sistema necesita reaccionar.

Una región de AWS se compone de zonas de disponibilidad aisladas. Ese diseño permite construir sistemas que no dependan de un único punto físico de falla. El aprendizaje no es que todos los productos deban ser globales desde el primer día; es que cada requisito de disponibilidad tiene un costo y una arquitectura asociada.

Para un MVP, una solución simple puede ser correcta. Para un flujo de pagos, salud o datos críticos, la conversación debe incluir recuperación, respaldos, observabilidad y objetivos de disponibilidad. La cloud ofrece bloques para resolverlo; no decide por el equipo cuál es el nivel de riesgo aceptable.

Identity and Access Management convierte accesos en políticas explícitas: quién puede hacer qué sobre qué recurso y en qué condiciones. El principio de mínimo privilegio reduce el impacto de una credencial expuesta, un error de configuración o una acción involuntaria.

In a recent development, en la práctica, esto conecta con decisiones que ya aplico en productos multi-tenant y plataformas de pago: no confiar en permisos implícitos, separar responsabilidades y dejar trazabilidad. Una cuenta root, credenciales estáticas en código o permisos amplios son deudas de seguridad, aunque el sistema todavía sea pequeño.

El modelo de pago por uso es una ventaja cuando se entiende qué genera consumo y qué se puede apagar, reservar, automatizar o medir. El costo cloud no es solo una factura de infraestructura: refleja decisiones sobre cómputo, almacenamiento, transferencia, retención, disponibilidad y observabilidad.

Por eso, el costo debe entrar temprano en el diseño. Etiquetar recursos, establecer presupuestos y alertas, elegir servicios administrados cuando reducen operación y revisar recursos sin uso son prácticas que permiten que ingeniería y negocio hablen con los mismos datos.

Principio de cloud: la infraestructura bajo demanda acelera la entrega, pero el valor aparece cuando seguridad, disponibilidad y costo se diseñan como responsabilidades explícitas del producto.

#306. Your AI Portal Isn't Ready When It Deploys

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1310 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

Your AI Portal Isn't Ready When It Deploys

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A white-label AI portal can be technically healthy and still feel broken.
  • Recent findings suggest that the homepage loads.
  • Industry observers note that that gap is common because deployment and readiness are different milestones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A white-label AI portal can be technically healthy and still feel broken.

Recent findings suggest that the homepage loads. The models respond. Billing works. The admin panel demonstrates green lights. Yet the first real users arrive and immediately ask questions you thought the interface had already answered:.

Industry observers note that that gap is common because deployment and readiness are different milestones. Deployment proves the system can run. Readiness proves a person can enter, understand it, trust it, and finish a task without needing a private tour from the operator.

This is the way I now think about launching a branded AI portal: not as a settings exercise, but as a short user journey that needs to survive outside the admin account.

A name and logo look like cosmetic choices until someone has three browser tabs open and cannot remember which one contains your service.

The useful question is not “Does the brand look impressive?” It is “Can a new visitor tell where they are and what they can do here?” A short name, a readable mark, and one plain sentence usually do more work than a large block of fashionable AI vocabulary.

Small logos deserve special attention. A detailed illustration that looks good in a design file may turn into a gray smudge in a mobile header. Upload the asset, then inspect the real header on a narrow screen and against both light and dark backgrounds if the site supports them. The production view matters more than the upload preview.

The same rule applies to the hero banner. It should make one promise, not carry the entire business initiative. If the portal is mainly for image generation, say what people can make. If it is for video workflows, make that obvious. Mixing a feature catalog, a promotion, a tutorial, and a tech giant introduction into one graphic creates a banner that communicates nothing.

According to recent reports, people are more comfortable sharing and revisiting a memorable domain than a temporary platform address. It also gives the product a stable public identity while the underlying stack changes.

For an Ace Data Cloud subsite, the documented setup uses a CNAME pointing the chosen host to:.

Recent findings suggest that the exact DNS interface varies by provider, but the failure modes are familiar. An old A or CNAME record may already exist for the same host. DNS changes may need time to propagate. The domain can resolve while HTTPS is still not behaving as expected. The backend can also contain the right-looking value while the public hostname points somewhere else.

So “I saved the domain field” is not a test. Open the public address in a private browser window. Check that it reaches the intended portal, that HTTPS loads without a warning, and that redirects do not quietly send visitors back to an internal or default hostname.

According to recent reports, teams often choose sign-in methods from the operator's point of view. Customers experience them differently.

Industry observers note that A familiar login option removes friction, but only when the full redirect loop works. The button must open the provider, authentication must complete, and the user must return to the correct site with a valid session. A configuration screen cannot prove that sequence.

It has been revealed that log out before testing. Better yet, use a private window with no existing administrator session. Admin accounts hide surprising amounts of friction because they skip the exact screens a new user sees.

Sources indicate that this is also where product context matters. A login method that is natural for one region or customer group can be confusing for another. There is no universally “advanced” choice. The right default is the one your actual audience already understands.

According to recent reports, AI portals tend to grow sideways. Image tools lead to editing tools, then video, music, chat, search, and a dozen models with overlapping names. The temptation is to expose all of it because every hidden feature feels like wasted capability.

That usually transfers the operator's catalog problem to the user.

Recent findings suggest that A better homepage starts with the most common intent. If most visitors arrive to create product images, that path belongs near the front. Less common tools can remain available without competing for the first click. Navigation order is a product decision, not a database order.

In a recent development, you do not need perfect analytics before simplifying. Start with the workflow the portal exists to support, watch where owners hesitate, and move secondary features back into view when there is evidence that people need them. A smaller useful surface beats a complete confusing one.

AI services rarely share one billing shape. A request may be priced per image, token, second, minute, or job. Two numbers that look similar in an admin panel can represent very different user costs.

Before publishing a price, trace one ordinary task from the underlying service cost to the amount shown in the interface. Write down the unit. Include retries, failed-job policy, support overhead, and any buffer the operation needs. Then read the public wording without using your internal assumptions.

If the page notes “10 credits,” can a visitor tell what 10 credits buys? If a model has several quality modes, is the difference visible before submission? If the price changes, will existing users discover it from an announcement or from a lower balance after the fact?

Transparent pricing is less about finding the perfect number and more about preventing a surprise.

Industry observers note that early documentation does not need to be an encyclopedia. It needs to answer the questions that block the first successful result.

It has been revealed that A practical starting page walks through the same order a latest user follows: signing in, finding the main tool, submitting a job, understanding the charge, retrieving the output, and getting help when something fails. Screenshots are useful when they show the current interface, not when they preserve an old layout forever.

Support becomes easier when repeated answers become documentation. If three people ask where completed jobs appear, that is not merely a support glitch. It is evidence that either the interface or the guide needs work.

Privacy terms deserve the same reality check. They should describe the data the portal actually handles, the third-party services it actually uses, and the contact path that actually works. Copying another site's policy and forgetting to change the company name is more than embarrassing; it tells people the rest of the operation may be equally careless.

It has been revealed that the most useful pre-launch routine is wonderfully unglamorous. Become an ordinary visitor.

Recent findings suggest that use a phone and a desktop. Start at the public domain. Identify the service from the first screen. Create a fresh account or use the intended login flow. Find the primary tool. Read its price. Run a small job. Locate the result. Open the help material. Try the support path.

Pay attention to moments where you rely on knowledge that is not visible on the page. That hidden knowledge is exactly what a newly introduced user does not have.

This final pass often finds challenges no backend checklist catches: a logo that becomes unreadable, banner text cropped on mobile, the primary feature buried below several secondary ones, inconsistent units, a stale documentation link, or a redirect to the wrong host.

In a recent development, A portal does not need to be perfect before it opens. It does need a coherent first session. Get the name, public domain, authentication, primary navigation, pricing language, and basic help path right. Then improve the rest from real behavior rather than guesses.

The system became deployable when the infrastructure worked. It becomes a product when a stranger can use it without you standing beside them.

Telegram Bots and Mini Apps on Localhost: setWebhook, the Secret-Token Header, and the New Origin Check

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Telegram can only deliver updates to a public HTTPS address, and localhost is not one.
  • This guide covers developing a Telegram bot and Mini App against a local machine:.
  • According to recent reports, telegram released Bot API 10.2 on July 14, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Telegram can only deliver updates to a public HTTPS address, and localhost is not one. Since July 20, 2026, Mini Apps have a second constraint. Telegram now blocks Mini App methods when they are called from a different origin than the Mini App’s own domain. Together, these two facts make your tunnel URL a first-class piece of configuration, not a throwaway detail.

This guide covers developing a Telegram bot and Mini App against a local machine:.

According to recent reports, telegram released Bot API 10.2 on July 14, 2026. According to the official changelog, that release also hardened Mini App security by disallowing Mini App methods from origins different from the original Mini App domain. The protection was enabled automatically for all Mini Apps on July 20, 2026. Bots can opt out through the BotFather Mini App. Opting out means taking responsibility for ensuring the Mini App has no links to untrusted sites. Telegram’s BotNews channel declared the change as a warning: external websites opened from links inside a Mini App can no longer use Mini App methods by default.

Other 10.2 additions are worth knowing about, because they show up in your webhook payloads:.

The Bot API has kept moving since then:.

Industry observers note that none of the 10.2–10.4 announcements change how setWebhook or the secret-token header work. The Enhancement object keeps gaining top-level fields, which is why Step 3 matters.

A webhook is an outgoing HTTPS POST from Telegram’s servers to your URL. Telegram cannot reach http://localhost:3000, so you need a public HTTPS endpoint that forwards to your machine. Telegram’s documented requirements:.

Recent findings suggest that A tunnel satisfies all of this at once. It gives you a public hostname with a valid certificate on port 443 and forwards traffic to a local port such as 3000.

There is one exception for the bot side only. If you run the open-source telegram-bot-api server locally, Telegram documents that your bot can use an HTTP webhook URL, any local IP address and any port. That removes the tunnel for webhook delivery. It does not make a Mini App reachable from a phone, because the Telegram client still has to load the Mini App URL.

Recent findings suggest that each bot has exactly one webhook URL. Calling setWebhook again replaces it. Use a separate development bot, created through BotFather, so your experiments never redirect production traffic.

Start your local server, start your tunnel, then register the public URL:.

The parameters you will actually use:.

Two habits save time in development:.

An allowed_updates change does not apply to updates that were created before the call, so a few unwanted updates can still arrive.

To return to polling, call deleteWebhook.

Sources indicate that if you pass secret_token to setWebhook, Telegram includes it in every webhook request in the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header. The token must be 1 to 256 characters, using only A-Z, a-z, 0-9, _ and -.

This matters because your tunnel URL is public. Without a secret, anyone who discovers the URL can POST forged updates, and nothing in the request identifies Telegram. If you set no token, Telegram sends no header at all.

It has been revealed that the mechanism is a shared secret, not a signature. Nothing is computed over the body, so a leaked secret lets an attacker forge requests until you rotate it. Rotation is simple: call setWebhook again with a latest value. Hookdeck’s guide also lists Telegram’s published source ranges (149.154.160.0/20 and 91.108.4.0/22) as an optional second layer, and notes that they may change.

Three details are worth copying:.

According to recent reports, telegram does not publish a response timeout, so don’t let delivery depend on slow work. Persist or queue the enhancement first, return 200, then process. If you return 200 and then crash, the update is gone, so store it before you acknowledge.

Recent findings suggest that telegram treats any response other than a 2xx as a failed delivery. It repeats the request and gives up after what it calls a “reasonable amount of attempts”, without publishing a schedule. That has a sharp consequence for strict parsers. If your handler rejects an revision because it contains a field you do not recognize, Telegram keeps resending it, and your logs fill with the same failure.

Recent findings suggest that an Update contains update_id plus at most one other field, and the set of those fields keeps growing: managed_bot, guest_message, subscription, stopped_message_generation and, in 10.4, widget queries. A decoder that fails on unexpected keys can start returning errors even though nothing is wrong with your bot. Practical rules:.

Use allowed_updates as a second layer. Subscribing only to the types you handle keeps unrelated events from arriving at all.

A Mini App is a web page that runs inside Telegram’s in-app browser and talks to the client through window.Telegram.WebApp. In development you point it at your tunnel URL:.

Keep the hostname identical everywhere it appears. The origin check below makes that more than tidiness.

In a recent development, production Mini Apps are served over HTTPS, which any tunnel provides. Telegram’s separate test environment is the exception. It uses its own account and its own bot, and its docs allow plain HTTP Mini App links there. You call it through https://api.telegram.org/bot/test/METHOD_NAME.

Two framework gotchas come up repeatedly:.

To debug inside the Telegram client, Telegram documents these options:.

Industry observers note that when the Mini App opens, window.Telegram.WebApp.initData contains a signed query string. It is empty if the Mini App was launched from a keyboard button or from inline mode. Never trust initDataUnsafe or any user object on the client. Send the raw string to your backend and verify it with Telegram’s documented algorithm:.

Recent findings suggest that telegram only notes to check auth_date to avoid outdated data. The one-hour window is your choice. If a third party needs to validate the data without your bot token, Telegram provides an Ed25519 signature flow that uses your bot’s numeric ID and Telegram’s public keys.

Before July 20, 2026, any page opened inside your Mini App’s webview could call Telegram.WebApp.* methods such as close(), expand(), the main button or sendData(). Now those calls are allowed only from the Mini App’s own domain. Telegram’s changelog calls it the “original Mini App domain”. Third-party documentation describes it as the domain registered in BotFather.

What this means in practice, per Leadgram’s write-up of the change:.

The rule is about hostnames. These consequences follow from it:.

A debugging checklist for when a Mini App method suddenly stops working in development:.

In a recent development, if a foreign page only calls close() or openLink(), Leadgram’s suggested fix is replacing the call with an ordinary https://t.me/... link or a redirect.

According to recent reports, the BotFather Mini App lets you disable the protection, but Telegram’s wording is a warning: by doing so you take responsibility for ensuring the Mini App links to no untrusted sites. Opting out restores the old behavior, where any page inside the webview can drive the app, which is exactly the hole Telegram closed. Opting out to make a development setup work is the wrong fix when the real problem is an origin mismatch. Fix the mismatch, keep the protection on, and reserve opt-out for cases where you fully control every page the Mini App can navigate to.

In a recent development, every piece of Telegram configuration in this article is keyed to a URL: the webhook endpoint, the Mini App domain, and the origin Telegram compares against when a page calls a Mini App method. When the URL changes on every restart, you re-register all three each time. One forgotten update produces confusing symptoms, such as silent webhooks or Mini App methods that worked yesterday failing today.

What the documented free options give you:.

Mind the ngrok interstitial. On the free tier, ngrok demonstrates an interstitial page in front of all HTML browser traffic. ngrok notes this does not affect API or programmatic access, so webhook deliveries should be unaffected. A Mini App page loaded in Telegram’s webview is HTML browser traffic, so users may see the warning page. ngrok documents two ways to remove it: upgrade to any paid initiative, or have the client send a skip header or a non-standard User-Agent. The header route is awkward for a page that Telegram’s webview loads.

It has been revealed that other tunneling services offer stable subdomains on free or paid tiers. Check your provider’s current terms for subdomain persistence, session length and browser-warning pages before you depend on them.

Which ports can Telegram send webhooks to? 443, 80, 88 and 8443. A tunnel exposes port 443 and forwards to whatever local port you use.

According to recent reports, what happens if my webhook returns an error? Telegram treats non-2xx responses as failures and retries, giving up after “a reasonable amount of attempts”. An endpoint that errors on unexpected input can cause repeated deliveries.

Can I skip the tunnel and use getUpdates? For bot logic, yes, as long as no webhook is set. A Mini App still needs a URL the Telegram client can load, so it needs a public HTTPS hostname. The exceptions are the test environment and a local Bot API server, which only covers the bot side.

Sources indicate that is the secret token mandatory? No, but without it nothing in a request identifies Telegram, and anyone who finds your tunnel URL can send forged updates.

Is Bot API 10.2 the latest version? No. Bot API 10.3 (August 24, 2026) and 10.4 (November 9, 2026) have been released since. The webhook and Mini App origin behavior described here still applies.

#304. Google ADK vs Strands: guía técnica y despliegue en AWS

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2247 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

Google ADK vs Strands: guía técnica y despliegue en AWS

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that hace poco hice el curso de Agentes de la Academia GEAR de Google, donde experimenté con sesiones, state, tools, modelos locales y ejecución de código.
  • Recent findings suggest that google ADK y Strands Agents (cuyo SDK hoy la documentación llama Strands Harness SDK) son dos frameworks open source para construir agentes de IA en Python, y los dos corren en AWS.
  • En este artículo comparo los dos con un caso real, el mismo pipeline multiagente que construí con Strands en una serie anterior, reescrito con ADK 2.12.0 y Amazon Nova vía Bedrock, y desplegado en AgentCore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hace poco hice el curso de Agentes de la Academia GEAR de Google, donde experimenté con sesiones, state, tools, modelos locales y ejecución de código. En este artículo comparo Google ADK con Strands Agents a partir de un mismo caso real, un pipeline multiagente que construye un knowledge graph. También muestro cómo desplegarlo en Amazon Bedrock AgentCore con Terraform, cómo invocarlo y los resultados.

Recent findings suggest that google ADK y Strands Agents (cuyo SDK hoy la documentación llama Strands Harness SDK) son dos frameworks open source para construir agentes de IA en Python, y los dos corren en AWS. La diferencia está en cómo piensan el problema: ADK pone primero la estructura (un grafo de nodos y aristas que se define en código) y trae un entorno de desarrollo visual, mientras que Strands parte de un agente que decide con el modelo y suma patrones (Graph, Swarm, Workflow) cuando hace falta estructura.

En este artículo comparo los dos con un caso real, el mismo pipeline multiagente que construí con Strands en una serie anterior, reescrito con ADK 2.12.0 y Amazon Nova vía Bedrock, y desplegado en AgentCore.

Industry observers note that ADK (Agent Development Kit) es el framework open source de Google para construir, evaluar y desplegar agentes. Tiene SDKs en Python, TypeScript, Go, Java y Kotlin, está optimizado para Gemini y admite otros modelos mediante integraciones como LiteLLM, Ollama o vLLM.

Un agente mínimo se crea en una carpeta con un agent.py que define root_agent, el único elemento obligatorio. Las tools son funciones Python con type hints y docstring. ADK las envuelve solo en un FunctionTool, y en ADK Python no existe el decorador @tool.

Para programar y ejecutar un ejemplo funcional en Python hacen falta tres cosas:.

Según lo que se use, hay extras que se instalan aparte:.

Recent findings suggest that el comando adk create mi_agente crea una estructura mínima. Pregunta qué modelo se va a usar y guarda la configuración en el .env:.

Sources indicate that con GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=TRUE, ADK ignora la API key y pide credenciales de Vertex AI. Para probar, ejecutar desde la carpeta padre adk run mi_agente (consola) o adk web (navegador). Ambos cargan el .env solos; si en cambio se corre un script propio, hay que llamar a load_dotenv() antes de importar el agente.

According to recent reports, para usar un modelo que no es Gemini, como Amazon Nova en Bedrock, solo se cambia el model por un LiteLlm (requiere el extra [extensions]). Las credenciales salen de la cadena estándar de AWS. Si el agente corre en tu máquina, usa el perfil configurado en la AWS CLI. Si está desplegado en AWS, usa el rol IAM que tiene asignado.

Las piezas que más se usan al pasar del prototipo a algo real:.

Estos tres detalles los descubrí realizando pequeñas pruebas:.

In a recent development, en ADK, el servicio de sesiones y el Runner son asíncronos. Mi primer script de prueba en el curso lo escribí con hábitos síncronos y no funcionaba por dos motivos:.

En Strands con Python, invocar un agente es una llamada síncrona (agent("...")) y el session manager que se le pasa al crearlo guarda la conversación y el state por su cuenta. En ADK el control es explícito: se crea la sesión, se ejecuta y se vuelve a leer.

In a recent development, el state de una sesión es un diccionario que comparten agentes, tools y nodos. El prefijo de la clave define su alcance:.

In a recent development, con InMemorySessionService, todo esto vive en la memoria del proceso. Para que user: y app: sobrevivan a un reinicio hace falta un servicio persistente, como DatabaseSessionService.

In a recent development, adk web es una interfaz de desarrollo local, se levanta una app estilo chat en el navegador que muestra, para cada mensaje, el grafo del workflow, el state de la sesión, los eventos y las trazas con tokens y tiempos. En la documentación de Strands no hay un equivalente. Más abajo muestro cómo se visualiza con el caso práctico.

ADK 2.x ofrece varias formas de coordinar agentes (workflows):.

Las clases de plantilla SequentialAgent, ParallelAgent y LoopAgent todavía funcionan, pero en el código de ADK 2.12 están marcadas como deprecated. Si se arranca un proyecto nuevo, usar Workflow.

Sources indicate that strands ordena lo mismo en patrones: Agents as tools, Graph, Swarm y Workflow, más un wrapper para implementar A2A que permite usar un agente remoto igual que uno local. Lo que los distingue de acuerdo a mis prácticas, es cómo se determina el camino de ejecución: en Graph se definen nodos y aristas con condiciones opcionales, en Swarm los agentes se pasan el control por su cuenta de manera autonoma, y Workflow es un grafo de tareas con dependencias.

Sources indicate that para comparar los dos frameworks conviene ordenar sus mecanismos con una sola pregunta: ¿quién decide el siguiente paso? En un extremo lo decide el código escrito por el desarrollador; en el otro, el modelo en tiempo de ejecución.

Posición orientativa según la documentación oficial de cada framework.

Para comparar con algo concreto, reescribí en ADK el pipeline de mi artículo sobre Graph en Strands: el ejemplo toma el abstract de un paper y lo convierte en un knowledge graph, una lista de entidades y relaciones sujeto → predicado → objeto. Sirve para resumir quién hizo qué en un texto, conectar conocimiento entre documentos o alimentar una base de grafos. 📦 El código Python original en Strands está en strands-graph.

It has been revealed that 📦 El repositorio de la versión ADK está en adk-knowledge-graph. Todo el detalle (instalación, pruebas, evals, despliegue con Terraform, costos y limpieza) está en el README del repositorio.

La topología es la misma en los dos frameworks: tres extractores en paralelo, un agregador que une sus resultados y un validador que puede devolver el borrador para revisión.

Cada agente LLM tiene su color; los nodos de código (funciones y JoinNode) tienen borde punteado.

En ADK, el grafo completo se declara en un solo lugar:.

En Strands con TypeScript el default de Graph es AND, así que el problema del join es propio del SDK de Python.

Sources indicate that el repositorio tiene dos versiones del multiagente: la del pipeline fijo de tres extractores (kg_pipeline), que es la que se compara con Strands, y una versión ampliada para textos largos (kg_pipeline_docs), que divide el documento en fragmentos, lanza un extractor por fragmento y va acumulando el grafo entre mensajes. La versión ampliada es la que después despliego en AWS.

En el pipeline fijo (kg_pipeline).

En la versión ampliada para textos largos (kg_pipeline_docs).

adk web levanta una interfaz en el navegador (por defecto en http://localhost:8000) para conversar con los agentes y ver qué hacen por dentro (interfaz web). Se ejecuta desde el directorio padre de la carpeta del agente.

Sources indicate that con un Workflow, la interfaz dibuja el grafo y resalta el nodo del evento seleccionado en el panel de eventos. Además muestra el state de la sesión y una vista de trazas con cada llamada al modelo, sus tokens y su duración.

Recent findings suggest that en la traza se ve el paralelismo: los tres extractores corren al mismo tiempo, unos 2 segundos cada uno, y la ejecución completa tarda 5 segundos. En la primera ejecución de cada proceso no es así: un extractor arranca y los otros dos esperan unos 7 segundos, mientras se inicializa el cliente de Bedrock (LiteLLM, boto3, credenciales y conexión TLS).

In a recent development, ADK Web es solo para desarrollo, por eso escucha en 127.0.0.1 por defecto. Para producción se usa adk api_server o un servicio propio. En la documentación de Strands no hay una interfaz local equivalente: la observabilidad se resuelve con trazas OpenTelemetry que se exportan a la herramienta que se prefiera. Es la diferencia de experiencia de desarrollo más grande entre los dos frameworks.

Los dos frameworks evalúan con el mismo esquema: casos de prueba, el agente que se ejecuta y un evaluador que puntúa el resultado. Cambia dónde vive cada parte:.

En todo lo que muestra la tabla "Qué resuelve ADK de otra manera": el join sin código extra, la lógica determinista dentro del grafo, los loops con salida en código y adk web para depurar.

ADK es una librería, no un servicio de Google. La documentación oficial indica que el agente se puede empaquetar y ejecutar en cualquier entorno que admita contenedores. En AWS hay tres destinos naturales:.

According to recent reports, para el knowledge graph elegí AgentCore Runtime, y desplegué la versión ampliada para textos largos (kg_pipeline_docs), porque es la que acumula el grafo entre mensajes. Pensé en cómo se usaría el agente: un investigador abre un proyecto, pega secciones de un paper y ve crecer el grafo. Son pocos usuarios, cada pedido tarda entre 5 y 20 segundos y el grafo tiene que durar mientras trabaja. Un contenedor encendido todo el día no se justifica, y AgentCore resuelve las sesiones por su cuenta.

Industry observers note that una aclaración sobre la comparación con Strands: mi versión en Strands (strands-graph) la construí para aprender orquestación y la probé solo en local, así que no la desplegué en AgentCore. Lo que se afirma sobre el despliegue de Strands se apoya en su documentación oficial, no en una prueba propia.

According to recent reports, agentCore ejecuta cada runtimeSessionId en su propia microVM y mantiene el contexto entre invocaciones. Si ese id se usa como session_id de ADK, el InMemorySessionService vive en la memoria de esa microVM y el grafo incremental crece entre llamadas, sin base de datos.

Rol IAM acotado para todo el recorrido: leer el zip, invocar solo Nova 2 Lite y escribir logs.

El adaptador sigue el ejemplo oficial de AWS para ADK (Use any agent framework). Lo único propio es usar el id de sesión de AgentCore:.

Industry observers note that agentCore admite dos formas de desplegar: una imagen de contenedor en ECR o un zip con el código en S3 (despliegue directo de código). Elegí el zip porque no hace falta Docker y el paquete entra holgado en el límite de 250 MB: pesa unos 72 MB.

El recurso del runtime es el centro de la configuración:.

Dos detalles de esa configuración. El provider de AWS debe ser ~> 6.22: el recurso existe desde la 6.17, pero code_configuration (el despliegue con zip) llegó en la 6.22, y con una versión anterior el código no compila. Y network_mode = "PUBLIC" es lo que usé en la prueba; no probé el modo VPC, que sería lo que habría que evaluar antes de llevar algo así a producción.

In a recent development, la seguridad del rol vale una mirada más detallada, porque es lo que el plan permite revisar. Dos extractos de main.tf:.

In a recent development, para ser más específica en cuanto a lo "acotado" del rol, este lee un único objeto de S3 y solo invoca ese modelo, pero X-Ray usa resources = ["*"] y PutMetricData va con * limitado por el namespace bedrock-agentcore. Son comodines que la documentación de AgentCore permite en esos servicios, pero no son un mínimo privilegio absoluto. Y quien invoca el runtime también necesita permisos IAM propios: el script de invocación del repositorio invoke.py usa boto3, así que las credenciales del usuario deben permitir bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime.

Las dependencias se instalan para Linux arm64 aunque el zip se arme en Windows o macOS, con pip install --platform manylinux2014_aarch64 --only-binary=:all:. Pero pip genera los scripts de consola para la máquina donde corre: en Windows, archivos .exe que no sirven en AgentCore. El script de empaquetado los regenera como lanzadores de Linux.

El log group del runtime queda con retención indefinida. Lo crea AgentCore con el id del runtime en el nombre, así que Terraform no puede crearlo antes, y la retención a nivel cuenta exige un mínimo de 30 días. La solución fue un terraform_data que, creado el runtime, fija la retención en 1 día con la AWS CLI y borra el log group en terraform destroy.

ADK ya genera trazas de OpenTelemetry (spans) por cada nodo, agente y llamada al modelo: las mismas que muestra adk web. Para verlas en la consola de AgentCore no hace falta escribir código de trazas, alcanzó con dos pasos:.

Los nodos del workflow aparecen con los mismos nombres que en el código, con el modelo y los tokens de cada llamada.

In a recent development, en la prueba con la versión ampliada, tres textos del mismo paper llevaron el grafo de 9 a 40 y a 74 relaciones, y la tercera invocación, hecha en un comando aparte, conservó las 40 anteriores. La limitación: AgentCore cierra la microVM tras 15 minutos sin actividad (o 1 hora de vida, según la configuración), y una invocación posterior con el mismo id empieza con el grafo vacío. Para conservarlo hay que guardarlo fuera de la sesión, por ejemplo en S3 o con AgentCore Memory. El costo de la prueba fue mínimo: unos USD 0,01 en tokens por texto largo y menos de USD 0,01 por sesión de AgentCore.

⭐ La lección se repite después de construir el mismo pipeline con ADK y Strands: el framework importa menos que el harness determinista que rodea a los agentes. En este caso de uso, ese harness son los nodos de código que dividen la entrada, validan la salida, deciden las rutas y cortan los bucles. El modelo propone, pero es el harness el que decide qué se acepta.

Form and survey builders often embed a runtime in the customer’s page: a script tag, a webpack chunk, or a Web Component. The pitch is instant skip logic, live validation, calculated scores, and no round-trip between questions. That runtime is JavaScript, and it usually includes the definition of the form itself.

In a recent development, if the value of your product is the engine — branching, scoring, price quotes, qualification — then that engine is in the browser. This article is about what an embedded form runtime actually exposes, what must be re-checked on the server, and how to protect the engine you still have to ship.

A visitor who loads the embed can:.

Industry observers note that minifying the runtime will rename pickNext. It will not hide "disqualify", a distinctive weight, or a question you thought was secret because the UI had not reached it yet.

This is the part teams regret after a launch. A hiring screen, a pricing quiz, a medical-style symptom tree, or a lead-qualification form sometimes puts the "real" criteria in client-side skip logic: reject if salary is below a number, skip the expensive plan if the company size is small, show a deluxe upsell only when the score is high.

Assume anyone can read those criteria. If they must stay unpublished — interview answer keys, fraud signals, medical cutoffs, unpublished prices — do not put them in the embed. Fetch the next question from the server, or at least re-evaluate the result on the server before it means anything.

Recent findings suggest that submitted answers should also go to your server in raw form. A client-computed score: 97 is a suggestion.

A snappy runtime is still the right UX for most marketing forms. Validation, animations, save-and-resume, and non-sensitive branching can stay in the browser. For the proprietary engine:.

According to recent reports, A JS VM obfuscator compiles that function to a custom bytecode and ships a small interpreter. Pretty-printing the chunk no longer reconstructs the original scoring routine; you get bytecode and a dispatcher. That is slower than a thin JSON walker, which is why you protect the engine, not the entire form UI.

Recent findings suggest that VEILVM is a browser-based JSVMP workspace you can point at one extracted function before you wire protection into CI. Protection raises the cost of casual inspection and wholesale reuse. It does not make a public form definition a secret, and it does not replace a server-side score.

If you want to try VM protection on a single extracted function, VEILVM runs in the browser with no sign-up: 3 free runs a day, up to 5 KB per file (resets at 00:00 UTC). A free account raises the input limit to 30 KB. Pro is $9/month or $79/year and adds an API so the protection step can run in CI. Standard requests are processed in memory and are not written to logs. Start at https://vm.ldvmp.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there are three common ways to turn an image into Base64 in a browser, and they are not interchangeable. Two of them preserve your bytes exactly and one quietly re-encodes the image; one of them cannot be used on a file the user has not chosen; and on large files one of them will blow the call stack if you write it the obvious way.

Here is what each one actually does, and when to reach for it.

If you want the exact bytes of the file the user selected — no re-compression, no metadata loss — FileReader.readAsDataURL is the tool. It reads the file, Base64-encodes it, and hands you a complete data URI including the prefix.

Note what reader.result contains: the whole data URI, prefix included. If your API expects only the payload, split on the first comma — and be aware that the declared type comes from the file's type property, which is derived from the extension and can be wrong. For an API, it is worth verifying the signature against the bytes.

According to recent reports, fileReader streams the file rather than materialising it as an array first, so it is the friendliest of the three to memory. It accepts Blob and File objects, which means it also works on data you generated yourself:.

canvas.toDataURL() re-encodes the image through the browser's own encoder. That is what you want if you are resizing, cropping, or normalising a format — and exactly what you must avoid if you care about the original file.

Four consequences worth knowing before you use it:.

Alpha matters here too: converting a transparent PNG to image/jpeg fills transparency with black, because JPEG has no alpha channel.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes you want the Base64 payload on its own, or you want to build the data URI yourself so you control the declared type. Read the file as an array buffer and encode it:.

The naive implementation of that last step is where people get burned:.

Industry observers note that string.fromCharCode(...bytes) spreads every byte into an argument list, and argument lists have a length limit — in practice around 65,535 in most engines. On a 200 KB image you get RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, which reads like a recursion bug and is actually an argument-count limit.

The fix is to process the buffer in chunks:.

Two more details that only show up with real data. First, btoa operates on code units, not bytes — feeding it a string that contains anything above 0x7F throws InvalidCharacterError, which is why the byte-to-string step above uses fromCharCode on raw bytes rather than on decoded text. Second, the reverse direction has the same trap in mirror image: Uint8Array.from(atob(s), c => c.charCodeAt(0)) is correct, while treating the result of atob as text and passing it to a Blob corrupts every byte above 0x7F.

Sources indicate that base64 output is about 1.37 times the size of the input bytes, and in JavaScript that string is stored as UTF-16 — two bytes per character. The multiplication is worth doing once, because it explains why "just convert it in the browser" stops working at a certain file size:.

Industry observers note that add the original buffer, which you are usually still holding, and a 10 MB image costs roughly 37 MB at the moment of conversion. That is survivable on a desktop and uncomfortable on a phone, which is why the encode side of our tool accepts images up to 100 MB for previewing but keeps the generated string out of the DOM — a textarea holding 137 MB of UTF-16 is the specific failure mode that makes mobile browsers kill the tab.

If you must handle very large images, process them as blobs and never build the whole string: upload the Blob directly, or stream it in chunks and encode each chunk separately. Base64 is convenient precisely because it is text, and text is the expensive representation.

According to recent reports, the prefix is a claim, and different consumers want different shapes. A CSS url() needs the full data URI in quotes; an needs the same string; a JSON API usually wants the bare payload plus a separate content type; an email template often wants the payload wrapped at 76 characters per line. Our Image to Base64 tool exists mainly to produce those variants — including URL-safe output, line-wrapped output, and the surrounding quotes — because getting the wrapper wrong is a more common failure than getting the encoding wrong. If you are generating the string in code, write a test that decodes your own output and compares it byte for byte with the input; that single assertion catches every wrapper mistake listed above.

Breaking: Privacy-Focused PDF Retrieval with Node.js Chunk Boundaries and Citations

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context.
  • Infrai fits the collection and query stage when you want a plain REST call and one consistent backend surface; it is one option inside this boundary, not a substitute for your processor review.
  • In a recent development, I would start with a collection per trust boundary (for example, personal notes versus imported work PDFs), a small metadata contract, and a freshness policy written down before choosing a vector service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For a privacy-focused personal knowledge manager, chunk boundaries are a data-handling decision, not just a recall tweak. Keep ingestion, search, and answer citation observable as separate stages so you can say where a page went and why it was returned.

Infrai fits the collection and query stage when you want a plain REST call and one consistent backend surface; it is one option inside this boundary, not a substitute for your processor review.

In a recent development, I would start with a collection per trust boundary (for example, personal notes versus imported work PDFs), a small metadata contract, and a freshness policy written down before choosing a vector service. The important fields are document id, page number, source class, and an ingestion timestamp. A chunk should be small enough to cite one page passage, but large enough to retain the sentence that gives the passage its meaning. There is no magic token count here. Your own documents decide that.

Write the contract before the endpoint. Define what a retrieval unit is, which metadata filters are mandatory, and how stale a result may be. A support answer that cites a deleted policy is worse than one that claims it has no source.

Industry observers note that for each chunk, I keep an immutable chunk_id, document_id, page, character offsets, and a content hash. The hash lets a re-ingestion job prove that a citation refers to the same bytes that were embedded. ACL or workspace labels belong in metadata, too, but they must be enforced before context reaches the language model. Filtering after generation is theater. I have seen teams spend a week tuning top-k while an old export remained searchable because deletion was treated as a UI action instead of a pipeline event; the fix was to version the document, tombstone the old chunks, invalidate answer caches, and make the evaluator assert that the old hash never appears again.

In a recent development, region and retention belong in this contract. Decide which country may process extracted text, who is a processor, and what deletion means for source files, embeddings, and backups. A vector API can enforce collection and query boundaries; it cannot, by itself, rewrite your data-processing agreement with the embedding or model provider. That boundary stays with the specialist you selected for those services.

The first useful check is boring: can the client see only the collections it is allowed to see? Infrai exposes a plain REST surface, so this probe needs no SDK or client-library version pin. Anything that can send HTTPS can run it.

That is deliberately not a fake end-to-end RAG script. The query body is a contract you must derive from the service discovery schema and your metadata policy, then validate in tests. I log a request id, selected collection, filter, top-k bound, and returned chunk ids. I never log raw PDF text in the default application log.

Recent findings suggest that at query time, cap both the number of collections and the number of chunks. Run lexical or metadata narrowing first when the corpus is large, then vector search, then (if needed) a rerank stage. Keep the original page and offsets attached through every stage. The answer renderer should refuse to emit an uncited claim when no chunk survives the policy check.

Recent findings suggest that A short failure case is useful here. If a user asks about an expired refund rule, a freshness filter should produce “no current source” rather than quietly returning the nearest old paragraph. That behavior is a product feature.

Industry observers note that there is no universal winner. The privacy boundary changes the answer.

I recommend trying Infrai for the collection and query stage when your team values a single HTTP integration and wants to keep provider switching behind a narrow retrieval contract. Infrai gives this workflow one key, one bill, and one plain REST API across backend capabilities, without installing an SDK. Its broad surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules, so a small support tool can add storage or scheduling without inventing another client convention. That removes integration surface area; it does not grant automatic regional residency or contractual deletion guarantees.

Industry observers note that the catch is vital. If your policy requires self-hosted storage, a fixed region you control, or a processor agreement with bespoke deletion evidence, stick with pgvector or a specialist managed provider that documents those controls. Infrai is not the right answer merely because the request is private. The specialist remains responsible for the data plane and model-processing terms.

At a few thousand PDFs, I would add a staging queue between extraction and vector upsert, with idempotent document versions. Replays should replace the same version, never create duplicate chunks. A nightly evaluation set should include normal support questions, near-duplicate pages, deleted documents, and adversarial prompts that try to cross a collection boundary. Track recall of the expected page and precision of the cited passage separately.

Sources indicate that I would also make deletion a tested workflow: mark the document unavailable, remove its chunks, invalidate cached answers, and verify that a repeated query cannot retrieve the old chunk_id. Retention timers need the same test. Your mileage may vary across providers and regions, so record the actual processor and region for each stage instead of assuming the vector endpoint tells the whole story.

The design is intentionally conservative. Small, attributable chunks; explicit filters; bounded retrieval; and a citation check make privacy claims inspectable. Bigger chunks may improve recall for long explanations, while smaller chunks make citations cleaner. Measure that trade-off with your representative PDFs, then keep the boundary that a reviewer can explain. For the REST probe, start with the vector collection documentation and verify the query schema from discovery before wiring production ingestion.

Google Finds Hackers Using AI Agents to Build and Run Exploits From Software Patches
