📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.
  • In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks to automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as observed in the case of PaperCut NG/MF flaws earlier this September.
  • The abuse of open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks is seen as a way to "automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report shared with The Hacker News.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.

In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks to automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as observed in the case of PaperCut NG/MF flaws earlier this September.

The abuse of open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks is seen as a way to "automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The tech giant said the adoption represents a paradigm shift in which cyber attacks take place at machine speed, allowing the operations to be scaled significantly by chaining together varied attack paths even if the underlying mechanics remain the same.

A number of threat actors have been observed experimenting with these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated and suspected espionage actors aligned with China.

"These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation," Google stated.

Another key area of misuse revolves around automating labor-intensive tasks like vulnerability analysis and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization using LLM-driven pipelines, allowing threat actors to collapse the window between patch disclosure and active exploitation.

"Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws," Google added.

Simultaneously, threat actors are also targeting AI infrastructure to illicit profit from LLMjacking attacks by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments, and then reselling the access through underground proxy services like APIMart and JetNight at discounted prices, otherwise known as LLM mixers.

The findings show that the emergence of open-source frameworks have further lowered the barrier to entry, enabling bad actors to easily integrate new exploits, autonomously scale attacks, and mount convincing phishing campaigns, further compressing attack timelines.

This includes a Chinese-language phishing platform called Jieyou that has integrated an LLM chatbot assistant to allow customers to configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands without necessarily having the technical expertise to do so.

It has been revealed that "The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier," Google said. "Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly.".

#294. Web corporativa en 2026: diseñar impacto sin sacrificar rendimiento ni control

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (503 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

Web corporativa en 2026: diseñar impacto sin sacrificar rendimiento ni control

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io.
  • Sources indicate that una web corporativa ya no compite solo por informar qué hace una empresa.
  • En ese tiempo, la persona tiene que poder entender qué hace la organización, por qué debería prestarle atención y cuál es el siguiente paso.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io.

Sources indicate that una web corporativa ya no compite solo por informar qué hace una empresa. Compite por comunicar criterio, diferenciar una propuesta y conducir una conversación comercial. El reto técnico es lograr una experiencia memorable sin convertir la página en una SPA frágil, lenta o difícil de evolucionar. Pambú 2026 fue construido desde ese equilibrio.

Una visita institucional dura poco. En ese tiempo, la persona tiene que poder entender qué hace la organización, por qué debería prestarle atención y cuál es el siguiente paso. La arquitectura de información no puede ser una lista de secciones intercambiables: necesita una narrativa que ordene propuesta de valor, enfoque, identidad, servicios y contacto.

En Pambú 2026, la estructura se organiza como una experiencia de una página con navegación a secciones. El scroll deja de ser solo una forma de desplazarse y se convierte en el ritmo de la presentación. Para negocio, esto permite guiar el mensaje; para ingeniería, mantiene un modelo de contenido directo y comprensible.

It has been revealed that el fondo animado con WebGL y Three.js incorpora profundidad y movimiento a una propuesta centrada en creatividad, tecnología e innovación. Pero el componente visual no puede cargar con el significado de la página. El contenido comercial, la navegación y el contacto deben permanecer disponibles como HTML semántico y legible sin depender de la capa gráfica.

Esta separación es un control de resiliencia. La experiencia enriquecida puede evolucionar, degradar de forma aceptable en hardware limitado o fallar sin bloquear el mensaje. El impacto visual es una capa de mejora progresiva, no una condición para que el sitio funcione.

GSAP y ScrollTrigger permiten sincronizar transiciones con la lectura de cada sección. Usarlos bien no significa animar todo: significa dirigir atención hacia un cambio de contexto, una jerarquía visual o una llamada a la acción. Cada animación debe justificar qué comprensión o conversión mejora.

En una página de alto impacto, el rendimiento es parte de la marca. El equipo debe tratar el peso de assets, el trabajo de renderizado y la ejecución en dispositivos de menor capacidad como restricciones de diseño. La elección de JavaScript vanilla para la capa de interacción reduce superficie de runtime y facilita que la experiencia se mantenga enfocada.

Pambú 2026 se implementa con HTML5, CSS3 y JavaScript vanilla, con Three.js y GSAP cargados desde CDN. Esta decisión no niega el valor de un framework; responde a un caso donde la página es una experiencia editorial acotada, no una aplicación con estados de negocio complejos.

La consecuencia es operativa: menos capas para desplegar, inspeccionar y modificar. El equipo puede concentrar su esfuerzo en narrativa, contenido, performance y calidad visual. Si el producto necesita luego CMS, personalización o funcionalidades transaccionales, la arquitectura puede crecer sobre una necesidad comprobada, no una hipótesis.

In a recent development, principio de experiencia corporativa: el alto impacto surge cuando la narrativa, la identidad visual y el rendimiento trabajan como un sistema. La tecnología debe intensificar el mensaje, no convertirse en el mensaje.

#293. Staggering Scroll-Driven Animations with animation-range-start

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1506 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Css-tricks

Staggering Scroll-Driven Animations with animation-range-start

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The other day on the CSS-Tricks Slack channel, Danny Schwartz shared an interesting recent Master.dev article by Ashutosh Biswas on how to stagger CSS scrolling animations using a clever combo of several emergent CSS features and a lot of math, which Ashutosh admits is “a huge formula and can look intimidating.”.
  • When Danny Slacked the link for the Frontend Masters article, he described it as “CSS on drugs.” Speaking of drugs, I am on heavy prescription painkillers while recovering from a serious injury, so that might not help my current comprehension skills.
  • It has been revealed that don’t get me wrong.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The other day on the CSS-Tricks Slack channel, Danny Schwartz shared an interesting recent Master.dev article by Ashutosh Biswas on how to stagger CSS scrolling animations using a clever combo of several emergent CSS features and a lot of math, which Ashutosh admits is “a huge formula and can look intimidating.”.

I’ll agree with Ashutosh there.

When Danny Slacked the link for the Frontend Masters article, he described it as “CSS on drugs.” Speaking of drugs, I am on heavy prescription painkillers while recovering from a serious injury, so that might not help my current comprehension skills. Nevertheless, after reading Ashutosh’s article a few times, here’s a meme showing how I’d feel using such an elaborate algorithm for something as mundane as staggering the animations of some characters as they scroll into view.

It has been revealed that don’t get me wrong. I know the complexity is because Ashutosh is going for a generic solution in which we can connect a “progress value to an animation, scroll progress, or any other input to drive the staggering.”.

In fact, I can dream up a scenario in which this might be what we want: Imagine a CSS karaoke machine that displays a ball bouncing on text that incrementally highlights, based on the user’s progress through the vocals measured via speech recognition. Running that kind of animation “not as a collection of independently timed objects, but as a single predictable, holistic effect driven by one progress value” might be exactly what the doctor ordered. This would be true because the staggered animations could be interrelated, and the overall animation would be driven by a custom input that’s not built into the browser.

Industry observers note that but unlike this hypothetical scenario, replacing the passage of time with scroll progress to control animations is already built into modern CSS. I contend that we’d need a better reason to roll our own implementation than the examples Ashutosh gives.

Ashutosh showcases a scroll-driven use case as “one of those ideal scenarios where the stagger formula shines.” But a red flag that we’re in danger of reinventing something we can get for free is that the spec for scroll-driven animations is cognizant that if we opt to base an animation on scroll progress rather than on time, then, as Ashutosh says, “the animation we are going to achieve is different from traditional ones because we don’t include time in our considerations.” This is no surprise to the creators of scroll timeline, and the MDN docs make Ashutosh’s point in different words when introducing scroll timeline.

The docs also point out that animation-delay is only meaningful when we are using the default time-based document timeline. Therefore, animation-delay does not affect scroll-driven animations. But this is why CSS introduced animation-range-start, which allows us to delay a scroll-driven animation relative to scroll progress and not time.

So, as esoteric and trippy as the math-heavy approach appears, that could be because we are doing something that should be simple in an unusual way.

Let’s see if I’m right by rewriting Ashutosh’s demo to remove reliance on custom CSS functions and use animation-range-start instead.

Ashutosh’s rework of Frontend Masters’ animated tally of donations in the site footer is a nifty, subtle use of scrollytelling that makes the user feel invested in revealing that number.

According to recent reports, sidenote: The only qualm I have about this use of scroll-driven animations for the donation tally is that it might be too subtle — if the user scrolls too quickly, the animated entrance of each digit might occur too quickly to notice. Therefore, the donation tally could be a good case study for comparing the merits of scroll-driven versus scroll-triggered animations as design options. However, that story will have to wait for another day, as the focus of this article is only to show that the staggered scrolling CSS animations can be greatly simplified.

In the video below, my eight-year-old narrates, as a reminder that simplicity is key to the web we’re choosing to leave to the next generation. He compares the complex math in the original demo source code with my animation-range-start fork. He shows the two versions working side by side, demonstrating that sometimes the only thing we lose by judiciously deleting complex code is a headache.

And for those using a Chromium-based browser, my fork of the Pen is below. You can peruse the CSS to see how it does away with the grand unified theory of staggered scrolling animations, and instead deals only with the problem at hand. Since I preserved the original functionality, you’ll need to scroll gradually to appreciate the staggered animations.

I once tackled a related problem with a mathematical formula in a previous article, which touched on how we can use sibling-index() to “increment animation-range-start to stagger the delay before characters fade in as the user scrolls.”.

The truth is, if we refuse to fall into the coding trap of possibly abstracting the wrong thing, we can use one line of CSS to replace a formula that took 1.3k words in the Frontend Masters article for me to still not fully grasp:.

The 2.5% increment for each sibling is because there are eight characters to stagger, and I wanted to choreograph the animations such that they are delayed in evenly-spaced increments till the last character makes its animated entrance when it reaches 30% of the containment range (10% + 20%).

It was inadvertently apt to describe the original post as “CSS on drugs.” Once you reinvent one built-in CSS feature, you can’t stop there. You find yourself having to recreate more stuff that CSS should be able to do by itself. Sure enough, even after we get through the custom formulas that make scroll timelines do what they already do, Ashutosh announces, “Unfortunately, we can’t use easing keywords or cubic-bezier() or linear() functions here. We are left on our own to create easing functions.”.

We shouldn’t have to because, despite the word “timing” in the name of the animation-timing-function property, MDN is clear that “animation-timing-function has the same effect when creating CSS scroll-driven animations as it does for regular time-based animations.” I know from experience that scroll-driven animations work with animation-timing-function because I used scroll-driven animations with steps() to animate a sprite climbing a ladder in my CSS scrollytelling game.

Industry observers note that the problem in the land of CSS on drugs is that after merging all the staggered animations into one, the easing applies to the entire master timeline rather than to each element. It’s not a flaw in CSS, but a logical consequence of the “holistic effect driven by one progress value.” Be careful what you wish for.

To be fair, over the years I have seen impressive results from developers reinventing things the browsers already do, usually because the reinvention gives us control we couldn’t obtain otherwise.

Industry observers note that I mention this to show that reinventing something like scroll timelines isn’t an inherently bad idea if we know why we’re doing it. After all, scroll timelines are only a reinvention of what developers were doing for decades prior in JavaScript. Having noted that, I believe my rewrite of the staggered scroll-driven tally demo indicates that the original approach was overkill for that example. Do let me know in the comments if you see any advantage to the custom CSS functions version over using animation-range-start.

And yet the thought that stuck with me about the Frontend Masters post is that it opens the door to linking the progress of a CSS animation to any arbitrary input value that could be used in a conceptually similar way to scroll timelines.

It has been revealed that this really appeals to me, because even when I first started writing about scroll timelines in 2024, I mentioned that “I would love to see other input controls that can manipulate animation timelines. Imagine text fields progressing animations as you fill them out.” Or how about an animation driven by how closely the new password you are typing matches a password scheme?

Sidenote: Adam Argyle’s Prop For That library, which Geoff recently wrote up, makes it more convenient than ever to expose validation information about a field via CSS custom properties.

Sources indicate that I can add my hypothetical karaoke machine scenario to the wishlist of custom progress inputs for controlling animations. How about an animation driven by the user’s progress through a quiz or a shopping cart?

Custom animation timelines would open the door to all sorts of engaging user experiences—but the code Ashutosh has shared may be the closest we are likely to get to driving CSS animations using values other than time or scroll progress.

Let me know in the comments if you can think of other types of progress inputs that could drive CSS animations to create immersive, interactive experiences.

Industry News: Onboarding clínico: cómo evitar que un producto de salud empiece vacío

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (404 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io.
  • In a recent development, milo Care nació de un problema de gestión de información: vacunas, medicación y controles repartidos entre una foto, un chat, una nota y la memoria.
  • According to recent reports, un registro clínico que abre vacío le pide al usuario que reconstruya meses o años de información antes de obtener algo a cambio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io.

In a recent development, milo Care nació de un problema de gestión de información: vacunas, medicación y controles repartidos entre una foto, un chat, una nota y la memoria. La primera decisión de producto fue evitar trasladar ese trabajo al usuario. Un onboarding útil no pide datos para llenar una base: transforma datos mínimos en un initiative de cuidado accionable.

According to recent reports, un registro clínico que abre vacío le pide al usuario que reconstruya meses o años de información antes de obtener algo a cambio. Para un producto de cuidado, ese costo inicial compite directamente con el papel, el chat o la nota que ya usan. No es un detalle de UX: es un problema de activación y retención.

En Milo Care, el alta del perro captura país y datos relevantes para iniciar un calendario vacunal. El resultado esperado no es una ficha más completa; es una primera sesión que ya muestra próximas acciones, fechas y un historial sobre el que se puede operar.

In a recent development, el calendario no podía ser una lista genérica de vacunas. Las recomendaciones cambian por país, fuente y contexto clínico. La solución fue modelar reglas de negocio que distinguen el calendario de Argentina y Uruguay, con SENASA y las guías WSAVA como referencias, sin presentar la plataforma como sustituto de una indicación veterinaria.

Sources indicate that ese límite es parte de la arquitectura de dominio. El sistema puede organizar, recordar y mostrar el initiative; la evaluación clínica y la decisión profesional siguen fuera del automatismo. Separar ambas responsabilidades evita que una recomendación de software se presente como diagnóstico.

Industry observers note that el calendario inicial se integra con módulos de vacunas, medicamentos, citas y síntomas. Cada módulo maneja su propio estado y vencimiento, pero alimenta un único historial por animal. Esa consolidación permite que el dashboard priorice el trabajo pendiente y que los recordatorios operen sobre datos estructurados.

In a recent development, para negocio, la decisión tiene un efecto claro: el producto entrega valor antes de pedir hábitos complejos. Para ingeniería, deja un dominio extensible para nuevas especies, clínicas veterinarias y planes premium sin convertir el onboarding en una colección de excepciones.

In a recent development, principio de producto: el onboarding debe convertir la información mínima en una primera acción valiosa. En dominios de salud, las reglas automatizadas organizan el seguimiento, pero no reemplazan el criterio profesional.

Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Iter

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters.
  • Industry observers note that GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the matter.
  • uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details.

Industry observers note that GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the matter. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed. I wrote all of the prose in this post myself; Claude wrote most of the code for the PoC.

uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page. You can use this to create a filter rule to block an element on the page without leaving the page.

It has been revealed that the element picker is implemented by injecting an iframe to a URL like moz-extension://76b2331a-894c-4d25-8b89-fcce37e79cc4/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html. That page can talk to the extension background script and tell it to add filters.

On Firefox, the only information we needed to figure out was the extension internal UUID which is random per-installation.

It has been revealed that on the default setup uBO has a lootdest.*##+js(no-fetch-if, adsbygoogle, war:googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js) filter rule (from uAssets), which hooks fetch. From inside the fetch hook, it makes an XHR request to moz-extension:///web_accessible_resources/googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js and returns the response from that as the fetch body, instead of actually making the request. The filter rule is intended to replace a network request for JS from an ad server with a dummy script that has the correct API but doesn’t do anything.

But the attacker website can itself hook the XHR made from inside the no-fetch-if hook to extract the random extension UUID.

Then the attacker website can run fetch('/adsbygoogle.js').catch(() => {}); to trigger the filter, and make their hooked XHR run. Note that there are several ways that the extension internal UUID could be leaked; it’s not just this one filter rule.

Then you can use that to iframe the element picker. Given an iframe element in the page, you just set its src to `moz-extension://${origin}/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html`.

Now we can drive the element picker. We can create a MessageChannel and do iframe.contentWindow.postMessage({ what: 'epickerStart' }, '*', [ch.port2]); to send it to the picker iframe. Then we talk to it: it sends us a start message, we send it a showDialog message with a filter and a resultsetDetails message1 to enable the create button and set opt.

According to recent reports, normally the picker restricts what filters you can enter, and doesn’t let you add scriptlet filters. But there’s a trick we can do to add arbitrary filters. There’s an opt field we set in the second message which is normally the type of network request to match (like image), and gets appended to the filter with a $ if set, like $image. But since we control it, we can put a newline in it and make it "image\ngoogle.com##+js(trusted-rpnt, script, ...)" to inject an arbitrary trusted filter that injects a script.2.

Sources indicate that this is where the main issue is - the element picker shouldn’t accept messages from the attacker. One of the fixes was having a secret password that the real element picker gets from the content script, that the element picker sends in the initial postMessage.

Sources indicate that I didn’t bother actually implementing this, but malicious websites could overlay stuff on top of the embedded element picker or make it invisible by setting the iframe opacity to 0. So as long as the website can get the user to click on the page, it can add arbitrary trusted filters for arbitrary domains.

Recent findings suggest that filters added by the element picker are always treated as trusted (at least until a recompile), which is why it can add a trusted filter. If the user later changes their custom filters it would cause a recompile, clearing the filter trust. But in practice the attacker could just immediately open the victim webpage, so this doesn’t help much.

Industry observers note that originally I sent that message in reply to a dialogSetFilter message from the picker, but it turns out you can just send it right away instead of waiting to reply. ↩︎.

It has been revealed that assuming the shown filter is a network filter. ↩︎.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WINUDF reads and writes UDF (versions 1.02 to 2.60), the file system of DVDs, Blu-ray discs, packet-written CDs and UDF-formatted USB sticks and disks: WINUDF.EXE gives DOS and Windows 1.0x–3.11 drive letters for them, WINUDF.VXD is a file system driver for Windows 95 / 98 / ME with long names.

WINUDF is one of the four WINDRV packages, each in its own repository and usable alone or together with the others:.

From DOS (or an MS-DOS box of Windows 95 / 98 / ME), in bin\DOS of this package:.

Industry observers note that DOS / Windows 3.x: WINUDF.EXE goes to AUTOEXEC.BAT after MSCDEX, LASTDRIVE=Z to CONFIG.SYS when needed. Windows 95 / 98 / ME: WINUDF.VXD goes to WINDOWS\SYSTEM and device=WINUDF.VXD to [386Enh] of SYSTEM.INI. The originals are saved as *.WNF. Uninstall: UNINUDF.

Industry observers note that files used by several systems are in each of their folders. The installer is run from bin\DOS; it takes the files of the other systems from the folders next to it, so the bin tree has to stay together (copy all of it to a floppy or a directory).

MANUAL.md (MANUAL.TXT in bin\DOS, WINUDF.TXT for Windows) describes everything else: all options, how the driver works, hardware and chipset notes, the programming interface, building from source, tests and known limitations.

1.0 (12 October 2026) — first release: UDF 1.02–2.60 read / write, WINUDF.EXE for DOS and Windows 1.0x–3.11, WINUDF.VXD for Windows 95 / 98 / ME.

1.0 update (14 October 2026): the package is split into bin/DOS, bin/WIN3X and bin/WIN9X; English documentation.

#280. Latest Update: It's always DNS, so why are we running our own?

📅 16 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1426 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 S2

Latest Update: It's always DNS, so why are we running our own?

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1426 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: S2

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This will be a rollercoaster story on how we ended up replacing Route53 and running our own authoritative DNS server.
  • Industry observers note that at some point, we decided we should be able to provide unlimited basins to our clients.
  • It has been revealed that for the purposes of this story, what is important is that each basin created by a customer becomes its own subdomain: my-basin.b.s2.dev (not different from the way buckets work on AWS S3).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This will be a rollercoaster story on how we ended up replacing Route53 and running our own authoritative DNS server.

Industry observers note that at some point, we decided we should be able to provide unlimited basins to our clients. Basins are a core namespace construct on S2 and act as top-level containers for streams (already unlimited in number). We found that customers were hacking around our not-so-arbitrary limit of 100 basins per account. That’s not a cool experience.

It has been revealed that for the purposes of this story, what is important is that each basin created by a customer becomes its own subdomain: my-basin.b.s2.dev (not different from the way buckets work on AWS S3). The DNS entry associated with each basin is a CNAME, which routes clients to the correct cell in our architecture. To support unlimited basins, we'd therefore need to support unlimited DNS records.

These records would need strong consistency too. When a basin is created, its address should be instantly resolvable, otherwise clients would be waiting around for a cached NXDOMAIN to expire.

My pulse went through the roof at the thought of running our own DNS server, yikes!

According to recent reports, my research phase started with hope. Hope that our existing DNS setup with AWS Route53 would work with these latest requirements. I really really did not want us to build and run our own DNS server.

In a recent development, route53 is an awesome system and can, it appears, support an unlimited number of records. But, there's a fatal limitation: their API rate limits at a max of about 5 UPSERTs per second (AWS throttling docs have recently changed, the limits may be higher now).

This was something we discovered the hard way, actually. I did read the docs but the API limits didn’t raise any concerns. It became obvious when a nefarious actor rapidly created 10s of thousands of basins, saturating our entire quota of Route53 records. This generated a backlog of work that required a few hours to process, during which our normal DNS updates were stuck, with processes trying to delete records while others tried to add fresh records. It did make for a great post-incident review though. This was when we started enforcing the 100 basins per account limit.

According to recent reports, we looked at the option of batching, but that would break our goal of making entries instantly available. And even with batching, the setup did not feel “unlimited”; it would still be possible for legitimate use of the system to hit the rate limit.

Other managed DNS providers we looked at (GCP Cloud DNS, Cloudflare, Azure DNS) have similar limitations: if you update/insert/upsert records using the provider API, there’s a heavy limiting component.

No way around it, a custom authoritative DNS server had to be built (double yikes!).

The technical requirements were pretty straightforward: given any DNS request that comes in, we need to query an up-to-date zone map, which should be able to hold unlimited records, and send a corresponding response back to the client.

According to recent reports, to avoid syncing to a separate system and having yet another moving piece, the DNS records would come directly from our existing basin database. A live SELECT would consistently “resolve” the required mapping in the DNS request. In other words, we wanted DNS to simply become a new caller of our existing, strongly consistent account database.

Our account database lives in Google’s Cloud Spanner where performance was expected to fare well (given enough money that is).

Next came the core functionality.

Recent findings suggest that we went back and forth between building on a library or writing a CoreDNS module. A library ended up feeling like the most flexible path, which would allow us to build something very specific to our use case. We are a Rust shop, but we decided to go with Go for this project, mostly because the Spanner tooling (and the GCP ecosystem) is comparatively more mature. We promptly settled on the miekg/dns library due to its excellent doc quality and the many RFCs under its belt.

We needed to be able to support authoritative DNS queries for several types of records: A, AAAA, NS, CNAME, SOA. Since we were using a library we had to build the responses ourselves. Our correctness testing focused on these, and consisted of unit tests, RFC compliance testing using Ferret (which we discovered in this great paper: SCALE: Automatically Finding RFC Compliance Bugs in DNS Nameservers) and a post-deploy smoke test with live data.

S2 uses wildcard certificates for the basin zone and they need ACME DNS-01 challenges to work. We decided not to serve the DNS challenge from our server and offloaded it to a separate Route53 zone using CNAME delegation, to avoid tweaking our cert renewal systems as well as serving dynamic TXT records.

It has been revealed that the more we pulled on this thread ... the scarier it got. There are many types of attacks that can happen at the DNS level, scary things I knew of and things I never heard of.

Sources indicate that NXDOMAIN attack is the one that made us the most afraid. Every random non-existent DNS query would be a fresh database lookup. We tried building in-app defenses for NXDOMAIN however, it is, in my opinion, the worst DDoS attack and nothing can really stop it. Not cool.

Long story short, the possible attacks on DNS infrastructure scared me more than I would like to admit. We went looking for a DNS firewall solution. We were sure there must be something like a reverse proxy setup for DNS serving. Either this is a niche setup or it’s a very dangerous world, but for our requirements of unlimited records and DNS reverse-proxy firewall type, we found only two companies: Cloudflare and Akamai. Both giants in their own rights, both with similar offerings (it’s the kind that has no public pricing).

Industry observers note that A few POCs later, we ended up picking Cloudflares DNS Firewall solution. Our DNS server origins were configured to only allow traffic from Cloudflare’s known IPs, a pretty standard reverse-CF setup (Cloudflare in front and nobody else gets to the origin, otherwise what’s the point). With this missing piece, we were now at our final design and ready to roll the upcoming system into production.

Recent findings suggest that as an authoritative DNS server, we have to reply to SOA and NS queries, and they point to nameserver IPs. We took extra care to ensure the IPs returned are always the Cloudflare IPs and not the load balancer ones, which included a ns-leak-test that ensures the origin IPs don't leak as part of some regression change.

For the final architecture and HA (yes, failures will always happen), we run the DNS server on two separate GKE clusters (in separate regions, choosing the closest possible to Spanner), each with multiple replicas behind a TCP and UDP load balancer.

Industry observers note that observability and training everyone on the latest system were another key component of the rollout. While I don’t think anyone gives Route53 a second thought and I don’t think anyone monitors it separately (managed services are someone else’s pager after all), we had to create alerts and runbooks with late-night processes to recover from failures.

Recent findings suggest that there is one funny part to this setup: explaining the full delegation chain. The main domain is managed by Cloudflare in a regular zone. Then it delegates the basin subdomain to Cloudflare, but not a zone, to a service (DNS Firewall). That service then connects to GKE. And there’s another zone in Route53 for the certs (good luck understanding that, Codex).

This isn’t even its final form, the internal TODO includes tuning DNS caching and how to properly optimize between clients/DNS Firewall/DNS app (no amount of AI can solve that), future DNSSEC extensions and many more. It is an unknown system when it comes to failures we don’t see (or the way I like to think about this, how do you know things fail when they look fine).

For now, things have been stable. Looking at stats for the past few weeks, live traffic looks good, the commit history for the past few weeks is mostly CVE fixes, dependency bumps and cost savings. Our customers now create thousands of basins, and they are instantly available for streaming.

I think we’re now in a place where we can blame DNS in one of our post-incident reviews.

#278. Alpine Linux Users Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (805 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq

Alpine Linux Users Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Alpine Linux Owners Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw.
  • Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.
  • The flaw comes from the way OpenSSH checks passwords when musl handles the underlying crypt() call.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Alpine Linux Owners Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw.

Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.

The flaw comes from the way OpenSSH checks passwords when musl handles the underlying crypt() call. On an affected system, a password longer than 256 bytes causes musl to return an error value. That value is an asterisk, the same character Linux uses in /etc/shadow to mark an account as having no password. OpenSSH then treats the returned asterisk as a match and permits the login.

The conditions to exploit the vulnerability are however quite narrow. The server must run OpenSSH before version 10.6p2, be built against the musl library rather than glibc, and operate without PAM. It must also have at least one account with a SHA-256 or SHA-512 password hash and another account marked with an asterisk in its shadow entry. When those conditions are met, any password between 257 and 1,024 characters can authenticate against the passwordless account.

Recent findings suggest that alpine Linux is the most prominent distribution affected, as it uses musl and its default OpenSSH configuration does not enable PAM. Other musl-based environments, including OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto, may also be affected where the same configuration applies. Systems using glibc, PAM, Dropbear or OpenBSD are not affected.

Ozgun Kultekin, a security researcher at Wakefield, published the technical explanation on the *sshole site. Kultekin traces the problem to two musl changes made in 2012: the first replaced the NULL error return from crypt() with an asterisk, and the second added a 256-byte limit to SHA-512 password hashing, so longer inputs caused an error. Together, the changes produced a value that could be mistaken for a password hash.

According to recent reports, the OpenSSH side of the problem dates from a 2016 fix for CVE-2016-6210, which was a timing attack that could reveal whether a username existed. To make responses take a similar amount of time for valid and invalid people, OpenSSH borrowed the salt from another account and hashed the supplied password anyway. That workaround also applied to real accounts whose shadow entry contained an asterisk.

Kultekin writes that the matter remained unnoticed for roughly a decade because the vulnerable combination was uncommon in testing. OpenSSH is tested on OpenBSD and glibc-based systems, while many Linux distributions route authentication through PAM, which does not call crypt() for asterisk entries in the same way. Kultekin says the bug was found after building OpenSSH in several configurations and testing about 17,600 unusual login attempts.

Sources indicate that on Alpine's official AWS and Azure images, the default alpine user is marked as passwordless and can use doas without a password. This means that an attacker who reaches that account can therefore obtain root privileges. Dan Goodin reports for Ars Technica that the matter can give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts within seconds on affected systems.

According to recent reports, openSSH 10.6p2 contains a fix. Operators who cannot enhancement immediately can disable password authentication by setting PasswordAuthentication no in the SSH server configuration and restarting sshd. Kultekin also advises checking authentication logs for evidence that an account with no password accepted a password. The project has published a detection and background repository.

Industry observers note that the vulnerability is being actively exploited. Goodin notes that GreyNoise reported that honeypots in Southeast Asia had been attacked by a group it is tracking known as GT10, which reportedly deploys a backdoor which supports shell commands, reconnaissance and persistence. Goodin reports that watchTowr linked the activity to botnets and cryptocurrency operations, while Previdian recorded 20 exploitation attempts from 13 IP addresses in nine countries. The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 9 November, according to Hackread.

Sources indicate that red Hat has mentioned that its products are not affected because they do not meet the required combination of musl and no PAM. Amazon has likewise marked Amazon Linux 2 and Amazon Linux 2023 as not affected. That does not remove the risk for teams running Alpine-based containers, embedded devices or custom musl builds. Administrators should look for SSH servers built against musl, check whether PAM is disabled, review shadow entries for asterisk-locked accounts, apply OpenSSH 10.6p2 and restart the service.

Industry observers note that the vulnerability was publicly disclosed on 5 November and exploitation reports followed within days. For organisations with internet-facing SSH services, the immediate action to take is fairly straightforward: revision OpenSSH, restart it, and remove password authentication where it is not needed.

#277. Uno Platform 7.0 Adds WebGPU Backend, Apple TV and Reactor Support, and Retires Native Rendering

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (630 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq

Uno Platform 7.0 Adds WebGPU Backend, Apple TV and Reactor Support, and Retires Native Rendering

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Uno Platform 7.0 Adds WebGPU Backend, Apple TV and Reactor Support, and Retires Native Rendering.
  • Nov 16, 2026 3 min read.
  • The Uno Platform team released Uno Platform 7.0, which unifies rendering on SkiaSharp 4 with an experimental WebGPU backend, adds Apple TV as a target platform and supports .NET 11 from day zero.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Uno Platform 7.0 Adds WebGPU Backend, Apple TV and Reactor Support, and Retires Native Rendering.

Nov 16, 2026 3 min read.

The Uno Platform team released Uno Platform 7.0, which unifies rendering on SkiaSharp 4 with an experimental WebGPU backend, adds Apple TV as a target platform and supports .NET 11 from day zero. The release also brings third-party .NET MAUI controls and Microsoft.UI.Reactor library to every target, and removes native rendering and Mac Catalyst.

Uno Platform is an open-source framework for building .NET applications with C# and WinUI XAML for Windows, Android, iOS, macOS, Linux and WebAssembly. The team describes 7.0 as its largest release, with 5,219 commits and 704 closed issues since 6.7. According to the team’s benchmarks, 7.0 is about 2x faster at the median and 5x smaller than 6.7, with some operations, such as brush creation, up to 38x faster. These figures come from the vendor and the workloads were not published in detail.

All targets now render through one pluggable pipeline. SkiaSharp 4 is the default, and Uno Platform is a co-maintainer of the library alongside the .NET team at Microsoft. On Android, Windows and Linux, Skia now renders through Vulkan by default. The WebGPU backend, available on all desktop, mobile and WebAssembly targets, is enabled by adding WebGpu to UnoFeatures and registering the backend on the host builder. It uses wgpu-native outside the browser and the browser’s own WebGPU support on WebAssembly. The team measured up to a 50% frame-rate improvement depending on the scene, and notes a WebGPU-only app drops about 6 MB of uncompressed native code from WebAssembly builds. A latest WebGpuCanvasElement lets applications issue their own WebGPU commands inside the UI.

Industry observers note that through .NET MAUI Embedding, controls from vendors such as Syncfusion, Telerik, Infragistics, DevExpress and Esri previously ran only on iOS, Android, macOS and Windows. They now work on every Uno Platform target, including the web and Linux. In the other direction, existing .NET MAUI apps can reach the browser and Linux through Uno Platform’s .NET MAUI handlers.

According to recent reports, microsoft.UI.Reactor, Microsoft’s declarative C# framework for WinUI with hooks such as UseState and no XAML, now runs on desktop, browser, Android and iOS. It is enabled with the Reactor UnoFeature, is in preview, and can coexist with existing XAML pages in the same visual tree. Apple TV support is added through the net10.0-tvos target framework, targets tvOS 15 and later, renders through Metal and uses the Siri Remote for focus navigation. .NET 11 is supported on every head, for example through dotnet new unoapp -tfm net11.0, while .NET 10 remains the long-term support option.

Recent findings suggest that richTextBlock and RichEditBox are now available on every platform, closing an concern opened in 2018. WinUI alignment continues with ItemsRepeater and ItemsView ported from current WinUI sources, LinedFlowLayout, the TitleBar control, multiple windows on iPad and Lottie rendering through Composition. AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field.
  • Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.
  • According to recent reports, AWS has introduced Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task, or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight virtual machine with a separate guest kernel, carved out of a running EC2 instance by the Nitro hypervisor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field.

Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.

According to recent reports, AWS has introduced Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task, or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight virtual machine with a separate guest kernel, carved out of a running EC2 instance by the Nitro hypervisor. On Amazon EKS, the whole change is one pod field: runtimeClassName: isolated-sandbox or confidential-sandbox.

Industry observers note that the feature is available in all commercial regions at no additional charge, and AWS positions it for workloads where the tenant or the code cannot be trusted, with coding agents named first. In an AWS blog post, Carlos Santana and Trishi Mehta write:.

Each pod gets its own operating system, completely separate from the host and from every neighbor.

Recent findings suggest that according to the EKS documentation, a containerd-shim-nitro-sandbox-v2 process on the parent instance introduces a Firecracker microVM as a first-level guest with hardware-assisted virtualization, after which an agent inside the VM runs the pod’s containers through its own containerd and the two sides communicate over virtio and vsock. The result is a sandbox that shares neither kernel nor memory mappings with the parent instance or any other sandbox, while the containers themselves start unchanged. How the nodes get there depends on the cluster type: on EKS Auto Mode the two RuntimeClasses ship with every cluster and sandbox-capable nodes are provisioned on demand, whereas on standard EKS a team builds a sandbox-enabled AMI for its node groups or Karpenter.

(Source: Amazon EKS User Guide).

What separates the two modes is which side of the boundary is trusted. Isolated mode trusts the parent instance and not the guest, which is why kubectl exec, logs, and process listing keep working, whereas confidential mode treats the parent as untrusted and moves enforcement inside the VM: a Cedar policy generated from the pod spec pins image digests, arguments, environment, mounts and capabilities, exec and stdin are denied, the Nitro Secure Module measures the image and policy into PCRs, and a KMS key policy can release secrets only to a sandbox whose measurements match. Image layers can be encrypted as well, so the parent moves ciphertext it never reads.

That chain only holds if something checks the measurements, and the documentation states so: without a KMS policy or external verifier checking the PCR values, "the attestation measurement is recorded but never verified, and the confidentiality guarantees of confidential mode are incomplete." Separately from either mode, a network-isolated annotation boots the sandbox with no network device at all, which also removes DNS, NTP, IMDS and Pod Identity and breaks HTTP and TCP probes.

Sandip Das, an AWS Container Hero, read the documentation the same way and drew out what isolated mode leaves to the operator: the protection "only runs in one direction," so a compromised parent can still observe or tamper with unencrypted traffic and DNS, writes the pod's /etc/hosts, and can mint Pod Identity credentials for any pod on the node. He also lists prerequisites the blog post does not, among them Kubernetes 1.36 or later, a launch template with Nitro Enclaves enabled on managed node groups, without which "sandboxed pods sit in Pending," and Pod Identity rather than IRSA for credentials. On AWS's description of performance as near-native, he advises treating it "as a vendor claim" and benchmarking startup latency, I/O throughput and tail latency.

Beyond agents, AWS lists multi-tenant SaaS, regulated workloads, CI builds and remote IDEs, and points to the open-source agent-sandbox project for warm pools that hand out a pre-booted VM in about two seconds.

The constraints are on the considerations page, and the largest is GPU and device passthrough, which is not supported at launch because Firecracker cannot pass host devices into a guest, so GPU pods run without the sandbox class. Density is capped twice over: total sandbox vCPUs may not exceed five times the node's vCPU count, and neither may the number of sandboxes, halved on CPU-overcommit types, which gives a 4-vCPU node room for twenty 1-vCPU sandboxes or five 4-vCPU ones. Simultaneous multithreading costs more than the arithmetic suggests, because core scheduling stops two sandboxes sharing the sibling threads of one core and leaves roughly half the advertised vCPUs usable; Graviton, with one thread per core, is unaffected.

It has been revealed that the nearest comparison is GKE Sandbox, which has offered a gvisor RuntimeClass since 2019 and more recently a microvm class built on Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor. gVisor intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel, starts in under 200 milliseconds and supports CUDA on a subset of GPUs; Google's microVM option carries a fixed 250 mCPU and 130 MiB per pod, starts in one to two seconds and does not support GPUs. AWS has taken the VM side of that split and expressed its overhead as density and threads rather than per-pod resources.

Sources indicate that on EC2, Amazon Linux and Firecracker are supported natively and patches are available for other virtual machine monitors. The EC2 User Guide carries the supported instance list and notes that snapshot, restore and live migration are not available.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News GitHub Rebuilds the Copilot App's Diff Surface to Open Million-Line Pull Requests Without Jank.

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.

GitHub engineering has published a detailed account of how it rebuilt the diff surface in the GitHub Copilot app to open a pull request with 2,200 files, over a million changed lines and more than 400 inline review comments without turning the review into a waiting exercise.

The post, by Principal Design Engineer Alberto Gimeno, lands at a moment when AI coding agents are producing far more pull requests than reviewers can digest, and the bottleneck has moved from writing code to reading it.

It has been revealed that at the heart of the rebuild is a decision to stop pretending a pull request is a single uniform list. Code rows have a known height at a known font size, so their geometry can be computed up front and never rebuilt. Comments do not. A markdown body wraps differently at different widths, sections can be toggled in place, reply composers grow as a user types, and images change height when they load. Rather than force one variable-height virtualizer to absorb both, the team split the document into two independent domains:.

Sources indicate that dynamic blocks are keyed by identity (file, line, side) rather than pixel position, with a fingerprint tracking content, open state and measurement width. A single idle-gated measurement pass reads mounted blocks in one batch, scoped to roughly 2,400 pixels around the viewport, and corrections are anchored to whatever the reader is looking at so the surface never fights an active scroll.

Gimeno is open about an early mistake, the team's first instinct was one ResizeObserver per block writing heights back into the layout, a classic feedback loop whose cost grows with every mounted block. The shipped design keeps the observer but defaults it to flagging rather than writing, with a deliberate frame-synchronous exception when the user toggles a or expands a reply composer, so the code below moves in the same frame.

The work builds on an April 2026 post from the main github.com files-changed team, who reported that unified-view diff lines previously rendered as roughly eight React components and ten DOM elements each, and cut both roughly in half.

GitHub's own stacked pull requests went into public preview on 30 July 2026 as an explicit answer to AI-generated monsters, and a DEV Community piece cited Microsoft research finding review quality degrades sharply once a pull request exceeds roughly 200 lines, a rounding error against the Copilot app's million-line test case.

Third-party tools have filled the gap from the review side. Graphite, Pullfrog and CodeRabbit each take different runs at agent-era review, with Codegen CEO Jay Hack arguing that the winners in this newly introduced era will be the teams that redesign their workflows around the fact that review, not code, is now the bottleneck.

According to recent reports, the team also describes the measurement loop built around the rebuild. The surface carries permanent structured probes for its own invariants, which run as CI budgets against a synthetic huge-pull-request fixture, and an autopilot drives the real desktop app through a scripted flow, cold and warm, so an agent can read the on-disk log and spot regressions without anyone at the keyboard. Gimeno's closing line is addressed to anyone who reviews code for a living: open the worst pull request you have got.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News AWS Open-Sources Emulator for Local Testing of 200+ Services by Coding Agents.
  • Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.
  • AWS has released AWS Emulator, a local program that serves an HTTPS endpoint for the public APIs of more than 200 AWS services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Open-Sources Emulator for Local Testing of 200+ Services by Coding Agents.

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.

AWS has released AWS Emulator, a local program that serves an HTTPS endpoint for the public APIs of more than 200 AWS services. AWS Emulator lets developers and coding agents create resources, hit the same errors AWS would return, and iterate without provisioning cloud resources or incurring service charges for the operations it emulates.

Teams point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at it with environment variables such as AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, leaving application code unchanged. On Linux it installs as an RPM or Debian package for x86_64 or aarch64; on macOS and Windows, AWS documents a short Dockerfile and does not publish a prebuilt image. Rust tests can use an embedded mode that runs the emulator inside the test process and wires its HTTP client into the AWS SDK for Rust. An aws-emulator skill can start the emulator for coding agents and check a project against published fidelity tests. Written in Rust, it is generated from more than 400 Smithy API models AWS publishes for the SDKs, according to Swaminathan Sivasubramanian.

It has been revealed that AWS says agents wrote and tested the code. Matthew Goldberg, a senior principal engineer at AWS, describes three teams: one writes fidelity tests from the public API models and verifies them against real AWS, one replays those tests and files concerns, and one implements each fix. Every change must pass a merge gate that checks compilation, coding standards, security, and fidelity regressions. The work runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit.

Industry observers note that how closely the emulator matches AWS varies by service. AWS publishes versioned fidelity tests and per-service scores with each release; a test passes only when every call matches AWS, including status codes, side effects, and exact errors. Unimplemented operations return HTTP 501 with the error code NotImplemented. AWS says fidelity is closest on control-plane APIs, while data-plane behavior and support for CloudFormation, Terraform, and the AWS CDK vary by service. Documented limits include no evaluation of IAM or resource-based policies, so it must not be used to test security; a single shared account and Region per process; in-memory state that disappears when the process stops; and no testing for long-running use or load. The evaluation suite includes tests the emulator does not yet pass.

Developers already have several local AWS stand-ins, including LocalStack, Floci, and moto. AWS Emulator is generated from AWS's own API models, ships official fidelity scores, and is dedicated to the public domain, but it is not a drop-in replacement for every workflow those tools cover, especially permission testing and infrastructure-as-code pipelines.

AWS just released a free local emulator of its APIs, made for coding agents and written entirely by agents. I counted its published fidelity tests: S3, DynamoDB and SQS pass about 2 in 3. CloudFormation passes under 1 in 5.

Yurii Serhiichuk compared it with existing emulators and published a container image and GitHub Action to cover a packaging gap:.

AWS shipped AWS Emulator today - think LocalStack/Floci but native. Rust, built by agents (so hopefully it gets updated pretty fast). No public docker image though, and no GitHub action. So I filled that part.

Industry observers note that AWS Emulator is generally available at no additional service fee. Source is on GitHub under the CC0 1.0 Universal public domain dedication, except third-party code in the vendor/ directory, which is under the Apache License 2.0. Setup details are in the user guide, and fidelity scores ship with each release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, two months ago, I got a new laptop. It’s a Lenovo Thinkpad z61t. I actually ordered a t61, but I accidentally got the z61 instead — and, I actually really like it. It’s quite similar to the t61, but a little smaller and lighter. I was worried that the smaller part would be a problem, but I’ve gotten used to it. I really like the fact that it’s much lighter than my old t42. It just makes it seem so much more usable on the go. Lugging out the t42 was always a chore.

Anyway, I was at the Office 2.0 conference today, where I was giving a little presentation on the Techdirt Insight Community, and about an hour before the presentation, I went to find a quiet place to practice the presentation… and discovered that my brand new laptop wouldn’t work. I knew something was wrong when the “sleep” light wasn’t lit. I started to get worried when I plugged in the laptop and the battery light didn’t light up. Then I noticed that even though the machine had been asleep, it was really really hot. Pushing the power button did nothing. No lights were on and nothing seemed to get them to turn on. I pulled out the battery and put it back in and that did nothing as well.

Industry observers note that so I called up IBM support and explained the situation. The guy on the other end then let me in on the secret power button code to revive your dead Thinkpad. After assessing the situation (totally dead laptop) he warned me: “Okay, this is going to sound totally bizarre, but I want you to give this a try…” He then had me unplug the AC adapter and take out the battery. Then, you push the power button 10 times in a row at one second intervals. Next, you push and hold the power button for 30 seconds. Then you put the battery back in and push the power button… and she lives. The computer came back, good as ever.

Industry observers note that I asked the guy what the power button pushing incantation did and he noted “static discharge” so apparently there was some sort of static that caused a short or something. I tried to get the guy to explain in more detail what happened, but he said “dude, you know as much as I do… but your machine is working.”.

So, if you happen to have a Thinkpad that suddenly drops completely dead for no reason, try the power button trick.

I think 2Smart is right. It’s not entirely uncommon for one to have to press the power button once or twice with no power attached to release the residual charge built up in capacitors. When the unit attempts to start it will use up the remaining power in the unsuccessful attempt. From there, you can sometimes start the machine. A common manifestation of this problem is fans spinning but no display. This can manifest after a power outage or other unexpected shut down.

It sounds to me like this particular system board has challenges discharging properly.

In a recent development, 1st off this works on any laptop/model not just think-pad. This isn’t a magic trick, the point of this besides the static discharge, this resets the Bios of computer by pulling all the charge out of the Internal 2032 CMOS Battery, which in return reboots the BIOS. This can happen for many reason not just a static charge, Some computers can have a bad infection that activates when the computer goes to sleep mode, this is a well known attacker, then the virus proceeds to overload your machine to shut down thus causing the bios to have the command programmed to stay shut down. Well by doing the manual BIOS RESET such as this, resets the configurations in the bios back to default.

According to recent reports, also you can try pulling battery out, unplugging charger, and then hold power button for 1 minute if the 10X an 30sec hold doesn’t work for you. And if for some reason it still don’t work, removing the 2032 CMOS Battery on the MOBO for 1 minute or replace it, the battery which is usually located near the RAM on most laptops, not all have the battery located in same place, I suggest if you need to go that far google your model of computer to locate the internal CMOS Battery.

Wine Computer Repair & Security.

If you are still having this glitch i suggest.

#272. Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix

Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Summer code change caused a Fall fail – frantic engineers had to patch the patch instead of rolling back.
  • Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email.
  • According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Summer code change caused a Fall fail – frantic engineers had to patch the patch instead of rolling back.

Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email.

According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The enhancement looked fine at the time, Microsoft notes, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact.

It has been revealed that however, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted.".

"The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware.".

Industry observers note that the fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued.

Recent findings suggest that it was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive.".

So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again.

"Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old.

Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored.

The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity problems.

At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in.

It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the concern. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over.

In a recent development, "Those services that were able – like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps – failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure," the report says. "But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons.".

Hence the length of time for which Exchange Online (or, from the perspective of many people, Outlook) was out of action.

By 0030 UTC on November 13, Microsoft had identified connection negotiation as the main culprit for the access failures and concluded that competing processes were preventing connections from being handled.

However, it took until 0720 UTC before "We identified a mitigation and applied the mitigation –  an enhancement that reverted the defective change.".

At 1610 UTC, Microsoft confirmed that things were once again looking healthy and, at 0415 on November 14, issued its final customer upgrade.

Industry observers note that A final post incident report is due on November 20. However, the preliminary report will do little to calm jangling nerves. An upgrade applied three months ago managed to cause Exchange Online (and other services) disruption on a global scale? With load testing that didn't reflect scenarios under Microsoft's control?

The engineers who worked feverishly to restore services deserve commendation and will hopefully never have to buy their own beverages in Redmond again (or at least escape the next round of firings). However, the processes that led to an update with a latent defect reaching production deserve a long, hard look. ®.

It combines technical configurations—such as enabling branch protection settings on source code repositories—with organizational controls, like publishing a clear security policy or documenting contributor onboarding and maintainer progression paths.

Recent findings suggest that the Security Baseline is structured across three maturity levels. Level 1 is the most straightforward, roughly equivalent to a mid-range Scorecard score, and takes an experienced developer about two hours to implement. It focuses heavily on documentation. While non-profit open-source maintainers are generally not legally bound by cybersecurity regulations like the EU CRA, downstream manufacturers and governments care immensely about compliance.

The EU CRA explicitly exempts open-source maintainers who do not profit from their work. However, commercial consumers must comply. The Security Baseline translates complex regulatory requirements—from the EU CRA, US Executive Orders, and Japanese legislation—into accessible, practical steps for maintainers without requiring them to digest raw legal texts.

By offering a tiered implementation aligned with modern security practices, the Security Baseline makes projects more attractive to downstream consumers. This increased visibility helps attract more contributors, users, feature requests, and code reviews to strengthen the project.

In a recent development, the second framework I recommend is SLSA (Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts), which addresses supply chain provenance, pedigree, and integrity. While Scorecard and Security Baseline focus on code and process quality, SLSA secures the underlying infrastructure—including IDEs, developer workstations, source repositories, CI/CD pipelines, and distribution systems.

SLSA defines progressive levels of maturity to harden development infrastructure. By pairing process-oriented frameworks like Scorecard or Security Baseline with SLSA, organizations can verify how software moves securely through the supply chain and assess infrastructure resilience.

#270. Google's A2UI in a bank app: the AI never sees the balance

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1642 w)
