📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on.
  • In a recent development, in this example, an agent posts unreviewed PRs to Slack for the first time.
  • Industry observers note that control what agents can do, not just what they can reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on. Agents call tools by writing short TypeScript programs, and save the ones that work as custom tools to reuse. Coral checks every call against your policy before it adds credentials and forwards the call.

Quickstart · Download · Demo video.

In a recent development, in this example, an agent posts unreviewed PRs to Slack for the first time. The agent searches for the GitHub and Slack tools and writes code that calls them. It isn't allowed to post to Slack without approval, so the user approves the post. The agent then saves its code as a custom tool. The next day, the agent runs the same task by calling that custom tool.

Industry observers note that control what agents can do, not just what they can reach. Most MCP gateways decide only which tools an agent can see. That is all or nothing: if an agent can call update_record, it can update any record in any way the tool allows. A custom tool is code, so it can hold the rule that Allow and Block cannot: closeStaleTicket changes one field, only on tickets with no activity for 30 days. You set Allow, Ask, or Block on the custom tool like any other tool, and Coral still checks every provider call inside it against your policy.

Less duplicated agent work. Agents start every task from scratch. They re-read tool schemas, retry failed calls, and spend tokens rewriting code for steps they got right yesterday. With Coral, agents save the code that worked as custom tools they call again in one step, and workspace owners can share them with the whole team.

Coral is used by thousands of developers at more than 450 companies for safer, more efficient agent work in customer support, SecOps, business intelligence, SRE, and more.

Add a provider. A provider is one service your agents can use, such as GitHub or Linear. Pick one from the catalog, or bring your own OpenAPI document or MCP server. By default, tools that read data run right away and everything else needs your approval. See Add a provider.

Connect your agent. Copy your workspace's MCP URL from the Coral UI and add it to your MCP client:.

For Cursor, VS Code, OpenCode, and other clients, see Connect an MCP client.

Sources indicate that ask a question. Ask your agent something that uses that provider, such as "What are my open pull requests?".

It has been revealed that we started Coral while building an AI SRE. To investigate an incident, the agent had to connect the dots across an ocean of telemetry and undocumented relationships between internal and external systems. It needed broad permissions and a lot of tokens, and it started from scratch the next time.

According to recent reports, we built Coral so that the agent remembers the route. Once a task succeeds, the agent saves the steps that worked as a custom tool. Next time, it finds that tool in the same search as provider tools such as Datadog and Slack. It started with SRE, and teams now use Coral for agent work across the organization:.

From one developer's laptop to an enterprise cloud, Coral fits your stack:.

In a recent development, agents write programs. Coral builds on code mode, and adds custom tools, policy controls, and managed identities. To use tools, an agent writes a short TypeScript program. One program can call several tools, filter the results, and return only what the task needs. Less raw data passes through the model's context.

According to recent reports, coral runs them on rails. Each program runs in a fresh V8 isolate with no network access, no credentials, and no imports. Coral checks every tool call against your workspace policy, then adds the credentials and forwards the call to the provider. A policy can also require a person to approve the call. Every run is attributed to the person or agent that started it.

The agent sends Coral programs through the exec tool. A program calls coral.search to find the tools the agent can use and read their TypeScript signatures. Then the agent sends a program that does the work. This one finds open pull requests that have no reviewer and posts them to Slack:.

Sources indicate that if posting to Slack needs approval, the run pauses there until you approve it. Only the pull request numbers go back to the agent, not the full GitHub response. The run happens on the Coral server, not in your agent, so it carries on even if the agent disconnects.

Recent findings suggest that what works becomes a custom tool. When a program succeeds, the agent saves it as a private tool and calls it next time in one step as coral.private.({ ... }). Agents find custom tools in the same search as provider tools, and reuse or edit them instead of starting over. A workspace owner can publish a private tool as a shared tool under coral.shared, so everyone in the workspace can call it.

To learn about providers, accounts, policy, and workspaces, read Concepts.

Sources indicate that running Coral for a team? See Run a shared server.

Coral Enterprise is coming soon under its own license. It adds organization-wide governance and support: SSO with SAML, SCIM provisioning, advanced RBAC, an immutable audit log, and support SLAs. See Coral Enterprise or book a demo.

Industry observers note that to run Coral from a checkout, follow the development guide. To contribute, read CONTRIBUTING.md. The release notes list what changed in each version.

Ask questions, share ideas, and show what you built in our Slack community or on GitHub issues.

Recent findings suggest that do not report security concerns in public issues or pull requests. See SECURITY.md.

Recent findings suggest that coral is ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certified. Each program runs in its own V8 isolate, and Coral logs every approval.

Industry observers note that coral is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE.

It has been revealed that the ee/ directory holds Enterprise Edition code under its own license, ee/LICENSE. A plain cargo build at the repository root builds only code under the Apache License 2.0. NOTICE sets out which license covers which files.

In a recent development, coral v1 replaces the SQL interface with TypeScript programs. It starts from fresh state and does not convert what 0.x stored. If Coral finds 0.x state, it tells you at startup. See Upgrade from Coral 0.x.
